0468.title: Can pattern matching run in linear time in the LZ77 input size?
0468.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and O(z+m) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
0468.answer_criterion: Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer. An algorithm linear in the uncompressed text length, or in a potentially larger grammar representation, does not attain this target.
0468.definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair (s,l) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require 1 <= s < p; the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy O(1) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word. There is no access to a separately stored decompressed text or precomputed index.
0468.why: This is a basic test of whether computation can follow the compressed input size rather than the size of the object it describes. Settling it would also clarify whether the representation gap between LZ77 and grammars creates an unavoidable algorithmic cost for a fundamental string operation.

progress.text: Gawrychowski gives deterministic O(z(1+log(N/z))+m) time for LZ-compressed occurrence detection, including self-referential parses.
Ganardi and Gawrychowski obtain O(g+m) time when the supplied text representation is a grammar of size g. This resolves the grammar-input version.
Gawrychowski asks whether the Lempel–Ziv version can be solved in time linear in compressed-text size plus pattern length.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary pattern matching scans the text and pattern in linear time. That guarantee can be too expensive for compressed input: a short sequence of copy instructions may describe a text many orders of magnitude larger than the representation. Here the algorithm only has to determine whether an occurrence exists, so a large number of matches does not force a large output.

A match can cross phrase boundaries or occur inside a repeated region. For example, a pattern may start near the end of one copied block and finish in the next. Inspecting each phrase in isolation therefore misses valid occurrences. The challenge is to summarize enough boundary and periodicity information while charging only constant total work per input phrase and pattern symbol.

Grammar compression provides an instructive comparison. Linear-time pattern matching is known when the input is a straight-line grammar, but converting an LZ77 representation to an appropriate grammar can increase its size. The existing grammar algorithm therefore does not immediately give linear time measured in z.

The 2025 seminar question explicitly retains the Lempel–Ziv target. This card fixes the decision version, permits self-references, and charges preprocessing. These choices prevent a reporting cost or an uncharged text index from changing the question.

0470.title: Can grammar random access use O(g log g) bits with logarithmic query time?
0470.formal: Is there a deterministic data structure that, for every binary straight-line program G with g rules generating a binary string T of length N, stores a representation in $O(g\log(g+2))$ bits and returns T[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in $O(\log(N+2))$ worst-case time? Preprocessing must take time polynomial in g and is given G, not an expanded copy of T. The space bound includes every persistent index and any retained grammar. Use the word-RAM model below. The representation may replace G; it need only answer queries to T correctly.
0470.definitions: A binary straight-line program has ordered variables X_1,...,X_g, one rule per variable, and start variable X_g. A rule is X_j -> 0, X_j -> 1, or X_j -> X_a X_b with a,b < j. All variables must be reachable from the start variable. Expansion is unique and finite; g counts rules, not expanded occurrences. The input specifies rule types and indices in O(g log(g+2)) bits. Machine words have $\Theta(\log(N+g+2))$ bits; random access, comparisons, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, Boolean operations, and shifts cost one step. Arithmetic results are restricted to a word. Stored bits may be packed; charge the final partially filled word as well. Queries may use O(log(N+2)) temporary words, initially empty and discarded afterward; this workspace contains no persistent advice. Every input-dependent table retained between queries counts toward the representation budget.
0470.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform representation, preprocessing algorithm, and query algorithm satisfying all bounds for every valid G, or prove that no such data structure exists. Space linear in g machine words is insufficient when log N is asymptotically larger than log g. A scheme whose preprocessing first expands an exponentially longer T does not meet the polynomial-in-g preprocessing requirement.
0470.why: Random access is the simplest useful operation on a compressed string. Resolving this target would determine whether the extra address-length information is an inherent price of efficient access or an artifact of current representations, and would make the distinction between compressed bits and machine words precise.

importance.reason: A basic compressed-space versus access-time frontier at the bit level, relevant to many grammar-based operations. The fixed logarithmic target gives a sharper scope than the broader random-access trade-off landscape.

progress.text: Navarro asks whether efficient grammar random access can avoid the extra space used to store all expansion lengths.
Takasaka and I obtain space-efficient SLP encodings supporting logarithmic access; their leading expansion-length term remains g log N in this card’s notation.

Duyster and Kociumaka sharpen and largely match grammar random-access trade-offs in their stated parameter regimes. Theorem 1.1 assumes a space budget above g log N bits; it does not supply the representation asked for here.

0470.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026 against the April encoding paper and ICALP 2026 trade-offs. This fixes a particular target within the source’s space-reduction question; results using O(g) words must not be read as O(g log g) bits.

context_blocks.text: A grammar rule stores references to smaller pieces, so its two references need only logarithmically many bits in the number of rules. A position in the expanded string can require many more bits. For example, a short chain of doubling rules can describe an exponentially long string. This difference is why a space bound stated in machine words can hide a substantial overhead relative to the grammar encoding.

To locate a position inside a concatenation, the usual navigation step compares that position with the length of the left expansion. Storing an exact expanded length with every variable is straightforward, but can consume g log N bits. The target asks whether this information can be organized or recovered using a representation comparable in bits to the original grammar, while keeping logarithmic access time.

The April 2026 encoding result improves the grammar representation and keeps logarithmic query time, but retains a g log N expansion-length term. The authors explicitly distinguish their encoding savings from removing that term. Their observation supports treating the latter as a separate question.

ICALP 2026 gives much sharper time-space trade-offs in a broad range of parameters. Its main upper-bound theorem uses a space budget above the g log N scale. Consequently, the optimality statements in that range do not automatically settle the smaller bit budget here. This card fixes logarithmic query time, a binary alphabet, polynomial preprocessing, and explicit workspace rules as a concrete specialization of the seminar’s fewer-auxiliary-bits direction.

0478.title: Can exact fully dynamic APSP have edge-linear amortized updates and polylogarithmic queries?
0478.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
0478.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
0478.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
0478.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

This is a deterministic bounded-integer-weight specialization; approximate and worst-case vertex-update results are recorded with their different guarantees.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

0481.title: Do single-pair shortest paths require cubic-size min-plus circuits?
0481.formal: For n >= 2, assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight x_{ij} to every unordered edge {i,j} of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates x_{ij} and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates min(a,b) or a+b, unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute f_n exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let s(n) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is s(n)=Omega(n^3)? Equivalently, do there exist constants c>0 and n0 such that every such circuit has at least c n^3 gates for every n>=n0?
0481.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences x_{ij} and x_{ji} denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
0481.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every c>0 and every n0 there is an n>=n0 with a correct circuit using fewer than c n^3 gates. An o(n^3)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.

A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

context_blocks.text: The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize d_0(1)=0 and d_0(v)=infinity otherwise, and compute d_k(v)=min(d_{k-1}(v), min over u distinct from v of d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}). After n-1 layers, output d_{n-1}(n). Each layer uses O(n^2) gates. Nonnegative weights ensure that deleting cycles cannot increase a walk’s cost, so these layers suffice for the simple-path optimum. This gives O(n^3) gates.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

For all-pairs shortest paths, a cubic lower bound is known in the same general min-plus framework. Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.

0491.title: Can every fixed-dimensional Tarski problem be solved with O(log² n) queries?
0491.formal: Let Q(n,k) be the minimum worst-case number of adaptive deterministic value queries needed to find any fixed point of an unknown monotone function $f:[n]^k\to[n]^k$, where [n]={1,...,n} and monotonicity is with respect to coordinatewise order. A query at x reveals the entire vector f(x). Is it true that for every integer k>=1 there is a constant C_k such that $Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2$ for every n>=2? Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. Constants may depend on k but not on n or f. This asks for an exponent independent of the fixed dimension, not a polynomial bound on C_k.
0491.definitions: For x,y in the grid, x<=y means x_i<=y_i for every coordinate i. The oracle is promised to satisfy x<=y implies f(x)<=f(y). A valid output is any x with f(x)=x; no minimum or maximum fixed point is required. An adaptive query procedure can choose each query using all earlier queries and answers, and must terminate correctly for every promised oracle. Equivalently, Q(n,k) is the minimum depth of a finite deterministic oracle decision tree whose leaves output valid fixed points for every monotone function consistent with that leaf. Neither a circuit description nor the table of f is part of the input. Query cost is one per returned vector, and places no restriction on the bit complexity of choosing the next query. The finite product grid is a complete lattice, so a fixed point always exists.
0491.answer_criterion: Prove the bound for every fixed k, or show that there is a fixed k for which Q(n,k)/(1+log_2 n)^2 is unbounded as n grows. A growing factor depending only on k is permitted. A bound whose logarithmic exponent grows with k does not answer yes. A lower bound obtained only by letting k grow with n does not answer no unless it implies failure at some fixed k.
0491.why: This probes the information cost of finding a guaranteed fixed point under monotonicity, a basic organizing principle in algorithms, semantics, and equilibrium computation. The same sharp bound in dimensions two, three, and four makes the dependence on dimension a substantive structural mystery rather than just a loose analysis of one algorithm.

importance.reason: A broad oracle-complexity question about monotone fixed points, with a surprising low-dimensional pattern and connections to equilibrium search. It distinguishes intrinsic information requirements from implementation time.

progress.text: Etessami, Papadimitriou, Rubinstein, and Yannakakis prove an Omega(log^2 n) lower bound already in two dimensions, including for randomized algorithms; the 2022 seminar records this starting point.
Fearnley, Pálvölgyi, and Savani give an O(log^2 n)-query algorithm in three dimensions, matching the two-dimensional lower bound.
Brânzei, Phillips, and Recker prove randomized query lower bound Omega(k log^2 n / log k) for n,k>=2. For fixed k this remains quadratic in log n, so it does not rule out the card’s target.

Chen, Li, and Yannakakis obtain O(log^2 n) queries in four dimensions and improve the exponent in every fixed dimension. Section 9 proposes the possibility of a generic dimension-dependent constant times log^2 n.

context_blocks.text: Starting at the bottom of the grid and repeatedly applying f gives a nondecreasing chain until a fixed point is reached. This directly proves existence constructively, but the chain can contain a number of steps proportional to n times the dimension. Since the coordinates need only log n bits to describe, dependence on n can be exponentially larger than dependence on the coordinate description length.

One-dimensional search can exploit order by repeatedly discarding a large interval. In a product order, two points can be incomparable: one coordinate is larger and another smaller. The oracle’s monotonicity then does not directly compare their images. The question asks whether these multidimensional interactions must eventually increase the power of log n, or whether they can be absorbed into a dimension-dependent constant.

The first surprise was that dimensions two and three both have Theta(log^2 n) query complexity. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis extend this equality to dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Their more general upper bound is O(log^(ceil((k-1)/3)+1) n) for fixed k. The concluding discussion explicitly raises a bound of the form f(k) log^2 n, which is the target on this card.

Query complexity and computational efficiency must be separated here. The 2026 algorithm uses expensive intermediate search and counting; its authors leave a time-efficient implementation open. Even a positive answer to this card would only limit how much oracle information is needed. Obtaining a polynomial-time algorithm when both k and log n are input parameters would require additional control of the constants and the work between queries.

0492.title: Is containment of conjunctive queries under bag semantics decidable?
0492.area: Database theory and finite model theory
0492.formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries q_1 and q_2 with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and D(A_j[h]) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
0492.definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function U^r to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
0492.answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
0492.why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.

progress.text: Chaudhuri and Vardi raise the bag-containment decidability question; the 2025 seminar traces the problem to their PODS paper.

0492.status_note: Open in the 2025 seminar, the June 2025 revised CQ-versus-UCQ paper, and the maintained problem list accessed 10 September 2026. No resolution was located in current searches. The problem includes bag input multiplicities and is not the separate bag-set variant.

context_blocks.text: Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let q(x) have body R(x), and let r(x) have body R(x),R(x). If R(a) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns m^2. Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as m=2. This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.

0506.title: Is private PAC sample complexity polynomial in VC dimension and log-star Littlestone dimension?
0506.formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class C on a finite nonempty domain X admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most 1/10 and confidence at least 9/10, while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
0506.why: The problem seeks a privacy analogue of a foundational characterization theorem in learning theory.

progress.text: The survey gives lower bound $\Omega(\mathrm{VC}+\log^*\mathrm{LD})$ and upper bound $\min\{O(\log|C|),\widetilde O(\mathrm{LD}^5)\}$. The $\mathrm{VC}=1$ case is nearly understood; the general gap remains.

references.authors: Kobbi Nissim; Uri Stemmer; Eliad Tsfadia
references.locator: Open Questions 1–2; Theorems 2–3

0506.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
0506.review_note: Concrete specialization of the quantitative target following Open Question 1: accuracy, confidence, epsilon, delta, and the meaning of polynomial overhead are fixed explicitly. The survey itself suppresses these parameters. Importance is editorial; cited proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.

0506.definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to {0,1}. VC(C) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. LD(C) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set {0,1}^X of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target h∈C and distribution D on X, with probability at least 9/10 over m independent draws x_i from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most 1/10. Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector (h(x))_{h∈C} can be identified, giving at most 2^|C| cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.
0506.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

importance.reason: Seeks a quantitative sample-complexity characterization of private learnability in terms of two basic dimensions, with consequences across hypothesis classes.

notes: Specified privacy for all labeled samples, measurable hypotheses, integer sample bound and the learning probability.

0679.definitions: H is a nonempty set of functions X→{0,1}; a finite subset B⊆X is shattered when all its binary labelings are restrictions of functions in H. Its VC dimension is the maximum shattered cardinality. Proper means that every output belongs to H. For z=((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^n, loss(h,z)=(1/n)Σ_i 1[h(x_i)≠y_i]. To define CMI_D, draw a supersample Z̃=(Z̃_i,0,Z̃_i,1)_{i=1}^n with 2n independent draws from D, and independent fair bits S=(S₁,…,S_n); feed the selected sample (Z̃_i,S_i)_i to A with independent randomness. Put W=A((Z̃_i,S_i)_i). CMI_D(A)=I(W;S|Z̃)=H(S|Z̃)−H(S|W,Z̃), with base-two conditional Shannon entropy of the finite random variable S. The learner may depend on H,n, but not on D. The source does not specify sigma algebras for arbitrary X,H, measurability of evaluation, or admissibility of learners and distributions; those choices affect the quantified statement. No domain restriction is silently added here.

sentences: Conditional mutual information measures what a learner’s output reveals about which examples were selected from an independent supersample.
The target is the proper agnostic-learning Conjecture 6 of Steinke and Zakynthinou: information O(d) and expected empirical excess loss O(√(d/n)).
Here d is the VC dimension, n is sample size, and the learner must work for every data distribution.
The paper’s separate proper realizable Conjectures 7 and 8 were refuted by Haghifam, Dziugaite, Moran and Roy in 2020.
Measurability conventions for the arbitrary-domain question remain to be specified, so this formulation is still marked unfinished.

context_blocks.text: A learner can fit its observed labels while retaining information that is irrelevant to future prediction. Conditional mutual information measures one aspect of this dependence: after revealing a pool of two candidate examples for each position, how much does the output reveal about which member of each pair was actually used? The hidden selection consists of n fair bits, so this information is between zero and n bits. The conjecture asks whether dependence can be limited by the class complexity d while retaining near-best training accuracy.

For a one-pair illustration, fix two different candidate observations. An output that identifies the selected observation reveals the selector bit completely; an output independent of that choice reveals nothing. This describes the information experiment, not a proposed learning algorithm. The conditioning removes uncertainty about the observations themselves, so even an observation with an arbitrarily long numerical description need not reveal more than that one selection bit.

Agnostic means that observed labels need not agree with any hypothesis in the class. The empirical comparison is therefore with the best in-class training loss, rather than with zero. Properness requires the output to remain in that same class. The learner may vary with the class and sample size but must be chosen before the data distribution; otherwise the distribution-free claim changes.

The source gives an empirical-risk minimizer with CMI at most d log n+2. Its question is whether the logarithmic dependence on sample size can be removed if expected empirical excess loss of order √(d/n) is allowed. The significance is that the ordinary CMI generalization inequality would then recover a dimension-dependent √(d/n) scale without an extra logarithmic loss.

The paper’s Conjectures 7 and 8 instead ask for proper realizable learners with expected empirical loss O(d/n), or zero. Haghifam, Dziugaite, Moran and Roy refute those claims in Theorem 4.2. Their negative theorem assumes that sharper empirical-loss requirement. Since d/n can be much smaller than √(d/n), it cannot simply be substituted for a refutation of the agnostic Conjecture 6 retained here.

Hafez-Kolahi and coauthors recover tighter VC generalization estimates through chained conditional mutual information. This shows that an information-theoretic analysis can eliminate the extra logarithmic factor by changing the bound being analyzed. It does not supply a proper learner whose unmodified output CMI obeys the conjectured O(d) bound. A statement about a successful analysis and a statement about how much information the learner itself retains are different.

One formulation issue remains explicit. On arbitrary domains, the probability distributions, hypothesis-valued random output and evaluation map require compatible measurable structures. Those conventions are not specified in the cited conjecture. This card preserves that gap instead of silently restricting the question to a finite domain. Its content and source distinction have been improved, but it is still an unfinished benchmark formulation.

0946.definitions: A hypergraph H=(V,E,w) has E⊆{e⊆V:|e|≥2} and weights w:E→ℝ_{≥0}. Its cut value is cut_H(S)=Σ_{e∈E: e∩S≠∅ and e∩(V\S)≠∅}w(e): a crossing hyperedge contributes its weight once, independently of how many of its vertices lie on either side. Zero-weight edges may be discarded; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. Empty or singleton hyperedges never cross a cut and are omitted without loss. H′=(V,E′,w′) follows the same conventions, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights. The output edge set E′ need not be a subset of E, following the original problem statement; new vertices are not permitted. Size means |E′|, not Σ_{e∈E′}|e|, weight-encoding length or total storage bits. C is independent of n, ε, edge count, rank and all weights. The empty edge set is allowed, and a zero input cut must remain exactly zero. This is a finite-object existence question: no construction algorithm, running-time or probability guarantee is imposed.
0946.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence statement with one constant C, or prove that the minimum required number of hyperedges times ε²/n is unbounded over the permitted inputs and accuracies. For a negative answer, the lower bound must allow arbitrary nonnegative hyperedges on the original vertex set. A growing logarithmic factor or a counterexample only to a particular sampling method does not resolve the target.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge {1,2,3,4} of weight one contributes one to both the partition {1}|{2,3,4} and the partition {1,2}|{3,4}. Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit O(n/ε²)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using O(n log n/ε²) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the Cn/ε² hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

1033.title: Does polynomial testability imply polynomial distance estimation for dense graph properties?
1033.formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with P_n nonempty for every n≥1, does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in 1/ε, independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-ε distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
1033.definitions: P_n is a nonempty subset of graphs on [n], invariant under vertex permutations. For n≥2, dist(G,P)=min_{H∈P_n}|E(G)△E(H)|/binom(n,2); for n=1 it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer t≥2, with ε=1/t, and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each G∈P_n with probability ≥2/3 and rejects each G with dist(G,P)≥ε with probability ≥2/3; no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants C,a≥1 with at most Ct^a adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants C′,b≥1, using at most C′t^b queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with Pr[|q−dist(G,P)|≤1/t]≥2/3 for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative q_P(poly(ε)) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.
1033.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
1033.why: Separates recognizing a robust violation from measuring its magnitude and asks whether polynomially efficient dense-graph testing automatically provides polynomial distance estimation.

importance.reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.

progress.text: Fischer and Newman prove a general tester-to-estimator conversion with a large quantitative overhead, leaving the polynomial regime open.
Gishboliner, Kushnir and Shapira revisit testing versus estimation and improve general conversion bounds, but do not obtain the conjectured polynomial transformation.
Gishboliner and Shapira state Problem 5.4: decide whether q_P(ε) testability implies estimation with q_P(poly(ε)) sample complexity.

1033.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The cited survey still states the polynomial tester-to-estimator implication as open; known conversions and positive special cases do not establish the universal claim.
1033.review_note: The former short index record is upgraded to the precise Problem 5.4 formulation from the 2025 survey. The exponent c is a normalization of q_P(poly(ε)); the dense-model distance and query quantifiers are explicit.

context_blocks.text: Testing asks only for a robust decision: accept graphs in the property and reject graphs that are ε-far from it. Estimation asks for the actual distance to the property, so it must distinguish every pair of nearby distance scales rather than only the two extremes used by a tester.

In the dense graph model the input has Θ(n²) possible adjacency queries, yet many properties can be tested with a number of samples depending only on ε. The central quantitative issue is whether this efficiency survives when the algorithm must estimate distance rather than detect a large violation.

Known reductions convert a tester into an estimator with very large overhead. The 2025 survey of polynomial property testing records an explicit open problem asking whether q_P(ε) can be replaced by q_P(poly(ε)); for polynomial testers this would yield a polynomial estimator. Existing results establish the implication only with exponential or otherwise much larger transformations in general.

Some important classes already have polynomial estimators, including selected hereditary partition properties and several induced-subgraph examples. Such positive cases show that the gap is not caused by a universal information-theoretic obstruction, but they do not give the transformation for every graph property.

The question is about query complexity in the dense model. A result in the bounded-degree model, a computational-time bound after reading the full graph, or a tester that estimates only whether the distance is above one fixed threshold addresses a different problem.

2997.title: How many rounds does triangle detection require in CONGEST?
2997.formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct O(log n)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate O(log n)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
2997.why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
2997.definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.

progress.text: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound.
Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round.
Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.

4245.title: Can parity games be solved in deterministic polynomial time?
4245.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants K,c>0 such that, on every finite parity game G and designated vertex s, A decides whether Even has a winning strategy from s in at most K(L+1)^c steps, where L is the explicit binary encoding length of (G,s)?
4245.definitions: G consists of a nonempty vertex set V={1,…,n}, a directed edge set E⊆V×V with at least one outgoing edge at every vertex, a partition V=V_Even⊔V_Odd, and a priority function p:V→N. Self-loops are allowed. The input explicitly lists all vertices, edges, owner bits and priorities, with integers in binary and delimiters; s∈V is included. A play is an infinite sequence v_0v_1… with v_0=s and (v_i,v_(i+1))∈E. At a vertex owned by a player that player chooses the next vertex. A strategy maps every finite valid play ending at a vertex owned by that player to a legal successor. Even wins a play if the minimum priority occurring infinitely often is even; Odd wins otherwise. A winning strategy for Even makes every play consistent with it winning for Even, irrespective of Odd’s choices. The algorithm must answer YES exactly when such a strategy exists. Strategies are not part of the input. The number and magnitude of priorities are unrestricted input data; the running-time exponent may not depend on them. The task has perfect information, alternating vertex ownership and no probabilistic transitions.

context_blocks.text: Parity games describe infinite behavior using a finite graph and a priority condition. The question is not how to simulate an infinite play; it is how to decide whether one player can force the eventual recurrence pattern of priorities to favor it. This decision problem underlies central constructions in logical verification and synthesis.

Positional determinacy says that a winning player can choose moves using only the current vertex. Thus finite strategies suffice even though the winning condition concerns an infinite play. Their existence does not by itself give a polynomial-time algorithm for finding or choosing the winning strategy. The problem lies in both NP and coNP, and more precisely in UP and coUP.

Calude and coauthors established a quasipolynomial-time algorithm in 2017. Czerwiński and coauthors proved quasipolynomial lower bounds for separating automata used by a broad collection of such algorithms. That lower bound concerns the specified approach, not arbitrary algorithms for parity games.

A November 2025 preprint by Rick van der Heijden claims a polynomial-time algorithm for the full problem. This review located and inspected the claim but did not independently verify its proof or find an authoritative resolution of its correctness. It must be visible on the card rather than omitted from a statement that the problem is confirmed open.

Suilen and Pérez’s April 2026 paper still describes polynomial-time parity-game solving as a longstanding open question while reducing parity games to a robust-MDP threshold problem. This later usage is evidence about the literature, not a proof that the earlier claim is false. The card therefore carries an explicitly unverified current status while completing the mathematical formulation and preserving its historical identifier.

4245.why: Determine the exact polynomial-time boundary for a central finite representation of infinite game behavior.
4245.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A defining algorithmic question of verification and infinite-duration games, with direct modal-logic and synthesis connections and a major quasipolynomial breakthrough. Its former rank came from a provisional unassessed score, not a low-significance assessment. The score does not certify the correctness or failure of the located solution claim.

5358.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
5358.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every n,s≥1, every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on {0,1}ⁿ, and all accuracy and confidence parameters ε,δ∈(0,1), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in n,s,1/ε and log(1/δ)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
5358.definitions: A literal is a variable x_i or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form (DNF) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers t,b≥2 and set ε=1/t and δ=2^(−b). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most p(n,s,t,b) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair (x,f(x)) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least 1−δ over the examples and internal randomness, Pr_{x drawn from D}[h(x)≠f(x)]≤ε. Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
5358.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

context_blocks.text: A DNF represents a union of rule-defined regions: an example is accepted when it satisfies at least one conjunction of feature conditions. The task is to infer accurate predictions from observations, without being given those rules. Feldman’s introduction identifies the general distribution-free question before studying more structured input distributions; that introductory question is the source of this catalogue record.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to using polynomially many examples. There are at most 3ⁿ simplified conjunctions, since each variable is absent, positive or negative. Padding a DNF with empty slots bounds the number of candidate formulas by (3ⁿ+1)^s. The finite-class union bound therefore gives O((ns+log(1/δ))/ε) samples sufficient for every consistent DNF in this class to generalize. Exhaustively finding such a DNF may still take enormous time. The question asks whether that computational search can be avoided, even by outputting a different representation.

The distinction between a constant and a growing number of terms is essential. The classical n^{O(s)} algorithm is polynomial for each fixed s, but does not provide a single polynomial in n and s. Servedio’s 2025 survey records the longstanding goal and the subexponential distribution-free upper bound 2^{Õ(n^{1/3} log s)}. For polynomially many terms and fixed learning accuracy, this still leaves a substantial gap to polynomial time.

A distribution-free learner must handle probability concentrated on any subset of the Boolean cube. An argument that a long conjunction rarely holds under independent uniform coordinates need not survive such a distribution. Feldman’s Fourier-based work uses uniform or product structure and, in some settings, additional query access. Its positive results should not be read as a solution from arbitrary-distribution random examples alone.

Allowing hypotheses outside the target class is substantive. A hardness proof for producing another DNF can leave open an efficient learner that outputs a Boolean circuit or a polynomial threshold function. Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz obtain hardness that also covers improper learning, under their assumption about refuting random K-SAT. The assumption is part of that theorem, so it supplies evidence against efficient learning without deciding the unconditional question posed here.

Daniely and Vardi later derive hardness for DNF with a growing number of terms from an assumption about local pseudorandom generators. This gives a second precise route connecting the computational difficulty of learning compact rules to average-case complexity. Neither theorem should be abbreviated to an unconditional assertion that DNF cannot be learned.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering paper obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning under a uniform training distribution in a framework permitting abstention under distribution shift. Those distribution, output and runtime guarantees differ from the present target. This recent result was included in the status check and does not supply the required polynomial-time distribution-free learner.

A positive resolution would also give the learner sought in TCS-6543: every k-junta can be written as a DNF with at most 2^k terms, and the uniform distribution is one allowed choice of D. This implication goes from general DNF learning to junta learning; learning juntas alone does not supply an algorithm for general DNF targets. The two cards retain distinct targets. The mislabelled legacy record TCS-0023 is consolidated with the junta card because its actual cited problem concerns growing junta support.

5358.why: Determine whether compact Boolean rules that need only polynomially many observations can also be learned with polynomial computation, without assumptions on the input distribution. A positive result would cover decision trees and uniform-example juntas; a negative result would identify a fundamental computational barrier in realizable learning even when the output representation is unrestricted.

importance.reason: A defining computational learning problem originating with the PAC framework, explicitly highlighted in successive surveys and connected to representation-independent learning hardness, decision-tree learning and junta learning. Selected for the Learning theory focus prefix after correcting the mislabelled junta record; the score reflects breadth and foundational significance, not the date of this review.

5773.title: Is the Skolem problem for integer linear recurrences decidable?
5773.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every input k≥1, c_0,…,c_(k−1)∈Z and u_0,…,u_(k−1)∈Z, and correctly decides whether the sequence defined by u_(t+k)=∑_(j=0)^(k−1)c_j u_(t+j) for all t≥0 has u_t=0 for some integer t≥0?
5773.definitions: All integers, including k, are given in binary with signs and delimiters; the input explicitly lists exactly k coefficients and k initial values. These data uniquely define the infinite integer sequence. The order k is unrestricted and is part of the input, not a fixed parameter. Coefficients may vanish, the supplied recurrence need not be of minimal order, and no simplicity, non-degeneracy or nonzero-leading-product promise is imposed. The search includes the given initial terms and all subsequent nonnegative indices. There is no supplied upper bound on t. The required output is YES exactly when a zero occurs and NO otherwise; only termination and correctness are demanded, without a time or space bound. This is the discrete recurrence problem over integers, not the continuous-time Skolem problem or the question whether every term is nonnegative.

context_blocks.text: A short recurrence determines infinitely many exact integer values. Testing any particular term is effective, but deciding that no term will ever be zero requires a terminating procedure for a global property. Even this elementary linear evolution leaves an unresolved boundary between arithmetic structure and algorithmic decision.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem constrains zero sets to a finite union of arithmetic progressions together with a finite exceptional set. That qualitative description is not, by itself, an algorithm that determines all exceptional zeros from the input. The distinction explains why a structural theorem about the sequence does not automatically settle the decision question.

Bilu and coauthors study simple recurrences and relate termination of their proposed procedure to transcendence conjectures. The arbitrary integer recurrence in this card also allows repeated characteristic roots and other cases outside the simple setting. Conditional termination for a subclass therefore has a different scope from an unconditional decision algorithm for the full input domain.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell improve the complexity of low-order and bounded-index versions. Their July 2026 revision places the unrestricted order-at-most-four problem in coRP. A bounded index range is additional input, and an order bound of four excludes general recurrences; neither restriction answers the unrestricted decision problem.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 paper obtains general decidability conditionally on a strengthened Cramér-type conjecture. Its unconditional density results for possible large zeros do not guarantee a decision for each individual recurrence. The new review preserves TCS-5773 and its original 2022 source rather than creating a second general Skolem entry.

5773.why: Locate the decidability boundary for exact zero reachability in discrete linear dynamics.
5773.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability problem with an elementary finite input, substantial arithmetic content, and direct links to verification and automata. The 2026 work confirms current specialist attention; the importance is independent of the record’s previous incomplete wording.

6446.title: Quantum PCP: a constant promise gap for local Hamiltonians
6446.formal: Do there exist integers k,d≥1 and a rational constant ε∈(0,1) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of m≤(n+1)^d k-local Hermitian terms H_i on n≥1 qubits and rational a<b in [0,1], with 0⪯H_i⪯I and b−a≥ε. For H=(1/m)Σ_i H_i, distinguish λ_min(H)≤a from λ_min(H)≥b.
6446.why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.

progress.text: The survey develops the Hamiltonian conjecture and obstacles to quantum PCP constructions.

Bafna–Vyas explicitly describe the general conjecture as open. Their classical private PCP uses $O(\sqrt n)$ queries; stronger parameters depend on a product-expansion conjecture. This does not prove Quantum PCP.

context_blocks.text: The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.

6446.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6446.definitions: Here 1≤m; each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. λ_min is the smallest eigenvalue. M⪯N means that N−M is positive semidefinite, equivalently z*(N−M)z≥0 for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with a<λ_min(H)<b are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs (Y,N₀) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |0⟩. H=2^(−1/2)((1,1),(1,−1)) is the Hadamard matrix, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For x∈Y some witness gives acceptance probability ≥2/3; for x∈N₀ every witness gives probability ≤1/3. A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and N₀ into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants k,d,ε are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.

importance.reason: A defining quantum-complexity conjecture connecting robust verification, approximation hardness, and the structure of many-body Hamiltonians.

6447.title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
6447.formal: Does every QMA promise problem admit a constant-round strong quantum interactive oracle proof with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, total prover-message length polynomial in the input length n, total query complexity O(1), completeness at least 2/3, and soundness at most 1/3? The strong access model is defined below. The prover may be computationally unbounded, and soundness quantifies over all prover strategies.
6447.why: The problem isolates the communication price of an extremely limited quantum verifier. A positive result would eliminate the exponential communication in the present strong construction.

progress.text: The general qIOP has polynomial communication but uses a polynomial private quantum resource. The strong construction operates on constantly many qubits but communicates $\exp(\operatorname{poly}(n))$ qubits. Question 1.9 asks for polynomial communication.

references.title: Quantum Interactive Oracle Proofs
references.locator: Definitions 1.1–1.2; Theorems 1.5, 1.7; Question 1.9

6447.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
6447.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: A quantum proof can be much larger than the portion a verifier actually inspects. An interactive oracle proof lets a prover supply such messages over several rounds, with the verifier charged for the qubits it touches. Communication volume and access complexity are therefore different resources.

The strong model requires the verifier to hand each received quantum message back in full and forbids sending an additional quantum message of its own. It still has private workspace. Returning a message does not mean undoing the measurement or channel applied to the queried qubits; the resulting state can be returned.

For example, a protocol might inspect only two qubits from an enormous register. That has constant query complexity but still transmits the enormous register. Conversely, allowing the verifier to retain part of a received message changes the protocol model even if the amount of communication is small.

The existing constructions meet different combinations of the desired bounds: general qIOPs have polynomial communication, while the strong construction has exponential communication. The question asks for polynomial communication in the strong model itself. The constant-round requirement and constant total query budget must hold together.

6447.definitions: In each round the prover supplies a quantum register W. The verifier chooses queried positions through a measurement and applies a quantum channel only to those qubits and its private register; query cost counts accessed message qubits, summed over rounds. It returns the entire W register, may send additional classical information, and sends no additional quantum register. It can retain its own private workspace, but cannot retain any part of a prover-message register. The parties have no initial shared entanglement. Total prover-message length counts the full incoming registers, not only queried qubits. This restates the strong model of Definitions 5.1–5.2 and 5.13–5.15.
6447.answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol for every QMA promise problem, or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no protocol meeting all these bounds. Polynomial communication in the weaker general qIOP model does not suffice.

importance.reason: Tests how far succinct interactive verification can extend to quantum proofs with explicit communication restrictions; affects a broad proof-system design space.

context_blocks.text: A quantum state may encode a proof that has no short classical description. Oracle separations test this idea but do not separate the standard classes.

The same quantum verifier is used on both sides of the comparison. What changes is the proof supplied by a prover: either a classical string or a quantum state. A classical proof is still allowed to instruct the verifier to perform a sophisticated quantum computation, so this is not simply a comparison between classical and quantum algorithms.

To prove a separation, one needs a verification task whose positive instances admit useful quantum proofs but no comparably short classical proofs for any efficient quantum verifier. Observing that a particular state has a long classical description is not sufficient: a different classical argument might certify the same claim without describing that state.

6448.answer_criterion: Prove QMA is contained in QCMA, or prove the existence of a promise problem in QMA outside QCMA. A separation relative to an oracle does not settle these unrelativized classes.
6448.definitions: Use uniform polynomial-time quantum verification, completeness at least 2/3 and soundness at most 1/3, with no shared advice or oracle. Classes here contain promise problems; the witness may depend on the whole input.

importance.reason: Separates quantum from classical witnesses and therefore addresses a basic source of quantum computational power.

6449.title: Quantum versus classical nonuniform advice
6449.formal: Is $\mathrm{BQP/qpoly}=\mathrm{BQP/poly}$? Advice for inputs of length $n$ depends only on $n$: a state on $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ qubits on the left, or $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ classical bits on the right. The computation must succeed on every input of that length.
6449.why: This distinguishes two basic ways to store auxiliary information for computation. It is different from QMA versus QCMA.

progress.text: The source gives the first separation of these advice classes using a standard classical oracle. It does not claim an unrelativized separation.

6449.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: Advice is not a witness chosen for an individual input. It is one nonuniform information resource shared by an entire input-length class.

For a fixed input length, the advice must support all inputs of that length. It cannot be tailored after seeing the particular instance. This makes it different from a witness, which is chosen to establish a claim about one input. A fresh copy of the same quantum advice state can be supplied for each computation.

The possible advantage is not that a measurement reveals an arbitrary amount of classical information from a few qubits. Instead, the algorithm might use the input to choose which computation to perform with the advice. The open question is whether polynomial-length classical advice can always support an equally effective computation for every input.

6449.answer_criterion: Prove that polynomial classical advice suffices for every language decidable with polynomial quantum advice, or prove a separation of the two unrelativized advice classes.
6449.definitions: The quantum computation is uniform and polynomial time, with error at most 1/3 on every input. Advice size is bounded by one polynomial. There is no computability restriction on the length-indexed advice family and no oracle.

importance.reason: Asks whether quantum information can encode useful nonuniform computational advice beyond classical advice of comparable size.
