6450.title: A polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication for total functions
6450.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
6450.formal: For a total Boolean function $F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}$, let $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)$ be public-coin randomized communication complexity and $Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F)$ quantum communication complexity with unlimited shared entanglement. Is there a universal polynomial $p$ such that $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)\le p(Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F))$ for every total $F$?
6450.why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

progress.text: For $F=f\circ\mathrm{AND}_2$, the source proves $D^{cc}(F)=O((Q^{cc,*}(F))^7\log^2 n)$. The polylogarithmic factor and the restriction to AND-composed functions prevent this from settling the general question.

references.title: Quantum–Classical Equivalence for AND-Functions
references.authors: Sreejata Bhattacharya; Farzan Byramji; Arkadev Chattopadhyay; Yogesh Dahiya; Shachar Lovett
references.locator: Introduction; communication model, PDF p. 9; revision 1

6450.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
6450.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: Partial functions can exhibit exponential quantum savings. Requiring correctness on every input pair may fundamentally restrict that advantage.

Alice receives x and Bob receives y. They need to compute a function of both inputs while exchanging as little information as possible. The classical protocol may use randomness, and the quantum protocol may begin with shared entanglement. The cost being compared is the communication, not the complexity of their local computation.

Totality means every pair of legal individual inputs must receive a correct answer, including pairs that a promise problem would exclude. A universal polynomial simulation would limit quantum communication savings across all such functions. A bound for a special composition, or one with an additional dependence on the input length, does not automatically supply that universal relation.

6450.answer_criterion: Establish one polynomial bound valid for every finite total Boolean communication problem, or prove that no universal polynomial bound holds. Promise problems and restricted subclasses do not suffice.
6450.definitions: X and Y are arbitrary finite sets. Cost is the worst-case total number of communicated bits or qubits, and error at most 1/3 is required on every input pair. Public random bits and prior entanglement, respectively, are not charged as communication.

importance.reason: A general classical-versus-quantum comparison across all total communication problems, with a sharp distinction from promise-problem separations.

category_assignment.reason: Boolean function analysis

sentences: Two parties must evaluate a Boolean function when each holds one part of the input.
The question asks whether randomized classical communication is polynomially bounded by quantum communication with shared entanglement for every total function.
Both models allow bounded error on each input, and their costs count transmitted bits or qubits rather than local computation.
A positive answer would limit quantum communication advantages whenever the function is defined on every input pair.
The totality condition is central: results for promise problems cannot be substituted, and the polynomial must be universal across all finite domains.

6454.title: Does worst-case Nearest Codeword hardness imply low-noise LPN hardness?
6454.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
6454.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.

references.title: Towards Worst-case Hardness for Low-Noise LPN
references.authors: Divesh Aggarwal; Rishav Gupta; Hai Hoang Nguyen; Kel Zin Tan; Prashant Nalini Vasudevan
references.locator: Revision 1, 8 September 2026

6454.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
6454.review_note: Editorial specialization of the NCP-only direction in Section 1.2 of the September 2026 revision. It fixes the starting problem, decision-LPN distribution, sample count, noise, uniformity, and asymptotic advantage, replacing the vague phrase natural worst-case problem. The source does not state this exact parameter specialization as a numbered conjecture.

context_blocks.text: LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.

6454.definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over F_2 and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least 2/3 on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
6454.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.

importance.reason: Would connect worst-case coding hardness to a central average-case cryptographic assumption in a concrete low-noise regime.

category_assignment.reason: Mapped from the existing subject category

sentences: Learning parity with noise asks for information about hidden binary linear equations when some answers have been flipped.
This project asks whether worst-case hardness of the binary nearest-codeword problem implies average-case hardness for a specified low-noise LPN distribution.
The chosen regime uses quadratically many samples and a noise rate inversely proportional to the square root of the secret dimension.
A reduction must produce that particular random-instance distribution rather than merely another hard coding problem or a different noise level.
Such a connection would strengthen the theoretical foundation of low-noise LPN in the way worst-case reductions support lattice-based assumptions.

6455.title: Doubly efficient IP = PSPACE for the full time range
6455.formal: Suppose a language is decided in polynomial space and time $T(n)$. Does it have an interactive proof with a $\operatorname{poly}(n)$-time verifier, a $\operatorname{poly}(T(n))$-time honest prover, and a constant completeness–soundness gap? Soundness must hold against arbitrarily powerful cheating provers. The target includes $T$ beyond the quasipolynomial range.
6455.why: This asks whether a long, space-efficient computation can be verified without hiding an excessive cost in the honest prover.

progress.text: The previous range cited in the paper was $T(n)=n^{O(\sqrt{\log n/\log\log n})}$.
The direct construction extends the range to $T(n)=n^{O(\log n)}$. It does not cover arbitrary polynomial-space computation times.

references.title: Towards a Doubly Efficient IP=PSPACE
references.authors: Liyan Chen; Matthew M. Hong; Yael Tauman Kalai; Zoe Xi
references.locator: Revision 1; Introduction

6455.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
6455.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: IP = PSPACE alone does not guarantee that producing the proof costs only a polynomial in the original computation time.

Interactive proofs separate the effort of checking a computation from the effort of producing a convincing transcript. The usual class equality allows an honest prover to use enormous resources. That is enough for a complexity-class statement, but does not establish that proof generation is efficient relative to the computation being certified.

The target compares the honest prover directly with the original running time T. A prover using a polynomial in T would have controlled overhead even when the verifier has only polynomial time in the input length. Soundness still has to hold against a cheating prover of unlimited power; restricting the honest prover does not weaken the adversary in the definition.

6455.answer_criterion: Prove the specified verifier/prover time guarantees for every polynomial-space language and its time bound, or prove the negation of that universal statement. Improving only a restricted range of T is partial progress.
6455.definitions: Use uniform classical randomized verification with completeness at least 2/3 and soundness at most 1/3. For every polynomial-space decider with time-constructible bound T(n) at least n, a protocol with the stated bounds is sought. Polynomial exponents may depend on the decider, but not on n.

importance.reason: Tests the efficiency limits of the IP = PSPACE phenomenon when both verifier and prover costs matter, across the full time range.

category_assignment.reason: The problem refines IP=PSPACE through honest-prover and verifier running times, rather than propositional proof length.

sentences: An interactive proof lets a verifier check a claim through conversation with a prover.
The question asks whether polynomial-space computations taking time T can be verified in polynomial input time using an honest prover running in polynomial T time.
The requirement extends across the full time range, beyond quasipolynomial computations.
This would make proof generation efficient relative to the computation being certified, strengthening the resource content of IP=PSPACE.
The saved review stresses that soundness must still withstand arbitrarily powerful cheating provers, despite the efficiency requirement imposed on the honest one.

6498.title: Are splay trees dynamically optimal?
6498.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost Θ(n), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by O((OPT(X)+n) log log n · log² log log n). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

6498.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
6498.definitions: Keys are [n]={1,…,n}, n≥1, ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence X∈[n]*, cost_splay(X;T₀) is the sum of these costs starting from T₀. A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. OPT(X) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

progress.text: Splaying has logarithmic amortized access cost and stronger guarantees for useful special patterns. These do not establish competitiveness against an arbitrary changing offline tree.
Tango trees give an online BST with an $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio. This result is for a different data structure and does not settle splaying.
The preprint proves $O((\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\log\log n\,\log^2\log\log n)$ total splay cost. Theorem 1 includes the initialization term explicitly. Constant competitiveness remains the target.

6499.title: Can distributed MIS be solved in sublogarithmic time on every graph?
6499.formal:
In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\in E\Rightarrow\{u,v\}
subseteq I$ and $v
otin I\Rightarrow N(v)\cap I
e\varnothing$. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each fixed constant $c>0$, allowing the constant in the running time to depend on $c$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\Delta\le n-1$.
6499.why: This isolates the communication needed for a basic symmetry-breaking task whose feasibility is easy to check locally. I include it because either outcome would change the benchmark for distributed graph algorithms: a faster algorithm would supply a stronger primitive, while a logarithmic lower bound would expose a substantial limitation of local coordination.
6499.definitions:
The network is the input graph. Rounds are synchronous; each edge can carry an arbitrarily large message in each direction. Vertices may have distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifiers and private random bits. Every vertex outputs its own membership bit. The measured time is the number of elapsed rounds until all outputs are available, not the number of rounds in which an individual processor stays awake.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree. Both the algorithm and the asymptotic time bound are uniform over input graphs and valid identifier assignments.

progress.text: Ghaffari gives the degree-sensitive MIS algorithm. With subsequent deterministic finishing routines, the standard bound is $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$.

Khoury and Schild give a randomized lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\log\Delta,\sqrt{\log n}\})$ for maximal matching and, by reduction, MIS on general graphs. This implies an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ worst-case barrier, not an $\Omega(\log n)$ barrier.

Their separate degree-reduction paper obtains $O(\log\Delta/\log(\log^{*}\Delta)+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds for girth at least seven. Its Open Question 1 asks for the general-graph improvement.

references.title: Breaking Barriers for Distributed MIS by Faster Degree Reduction
references.locator: Introduction, Open Question 1 and Theorem 1

references.title: An Improved Distributed Algorithm for Maximal Independent Set
references.locator: SODA 2016; local-complexity theorem and global consequence

references.locator: Introduction and Theorem 1

6499.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. General-graph sublogarithmic elapsed-round complexity remains open in the checked literature; awake-time and high-girth results have different guarantees.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.

Maximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.

Degree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\log\Delta+\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.

Recent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six. It does not extend to arbitrary graphs. Together with stronger lower bounds, this leaves a concrete question: can local choices still make sufficiently rapid progress when short cycles create dependencies between nearby decisions?

6499.review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.
6499.answer_criterion: Give one randomized LOCAL algorithm with a uniform o(log n) round bound and the stated success probability on all graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A degree restriction does not settle the proposition.

importance.reason: A basic randomized symmetry-breaking question on arbitrary graphs whose resolution would sharpen the global locality frontier.

The question asks for a randomized LOCAL algorithm that finds such a set in o(log n) rounds on every graph with high probability.
Message sizes and local computation are unrestricted, so the resource measures the distance over which decisions must be coordinated.

Degree-sensitive algorithms already improve some cases, but the target requires a mechanism that also avoids logarithmically many phases on unrestricted graphs.

6500.title: Erdős girth conjecture: is the classical spanner size bound tight?
6500.formal: For every fixed integer $k\ge 2$, do there exist a constant $c_k>0$ and arbitrarily large simple undirected graphs $G$ with $n$ vertices, at least $c_k n^{1+1/k}$ edges, and no cycle of length at most $2k$? Equivalently, can the $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ extremal upper bound for girth greater than $2k$ be attained up to a constant factor for every $k$? The first unsettled value is $k=4$: girth at least nine and $\Omega(n^{5/4})$ edges.
6500.why: This is a structural problem with a short, rigorous reduction to an algorithmic limit. I include it because many claims that a distance-preserving graph representation is optimal depend on precisely this unproved construction. A proof would establish those lower bounds; a counterexample would force a re-examination of the expected stretch–space tradeoff.
6500.definitions: The girth is the length of a shortest cycle, with infinite girth for a forest. A $t$-spanner is a spanning subgraph $H\subseteq G$ satisfying $d_G(u,v)\le d_H(u,v)\le t\,d_G(u,v)$ for every reachable pair. The parameter $k$ is fixed as $n$ grows, and constants may depend on $k$. The question asks for existence; an efficient explicit construction would be a stronger result.

progress.text: Althöfer, Das, Dobkin, Joseph, and Soares give sparse multiplicative spanners: every weighted $n$-vertex graph admits stretch $2k-1$ with $O_k(n^{1+1/k})$ edges. High-girth graphs give the corresponding obstruction to improving size.

Bodwin and Lopez review the remaining girth conjecture in Section 1.1. Their degree-fault-tolerant spanner lower bound is unconditional, separating a new algorithmic result from the still-open underlying conjecture.

references.title: Unconditional Lower Bounds for Degree Fault Tolerant Spanners
references.locator: Section 1.1, pp. 31:1–2; new result in the abstract

references.title: On Sparse Spanners of Weighted Graphs
references.authors: Ingo Althöfer, Gautam Das, David Dobkin, Deborah Joseph, and José Soares
references.locator: Discrete & Computational Geometry 9, 81–100

6500.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The general conjecture remains unresolved; several individual values of k are settled.

context_blocks.text: High degree tries to make short cycles unavoidable. In a graph whose small neighborhoods contain no cycles, a breadth-first search keeps discovering new vertices rather than revisiting old ones. Sustaining large branching for several levels consumes the available vertices rapidly. This is the reason a ban on short cycles forces an upper bound on density; the conjecture asks whether graphs can pack edges as efficiently as that counting argument permits.

The algorithmic connection is direct. Suppose a unit-weight graph has girth greater than $2k$. If a subgraph omits an edge $uv$, every remaining $u$–$v$ path has at least $2k$ edges: a shorter path together with $uv$ would create a forbidden cycle. Thus any $(2k-1)$-spanner must keep every edge. A dense graph of this kind is a certificate that no smaller spanner can preserve the required distances.

For example, a triangle-free graph alone is not enough for the $k=2$ application: a four-cycle allows one edge to be replaced by a three-edge detour. Excluding both triangles and four-cycles makes every edge indispensable for stretch three. This example explains why the exact girth threshold appears in the conjecture.

The conjecture is not an established law of graph sparsification. The 2026 source records that only the parameters 1, 2, 3, and 5 are known and discusses reasons to question the general statement. Its new fault-tolerant lower bound bypasses the conjecture for that model; it does not construct the missing high-girth families.

6500.answer_criterion: Prove the required graph families exist for every fixed k, or refute the universal claim for at least one fixed k. Proving the k=4 case alone would resolve the first unknown case but not the whole conjecture.

importance.reason: Connects extremal graph density with the optimal size of sparse distance-preserving structures; consequences extend across graph theory and algorithms.

6504.title: Is perfect matching in general graphs in deterministic NC?
6504.formal: Do there exist constants C,a,b>0 and a logspace-uniform family of Boolean circuits which, on the adjacency matrix of every n-vertex simple undirected graph, output a perfect matching or correctly report that none exists, with at most C(n+2)^a gates and depth at most C(log₂(n+2))^b?
6504.why: I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way. The question asks whether randomness is needed to find globally compatible choices quickly, and whether the structural tools for odd cycles can be made as parallel as the algebraic ones.
6504.definitions: The input is the n×n binary adjacency matrix of a graph on [n], with symmetry and zero diagonal promised. A perfect matching is a set of edges with exactly one edge incident to each vertex. Output is a flag and an n×n binary incidence matrix for the chosen matching; when the flag reports nonexistence the remaining output bits are ignored. The empty graph has the empty perfect matching. Circuits use fan-in-two AND/OR, fan-in-one NOT, constants 0,1 and unrestricted fan-out. Depth counts gates on the longest input-output path and size counts gates; the n² output positions are specified as part of the description. A deterministic Turing transducer on unary input 1^n writes the description using O(log₂(n+2)) work bits, with read-only input and write-only output. Constants and generator are fixed across n; every valid input must receive an exact answer. No randomness, oracle, advice, bipartiteness or other structural graph promise is supplied.

progress.text: The randomized parallel approach of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani uses isolation to single out a matching. Svensson and Tarnawski review this starting point and the need to derandomize it.

Svensson and Tarnawski give a deterministic general-graph algorithm in $O(\log^3 n)$ parallel time with $n^{O(\log^2 n)}$ processors. It achieves quasi-NC, leaving a quasipolynomial-versus-polynomial resource gap.
Chakraborty and coauthors’ revision constructs maximum matchings in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. The restored auxiliary-memory model does not by itself yield ordinary NC.
The bipartite NC preprint reaches revision 2, covering weighted and search versions and extending to linear matroid intersection. General-graph matching is outside the stated theorem.

6504.status_note: The general quasi-NC result, the bipartite preprint’s revision 2 of 15 July 2026, and the catalytic-logspace revision of 1 June 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. Subsequent-result searches found no deterministic NC search algorithm for arbitrary graphs. The newly cited preprint proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the issue is how many dependent stages remain when the work is spread across many processors. Polynomial total size is essential: evaluating exponentially many candidate matchings in parallel is outside NC. The output requirement is also explicit. The circuit must select a set of edges forming one matching, or certify nonexistence with its output flag.

Choosing matching edges independently can give incompatible decisions. On a four-cycle, deleting any one edge leaves a perfect matching. Deleting all four edges at once leaves none. This small example distinguishes a collection of individually valid existence statements from the coordinated selection required for a search output.

General graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.

The June 2026 bipartite preprint, updated on 15 July, gives NC algorithms for bipartite matching and extends the results to search and weighted variants and to linear matroid intersection. Its scope restriction matters: an arbitrary graph need not be bipartite. The July revision does not state the general-graph theorem asked here.

A separate June 2026 revision places maximum-matching construction in general graphs in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. Catalytic space means a larger auxiliary memory tape may begin in an arbitrary state and must be restored on termination. This additional resource is different from ordinary logarithmic workspace, and the result does not establish an NC circuit family. It is a nearby complexity improvement whose model must remain attached to its conclusion.

The 2017 quasi-NC result already obtains polylogarithmic parallel time, but permits n^{O(log² n)} processors. Such a quantity eventually exceeds every fixed polynomial. The open gap is therefore the total resource bound for arbitrary graphs, not simply finding any parallel algorithm with a short dependency chain.

6505.title: One cycle versus two: is logarithmic time necessary in low-memory MPC?
6505.formal: For every fixed $0<\delta<1$, must every randomized MPC algorithm distinguishing one n-cycle from two vertex-disjoint (n/2)-cycles use $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds in the worst case over even n and input placement? Each machine has $O(n^\delta)$ words and total memory is O(n) words. Require success probability at least $1-n^{-c}$ for each requested fixed $c>0$. An $o(\log n)$-round algorithm for one fixed $\delta<1$ would refute this lower-bound conjecture.
6505.why: I include this because the input removes most graph-theoretic complications and leaves the cost of assembling global connectivity information. It is a standard conditional-hardness benchmark for massively parallel algorithms, and a resolution would clarify whether limited memory creates an inherent logarithmic coordination cost even on degree-two graphs.
6505.definitions: Words have $O(\log n)$ bits. The input edge list is distributed across machines without exceeding their local memory. Each synchronous round allows arbitrary local computation followed by sending and receiving at most $O(n^{\delta})$ words per machine. The desired success probability is $1-n^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. This card fixes linear total memory; variants allowing more total space must be stated separately.

progress.text: Nanongkai and Scquizzato develop equivalence classes and conditional-hardness connections around this cycle problem and logarithmic-space computation. Their reductions have explicit global-memory requirements; those should be checked before transferring them to the linear-total-memory variant here.

Gan, Wirth, and Zhang explicitly state the linear-total-memory 2-CYCLE conjecture while giving a constant-round algorithm for embedded grid graphs. The promised arbitrary-cycle problem is left unresolved.

6505.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The lower bound is conjectural. Constant-round results for geometric graphs or larger local memory do not establish this variant.

context_blocks.text: Both promised inputs have exactly n vertices and n edges, and every vertex has degree two. Counting vertices, counting edges, and checking degrees therefore gives the same answer. The difference is how those edges join into components. Vertex identifiers are arbitrary, so the labels do not reveal where a cycle begins or whether two pieces belong together.

A sequential scan with graph traversal solves the problem in linear time. With the edge list spread across machines, no one machine can store the whole instance. Repeatedly joining path fragments or doubling the length represented by a pointer gives a natural logarithmic-round approach. The conjecture says that general distributed computation cannot compress this process into asymptotically fewer communication rounds under the stated memory limits.

It is tempting to justify the conjecture by saying that information travels only one graph edge per round. That would be incorrect here. Any machine may send to any other machine, and local computation between exchanges is unrestricted. The restriction is how much information a machine can store, send, and receive at once. A valid lower bound must cope with arbitrary encodings and nonlocal communication.

Extra geometric structure can change the answer. The 2025 grid-connectivity algorithm uses an embedding with bounded edge lengths to obtain constant rounds in its parameter regime. An arbitrarily labelled cycle does not provide that embedding, so the geometric result does not refute this promise-problem conjecture.

6506.title: Can deterministic LOCAL algorithms find an MIS in O(log n) rounds?
6506.formal: Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.
6506.why: This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An O(log n) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.
6506.definitions:
LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output. The target is uniform over arbitrary graphs, not restricted to bounded degree, planar graphs, or trees.

Nodes may know n and the maximum degree; the time guarantee must still be O(log n) uniformly over degrees.

progress.text: Balliu and coauthors prove a deterministic lower bound $\Omega(\min\{\Delta,\log n/\log\log n\})$. In particular, the general worst-case complexity cannot be substantially below logarithmic up to a log-log factor.
Rozhoň and Ghaffari obtain polylogarithmic deterministic network decomposition and consequently polylogarithmic deterministic MIS.
Ghaffari and Grunau improve MIS to $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ rounds, where the hidden factors are polylogarithmic in $\log n$.
Bourreau, Brandt, and Nolin use the same deterministic MIS benchmark to improve Δ-coloring; their result does not give an O(log n) MIS algorithm.

6506.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is solved; the O(log n) target remains open in the checked literature.

context_blocks.text: Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.

Randomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.

Network decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.

The 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.

6507.title: Can directed reachability have near-linear work and polylogarithmic depth?
6507.formal: Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Both bounds must hold on arbitrary inputs, including sparse graphs with long directed paths. Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.
6507.why: I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.
6507.definitions:
The model is a standard word-based PRAM/shared-memory parallel model, with $O(\log n)$-bit words and concurrent access handled by standard PRAM conventions. Local primitive operations, auxiliary data construction, and shortcut generation count toward work. $\widetilde O$ hides polylogarithmic factors. High probability means $1-n^{-c}$ for a requested fixed $c>0$. The output is reachability, not shortest-path distances.

For definiteness fix a CREW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed, and concurrent writes to one cell are prohibited. Word operations are arithmetic, multiplication, bitwise operations, shifts, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of logarithmic-size words. The target permits the polylogarithmic overhead of simulating common alternative PRAM conventions.

progress.text: Jambulapati, Liu, and Sidford obtain almost-linear work with $n^{1/2+o(1)}$ depth for directed reachability.

Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, Probst Gutenberg, and Saranurak improve the near-linear-work depth bound as graph density increases; their dense-graph reachability bound is $n^{0.136}$. The theorem does not give polylogarithmic depth for every density.

Kogan and Parter give polylogarithmic depth with $\widetilde O(T^{\omega/2})$ work, where $T=|TC(G)|$ and $\omega$ is the matrix-multiplication exponent. Even the hypothetical $\omega=2$ gives work in terms of $T$, which may be quadratic for a linear-size input.

6507.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 closure-sensitive algorithm. Near-linear input work with polylogarithmic depth remains the target.

context_blocks.text: A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.

The size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.

Shortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.

The August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”

6511.title: Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?
6511.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
6511.answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
6511.why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
6511.definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.

progress.text: Mulmuley, U. Vazirani, and V. Vazirani provide the randomized algebraic matching framework underlying polynomial-time Exact Matching algorithms.

Du claims a deterministic bipartite algorithm. Version 3 states eight explicit hypotheses in its Lean formalization. That paper does not claim a general-graph solution.

Sato and Yamaguchi’s revised preprint tests all possible red counts simultaneously with high probability using O(n^ω) finite-field operations, where ω denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent used by their algebraic routines. The algorithm remains randomized; the introduction explicitly retains deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.

6511.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026, including the August 2026 revision of the randomized algorithm and the April 2026 bipartite claim. The revised randomized-algorithm paper explicitly states that deterministic polynomial time remains open. This question allows nonbipartite graphs.

context_blocks.text: Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.

6513.title: Does the smallest grammar problem admit a constant-factor approximation?
6513.formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
6513.answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on P != NP should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
6513.definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
6513.why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

progress.text: Charikar and coauthors give an O(1+log(|s|/g*(s))) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below 8569/8568 unless P = NP.
Casel and coauthors establish hardness over fixed alphabets of size at least 17 and retain constant-factor approximation as Open Problem 2. The hardness result does not rule out every constant.

6513.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026 using the primary approximation and fixed-alphabet papers, with a search for later results. No general constant-factor algorithm was located. Recent assembly-index work uses additional size conventions and is not treated as resolving this proposition.

context_blocks.text: A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under P != NP, but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.

6516.title: An entanglement entropy area law for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
6516.formal: For every fixed local dimension q≥2, interaction range r≥1, interaction incidence bound g≥1, norm bound J>0, and spectral gap Δ>0, is there a finite constant C=C(q,r,g,J,Δ) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice Λ_L, has unique ground state ψ satisfying S(ρ_A)≤C|∂A| for every A⊆Λ_L?
6516.definitions: Let L≥1 be an integer, Λ_L={1,…,L}² with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of C^q over its sites. Write H=Σ_a h_a, where each h_a is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support X_a⊆Λ_L of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every h_a is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector ψ and its next eigenvalue is at least Δ above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For A⊆Λ_L, let A^c be its complement in Λ_L and ρ_A=Tr_(A^c)(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|) and S(ρ_A)=−Tr(ρ_A log_2 ρ_A), with 0 log_2 0=0. The boundary ∂A is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
6516.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6516.why: A central problem in quantum Hamiltonian complexity: whether locality plus a uniform gap controls the quantum information in ground states in two dimensions. It would sharpen the structural foundations of tensor-network methods and separate the task of bounding entanglement from the further task of computing the state.

importance.reason: A fundamental unresolved link between spectral gaps, geometric locality, entanglement, and the resources needed to describe quantum many-body ground states.

6516.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The February and April 2026 results retain extra hypotheses; the general globally gapped 2D entropy area law remains unresolved. The formulation explicitly requires a size-independent constant and fixes the geometric boundary, interaction norms, local dimension, uniqueness, and global gap.

context_blocks.text: A region with m spins has enough Hilbert-space dimension for entropy m log_2 q. For a square block of side length ℓ, that is proportional to ℓ², whereas this conjecture allows only a constant times ℓ. The physical idea is that finite-range interactions and a gap should constrain how much quantum information crosses the boundary. Fixing both interaction strength and the gap prevents an artificial rescaling from making a gapless family appear uniformly gapped.

In one dimension, Hastings proves the corresponding entropy bound for gapped local systems. Since an interval has only a constant number of boundary points, its entropy remains bounded as the chain grows. Matrix-product-state approximations then connect this structure to classical numerical methods. Grouping columns of a two-dimensional lattice into single one-dimensional sites does not directly extend the theorem: each new site has dimension q^L, which grows exponentially with the width.

Anshu, Arad, and Gosset make major progress for frustration-free systems with a local gap. Frustration freeness means one state minimizes every local term; the local-gap assumption controls Hamiltonians obtained from subsets of terms, and is stronger than the global gap here. Their cited version proves a vertical-cut entropy bound n^(1+O((log n)^(−1/5))) for cut length n. It is asymptotically almost linear, but the remaining factor is not a constant and neither extra assumption follows from the statement in this card.

Anshu, Harrow, and Soleimanifar prove an area law for entanglement spread, a measure of variation among the Schmidt coefficients after an appropriate smoothing. This controls a different feature of entanglement from its entropy. For intuition, a maximally entangled state can have arbitrarily many equal Schmidt coefficients: its spread is zero while its entropy is the logarithm of their number. A spread bound therefore does not by itself answer the entropy question.

Arad, Firanko, and Jain’s February 2026 theorem treats mutual information of the maximally mixed ground state. It assumes a sufficiently accurate approximation to the ground-space projector whose operator Schmidt rank is suitably small. Constructing such an approximation for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians remains a missing ingredient; the general wording of the title does not remove this hypothesis.

Garratt and Abanin’s April 2026 preprint provides thermodynamic upper bounds and proves area laws for frustration-free systems when ground-space degeneracies of the relevant subsystem Hamiltonians have suitable boundary scaling. A unique ground state for the full system does not impose that condition on each subsystem. These results retain additional assumptions.

The computational significance also needs care. Huang proves that two-dimensional local Hamiltonian instances whose ground states satisfy area laws can still be QMA-complete. Those instances are not claimed to have the uniform gap fixed here. The result nevertheless shows why an entropy bound alone should not be advertised as a general efficient classical algorithm for finding or manipulating two-dimensional ground states.

6518.title: Does NPT bound entanglement exist?
6518.formal: Do there exist finite integers a,b≥2 and a bipartite density matrix ρ on ℂᵃ⊗ℂᵇ such that ρ has negative partial transpose, but ⟨ψ|(ρ^{Γ_B})^{⊗k}|ψ⟩≥0 for every integer k≥1 and every unit vector ψ of Schmidt rank at most two across (ℂᵃ)^{⊗k}:(ℂᵇ)^{⊗k}?
6518.definitions: A density matrix is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix with trace one. In fixed local orthonormal bases, partial transpose on B is defined by (ρ^{Γ_B})_{ij,kℓ}=ρ_{iℓ,kj}. Negative partial transpose (NPT) means that ρ^{Γ_B} has at least one negative eigenvalue; it does not mean that the whole matrix is negative semidefinite. Schmidt rank is the minimum number of product vectors whose sum is ψ. Tensor powers represent independent copies of the same fixed state. A state is k-copy distillable exactly when a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two vector makes the displayed expectation strictly negative. Thus the proposed state is undistillable for every finite number of copies. Operationally, Alice and Bob may use arbitrary local quantum operations, local auxiliary systems and unlimited classical communication in both directions, but no quantum communication or additional shared entanglement. Distillability means that they can asymptotically obtain Bell pairs (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 at a positive rate with error tending to zero. The finite-copy criterion above is equivalent to positive distillability in this model.
6518.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6518.why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

importance.reason: A central structural boundary in entanglement theory, with canonical finite-dimensional candidates and consequences for what quantum correlations can accomplish under local operations.

6518.status_note: The all-copy NPT bound-entanglement question remains explicitly open in the July 2026 primary sources. New two-copy solutions and restricted three-copy progress do not settle this formulation. Reviewed through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

Low local dimension explains why a spectral test alone can be misleading in larger systems. If one party has dimension two, every vector has Schmidt rank at most two. A negative eigenvector then immediately certifies one-copy distillability. In higher dimensions, a negative eigenvector can require three or more product terms. Combining copies enlarges both local spaces and permits collective operations, creating additional opportunities to extract a useful two-dimensional entangled subsystem.

The systematic search for NPT bound entanglement dates at least to the families studied by DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal. Their work provides evidence and reductions to structured states rather than a proof of an all-copy counterexample. Such reductions matter because the original statement quantifies over all finite dimensions and all density matrices; symmetry can expose a tractable algebraic problem inside that enormous search space.

A canonical family is ρ_W(d,α)=(I+αF)/(d²+αd), where d≥3, −1≤α≤1 and F swaps the two d-dimensional systems. These Werner states are NPT exactly when α<−1/d, and one-copy distillable exactly when α<−1/2. Consequently the interval −1/2≤α<−1/d consists of particularly important candidates. It is nonempty for d≥3. The endpoint α=−1/2 is NPT even though its minimum expectation on rank-two vectors is zero.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example ρ_W(4,−1/2). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

A two-copy proof cannot simply be iterated. In the corresponding matrix formulation, taking a partial trace can increase rank; tensor products also need not preserve the relevant positivity property. Bharti, Gajjala and Haug make these obstacles explicit while giving restricted many-copy extensions. Likewise, a sequence of examples that resists progressively larger numbers of copies can approach the PPT boundary without yielding one fixed NPT state that resists all of them.

Wu and Zou’s subsequent three-copy analysis proves endpoint nonnegativity for the normal rank-two coefficient sector, among other restricted sectors, and studies genuinely nonnormal cases separately. It does not settle the unrestricted three-copy question, much less the all-copy target. The distinction makes the remaining challenge concrete: control every admissible rank-two witness across the full collection of copies, rather than only witnesses with a convenient internal structure.

6520.title: Computability of quantum channel capacity
6520.formal: Does there exist a single classical Turing algorithm that, given any effectively described finite-dimensional memoryless quantum channel Φ and a positive rational ε, halts and outputs a rational r satisfying |r−Q(Φ)|≤ε, where Q is the unassisted quantum capacity in qubits per channel use?
6520.definitions: The input includes positive integers d_A,d_B and a program describing the unnormalized Choi matrix J(Φ)=Σᵢⱼ |i⟩⟨j|⊗Φ(|i⟩⟨j|), a matrix of order d_A d_B. On input k≥1, that program must halt and output a rational complex matrix whose real and imaginary entries approximate the corresponding entries of J(Φ) within 2⁻ᵏ. It is promised that the limiting matrix is positive semidefinite and Tr_B J(Φ)=I_A, so it defines a completely positive trace-preserving linear map from d_A-dimensional input states to d_B-dimensional output states. This explicitly specifies “effective description”; finite algebraic matrix descriptions are included. The requested algorithm need only meet its guarantees on inputs satisfying these promises. Memorylessness means n uses implement Φ^{⊗n}, allowing arbitrary joint encoding and decoding across those uses. No preshared entanglement, additional classical communication, feedback or auxiliary channel is free. Operationally Q(Φ) is the supremum of asymptotically achievable quantum transmission rates with error tending to zero. Equivalently, Q(Φ)=sup_{n≥1} n⁻¹ max_ρ I_c(ρ,Φ^{⊗n}). Here ρ ranges over density matrices on A^{⊗n}; if ψ_{RAⁿ} is any purification and ω=(id_R⊗Φ^{⊗n})(ψ), then I_c=S(ω_{Bⁿ})−S(ω_{RBⁿ}), with S(τ)=−Tr(τ log₂τ) and 0 log₂0=0. There is no running-time bound beyond eventual halting for every valid channel description and every ε>0.
6520.answer_criterion: A positive answer requires a uniform algorithm with a proved finite stopping rule and additive error guarantee for every promised input. A negative answer must prove that no such approximation algorithm exists in this specified representation. An asymptotic formula without an effective convergence bound, hardness only for polynomial-time computation, or undecidability of a different assisted, zero-error or memoryful capacity is insufficient. Undecidability of testing the exact equality Q(Φ)=0 alone would also not disprove computable additive approximation.
6520.why: Determine whether the fundamental reliable quantum communication rate is algorithmically accessible even without efficiency constraints.

importance.reason: A foundational computability question about regularized information quantities, separating lack of efficient algorithms from the possible absence of any certified approximation algorithm.

6520.status_note: No uniform computability theorem or impossibility proof for this finite-dimensional memoryless unassisted capacity found through 11 September 2026. The corrected 2026 paper explicitly leaves the general question open: its quantum-capacity result is QMA-hardness, while its undecidability result concerns a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity.

context_blocks.text: Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem expresses capacity through regularized coherent information: optimize over a block of n uses, divide by n, and take the supremum over every block length. Devetak’s coding theorem gives an operational justification for this expression. It is an exact mathematical characterization, but it involves infinitely many optimization problems. A numerical procedure needs an additional way to know when unexamined block lengths cannot improve the answer by more than ε.

For each fixed block length, the input dimension is finite and the coherent-information objective can be approximated on the compact space of density matrices. Exhaustive computation can therefore produce successively better certified lower bounds on Q. This can be absurdly expensive and still count as computation here. The obstruction is that increasing lower bounds need not come with a computable certificate of how far they remain below their limit.

Cubitt, Elkouss, Matthews, Ozols, Pérez-García and Strelchuk show that no universal constant number of channel uses suffices even to expose positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there, but becomes positive at a larger block length. These are different channels as the chosen length changes. The theorem does not rule out an algorithm whose stopping time depends on the channel description and requested precision.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating Φ independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least 3/4 from capacity at most 1/4, even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.

6523.title: Does every isotropic log-concave measure have a dimension-free Poincaré constant?
6523.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C<∞ such that, for every dimension n≥1, every isotropic log-concave probability measure μ on ℝⁿ, and every locally Lipschitz f:ℝⁿ→ℝ with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
6523.definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density ρ=e^{−V}, where V:ℝⁿ→ℝ∪{+∞} is convex and ∫ρ=1; allowing V=+∞ includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means ∫x dμ(x)=0 and ∫xxᵀ dμ(x)=Iₙ. Variance is Varμ(f)=∫(f−∫f dμ)²dμ, and ∇f is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let C_P(μ) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is supₙ supμ C_P(μ)<∞, with μ ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in ℝⁿ. There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of n, μ, or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, ψμ is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; ψμ² is comparable to C_P(μ) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on ψμ must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
6523.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6523.why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

progress.text: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies.
Klartag and Lehec obtain the first polylogarithmic bounds for the KLS isoperimetric constant using stochastic-localization techniques.
Klartag proves ψμ=O(√log n), equivalently C_P(μ)=O(log n), through an improved log-concave Lichnerowicz inequality.
Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls E(‖X‖₂−√n)² uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality.

Letwin’s preprint reports Var(XᵀMX)≤2E‖∇(XᵀMX)‖₂² for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives ψₙ=O((log n)^{1/4}). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is C_P=O(√log n), not O((log n)^{1/4}).

6523.status_note: The full KLS conjecture is explicitly open in the primary sources, including Letwin’s July 2026 preprint. Research through 10 September 2026 found no dimension-free general-function resolution. The recent quadratic-form and thin-shell results are not treated as proofs of the full conjecture; the July bound is labeled as a preprint result.

context_blocks.text: The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable ‖X‖₂. Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds E(‖X‖₂−√n)² by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives C_P(μ)=O(log n). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives ψμ=O((log n)^{1/4}), hence C_P(μ)=O(√log n). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.

6525.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
6525.formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant C_H≥1 such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric d_G admits a map f:V(G)→ℝᵐ into some finite-dimensional ℓ₁ space satisfying d_G(u,v)≤‖f(u)−f(v)‖₁≤C_H d_G(u,v) for all vertices u,v?
6525.definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and d_G(u,v) is the minimum path length. In ℝᵐ, ‖x−y‖₁=Σⱼ₌₁ᵐ |xⱼ−yⱼ|. The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant C_H may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |V(G)|, the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
6525.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6525.why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded ℓ₁ distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.
