context_blocks.text: The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and ℓ₁ embeddings.

The target ℓ₁ space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an ℓ₁ embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their ℓ₁ distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is O(√log n) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by γ faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion O(√log(γ+1)). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed γ and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of K₂,ₙ as (3k−2)/(2k−1), where k=⌈n/2⌉. The values approach 3/2. This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.

6532.title: Is the polynomial hierarchy strict at every finite level?
6532.formal: Is $\Sigma_k^{\mathrm P}\subsetneq\Sigma_{k+1}^{\mathrm P}$ for every integer k≥0? Here Σ₀^P=P, and Σₖ^P for k≥1 consists of languages definable by k alternating blocks of polynomially bounded Boolean quantifiers, beginning existentially, followed by a deterministic polynomial-time predicate.
6532.definitions: A language L is in Σₖ^P if there exist a polynomial p and a deterministic polynomial-time predicate R such that, for every binary input x, $x\in L\iff\exists y_1\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\ \forall y_2\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\cdots Q_k y_k\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:R(x,y_1,\ldots,y_k)=1$, where Qₖ is existential for odd k and universal for even k. Each yᵢ is an entire string, so k counts quantifier blocks, not individual bits. The predicate is polynomial-time in the combined input length. k is fixed for a class membership claim and cannot grow with |x|; p and R may depend on k and L. Let Πₖ^P consist of complements of Σₖ^P languages, and let PH=⋃ₖ≥0Σₖ^P. In particular Σ₁^P=NP and Π₁^P=coNP. These are uniform, unrelativized classes of total decision languages. Strictness at level k means that some language in Σₖ₊₁^P is absent from Σₖ^P. The separating language may depend on k. All classes use ordinary Turing computation with no advice or external oracle.
6532.answer_criterion: Prove strict containment at every finite level, or prove equality Σₖ^P=Σₖ₊₁^P for some fixed k. Equality at any adjacent pair collapses all higher levels to that level, so a collapse at even one finite level answers no. Proving strictness for finitely many levels or relative to an oracle does not answer yes.
6532.why: This is the organizing conjecture behind the computational cost of alternating existential and universal reasoning. It strengthens the basic P-versus-NP distinction across all fixed quantifier depths and underlies many conditional lower bounds in complexity, verification, and graph problems with nested solution requirements.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture asserting that every further alternation increases computational power. It governs a large family of complexity classifications and has major circuit-lower-bound consequences.

progress.text: Meyer and Stockmeyer introduce the hierarchy; Stockmeyer develops its structural properties and complete problems.
Oracle constructions show that all levels can be distinct in a relativized world. Karp–Lipton-type theorems connect small circuits for NP to a collapse of the unrelativized hierarchy.
Rossman, Servedio, and Tan establish infinitude relative to a random oracle with probability one. Their proof comes from an average-case lower bound separating consecutive constant circuit depths.

Hirsch and Volkovich study the Linear Ordering Principle, related small complexity classes, and Karp–Lipton-style conditional collapses. These are implications under hypotheses, not an unconditional collapse or separation of PH.

6532.status_note: Explicitly conjectured in the primary-source survey and Wigderson’s hierarchy discussion. Research through 10 September 2026 yielded no unrelativized proof of infinitude or finite collapse. Random-oracle infinitude and conditional Karp–Lipton collapses are not recorded as resolutions.

context_blocks.text: NP captures a single existential choice of a certificate. A second block permits a statement of the form “there is a candidate that survives every challenge”; a third permits a response to every challenge. Polynomially many bits may be chosen at each stage. The question is whether every additional fixed stage enables some decision problem that cannot be expressed with fewer stages and a polynomial-time final check.

The hierarchy is monotone because unused quantifier blocks can be inserted. Its collapse property is much stronger: if two neighboring levels coincide, all later alternations can be eliminated down to that level. Consequently the target is a single binary statement, not a request to classify an unspecified collection of logical formulas.

Strictness includes P≠NP at its first step, but P≠NP alone would leave the possibility of a later collapse. The conjecture also implies that PH is a proper subclass of PSPACE: if TQBF belonged to PH, it would belong to one fixed level, and PSPACE-completeness would force the whole hierarchy into that level. Allowing arbitrarily many quantifier alternations in the input is therefore a separate issue from allowing any fixed number.

The Karp–Lipton implication connects this conjecture to circuit complexity. Polynomial-size circuits for NP would collapse PH, so an infinite hierarchy would imply an NP language without polynomial-size circuits. Conditional collapse arguments are useful precisely because they can turn an assumption about nonuniform circuits into a conclusion about uniform classes; the conditional conclusion is not an established collapse.

Rossman, Servedio, and Tan prove that PH is infinite relative to a random oracle with probability one, through an average-case circuit-depth hierarchy theorem. Random membership bits supplied by an oracle are an extra computational resource. The result shows that strictness is compatible with, and typical in, that oracle model; it leaves the unrelativized hierarchy open.

6533.title: NL versus UL
6533.formal: Is NL=UL? Equivalently, is there a single nondeterministic Turing machine that decides directed s–t reachability using O(log N) work space and polynomial time, has exactly one accepting computation on every reachable instance, and has no accepting computation on every unreachable instance, where N is the explicit input length?
6533.definitions: An input consists of a finite directed graph with labelled vertices and explicitly listed edges, together with vertices s,t. Reachability asks whether a directed path from s to t exists; the length-zero path is allowed when s=t. A machine has a read-only two-way input tape, O(log(N+2)) read/write work-tape cells over a fixed finite alphabet, and a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation. Every computation branch must halt within a polynomial in N. NL permits any positive number of accepting branches on yes inputs; UL permits exactly one. On no inputs both classes require zero accepting branches. A branch is a sequence of transition choices, not merely its endpoint or output. Rejecting branches need not be unique. Machines are uniform finite programs without advice, randomness, oracle access or additional catalytic storage. The equality asks whether every NL language has some equivalent UL machine; it does not require a computable compiler converting descriptions of arbitrary machines. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logspace reductions, so its UL membership suffices.
6533.answer_criterion: Prove a uniform O(log N)-space unambiguous algorithm for all directed reachability inputs, or prove that some NL language is not in UL. Any positive construction must remain unambiguous on every input without assuming that the supplied graph itself has a unique path. A polynomial-time algorithm using O((log N)^{3/2}) space, nonuniform advice, catalytic memory, or an unproved hardness hypothesis is progress rather than a solution.
6533.why: Determine whether the multiplicity of accepting computations adds power to logarithmic-space computation.

6533.status_note: The checked general unconditional simulation still uses O(log^{3/2} N) space. The 2025–2026 hardness-based results remain conditional, catalytic results use additional resources, and Hoza’s July 2026 lower bound excludes only oblivious isolation. No settlement of uniform NL=UL found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic reachability algorithm can guess the next vertex of a path, checking each edge as it goes. It needs only a current vertex and a step counter, so logarithmic memory suffices. The difficulty is that a graph can offer many successful sequences of guesses. An unambiguous algorithm must retain the ability to recognize a path while allowing only one successful computation.

This restriction is weaker than determinism. The machine may still branch many times and have many rejecting computations. On a reachable graph, only one complete branch may accept. Consequently, NL=UL would explain something about the source of nondeterministic power without establishing L=NL. A proof that NL≠UL would, however, also separate deterministic and nondeterministic logspace, since L⊆UL⊆NL.

One approach is to assign positive integer weights to edges so that every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. Reinhardt and Allender show how such min-isolating weights support an unambiguous reachability algorithm. If the weights are polynomially bounded and can be generated in deterministic logspace from the graph, the resulting memory use remains logarithmic. Randomly choosing suitable weights can give isolation, but does not provide a uniform deterministic construction.

Reinhardt and Allender also prove NL/poly=UL/poly. Here a polynomial-length advice string may depend on the input length and be shared by every input of that length, without any requirement that the string be generated efficiently. This is evidence that isolation is possible in a broad nonuniform sense. Removing the advice is essential to the ordinary NL=UL question.

The strongest checked unconditional general simulation uses more than logarithmic memory. Van Melkebeek and Prakriya give an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation of NL using O((log N)^{3/2}) space. Their work reduces the randomness and weight-description costs of isolation. The remaining square-root-of-logarithm factor is small numerically, but it is an unbounded factor in the resource defining the target class.

The inherited 2025 paper by Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams develops new hardness-versus-randomness tools for isolation. Its main conditional unambiguity theorem concerns the linear-space analogue NSPACE[n]⊆USPACE[O(n)], under uniform circuit lower bounds with specified oracle access. The March 2026 Pyne–Tell survey gives a refined version. These assumptions are unproved, and the linear-space conclusion should not be reported as an unconditional logspace equality.

A February 2026 revision by Arvind, Chakraborty and Datta gives reachability algorithms in a catalytic model with UL oracle access. Catalytic computation permits extra memory initially containing arbitrary data, provided that the data are restored at the end. This is an interesting way to use storage, but it supplies resources absent from a plain UL machine. The headline about derandomizing isolation therefore does not resolve this card.

Hoza proves a new limitation in July 2026. Suppose one weight assignment must work for every layered graph of given width w and length ℓ, without examining which edges are actually present. Such an oblivious min-isolating assignment requires weights of magnitude 2^{Ω(log w·log ℓ)}, so polynomially bounded universal weights cannot solve the general problem by this route. This restriction does not cover assignments that depend on the actual graph or other unambiguous algorithms.

A solution would determine whether many successful paths are ever intrinsically necessary when computation has only logarithmic memory. It would also clarify how much information must be retained to select a unique witness from a large implicitly represented family. 6535.title: Is nonuniform TC⁰ strictly smaller than nonuniform NC¹?
6535.formal: Is TC⁰⊊NC¹ for the nonuniform circuit classes defined below? Equivalently, does there exist a Boolean function family f=(f_n:{0,1}^n→{0,1}) in NC¹ such that for every fixed depth d≥1, exponent k≥1, and constant M≥1, there is an n for which every depth-at-most-d majority circuit computing f_n exactly has size greater than M(n+1)^k?
6535.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes x_1,…,x_n, optional constants 0,1, and one output. Depth is the maximum number of gates on an input-to-output path. Size is the number of gates plus the number of wires; if an input is repeated at a gate, each occurrence counts as a wire. A majority circuit has AND and OR gates of arbitrary positive fan-in, NOT gates of fan-in one, and MAJ gates of arbitrary positive fan-in m, with output 1 exactly when strictly more than m/2 inputs equal 1. TC⁰ consists of all families with such circuits of size M(n+1)^k and depth at most d for every n, for some constants M,k,d depending on the family. NC¹ consists of families with circuits over AND, OR, NOT, with fan-in at most two (one for NOT), size M(n+1)^k, and depth at most b log_2(n+1), for fixed M,k,b. Circuits may share intermediate gates. Both classes are nonuniform: an arbitrary separate circuit may be chosen for each input length, without any requirement to compute its description. The output must be correct on every input; no randomness, approximation, promise, or distributional error is allowed.
6535.answer_criterion: Prove TC⁰⊊NC¹ or TC⁰=NC¹ for the nonuniform families defined here. Strictness requires a single NC¹ family with no polynomial-size constant-depth majority-circuit family; equality requires that every NC¹ family admit such a family.
6535.why: One of the central small-circuit questions: whether a constant number of counting layers can perform every logarithmic-depth Boolean computation. A resolution would clarify the power of threshold circuits, finite-group computation, and the role of sequential dependence in parallel computation.

importance.reason: A flagship unresolved containment between basic circuit classes, with explicit complete problems and connections to arithmetic, algebraic automata theory, and lower-bound amplification.

progress.text: Hesse, Allender, and Barrington place division and iterated multiplication in DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰, demonstrating the arithmetic power already available at constant depth.

Dawar and Evans characterize uniform NC¹ with typed monoids and unary generalized quantifiers. The containment comparison remains open.
Chen, Tal, and Wang prove superquadratic gate lower bounds for depth-two weighted threshold circuits for an E^NP function; the result does not supply an NC¹ separation against every constant depth.

6535.status_note: The source and subsequent-work checks on 11 September 2026 found no equality or separation of these nonuniform classes. The 2026 depth-two result concerns a function in E^NP and polynomial circuit size; the typed-monoid result concerns uniform classes. These conclusions have different quantifiers and models from the target.

context_blocks.text: The two models trade different resources. A majority gate can aggregate arbitrarily many bits in one step, whereas a binary Boolean gate sees only two. NC¹ permits logarithmically many layers of binary computation. A majority of polynomially many bits can itself be computed by a polynomial-size logarithmic-depth Boolean circuit, so a constant number of majority layers gives TC⁰⊆NC¹. The open issue is whether counting in a fixed number of layers can also replace every logarithmic-depth computation.

Arithmetic tasks are an instructive warning against judging depth from familiar sequential algorithms. Hesse, Allender, and Barrington prove that integer division and iterated multiplication have even DLOGTIME-uniform TC⁰ circuits. A binary long-division procedure takes many dependent steps, but that procedure does not establish a lower bound on all circuits for division. These arithmetic problems therefore cannot serve as the missing separation.

There are concrete complete problems on the NC¹ side. Evaluating a Boolean formula, and evaluating a product of elements of the fixed permutation group S_5, capture NC¹ under very simple reductions. S_5 consists of the 120 permutations of five objects, with permutation composition as its operation. Chen and Tell study these complete problems in their lower-bound amplification results.

Chen and Tell prove a conditional amplification theorem connecting certain mildly superlinear wire lower bounds to a separation of the full classes. Its hypothesis imposes a specific quantitative dependence on circuit depth. Thus a lower bound proved only at one fixed depth, or with an insufficient exponent at growing constant depths, is a different statement from their theorem’s hypothesis and from the conjecture here.

Dawar and Evans give an algebraic characterization of uniform NC¹ using typed monoids in FSTTCS 2025, extending earlier work on uniform TC⁰. Typed monoids allow infinite algebraic structures while restricting recognition through finitely many types. This supplies another mathematical language in which to compare the classes. Their theorem is a characterization, not a separation, and its uniform scope must be kept distinct from this card’s formulation.

Chen, Tal, and Wang’s 2026 preprint proves n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds for depth-two linear-threshold circuits computing a function in E^NP. Here E^NP allows deterministic time 2^{O(n)} with an NP oracle. A linear-threshold gate tests a weighted sum, while this card fixes unweighted majority gates. More decisively, the result treats one depth, a polynomial size bound, and a hard function not shown to belong to NC¹. The target here concerns an NC¹ family against every fixed depth and every polynomial size bound.

6536.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
6536.formal: Is there one deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, on every connected simple undirected graph with n vertices, m edges and arbitrary real edge weights, outputs a minimum spanning tree in O(m+n) worst-case time in the comparison RAM model below?
6536.definitions: The graph is explicitly supplied as vertex and edge records, with vertices numbered 1,…,n and edges given distinct identifiers. An edge record contains its two endpoints and a weight key representing an arbitrary real number. A spanning tree is a set T of n−1 edges connecting all vertices without a cycle; it is minimum when Σ_{e∈T}w(e) is smallest among all spanning trees. For n=1 the output is empty. Equal and negative weights are permitted, and any minimum tree is acceptable. Weight keys may be copied and compared, but their bit representations cannot be inspected, and arithmetic on their numerical values is unavailable. Each comparison has unit cost. Nonweight data, addresses and indices use O(log(m+n+2))-bit words on a random-access machine, with unit-cost reads, writes, comparisons, standard word arithmetic, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts; arithmetic is restricted to these words. All ordinary operations count in the running time, not just weight comparisons. The algorithm has a fixed finite description and no input-length-dependent advice or free precomputed tables. Any tables it constructs, as well as writing the output, are charged to its time. The hidden linear-time constant must be independent of graph topology, n,m and the weights. This fixes a conventional uniform sequential comparison model. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6536.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6536.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

6536.status_note: The deterministic linear-time comparison problem remains open in the primary-author material checked through 11 September 2026. Integer-word algorithms, high-girth results and the optimal-decision-tree theorem do not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is among the basic examples where a local greedy rule produces a global optimum, and it appears in network design and clustering. The optimization objective is well understood; the unsettled issue is how much computation is fundamentally needed to identify the right n−1 edges when the input already contains m edge records.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for Kruskal’s algorithm, but sorting is a stronger task than the required output. On a graph that is itself a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of their relative weights. On a triangle, only the identity of a largest-weight edge is needed: discard it. Thus the familiar comparison lower bound for sorting all keys does not automatically become a lower bound for finding an MST. A faster algorithm must exploit the graph’s structure to avoid unnecessary ordering information.

The cut and cycle rules make this possible. A lightest edge across a cut can be selected safely, and a strictly heaviest edge on a cycle can be discarded. Equal weights can be handled consistently by comparing pairs consisting of the weight and the edge identifier. These rules avoid numerical arithmetic on weights, so the problem is meaningful for arbitrary real keys even though the objective is expressed as a sum.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected O(m+n) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm achieves O(mα(m,n)) time, where α is a slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function. Its soft-heap machinery deliberately permits a controlled set of key increases inside an auxiliary data structure while the surrounding algorithm preserves the exact MST answer. The extra factor is tiny for practical input sizes, yet unbounded asymptotically. Removing it asks for an exact structural understanding of the problem’s complexity, not merely an implementation improvement.

Pettie and Ramachandran establish a different kind of optimality: total algorithmic running time can match, within a constant factor, the optimal worst-case number of edge comparisons for MST. Their algorithm is uniform; it constructs the small optimal decision trees it needs within the time analysis. But the asymptotic size of that optimum is itself unknown. Consequently a proof that linear-size comparison decision trees always suffice would settle the algorithmic question through their theorem.

The graph family also matters. Eisenstat and coauthors show that it is enough to solve graphs with at most 3n/2 edges, and separately relate the general problem to graphs with any fixed lower bound on girth, the length of a shortest cycle. Their available high-girth algorithm requires a lower bound that grows with n. That difference between a fixed girth threshold and a slowly growing threshold leaves the general deterministic question open.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

The remaining challenge can therefore be stated without ambiguity: retain exactness, arbitrary real-key weights and all graph topologies, and make every part of the computation linear without random choices. A negative answer would be equally significant, by establishing an intrinsic cost for deterministic comparison-based optimization that expected-time random sampling avoids.

6537.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
6537.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant C such that, for every n≥2, every integer word length w≥⌈log₂(n+1)⌉, and every list x₁,…,xₙ∈{0,…,2ʷ−1}, the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most Cn?
6537.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
6537.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
6537.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

6537.status_note: The checked primary bounds and the CMU Spring 2025 source leave expected linear-time sorting across all word lengths open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no result settling this full target. Recent parallel sorting results for keys in [n] concern a restricted universe and a different performance model.

context_blocks.text: Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles w=O(log n). Divide each key into digits of about log₂n bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size O(n). There are O(1+w/log n) passes, giving O(n(1+w/log n)) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If w=(log n)^{3/2}, however, that same argument takes about √log n passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for w=Ω((log n)² log log n), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’s O(n√log log n), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic O(n log log n) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

6538.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
6538.formal: Is there one randomized sequential algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with n vertices and m edges, outputs an exact maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least 2/3 and has expected running time (n+m+2)^{1+o(1)} in the word-RAM model below?
6538.definitions: A matching M⊆E(G) is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Its size is |M|, and ν(G)=max{|M|:M is a matching in G}. The algorithm must output valid edge identifiers forming a matching on every terminating execution, and |M|=ν(G) with probability at least 2/3 on each input. It must terminate with probability one. Vertices are labelled 1,…,n and the input is an adjacency-list or edge-list representation of size O(n+m); isolated vertices are included in n. Put N=n+m+2. Use a random-access machine with Θ(log N)-bit words, supporting constant-cost reads, writes, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on words, and fresh uniform random words. Intermediate larger integers require multiple words and their processing is charged. Preprocessing and output writing are included. The program is uniform, with no advice or free precomputed tables. The time statement means that this same algorithm satisfies: for every real ε>0 there are constants Cε and Nε such that for every input with N≥Nε, its expected number of operations is at most Cε N^{1+ε}. The expectation is over its own random choices, not a distribution on graph inputs. No edge weights, degree restriction, bipartiteness promise, approximation slack or auxiliary communication model is assumed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6538.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

6538.status_note: No almost-linear exact general-graph algorithm was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Bipartite flow algorithms, approximation schemes and the 2026 catalytic-space result do not meet the stated target. This card explicitly permits bounded-error randomization and expected running time.

context_blocks.text: Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Alternating paths explain how a nonmaximum matching can improve. Such a path alternates edges outside and inside the matching and starts and ends at unmatched vertices. Flipping its edge membership increases the matching size by one. In general graphs, odd cycles complicate the search for shortest augmenting paths; contracted structures called blossoms keep track of these possibilities. Micali and Vazirani’s classical algorithm achieves O(m√n) time, with later work developing its proof and presentation.

Bipartite graphs have a particularly effective flow formulation. Direct each edge from the left side to the right, join a source to left vertices and right vertices to a sink, and give every edge capacity one. Integral maximum flow gives a maximum matching. Almost-linear exact flow algorithms therefore solve bipartite matching within the desired time scale. There is no supplied bipartition in the present question, and the same construction does not automatically encode odd-cycle constraints.

A triangle illustrates the polyhedral obstacle without requiring a large example. If a fractional variable of one half is placed on each edge, every vertex has total incident value one, but the total value is 3/2 while an integral matching has size at most one. For any odd vertex set S, an integral matching uses at most (|S|−1)/2 edges entirely inside S. Handling these additional odd-set restrictions efficiently is part of what distinguishes general matching from its bipartite counterpart.

Algebraic algorithms offer another route. Mucha and Sankowski use Gaussian elimination to construct maximum matchings in randomized time governed by matrix multiplication, conventionally written O(n^ω) for an available exponent ω>2. This is a major improvement over combinatorial bounds on dense graphs. It still does not yield input-size almost-linear time on all sparse graphs, where a dense n-by-n matrix representation can itself exceed the input size by a large factor.

Approximation also behaves differently. Duan, Pettie and Su obtain a (1−δ)-approximation for maximum weight matching in O(mδ⁻¹ log δ⁻¹) time, hence linear time for fixed δ; unit weights cover cardinality. To force exact cardinality purely by rounding this guarantee, one would need δ small enough that the possible loss is below one edge. When the optimum is Θ(n), that requires δ=O(1/n), so substituting it into the approximation running time loses the desired almost-linear bound.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

6540.title: An explicit static problem requiring superlogarithmically many cell probes
6540.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥2 and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions F_n on an n-word database and a k⌈log₂ n⌉-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity t*F(n), with word size ⌈4log₂ n⌉ bits and n⌈log₂ n⌉² memory cells, satisfies t*F(n)/log₂ n→∞ as n→∞?
6540.definitions: For each integer n≥2 put w=⌈4log₂ n⌉ and s=n⌈log₂ n⌉². A database is D∈({0,1}^w)^n, a query is q∈{0,1}^{k⌈log₂ n⌉}, and F_n(D,q)∈{0,1}. Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes F_n(D,q), given (1^n,D,q), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map E_n into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output F_n(D,q) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through E_n(D). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define t*F(n) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
6540.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real B>0 there is N such that t*F(n)>B log₂ n for every n≥N. Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite B>0 such that t*F(n)≤B log₂ n for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an O(log n) bound for all sufficiently large n.
6540.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

importance.reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.

6540.status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least n² possible queries, while the stored representation has only O(n log³ n) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is O(log n), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to Θ(log n)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is Ω(min{log(m/s), n/log s}) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most O(log n). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Static and dynamic memory have different sources of hardness. Larsen, Weinstein and Yu crossed the logarithmic barrier for dynamic Boolean problems, where updates limit how information can be reorganized. Ko’s March 2026 preprint claims a further Ω((log n/log log n)²) bound for a dynamic multiphase problem. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

6541.title: Does every VC class admit linear-size sample compression?
6541.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class H⊆{0,1}^X of finite VC dimension d≥1 admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying k+b≤Cd, in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
6541.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept h∈H is a total function X→{0,1}. A finite set A⊆X is shattered if {h|_A:h∈H}={0,1}^A; d is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set S⊆X×{0,1} agreeing with some h∈H. A scheme consists of deterministic maps κ and ρ, which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable S, κ(S)=(T,z), where T⊆S is an unordered labeled subset with |T|≤k and z∈{0,1}^b. The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor ρ(T,z):X→{0,1} agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
6541.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6541.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

importance.reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.

progress.text: The framework of Littlestone and Warmuth led to the conjecture that compression size can be linear in VC dimension; the general conjecture remains explicit in the 2025 survey of reductions.
Moran and Yehudayoff prove a general 2^{O(d)} bound for binary classes. The corrected arXiv v2 is the appropriate preprint; the journal version appeared in JACM in 2016.
Chase and coauthors prove an exponential dimension obstruction to embedding arbitrary VC classes in extremal classes, limiting a major proposed approach without refuting sample compression itself.
Bourneuf and coauthors obtain almost-linear proper compression in treewidth and cliquewidth for graph-ball classes, while retaining the general conjecture as open.

The latest version of arXiv:2603.23561, which had earlier claimed a compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result, is withdrawn. Its authors identify an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. This is not a resolution.

6541.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general linear bound remains open in the primary sources checked. The 2026 graph-ball theorems concern structured classes. The claimed breakthrough at arXiv:2603.23561 is withdrawn and is included only to document its status. This card fixes labeled, possibly improper, unordered-subset compression with all side bits counted.

context_blocks.text: The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size 2^{O(d)}, settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size O(t log(t+1)) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.

6542.title: Polynomial-time learning parity with constant random noise
6542.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate η with 0<η<1/2, does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret s∈{0,1}^n, recovers s with probability at least 2/3 from independent samples (a,⟨a,s⟩⊕e), where a is uniform in {0,1}^n and e is independently Bernoulli(η)?
6542.definitions: The inner product ⟨a,s⟩ is Σ_i a_i s_i modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with Pr[e=1]=η. The learner knows n and the fixed rate η, and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed η the algorithm and its polynomial bound pη may depend on η, but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most pη(n) bit operations and requests at most pη(n) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational η does not demand a running-time bound uniform as η approaches 1/2 with n.
6542.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6542.why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.

6542.status_note: The primary literature checked through 11 September 2026 leaves classical polynomial-time learning at fixed constant noise open. The card asks for all fixed rational rates separately, allowing rate-dependent polynomial bounds. The September 2026 reduction is conditional; sparse, quantum-example and limited-memory models do not replace the specified problem.

context_blocks.text: A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability 1−η. Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the 2^n candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At η=1/4, for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement 3/4, while every incorrect parity has expected agreement 1/2. A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a 2^{O(n/log n)}-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only n^{1+ε} examples for each fixed ε>0. The resulting running time is 2^{O(n/log log n)}. This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either Ω(n²/(1/2−η)) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed η, the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by b⊕⟨a,r⟩, learn the masked secret s⊕r and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.

6543.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
6543.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in n, 2^k and 1/ε, with uniform-distribution error at most ε and success probability at least 2/3?
6543.definitions: For integers 0≤k≤n, a k-junta is a function f:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1} for which there is an unknown set S⊆{1,…,n}, |S|≤k, and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that f(x)=g(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer t≥3, setting ε=1/t. Each requested example consists of an independently uniform x∈{0,1}ⁿ and its exact, noiseless label f(x). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least 2/3 over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that h(x)≠f(x) is at most 1/t. One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most (n+2^k+t)^C steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting ε to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.
6543.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6543.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

importance.reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.

Beretta’s revised RANDOM paper distinguishes junta-distribution learning from noiseless function learning and records the continuing computational gap.
Servedio’s survey explicitly retains the uniform-example junta barrier and contrasts it with efficient learning using membership queries.
A new gradient-based learning result uses labelled samples from a lazy random walk; its temporal dependence is outside the independent-example model.

context_blocks.text: A junta is a model of prediction with many irrelevant features. The target may use only a small hidden subset of a very long input, but its behaviour on those relevant features is unrestricted. The goal is accurate prediction on a new uniform input. Identifying the support exactly is not required: variables that affect too little probability mass may be ignored at the requested accuracy.

The allowance of 2^k is deliberate. An arbitrary function on the relevant coordinates can have a truth table with 2^k entries, so a polynomial dependence on that quantity accommodates the complexity of the target itself. The desired improvement is in locating useful coordinates among n possibilities. For k proportional to log n, the proposed bound would give polynomial-time learning. Brute-force support enumeration has about n^k possibilities and becomes quasipolynomial in that regime.

The sample requirement already fits the target. There are at most (k+1)n^k·2^{2^k} juntas on n variables. A union bound shows that O((2^k+k log(n+1)+log(k+1)+1)/ε) independent examples suffice for every consistent hypothesis in this finite class to have error at most ε, with constant confidence. Such a hypothesis exists because the labels come from a junta. The difficulty is finding it efficiently; enumerating supports and filling their truth tables gives a direct but expensive method.

Mossel, O’Donnell and Servedio obtained the first constant-factor improvement in the exponent of this search. Their algorithm combines structural information about Boolean functions with algebraic computation and learns exactly in approximately n^{0.704k}·poly(n,2^k) time at the matrix-multiplication exponent used in the paper. This is an algorithm for arbitrary juntas from uniform random examples, so it addresses the same access model.

Gregory Valiant subsequently improved the exponent to below 0.6k, with polynomial factors in n and 2^k, through algorithms for finding correlations and learning sparse parities with noise. His argument combines a noise-robust parity learner with the junta structure used in earlier work. The approximately n^{0.6k} benchmark is still stated in Servedio’s November 2025 survey. It is a major improvement over exhaustive search, but the exponent on the ambient dimension still grows with k.

Simple correlation screening is insufficient. For example, f(x)=x₁ XOR x₂ XOR x₃ is independent of each individual input bit under the uniform distribution, although all three are relevant. This does not make noiseless parity computationally hard: one can learn an unknown parity by solving linear equations over the two-element field. It explains why a limitation of low-order correlations or statistical queries cannot automatically be converted into a lower bound for every algorithm using actual examples.

Membership queries change the task substantially. They allow the learner to choose an input and ask for its label, making it possible to isolate relevant variables by carefully comparing nearby points. Learning juntas in polynomial time in n and 2^k is known with this additional access. Servedio’s survey also notes that monotone juntas admit the desired bound from ordinary uniform examples; arbitrary juntas need not expose their variables through such first-order information.

The phrase “learning junta distributions” describes another problem: recovering a probability mass function that depends on a small coordinate set. Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper relates that distribution-learning task to learning sparse parities with noise. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes noiseless Boolean junta learning and reports the existing n^{0.6k} benchmark. An equivalence for distribution learning is not an unconditional lower bound for the noiseless prediction task here.

Cornacchia, Mikulincer and Mossel show in May 2026 that a suitable neural-network training procedure can learn juntas efficiently from a lazy random walk on the hypercube, with essentially linear sample complexity in ambient dimension for each fixed k. Their loss uses differences between consecutive samples. Even if each sample has a uniform marginal distribution, consecutive samples are correlated; an independent-example oracle does not provide those labelled neighbouring points. This result therefore leaves the present question intact.

The problem is a gateway to learning richer representations. A k-junta has both a decision tree and a DNF representation of size at most 2^k. Efficient uniform-example learners for those general classes would consequently learn juntas within the requested resource bound. A positive result here would solve a central obstacle, while a negative result for unrestricted learners would explain a computational limitation of feature selection even under a particularly simple input distribution.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, the source inherited as TCS-0023, concerns the class F_k of functions depending on at most k input bits. The old catalogue title incorrectly described it as growing-size DNF learning. Its challenge is to go beyond constant support size with polynomial-time learning, or justify a hardness assumption. This card retains the precise stronger target poly(n,2^k,1/ε) for every k. A positive answer supplies polynomial time when k=O(log n); a learner for only one slower-growing support regime need not meet the full target. Conditional hardness allowed as an outcome in the source is also weaker than an unconditional negative answer here. The source record is consolidated as a related milestone, not asserted to be an equivalent formulation; The removed TCS-0023 keeps its reserved ID and deletion reason; its bibliography and weaker milestone are preserved here.

6546.title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
6546.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries imply the existence of a classical, efficiently generated family of full-domain one-way permutations with the same security convention?
6546.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_n:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}^{ℓ(n)}, for a polynomially bounded, computable output length ℓ, such that for every randomized polynomial-size circuit family A_n, Pr[f_n(A_n(1ⁿ,f_n(X)))=f_n(X)] is negligible in n for uniform X∈{0,1}ⁿ; outputs outside {0,1}ⁿ fail. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all sufficiently large n. A permutation family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1ⁿ) and deterministic polynomial-time evaluation Eval(1ⁿ,pk,x), with a fixed polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer m(n)≥n. For every pk in the support of Gen(1ⁿ), Eval defines a bijection π_pk:{0,1}^{m(n)}→{0,1}^{m(n)}. For every randomized polynomial-size adversary A_n, Pr[π_pk(A_n(1ⁿ,pk,π_pk(X)))=π_pk(X)] must be negligible, with pk←Gen(1ⁿ), independent uniform X and independent adversary coins. Malformed outputs fail. The public key is available to the attacker; no trapdoor is required or given. All security is classical. “Full-domain” fixes the input set to the whole Boolean cube; the valid public-key set need not be all bit strings of its length. The implication is an ordinary existence implication, without restrictions to black-box constructions and without extra assumptions such as obfuscation or subexponential security.
6546.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, allowing any mathematical construction or proof technique, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. Proving that one-way functions do not exist would make the implication vacuously true. An oracle separation or a theorem excluding a restricted class of reductions is a construction barrier, not a refutation of the unrestricted implication. A permutation family on special sparse domains does not meet the full-domain convention fixed here; an additional trapdoor property would be a stronger positive result.
6546.why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.

importance.reason: A longstanding question about the structure obtainable from minimal cryptographic assumptions, with strong construction barriers and a recent full-domain breakthrough under additional assumptions.
