6546.status_note: No derivation from ordinary one-way functions alone, or refutation of the unrestricted existence implication, was found through 11 September 2026. The 2025 full-domain trapdoor construction requires subexponential iO and OWF assumptions. Existing oracle and black-box barriers do not settle the unrestricted question. This card explicitly fixes the full-domain keyed convention.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a random input. It may identify many different inputs and need not cover its output space. A one-way permutation has exactly one preimage for every output in its domain. The extra requirement is structural: nothing is lost mathematically, yet efficiently recovering the uniquely determined input must remain infeasible.

This card fixes the full-domain, public-key family version because the original phrase “one-way permutation” leaves several conventions unspecified. A public key chooses a permutation of an entire Boolean cube; all input strings of that length are valid. A stronger unkeyed formulation asks for a single length-preserving permutation on all bit strings. A more permissive formulation allows key-dependent sparse domains. Results in those settings must be compared with their domain and sampling requirements visible.

Making a computation reversible is not enough. The map (x,z)↦(x,z XOR f(x)) is a bijection for any efficiently computable length-compatible f, but its inverse is obtained by applying exactly the same map. Likewise, simply attaching x to f(x) makes the output injective while revealing the desired preimage. The construction has to preserve computational difficulty while removing collisions and covering the domain, without publishing the information needed for inversion.

Many other forms of cryptographic structure can be derived from bare one-wayness. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby show that every one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator. That success does not enforce bijectivity. The permutation question tests whether computational hardness can always be reorganized into a particularly rigid, uniquely invertible mathematical object.

Rudich’s 1988 thesis developed the oracle-separation approach and gave a barrier for this implication conditional on a combinatorial conjecture. The thesis abstract states that qualification explicitly. It is misleading to describe the original thesis alone as an unconditional separation of the ordinary existence assumptions. An oracle world changes what algorithms can access, so it diagnoses limitations of proof techniques rather than settling the actual implication.

Matsuda and Matsuura subsequently prove a fully black-box barrier even when the starting function is injective, increases length by only one bit, and satisfies their stronger adaptive one-wayness condition. Thus an apparently tiny departure from a permutation already defeats a broad class of generic constructions. Their result concerns constructions that treat the supplied primitive and adversary through specified interfaces; it does not exclude exploiting the code or other structure of a concrete function.

Asharov and Segev address another subtlety: earlier negative arguments could fail when the construction’s domains depended on the underlying primitives. They exclude black-box constructions from one-way functions even without that domain-invariance requirement. They also give a separate barrier for constructions using oracle-aided indistinguishability obfuscation, under domain-invariance conditions. The two statements have different assumptions and should not be merged into an unrestricted impossibility theorem.

There is significant progress with stronger assumptions. Shmueli and Zhandry’s July 2025 paper constructs full-domain trapdoor one-way permutations assuming subexponentially secure indistinguishability obfuscation and subexponentially secure one-way functions. It uses a new kind of pseudorandom permutation that supports controlled permutation of its outputs. The trapdoor guarantee is stronger than this card requests, but both the extra primitive and the stronger hardness assumptions prevent this from proving the target implication.

The same paper explains why its full-domain result is compatible with the earlier obfuscation barrier. Its input domain is the whole cube, but its public keys are obfuscated programs. The valid-key domain therefore depends on the building blocks. The older formal domain-invariance condition constrains both input and key domains. Keeping these two notions separate prevents an erroneous claim that a published barrier has been contradicted.

A positive answer would show that unique, length-preserving inversion hardness is available whenever basic cryptographic hardness exists. A negative answer would reveal a structural separation inside foundational cryptographic assumptions. Existing barriers make the problem especially informative: a successful construction from ordinary one-way functions would need to escape the established generic approaches, rather than merely improve their efficiency.

6547.title: Does one-wayness suffice for collision-resistant hashing?
6547.formal: In the ordinary classical computational model, does the existence of a polynomial-time computable one-way function secure against all polynomial-size circuit families imply the existence of a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family H_k:{0,1}^{2λ}→{0,1}^λ secure against all polynomial-size circuit families?
6547.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic uniformly polynomial-time computable map f on finite binary strings, with output length bounded by a polynomial in the input length, such that for every family of possibly randomized Boolean circuits A_n of size polynomial in n, Pr[f(A_n(1^n,f(X)))=f(X) and |A_n(1^n,f(X))|=n] is negligible in n, where X is uniform on {0,1}^n. The same invocation of A_n supplies the candidate preimage in both parts of this event. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0 there is N_c such that μ(n)≤n^{-c} for all n≥N_c. A hash family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator Gen(1^λ) producing a polynomial-length public key k, and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator H(1^λ,k,x). For every key in the generator’s support, H_k maps every 2λ-bit input to a λ-bit output. Collision resistance means that for every polynomial-size possibly randomized circuit family B_λ, the probability that B_λ(1^λ,k) outputs distinct x,x′∈{0,1}^{2λ} with H_k(x)=H_k(x′) is negligible in λ, over k←Gen(1^λ) and the attacker’s coins. Both messages may be chosen after the attacker sees k. Circuit descriptions may depend on the security parameter, but not on the freshly sampled key. The implication permits arbitrary use of the description of f and arbitrary proof techniques; no random oracle, additional setup assumption, quantum resource, trapdoor, or stronger quantitative hardness assumption is supplied.
6547.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without additional assumptions, or refute it in the ordinary unrelativized model. A positive result may use non-black-box techniques. An oracle world where one-way functions exist but collision-resistant hashing fails proves only a relativizing barrier. Failure of a particular construction, even for a specific one-way function, is also insufficient to refute the existence implication. Producing only target-collision resistance, noncompressing injective functions, or a construction from stronger product-hardness assumptions does not settle the proposition.
6547.why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.

6547.status_note: No unrestricted implication or refutation was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Existing black-box separations do not settle this ordinary-model existence statement. The definitions explicitly use uniform honest algorithms, nonuniform classical adversaries, public fresh keys and factor-two compression.

context_blocks.text: A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are 2^{2λ} possible inputs and only 2^λ outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi give a positive route under stronger assumptions about simultaneously inverting independent challenges. Their one-way product functions require quantitative batch hardness beyond ordinary one-wayness. They construct collision-resistant hashing from suitable such functions and connect the missing assumption to unusually strong parallel repetition. This identifies a concrete intermediate target without showing that every ordinary one-way function possesses the required batch security.

The separation also connects hashing to total search problems. Given a circuit for a compressing map, a collision is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently. Folwarczný and coauthors study whether one-way functions can establish hardness for total NP search more generally, extending limitations for a class of single-query reductions. These are restrictions on reductions, not an unconditional proof that collision-resistant families cannot follow from one-wayness by any method.

Applications can sometimes avoid the full primitive. Rothblum’s July 2026 work constructs efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computations from one-way functions. Communication depends on the space bound times a polynomial in log T and the security parameter, and the security loss depends polynomially on the computation time T. This weakens assumptions for that interactive application; it does not construct a publicly evaluable compressing hash that withstands arbitrary key-dependent collision attempts.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

Inverting a random function output and deliberately constructing a colliding pair are different challenges.
Resolving their relationship would identify whether collision resistance is an additional cryptographic assumption or a consequence of basic one-wayness.

6548.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
6548.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption imply the existence of IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption in the plain model, with classical security against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries and no additional computational assumption?
6548.definitions: A public-key encryption scheme has uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms Gen(1ⁿ)→(pk,sk) and Enc(pk,m)→c and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm Dec(sk,c)→m or ⊥. It supports bit-string messages of any polynomially bounded length. For every polynomial p, the maximum decryption-error probability over messages |m|≤p(n) is negligible in n, with probability over key generation and honest encryption. In the IND-CPA game an adversary receives pk, chooses equal-length messages m₀,m₁ and state, receives c*=Enc(pk,m_b) for an independent uniform bit b, and guesses b. Its advantage is |Pr[guess=b]−1/2|. In the IND-CCA2 game it also has adaptive access to Dec(sk,·), both before and after choosing the challenge messages and receiving c*. After the challenge, the oracle rejects the exact bit string c*; all other ciphertext queries are allowed. Security requires negligible advantage for every nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, allowing any polynomial number of oracle queries. Negligible means eventually smaller than n^{-a} for every a>0. Each adversary has its own polynomial resource bound, but the scheme is fixed independently of that bound. The plain model has no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, hardware or trusted setup beyond the recipient generating its own key pair. This is an unrestricted existence implication, not a requirement that a compiler treat the original scheme as a black box.
6548.answer_criterion: Prove that an IND-CCA2 scheme with these guarantees exists whenever an IND-CPA scheme exists, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. A conversion assuming additional trapdoor functions, suitable proof systems, special pseudorandom generators or ideal random oracles does not by itself suffice. A theorem excluding a restricted class of black-box conversions is a barrier, not a negative answer to the unrestricted implication. Fixed-query bounded CCA2, pre-challenge-only CCA1 and non-malleability without adaptive decryption access are weaker targets.
6548.why: Determine whether public-key confidentiality alone can always be strengthened to resist adaptive decryption attacks, without importing another cryptographic assumption.

importance.reason: A central question about the minimal assumptions for robust public-key encryption, connecting encryption, proof systems, trapdoor structure and generic security transformations.

The revised threshold-encryption work retains additional-model or stronger-security requirements in its CPA-to-CCA transformations.

Bounded-CCA results and constructions with injective trapdoor functions, hinting PRGs, batch arguments or random oracles leave this target open.

context_blocks.text: Public-key encryption already allows anyone, including the attacker, to create ciphertexts. Ordinary chosen-plaintext security protects the contents of an honestly generated challenge ciphertext. Chosen-ciphertext security additionally protects it while the attacker submits other ciphertexts for decryption and uses the responses to decide what to ask next. The only forbidden query is the challenge itself, because returning its plaintext would make confidentiality impossible by definition.

A simple modification illustrates the gap between definitions. Start with a secure ordinary scheme, append an unused bit to every ciphertext, and make decryption ignore that bit. The modification preserves chosen-plaintext security. A chosen-ciphertext attacker flips the challenge’s unused bit and submits the resulting different string to the oracle, which returns the challenge plaintext. This proves that a particular CPA scheme need not itself be CCA-secure; it does not rule out building another scheme from its existence.

This is why the question concerns a construction or existence implication. A successful transformation may change the ciphertext format, use many public keys, encode messages, and inspect the original algorithms’ descriptions. It must arrange that responses to every other ciphertext remain harmless. A proof faces the corresponding simulation problem: how can it answer decryption queries while relying only on a challenge from the weaker security game?

The source proposal points to Trevisan’s cryptography project list, which explicitly asks whether CCA security can be derived from CPA security by black-box techniques or by any techniques. Its bibliography juxtaposes partial negative results with positive results for non-malleability. That distinction remains important: an advance for one attack model should not silently be reported as a solution for another.

Gertner, Malkin and Myers give a black-box separation for constructions whose new decryption algorithm never calls the original encryption algorithm. This covers a substantial class of natural attempts. It still leaves constructions that re-encrypt during decryption, and does not cover arbitrary use of the source code. The scope of that restriction is central to the theorem, rather than a technical detail that can be omitted.

Choi, Dachman-Soled, Malkin and Wee construct non-malleable encryption from any semantically secure scheme and extend their approach to bounded chosen-ciphertext attacks. In the bounded version, the permitted number q of decryption queries is fixed before constructing the scheme. Full CCA2 instead asks for one scheme that withstands every polynomial-time attacker, whose query polynomial can be larger than any particular bound built into that scheme.

Another productive route adds a primitive that helps enforce ciphertext validity. Hohenberger, Koppula and Waters prove in CRYPTO 2020 that injective trapdoor functions suffice for CCA-secure public-key encryption, without requiring lossiness or correlated-product security. This removes significant earlier restrictions. An arbitrary encryption scheme is not automatically such a trapdoor function: its decryption need only recover the message, not a unique full input including encryption randomness.

Koppula and Waters obtain generic upgrades using a hinting pseudorandom generator, whose security survives a special kind of auxiliary information. Ordinary pseudorandomness does not state that guarantee. Their construction offers another way to organize the decryption proof, but applying it to arbitrary public-key encryption still requires establishing the additional hinting property from the original assumption.

Matsuda’s PKC 2025 work shows that a publicly verifiable noninteractive batch argument for NP can supply the additional ingredient. The May 2025 revision weakens the required proof-length savings: they need not be strong enough for currently known constructions of noninteractive zero knowledge. This is progress in reducing the extra structure needed for the upgrade. The paper still assumes the batch argument; it does not construct it from arbitrary CPA encryption.

A PKC 2026 paper by Brzuska, Klooß and Woo gives CPA-to-CCA transformations for threshold encryption, where several parties jointly decrypt. Its generic transform from arbitrary CPA-secure threshold encryption uses a random oracle. Its other route has additional requirements, including a stronger semi-malicious CPA notion. The July 2026 revision therefore does not establish the plain-model implication in this card.

Resolving the implication would clarify whether protection against active ciphertext manipulation is an additional foundational assumption or a consequence of ordinary public-key confidentiality. It would also explain why existing general approaches repeatedly need structure beyond the weak starting primitive. The target is a foundational security theorem; it does not ask that the resulting construction be practical or preserve the original scheme’s efficiency.

6549.title: Does public-key encryption imply oblivious transfer?
6549.formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
6549.definitions: The security parameter is λ, supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function μ is negligible if for every c>0, μ(λ)<λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Public-key encryption consists of KeyGen(1^λ)=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r), and Dec(sk,c), for m∈{0,1}; decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes Enc(pk,0) from Enc(pk,1) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits (m_0,m_1), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output m_c except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators Sim_S(1^λ,m_0,m_1) and Sim_R(1^λ,c,m_c) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond (c,m_c). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
6549.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
6549.why: Determines whether the ability to send secrets to a designated receiver already suffices for general private computation between mutually distrustful parties. It is a basic boundary in the hierarchy of cryptographic assumptions, with a longstanding black-box barrier and no known unrestricted implication.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.

The journal version of Tanishita and coauthors’ work derives OT from updatable encryption with additional sampling properties. It does not remove all extra assumptions on the starting primitive.

6549.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unrestricted classical implication from arbitrary IND-CPA public-key encryption to OT was identified. Known oracle/black-box separations and positive results for rerandomizable or suitably samplable encryption do not settle this formulation. The card fixes semi-honest standalone security with classical communication and no setup.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.

6550.title: Does ordinary polynomial-hard LWE suffice for circuit obfuscation?
6550.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
6550.definitions: Fix q(n) to be the least prime at least n^4 for every integer n≥2. Let χ_n be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to exp(−πe²/n²). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial m(n), the ensembles (A,A s+e mod q) and (A,u) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in Z_q^(m×n), s is uniform in Z_q^n, the m coordinates of e are independent χ_n samples, and u is independent uniform in Z_q^m. Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than n^(−c) eventually for every constant c>0. No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in λ+|C| that outputs a Boolean circuit O(1^λ,C) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic AND/OR/NOT circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible μ_p such that for every |C|≤p(λ), with probability at least 1−μ_p(λ) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences C_0,λ and C_1,λ with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6550.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6550.why: Asks whether a single basic noisy-linear-equation assumption supports general program obfuscation. Resolving the implication would clarify the strength of LWE and the assumption cost of a broad family of cryptographic constructions that currently use iO as a separate resource.

importance.reason: A central assumption-minimization problem for general obfuscation, with consequences throughout cryptography and a crucial distinction between ordinary LWE and strengthened LWE-based assumptions.

progress.text: Barak and coauthors establish impossibility for general virtual-black-box obfuscation while introducing weaker obfuscation notions, including the indistinguishability target.
Regev develops LWE, lattice-hardness connections and public-key encryption; these results supply the standard noisy-equation foundation, rather than general obfuscation.
Jain, Lin, and Sahai construct general iO from four well-founded assumptions with the quantitative security specified in their theorem. The JACM publication does not reduce the list to LWE.
Their follow-up removes LWE, obtaining iO from LPN over prime fields, DLIN, and local PRGs under subexponential security. It explicitly leaves minimal assumption sets open.

Brakerski and coauthors obtain iO from circular-security properties of LWE-based encryption, including randomness-leakage resilience. They also repair a limitation in a previous exponentially-efficient-obfuscation transformation.

6550.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.

context_blocks.text: Indistinguishability obfuscation compares two implementations of exactly the same function. After obfuscation, an efficient observer should not tell which implementation was used. Equality of size prevents a trivial distinction from the amount of code supplied; padding can put implementations under a common size bound. This definition does not say that every secret written into an arbitrary program is hidden. A secret that the function itself reveals through its outputs remains visible.

That distinction is necessary. Barak and coauthors rule out general obfuscation under the stronger virtual-black-box requirement, which would make code reveal no more than oracle access to its function. Their impossibility theorem does not rule out indistinguishability obfuscation. The weaker comparison between equivalent implementations has therefore become a central target, rather than an informal promise to make arbitrary software unreadable.

LWE supplies a particularly concrete potential foundation. Its samples are linear equations modulo a public integer, perturbed by small independent errors. Exact equations would reveal the secret by linear algebra; the errors obstruct that approach. Regev introduced reductions connecting LWE to worst-case lattice problems and used it to build public-key encryption. This card fixes a particular ordinary decisional-LWE ensemble so that the noise distribution, modulus, number of samples, and adversarial resources cannot vary silently.

Jain, Lin, and Sahai established general-circuit iO from a combination of four assumptions: LWE, LPN over large fields, a local Boolean pseudorandom generator, and a bilinear-group assumption. Their theorem uses stronger quantitative security than mere polynomial hardness. Its Journal of the ACM version appeared in February 2026, following the STOC 2021 work. That publication is an important foundation for iO, but is not a 2026 construction from plain LWE alone.

A follow-up by the same authors removes LWE from that combination, leaving the other three assumptions. Eliminating LWE from a sufficient set is logically different from eliminating all the other assumptions while retaining LWE. The follow-up explicitly poses the possibility that LWE alone might suffice, without claiming a resolution.

Brakerski, Döttling, Garg, and Malavolta give another route using LWE-based encryption with circular randomness-leakage resilience. The construction uses that stronger assumption. Its security experiment exposes structured information related to keys and encryption randomness, whereas ordinary LWE supplies only the noisy linear samples defined above. Calling the construction LWE-based therefore does not remove the extra security hypothesis.

A solution would unify the assumptions behind many uses of obfuscation with an established lattice-learning problem. The specific target here is deliberately demanding: ordinary polynomial security and a polynomial modulus-to-noise ratio. Even a construction from plain LWE with stronger quantitative hardness would be substantial progress, but the security loss would still need attention before it established this exact implication. The question concerns mathematical feasibility; it does not impose practical code size or execution speed.

6551.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
6551.formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
6551.definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer c≥3 and polynomial sample count M(d), let q(d) be the least prime at least d^c, let s be uniform in Z_q^d, let A be uniform in Z_q^{M(d)×d}, and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to exp(−πz²/(4d)), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and (A,u), for independent uniform u∈Z_q^{M(d)}, are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian D_{Z,2√d}; only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms Gen(1^λ)→(pk,evk,sk), Enc(pk,b), Eval(evk,C,c₁,…,c_t), and Dec(sk,c), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by P(λ), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in λ and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most p(λ) and all input bits b₁,…,b_t, decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals C(b₁,…,b_t), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than λ^{-a} eventually for every a>0. No subsequent secret-key assistance, ideal oracle, external trusted setup, superpolynomial adversary-hardness assumption, functional-encryption assumption or obfuscation assumption is allowed. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.
6551.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6551.why: Determine whether ordinary LWE alone supports compact encrypted computation at arbitrary polynomial depth with one fixed key set.

6551.status_note: No classical unleveled compact FHE construction from the specified ordinary LWE assumption alone was found through 11 September 2026. Functional-encryption constructions use additional assumptions. The inspected February and April 2026 no-circularity proposals retain explicit level bounds; the latter also uses quantum evaluation. This card fixes polynomial-modulus LWE, nonuniform classical security and fresh-input FHE correctness.

context_blocks.text: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on encrypted data and return an encrypted answer. Compactness makes this substantive: the client should decrypt a short answer, rather than receive the original ciphertexts together with the whole circuit and perform the computation itself. Here all four algorithms are classical, and the ciphertext for one output bit remains bounded by a fixed polynomial in the security parameter.

The order of choices is the heart of the problem. In a leveled scheme, the user first chooses a maximum depth L and generates keys suitable for that level. This can support every circuit up to L without revealing the data. The present question asks for one key-generation algorithm that receives only the security parameter and supports every polynomial-depth circuit later supplied to the evaluator. Choosing L=λ¹⁰ during setup still leaves deeper polynomial computations outside the guarantee.

Lattice ciphertexts generally include small errors that hide the plaintext. Homomorphic operations transform the desired message and these errors together. Once the error exceeds the decryption tolerance, the output may no longer decode correctly. Gentry’s bootstrapping idea refreshes a ciphertext by homomorphically evaluating a decryption circuit, with the secret key itself provided in encrypted form. Micciancio’s teaching slides explain both this noise issue and the associated circular-security question.

A chain of independent keys avoids the immediate circularity. Encrypt the secret key at level i under the public key at level i+1, then use the next level to refresh the current ciphertext. The usual hybrid proof can replace those encryptions in reverse order because the chain has an endpoint. But the public material grows with the number of refreshes planned in advance. Closing the chain into a cycle reuses a bounded collection of keys and changes the security argument.

Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan’s construction makes the distinction explicit in its journal abstract: ordinary LWE gives leveled FHE, while removing the depth restriction uses an additional weak circular-security assumption. Later bootstrapping work supports polynomial-modulus parameters and polynomial lattice approximation factors. Improvements in error growth and efficiency do not themselves justify exposing the secret-key encryptions needed to reuse the keys.

The requested proof need not avoid bootstrapping, or even avoid encrypted keys. It must justify the actual public evaluation information using ordinary LWE alone. Conversely, it is not enough to prove that some artificially designed CPA-secure encryption scheme becomes insecure when encrypting its own key. Such a counterexample refutes an automatic upgrade for every scheme; it does not rule out designing a particular FHE scheme with a valid ordinary-LWE proof.

Bitansky and Solomon obtain FHE without circular-security assumptions using functional encryption, under polynomial hardness assumptions. This is a significant positive result for a broader assumption set. In their ITCS 2023 construction, the available functional-encryption instantiation uses assumptions including LPN, bilinear SXDH and shallow pseudorandom generators, in addition to the LWE-based homomorphic component. The basic theorem protects against uniform adversaries; their nonuniform extension requires an additional worst-case complexity assumption. Neither version establishes LWE alone under the convention here.

Recent claims also require checking the formal setup. Wang, Huang and Tang’s February 2026 dynamic multi-key scheme advertises avoiding a common reference string and circular security. Definition 2.2 nevertheless gives Setup the depth parameter L, and the construction chooses its dimension and modulus using L. Its stated compactness also permits dependence on L. This is a leveled guarantee, even though the number of participating keys can change dynamically.

Liu and coauthors’ April 2026 quantum homomorphic proposal also advertises classical LWE and no circular-security assumption. Its Section 3.4 uses L+1 independent key layers; a later discussion explicitly preallocates L evaluation gadgets. It therefore retains a level bound, and its evaluator performs quantum operations. These scope differences already prevent it from settling the classical, depth-independent target; this review does not validate its separate efficiency or quantum-security claims.

There is a further definitional distinction between evaluating one arbitrary circuit on fresh ciphertexts and repeatedly evaluating new circuits on the resulting ciphertexts. Micciancio’s slides show that correctness for the first task does not automatically imply correctness for the second. This card asks for the usual fresh-input FHE guarantee. Establishing full composability would be an additional accomplishment, rather than an implicit condition that makes the target harder.

A solution would remove a central gap between the clean assumption used to prove the security of leveled lattice encryption and the extra assumption used to reuse a fixed key set indefinitely over polynomial computations. It would clarify the foundation of FHE independently of practical parameter optimization, and could improve the assumptions of constructions that use unrestricted encrypted computation as a component.

6552.title: Noninteractive zero knowledge from one-way functions
6552.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions imply reusable, adaptively secure noninteractive zero-knowledge arguments for circuit satisfiability in the honestly generated common-reference-string model, with computational soundness and computational zero knowledge against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries?
6552.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family f_n on uniform n-bit inputs with polynomial-length outputs, such that every nonuniform randomized polynomial-size adversary given 1ⁿ and f_n(X) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability. Circuit satisfiability has statements x encoding Boolean circuits and witnesses w assigning their inputs, with R(x,w)=1 exactly when the circuit outputs 1. A proposed argument consists of uniform algorithms Setup(1^λ,1^B)→crs, Prove(crs,x,w)→π, and Verify(crs,x,π)→{0,1}; their time and output length are polynomial in λ+B, where B bounds statement and witness lengths. Setup is independent of the later statements; its private coins are not published. For every polynomial B=B(λ), completeness error is negligible uniformly over valid (x,w) of length at most B. Adaptive computational soundness means that every nonuniform polynomial-time adversary given crs has negligible probability of outputting an unsatisfiable x and an accepted π. Reusable computational zero knowledge means there exist uniform polynomial-time SimSetup and SimProve such that no nonuniform polynomial-time distinguisher separates these experiments: (i) it receives honest crs and can adaptively request Prove(crs,x,w) for polynomially many valid pairs; (ii) it receives simulated crs from SimSetup, and each valid query is answered by SimProve using the simulation trapdoor and x, without receiving w. Both experiments reject invalid queries, and the distinguisher retains arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information. All negligible bounds are in λ: for each a>0 the error is eventually below λ^{-a}. Only crs is public in the real system, and one proof message is sent for each statement. No random oracle, extra cryptographic assumption, online verifier challenge, proof of knowledge or succinctness requirement is included. Circuit satisfiability covers every NP language through witness-preserving polynomial reductions.
6552.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, or refute it in the ordinary computational model. The result may use the code of the one-way function and need not be black-box. A construction adding LWE, an appropriate batch argument, trapdoor hashing, or strong extra complexity assumptions does not suffice unless those ingredients are themselves derived from the same ordinary OWF premise. An interactive proof, a witness-indistinguishable argument, or a single-theorem result without a justified reusable upgrade is not the specified conclusion.
6552.why: Determine whether the minimal assumption supporting basic cryptography is sufficient for reusable, publicly verifiable proofs that reveal no witness and require no online interaction.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between interactive and noninteractive zero knowledge, with implications for the assumptions behind privacy-preserving proof systems and cryptographic transformations.

6552.status_note: No construction of reusable adaptive NIZK arguments from ordinary OWFs alone, or refutation of that unrestricted implication, was found through 11 September 2026. The cited BARG, trapdoor-hash and derandomization constructions retain extra assumptions; recent OWF-only succinct proofs are interactive, and high-error characterizations run in the reverse direction.

context_blocks.text: An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. The title “Batch Arguments to NIZKs from One-Way Functions” must be read with its starting resource intact: the batch argument is an additional primitive, rather than something their theorem constructs from a bare one-way function.

Branco and coauthors develop a vector-trapdoor-hash approach, with an updated version in March 2026. Their constructions use either LWE or a combination of DDH and LPN assumptions. The initial black-box constructions provide single-theorem zero knowledge, and their multi-theorem upgrade uses cryptography in a non-black-box way. This distinction is compatible with the target here, which allows any construction technique but requires the OWF-only assumption and reusable security.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell pursue a different route through derandomization and strong computational hardness. Their construction combines a subexponentially secure one-way function with an additional complexity assumption and obtains computational soundness against uniform adversaries. It is progress toward avoiding highly structured cryptographic primitives, but the extra hardness and the adversary convention both differ from this card.

Recent results in the reverse direction should not be read as a construction. Chakraborty, Hulett, Khurana and Tomer show in February 2026 that nontrivial NIZK arguments imply one-way functions under the hypothesis that NP is not contained in ioP/poly, even in a broad high-error regime. Their amplification consequences improve existing weak NIZK systems. Neither direction starts with an ordinary OWF alone and produces the desired NIZK system.

Another 2026 result gives succinct zero-knowledge proofs using one-way functions as black boxes. Florentz–Konopnicki and Rothblum’s protocol is interactive: its theorem explicitly bounds a number of public-coin rounds that depends on the relation’s parameters. Its noninteractive commitment component does not make the whole protocol noninteractive. A resolution of this card would isolate exactly how much cryptographic structure is needed to remove that interaction after a single reusable setup.

6554.title: Distributed Lovász Local Lemma in O(log log n) rounds
6554.formal: Does there exist an integer c≥2 such that, for every fixed integer d≥2, a uniform randomized LOCAL algorithm A_d and a constant K_d solve every n-event variable Lovász Local Lemma instance of dependency degree at most d and maximum bad-event probability p with p·d^c<1/2, within K_d(1+log₂log₂(n+2)) rounds, with probability at least 1−n^(−3) of avoiding all bad events simultaneously?
6554.why: The question asks whether sparse dependencies can always be resolved within a log-logarithmic communication radius under fixed polynomial slack. This would determine the complexity of a widely used distributed primitive and clarify a central scale in the LOCAL complexity hierarchy.

6554.definitions: There are n≥2 bad events, each a predicate on a specified finite subset of finitely many mutually independent variables. Each variable has a finite nonempty alphabet and a rational probability distribution; event predicates and distributions are given by finite tables. Variables occurring in no event can be omitted. Two distinct event nodes are adjacent exactly when their variable sets intersect; this graph is the communication network. Its maximum degree is at most d. The number p is the largest probability of an event under the product of the specified distributions. Each node initially knows n,d, its own event table, its variables and their distributions, its neighbours and their identifiers. Node identifiers are distinct integers in [n²]; shared variables have consistent names. LOCAL means synchronous rounds with arbitrarily long finite messages in each direction on each edge, and unrestricted terminating local computation. Nodes have private independent fair random bits. A single finite program is used at all nodes, independently of n and the instance. Each node outputs one value for each of its variables. Success requires agreement on shared variables and falsity of every event. The round bound holds on every random tape; the success probability is over all node coins for each fixed instance and identifier assignment. Constants and the algorithm may depend on d; the slack exponent c is chosen before d. No preprocessing using the full instance is supplied. The factor 1/2 removes the low-degree ambiguity recorded in the source conjecture.
6554.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed integer c≥2 admits, for every fixed d≥2, algorithms A_d and constants K_d with the stated round and global-success bounds on all eligible instances. Alternatively, prove that for every candidate c there is a fixed d for which no such algorithm and constant exist. An obstruction at one slack exponent alone does not refute the existential choice of c. Bounds averaged over nodes, expected round bounds, or a higher fixed power of log log n do not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.text: The Lovász Local Lemma concerns many individually unlikely failures that share only limited dependencies. In a variable instance, a bad event is a condition on some independent random variables. The goal is to choose the variables so that none of these conditions holds. The distributed question asks how quickly processors located at the events can agree on such choices when communication follows the dependency graph.

For an illustrative instance, independently color the vertices of a hypergraph red or blue, and let each hyperedge define the bad event that all its vertices receive the same color. A hyperedge containing k vertices is monochromatic with probability 2^{1−k}. Events are adjacent when their hyperedges share a vertex. A successful assignment is a two-coloring with no monochromatic hyperedge. This example explains the objects; the card allows arbitrary finite event tables, rather than only coloring events.

Small individual probabilities do not mean that one simultaneous random assignment succeeds with high probability globally. Even n mutually independent events of probability p are all avoided with probability (1−p)^n, which can be tiny. The LLL guarantees existence in a suitable probability-and-dependency regime. A distributed algorithm must obtain a globally valid assignment with the much stronger success guarantee stated on the card.

The slack condition p·d^c<1/2 is deliberately stronger than the usual existence threshold. One universal constant c must work before the degree bound d is chosen; choosing an exponent that grows with n would answer a different question. Each d is fixed while n grows, so constants in the round bound may depend on d. This bounded-degree convention is essential to interpreting the conjecture.

In LOCAL, messages have no bandwidth limit, but information still crosses only one dependency edge per round. After r rounds a node can depend only on information and random choices within its r-hop neighborhood. Shared variables also require agreement: two neighboring event processors cannot assign different colors to the same underlying variable and count that as a solution.

Fischer and Ghaffari gave a sublogarithmic algorithm under polynomially strengthened criteria. Subsequent derandomization tools and Davies’s algorithm yield bounds of the form O(d/log d + (log log n)^{O(1)}) in the relevant regime. For fixed d this is polynomial in log log n, but it does not give a bound linear in log log n. The conjecture targets that remaining distinction.

The 2025 locality paper gives an O(log log_{1/p} n) node-averaged guarantee while retaining a larger worst-case round bound. The average measures how long a typical node remains active; it can be small while a few nodes keep working. This card requires every node to finish within the same O(log log n) budget. Results for local-computation queries, MPC or the congested clique also have different access and communication rules.

The 2026 resilient-LLL paper broadens the coloring applications with polynomial-log-log round algorithms. It also distinguishes those applications from unrestricted dependency degree. Its broader general-LLL question must not erase the bounded-degree upper bounds already known here. Lower bounds from sinkless orientation explain why log log n is a central scale, with the precise LLL criterion relevant when transferring such a bound.

The question has broad consequences because distributed conflict-resolution tasks can be expressed as avoiding overlapping bad events. Chang and Pettie’s connection to locally checkable labeling problems gives the LLL a structural role in distributed complexity, beyond its use in any one coloring algorithm.

6555.title: Optimal exact single-source shortest paths in CONGEST
6555.formal: For every fixed integer b≥1, do there exist constants K,c>0 and a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm which, on every connected simple undirected graph with n≥2 vertices, integer edge weights in [0,n^b] and a designated source s, makes every vertex output its exact weighted distance from s in at most K(√n+D)(log₂(n+2))^c rounds on every execution, with simultaneous correctness probability at least 1−n^(−3)? 6555.why: This asks whether exact weighted shortest distances can be computed as quickly as the general communication lower bound permits, up to logarithmic factors. It separates the cost of exact optimization from the costs of network diameter and limited link bandwidth.

6555.definitions: A path length is the sum of its edge weights; the distance is the minimum path length, and the source distance is zero. D is the maximum over vertex pairs of the minimum number of edges on a path between them. The graph itself is the network. In each synchronous round, each endpoint of each edge can send at most B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits to the other endpoint, for a constant B depending only on b. Nodes initially know n,b, the source identifier, their own identifiers, and the identifiers and weights of incident neighbours. Identifiers are distinct integers in [n²]. Local computation and memory are unrestricted, but each local computation between rounds terminates. Nodes use independent private fair random bits. One finite program, allowed to depend on b, runs at all nodes; no global graph description, advice, routing tables or preprocessing is supplied. The graph, weights, source and identifiers are fixed before randomness is drawn. Output at v is an ordinary binary integer for dist(s,v), stored locally. The guarantee concerns all vertices together, over all coins. All communication, including finding termination and any preprocessing, counts in the round bound. K,c,B are independent of n,D and the instance; no value of D is initially supplied.
6555.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed weight exponent b there is a single uniform algorithm meeting the stated O((√n+D)polylog n) round bound on every execution and the simultaneous 1−n^(−3) correctness probability on every eligible network. Alternatively, prove that this is impossible for at least one fixed b, for every choice of algorithm and fixed constants K,c,B. An approximation guarantee, an n^{o(1)} overhead not bounded by a fixed power of log n, or a result for only one diameter regime is not the stated affirmative answer.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex must learn its distance from one designated source, measured by the sum of edge weights. The processors sit at the vertices and can communicate only along the graph’s edges. The question is about the number of synchronous communication rounds, rather than the time a single processor would spend on an adjacency-list representation.

There are two different notions of distance. If s is joined directly to v by an edge of weight 10, but a two-edge route has weights 2 and 2, the weighted distance is 4 even though v is one communication hop from s. The parameter D ignores weights and measures the largest hop distance between vertices. A minimum-weight path can contain many more edges than a minimum-hop path.

Each edge transports only O(log n) bits per direction in one round, while different edges can communicate simultaneously. A distance fits in O(log n) bits because weights are polynomially bounded, but many different pieces of information may need the same link. The √n term in the benchmark reflects a bandwidth obstacle in worst-case networks; the D term reflects how far information has to travel.

The requested output is distributed: vertex v stores dist(s,v). Collecting all distances at s, printing full paths, or making every vertex learn the whole distance table would impose additional communication requirements. Conversely, a local estimate that is merely close to the shortest distance is not the exact output required here.

Chechik and Mukhtar give an exact randomized bound Õ(√n D^{1/4}+D), where the tilde hides factors polynomial in log n. Their theorem also handles directed weighted graph inputs over an undirected communication network, so it covers the undirected case retained on this card. The extra D^{1/4} factor is not absorbed by the logarithmic allowance when D grows polynomially with n.

Cao and Fineman’s 2023 theorem supplies another bound, Õ(n^{2/5+o(1)}D^{2/5}+√n+D), for polynomially bounded weights. This improves the comparison in part of the diameter range. For D≈n^{1/2}, its displayed terms give n^{3/5+o(1)}, while the target is Õ(n^{1/2}). This comparison of proven bounds displays a remaining gap; it does not prove that any particular graph requires n^{3/5} rounds.

The notation n^{o(1)} allows factors larger than every fixed power of log n. Such a factor cannot automatically be treated as the polylogarithmic overhead specified in the statement. Similarly, a theorem for one fixed diameter regime does not supply the single bound required for all connected networks.

Near-optimal algorithms for (1+ε)-approximate undirected distances provide an important contrast. For fixed ε they may return a nonzero relative error. Since integer distances can be as large as n^{b+1}, forcing exactness by taking ε extremely small can increase the algorithm’s complexity through its ε dependence. A fixed-accuracy approximation theorem therefore does not imply this exact result.

The inherited 2026 reference studies programmable matter with reconfigurable circuits that transmit signals in a different way. Its related-work section is useful background for CONGEST, but its own polylogarithmic algorithm is not a solution in the present model. The card now cites the original CONGEST results as well, including the 2023 bound missing from that summary.

Resolving the question would determine whether exact numerical optimization has an additional distributed cost beyond the familiar bandwidth-and-diameter benchmark. Shortest distances are also a primitive in other distributed constructions, so a faster exact computation would affect more than routing from one source.

6556.title: Directed reachability with nearly linear memory and polylogarithmic passes
6556.formal: Do there exist constants a,b,C and a uniform randomized streaming algorithm that decides directed s–t reachability on every n-vertex graph using at most Cn(log(n+2))^a bits of memory and C(log(n+2))^b passes, with success probability at least 2/3 for every adversarially ordered edge stream?
6556.definitions: The input is a finite simple directed graph on the labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, with distinct designated vertices s,t. The algorithm knows n,s,t before reading the edges. Each directed edge occurs once in an insertion-only stream, in an arbitrary order fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Each pass scans this same stream in the same forward order. The input is read-only: there are no adjacency queries, random-access reads, sorting operations on external storage, or writable auxiliary streams. All mutable working storage counts toward the bit bound; fresh independent random bits may be read from a one-way random source. The memory and pass bounds hold on every execution. Computation between successive input items is unrestricted but must terminate; no running-time bound beyond termination is imposed. A yes answer means that there is a directed path from s to t in the input graph. The constants and algorithm are independent of n, the graph, and the edge order.
6556.answer_criterion: Prove that one uniform randomized decision algorithm has simultaneous O(n logᵃ(n+2))-bit space and O(logᵇ(n+2))-pass bounds for fixed constants a,b on every execution, and success probability at least 2/3 on every fixed graph and edge order. Alternatively, prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. Ruling out a fixed pass count, requiring the output of a path, or restricting computation between stream items does not establish the stated negation.
6556.why: Determine whether global directed reachability can be recovered from repeated sequential scans with only nearly linear memory, a central unresolved graph-streaming tradeoff.

importance.reason: A basic directed-graph primitive with a polynomial-versus-polylogarithmic pass gap, connections to communication lower bounds and consequences for other streaming tasks.

6556.status_note: The primary survey, cited multipass bounds and the revision of 9 September 2026 were checked on 11 September 2026. The recent paper explicitly retains the n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass upper benchmark. No polylogarithmic-pass algorithm or lower bound ruling out every polylogarithmic pass bound in the stated memory model was found. This check covers decision with adversarial fixed order, rather than a changed stream or a path-output requirement.

context_blocks.text: Directed reachability asks an elementary question: can one vertex eventually lead to another by following arrows? With the whole graph in memory, a search answers it in linear time. In a graph stream, the difficulty is that the next useful edge may already have gone past before the algorithm learns that its tail is reachable. Repeated scans provide another opportunity to use the edge, but every scan revisits the entire input.

Nearly linear memory means linear in the number of vertices, up to powers of a logarithm. It can store labels, several values per vertex and a sparse auxiliary graph, but a dense input may have quadratically many edges. The card allows every fixed polylogarithmic memory overhead: it does not ask for an especially restrictive exact n-bit implementation. Conversely, allowing storage proportional to all the edges would erase the intended obstacle.

A simple baseline maintains the set of vertices already reached from s. Whenever an edge leaves this set, its head is marked reachable. After at most n−1 scans every reachable vertex has been found, using a bit per vertex and counters. A path whose edges appear in reverse path order makes this particular algorithm advance slowly. That example is not a lower bound for all algorithms: a path has only linearly many edges and fits entirely in the permitted memory.

The undirected analogue has a much stronger one-pass solution: maintain connected components with union–find. Direction removes the equivalence-relation structure that makes this summary sufficient. Strongly connected components can still be contracted in a digraph, but their directed reachability relation is another graph rather than just a partition. A small summary must somehow preserve the information needed for the specified source and target.

Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford give a randomized parallel reachability algorithm using nearly linear work and n^{1/2+o(1)} depth. Their shortcut construction can also be implemented in the streaming model. Assadi and coauthors explicitly state the resulting n^{1/2+o(1)}-pass semi-streaming path-finding algorithm as Proposition 4. This supplies the relevant upper bound through a concrete simulation, rather than through an assumption that every shallow parallel computation automatically yields a streaming algorithm.

A reachability-preserving shortcut is an extra arc (u,v) added only when the original graph already contains a directed path from u to v. Such arcs can reduce the number of edges in a path without changing which vertices are reachable. The cited streaming upper bound constructs and uses a sparse collection within its memory budget; its pass guarantee is part of that implementation, not a consequence of the existence of shortcuts alone.

On the lower-bound side, Guruswami and Onak extend earlier path-output barriers to the decision problem itself. Their multipass space bound implies that semi-streaming reachability requires Ω(log n/log log n) passes. The exact theorem includes polynomial factors in the pass count and logarithmic factors in n; these should not be dropped when comparing parameters. The conclusion rules out constant passes but leaves the polylogarithmic target available.

Chen, Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, Song and Yu prove that o(√log n) passes require n^{2−o(1)} space. This is a striking strengthening of how much memory is necessary when the pass budget is very small. It is not a larger asymptotic lower bound on the number of passes with nearly linear memory than the Ω(log n/log log n) statement above. The two results describe different parts of the tradeoff.

Azarmehr and coauthors’ September 9, 2026 revision still identifies n^{1/2+o(1)} as the fastest known semi-streaming reachability pass bound. Their Theorem 9 links an improved streaming approximation for distance to monotonicity to an improved reachability algorithm. This is evidence that the question controls progress beyond reachability itself, and gives a recent explicit check of the benchmark used on this card.

A positive answer would show that repeated sequential access with a compact memory can recover global directed information surprisingly quickly. A negative answer would establish a fundamental barrier to that access pattern, even without restricting local computation time. Either result would help explain the difference between graph problems admitting compact summaries and those that require many rounds of discovering dependencies.

6557.title: Explicit superconstant lower bounds in the congested clique
6557.formal: Does there exist a Boolean predicate P of finite simple undirected graphs on [n], decidable from the full adjacency matrix by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, such that every uniform deterministic unicast congested-clique algorithm computing P has worst-case round complexity R_A(n)=ω(1)? 6557.why: A central unbroken barrier in unconditional lower bounds for a powerful distributed model.

6557.definitions: For each n≥2, the communication network is the complete graph on processors 1,…,n. The input is a separate simple undirected graph G on the same labeled vertex set. Initially processor v knows n, its identifier v and the n−1 adjacency bits for edges incident to v in G. No other input or certificate is supplied. In a synchronous round every processor performs a finite, otherwise unrestricted amount of local deterministic computation and sends a separate message of at most ceil(log₂ n) bits to each other processor; all messages arrive before the next round. Local memory is unrestricted. All processors execute one fixed finite algorithm with their identifiers and n as inputs; no nonuniform advice, randomness, oracle or free communication is allowed. The cost counts communication rounds only, not local computation. Node 1 must halt with P(G) on every input; requiring all nodes to receive this one bit changes the cost by at most one round. R_A(n) is the maximum number of rounds until node 1 outputs, over all n-vertex input graphs. The statement R_A(n)=ω(1) means that for every integer B≥1 there is N such that R_A(n)>B for every n≥N; it is stronger than a lower bound at only infinitely many sizes. The chosen predicate may depend on vertex labels, as in Korhonen–Suomela’s graph-language model. “Explicit” is fixed by the source proposal’s centralized polynomial-time condition: one deterministic Turing machine computes P on every adjacency matrix within C(n+1)^k steps for constants C,k independent of n. There is no polynomial bound imposed on processors’ local work. A constant multiple of log n message bits can be simulated by a constant factor more rounds and does not change the ω(1) target.
6557.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a single graph predicate with a proved centralized polynomial-time decision procedure and proves the displayed ω(1) lower bound against every correct uniform deterministic protocol in the specified model. A negative resolution proves the logical negation of that existence statement. A two-round lower bound, a lower bound for broadcast messages or restricted local computation, or a hard predicate without the centralized polynomial-time guarantee does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: The network and the input graph differ
context_blocks.text: Even if the input graph is a long path, the processors can communicate directly with every other processor. The path’s large diameter therefore does not force a long wait for information to travel from one endpoint to the other. The obstacle, if any, must arise from the amount and arrangement of the information needed for the decision, while each individual communication link carries only logarithmically many bits.

context_blocks.title: One bit can be much easier than collecting the input
context_blocks.text: For example, deciding whether G has an edge takes two rounds: every processor sends node 1 one bit saying whether it has an incident edge, and node 1 can broadcast the answer. Computing the decision at node 1 itself takes just the first round. Although the whole input contains quadratically many potential edge bits, this predicate does not need those bits collected individually. Input size alone is not a lower bound for an arbitrary one-bit output.

context_blocks.title: Why unicast is essential
context_blocks.text: In the unicast model, a processor may send different pieces of information to different recipients in the same round. Broadcast restricts it to one common message. The latter can admit bottleneck arguments that do not remain valid once a sender uses all its links separately. Drucker, Kuhn and Oshman study both versions and explicitly distinguish their lower bounds. A theorem for the broadcast version cannot be silently transferred here.

context_blocks.title: The explicitness requirement
context_blocks.text: Counting arguments show that some Boolean functions require many rounds. Korhonen and Suomela also establish a uniform time hierarchy by selecting hard functions through exhaustive enumeration. Such a selection supplies computability, but not the polynomial-time centralized algorithm demanded by this card. The desired separation concerns a task that is computationally manageable once its entire graph is available, while still resisting distributed communication with unrestricted local computation.

context_blocks.title: Connections and known limitations
context_blocks.text: The 2014 circuit simulations relate distributed lower bounds to difficult circuit lower bounds, with important bandwidth and depth qualifications. In particular, the introduction distinguishes a superconstant bound with one-bit links from an Ω(log log n) bound with logarithmic links. These are not interchangeable claims for the weaker ω(1) target here. Robinson’s PODC 2023 result rules out one-round MST computation at logarithmic bandwidth under its edge-output convention. It proves a genuine limitation, but two rounds are still a constant, and outputting a spanning tree differs from computing one decision bit.
