6558.title: Černý conjecture: a reset word of length at most (n−1)²
6558.formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n≥1 states have a reset word of length at most (n−1)²?
6558.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system A=(Q,Σ,δ), with |Q|=n, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, and a total function δ:Q×Σ→Q. Extend δ to words by δ(q,ε)=q and δ(q,wa)=δ(δ(q,w),a). A word w is a reset word when |{δ(q,w):q∈Q}|=1. The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold rt(A) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles n=1. No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models.
6558.answer_criterion: Prove that rt(A)≤(n−1)² for every synchronizing complete deterministic n-state automaton, or exhibit such an automaton with rt(A)>(n−1)² and prove that strict inequality. Alphabets and state counts are unrestricted as specified above.
6558.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

importance.reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.

progress.text: Černý constructs an n-state family with reset threshold exactly (n−1)², establishing the sharp lower-bound target.

Shitov improves that argument to a leading constant approximately 0.1654; the exponent remains three.

Zhu reports a proof for the one-cluster subclass in a preprint. This card does not independently certify that proof or extend it to unrestricted automata.

6558.status_note: Szykuła’s survey posted 25 August 2026 explicitly states the unrestricted conjecture as open and records the cubic upper bound. Sources and later work were checked on 11 September 2026. The July one-cluster preprint is a restricted-class claim whose proof was not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states 0,…,n−1, let a cyclically increment the state and let b send n−1 to 0 while fixing the other states. For n≥2, the word b(a^{n−1}b)^{n−2} has length (n−1)² and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. A proof of the conjecture must match this obstruction exactly.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately 0.1654n³+o(n³), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound (n−1)². Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

6559.title: Does any regular language require generalized star height greater than one?
6559.formal: Does there exist a finite nonempty alphabet Σ and a regular language L⊆Σ* such that every generalized regular expression denoting L has Kleene-star nesting depth at least two, when complement is allowed without increasing that depth?
6559.definitions: Σ* is the set of all finite words over Σ, including the empty word ε. A regular language is one accepted by a finite deterministic automaton. Generalized expressions are finite expressions built from ∅, ε, and the letters a∈Σ using binary union E∪F, concatenation EF, complement E^c, and Kleene star E*. Their meanings are respectively the empty language, {ε}, {a}, language union, all concatenations uv with u∈L(E) and v∈L(F), Σ*∖L(E), and the union of all finite concatenation powers of L(E), including power zero {ε}. Set h(∅)=h(ε)=h(a)=0, h(E∪F)=h(EF)=max{h(E),h(F)}, h(E^c)=h(E), and h(E*)=h(E)+1. Define h_g(L)=min{h(E):L(E)=L}, which exists because every regular language has an ordinary regular expression. The question is whether h_g(L)>1 for at least one such L. There is no bound on expression size, number of complements, union or concatenation depth, automaton size, or alphabet size. Intersection is permitted as the abbreviation (E^c∪F^c)^c and does not add star depth. Backreferences, infinite words, additional predicates and auxiliary alphabets in the final expression are not part of the syntax.
6559.answer_criterion: Prove that some regular language has generalized star height at least two, including a lower bound over all generalized expressions for that language, or prove that every regular language over every finite nonempty alphabet has a generalized expression of star height at most one. Expression size is unrestricted in both alternatives.
6559.why: A basic unresolved expressive-depth question for regular languages: determine whether Boolean operations eliminate every need for nested iteration, or whether a genuine second level exists.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem connecting regular expressions, finite automata, algebraic language theory and logical descriptions.

progress.text: Schützenberger characterizes generalized height zero by aperiodic syntactic monoids; height one is already necessary for simple parity languages.

6559.status_note: The checked author sources distinguish the open generalized question from the solved ordinary star-height problem. A later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no verified height-two example or universal height-one theorem. The inspected factor-counting results establish additional height-one subclasses only.

context_blocks.text: Kleene star represents arbitrary finite repetition. Nested stars arise naturally when repetitions occur inside other repeated blocks. The question is whether such nesting expresses a real hierarchy once a language can also be complemented at no cost to the height measure. Complement preserves regularity, so it does not enlarge the class recognized by finite automata. It may nevertheless radically change the shape of the shortest-depth expression for the same language.

Even elementary examples demonstrate that syntax and language height must be separated. Over Σ={a,b}, the language of all words has the ordinary expression (a∪b)*, with a star. With complement, it is simply ∅^c and has height zero. The language avoiding the factor ab is (Σ*abΣ*)^c; replacing each displayed Σ* by ∅^c makes this a star-free expression. Infinitely many words can therefore belong to a language of generalized height zero.

Height zero does not capture all regular languages. Over the unary alphabet {a}, the even-length language (aa)* has generalized height exactly one. Its two-state automaton remembers length modulo two. Schützenberger’s theorem characterizes height zero through an aperiodic syntactic monoid, and this parity language has a nontrivial two-element group. Thus the first separation, between zero and one, is known; the question asks for the next separation.

The syntactic monoid packages how words behave inside arbitrary contexts: u and v are equivalent when puq belongs to L exactly when pvq does, for every pair of words p,q. Concatenation induces multiplication on the finitely many equivalence classes. A finite monoid is aperiodic when some exponent N makes x^N=x^{N+1} for every element x. Schützenberger’s characterization gives an effective algebraic test for star-freeness, but no corresponding complete height-one criterion is known.

The ordinary, or restricted, star-height problem disallows complement. In that setting, arbitrarily high heights exist and the minimum height is computable. These facts cannot be transferred to generalized height by reusing an ordinary expression or an automaton cycle measure: allowing complement introduces additional descriptions that the old lower-bound argument may not exclude. Pin’s problem page explicitly distinguishes these two versions and separately lists the existence of height two and the algorithmic computation of height.

Pin, Straubing and Thérien prove height at most one for several algebraic classes, including languages recognized by finite nilpotent groups of class at most two, and eliminate a proposed height-two example. They also show that every regular language is the inverse image of an ordinary height-one language under a suitable word morphism. That representation does not bound generalized height without an additional closure statement: inverse morphisms preserve regularity, but their preservation of generalized height one is part of the unresolved issue.

Bourne and Ruškuc extend the height-one territory using factor-counting arguments. Their results cover specified counting cases and languages recognized by Rees zero-matrix semigroups over abelian groups. A factor here is a contiguous occurrence of a word, which differs from counting scattered subsequences. The theorem handles a substantial recognizing-semigroup class, while leaving the existence of a language above height one unresolved.

Daviaud and Paperman study languages generated from sets u* with a single word u, under Boolean or lattice operations and, in some cases, quotients. They give effective equational characterizations of those particular classes. These are deliberately restricted families inside the broader problem: a full height-one expression may take the star of an arbitrary star-free language and combine the resulting languages by concatenation and Boolean operations. Their paper describes its result as a step toward that larger structural challenge.

Cotumaccio’s 2025 account of connections between compressed indexing and automata again identifies generalized star height as an open structural question. It does not supply a new separation or universal flattening theorem. The relevance extends beyond a formal-expression puzzle: a solution would clarify how finite-state iteration, modular behaviour and Boolean operations interact, while allowing descriptions to grow arbitrarily large.

6561.title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
6561.formal: For every fixed integer k≥0, is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to DD_k(A), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
6561.definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, ε the empty word, and A+=A*∖{ε}. Set DD₀(A)={∅,{ε},A+,A*}. For a class C of languages over A, Pol(C) consists of all finite unions of marked products L₀a₁L₁⋯a_rL_r, where r≥0, each a_i∈A, and every L_i∈C; r=0 gives L₀. Let Bool(C) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define DD_{k+1}(A)=Bool(Pol(DD_k(A))). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is L(M). The question quantifies ∀k∃a total Turing algorithm A_k∀M, with A_k(M)=yes exactly when L(M)∈DD_k(A). Each A_k must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6561.answer_criterion: Prove that membership in DD_k is decidable for every fixed integer k≥0, with each decider handling all finite alphabets, or prove that membership is undecidable for at least one fixed level k. The positive statement does not require an effective procedure that takes k as an additional input.
6561.why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.

importance.reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.

6561.status_note: Checked on 11 September 2026. Place–Zeitoun’s full-level-three decidability theorem remains distinct from the all-level target. The January 2025 alternation-hierarchy announcement is still explicitly withdrawn because of a fatal flaw in Lemma 19. No corrected result settling every fixed full dot-depth level was located.

context_blocks.text: Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and b, A*aA*bA* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by {ε} requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation asks whether a language from a prescribed class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering asks whether a given language can be covered by finitely many languages from the class such that each covering language is disjoint from at least one member of a given finite list of forbidden regular languages. These are stronger classification tasks than membership. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 result decides separation and covering for dot-depth two.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

MeSCaL implements established membership tests, including computations for level two and intermediate levels, while its 2025 account explicitly retains the general hierarchy problem. Such tools make existing decision theorems usable without implying that every level is decidable.

Lambert’s July 2026 paper develops effective methods that turn automata into logical descriptions for dot-depth one and specified extensions. Its target classes are fixed; it does not claim a procedure for every level of this hierarchy.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.

6562.title: Are word equations with linear length constraints decidable?
6562.formal: Is there a Turing machine that halts on every finite input consisting of a system of word equations U_i=V_i and a system of integer linear equalities and inequalities on the variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when a simultaneous solution exists in the free monoid Σ*? The alphabet, equations, variables, and arithmetic coefficients are part of the input, with the conventions below.
6562.definitions: Σ is a finite nonempty alphabet of constant symbols and X={X_1,…,X_k} is a disjoint finite set of variables. Each U_i,V_i is an explicitly written finite word over Σ∪X; repeated occurrences of a variable must receive the same substitution. A solution assigns a finite word σ(X_j)∈Σ* to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing every letter of Σ. The empty word is allowed. Every substituted equality σ(U_i)=σ(V_i) must hold as a literal equality of words. The additional constraints are a finite conjunction of atoms sum_j a_j|σ(X_j)|≤b or sum_j a_j|σ(X_j)|=b, where all coefficients and constants are signed binary integers. Length is the number of alphabet symbols. There is no product of two variable lengths, letter-frequency counter, regular-expression predicate, string-to-integer conversion, or universal quantifier. The requested decider need not run in polynomial, elementary, or any specified computable time bound, but must terminate on satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs alike. Nonempty-substitution requirements can be imposed using |σ(X_j)|≥1. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6562.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6562.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

importance.reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.

6562.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The IJCAR 2026 primary source explicitly leaves general word-equation satisfiability with length constraints open. The two-variable quadratic theorem is a restricted case, and the July NEXP-hardness claim is a lower bound rather than a decidability result. This card fixes existential satisfiability with concatenation and integer linear length constraints only.

context_blocks.text: The two ingredients are individually manageable: plain word equations are decidable by Makanin’s theorem, and integer linear arithmetic is decidable. Their combination is difficult because string equality constrains how letters align, while arithmetic constrains the lengths of pieces across those alignments. A decision procedure for either component does not automatically decide their interaction. Ciobanu’s survey identifies this specific combination as a major remaining question.

Taking lengths gives useful necessary conditions, but can lose decisive information. For distinct letters a and b, the equation Xa=bX yields the harmless length identity |X|+1=1+|X|. Nevertheless, it has no finite-word solution. If X is nonempty its first letter must be b, and cancelling that b leaves the same equation for a shorter word; eventually one obtains the false equality a=b. This example shows why satisfying the induced linear equations alone cannot certify a word solution.

There is an elementary way to recognize every YES instance eventually: enumerate all tuples of finite words and test the equations and length constraints. If a solution exists, this search reaches it. For a NO instance, however, there is no prescribed point at which enumeration can stop. A computable bound on the size of some solution to every satisfiable input would therefore be sufficient for decidability. The existence of large witnesses by itself does not establish undecidability.

Several nearby theories have a different status. Constraints on the numbers of individual letters, or on the full vector of letter counts, can make word-equation satisfiability undecidable. Those predicates carry information beyond total length. Similarly, results with alternating quantifiers concern a stronger logical language. Importing either kind of undecidability theorem into this purely existential length-only question would change the problem.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic word equations in at most two unknowns, using a connection with matrix-semigroup reachability. Quadratic means each unknown has at most two occurrences across the equation. The two-unknown restriction is essential to the result stated in their RP 2025 paper. Its abstract also explains that sets of possible solution-length vectors need not be semilinear, so representing every such set by ordinary Presburger arithmetic cannot simply be assumed.

Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 work analyzes when extended Nielsen transformations terminate. These transformations reason about prefixes of variable values while tracking partial length information. Their cut graph records dependencies between occurrences, giving a sufficient termination criterion and a partial converse. This advances a procedure used in string solvers, but neither guarantees termination for every input nor decides the unrestricted problem.

Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez’s July 2026 preprint claims NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints, already over two letters. This strengthens the PP-hardness stated in its first version. Its NEXP-completeness theorem is for arithmetic with divisibility, not for unrestricted word equations with lengths. Positive Boolean formulas can be expanded into finitely many conjunctions for purposes of decidability, but that expansion need not be polynomial. The result therefore records a substantial complexity barrier without establishing a general decider or undecidability.

6563.title: Equivalence of deterministic macro tree transducers
6563.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given two deterministic macro tree transducers with the same finite ranked input and output alphabets, decides whether they define exactly the same partial function from finite ordered input trees to finite ordered output trees?
6563.definitions: Fix the ordinary inside-out, or call-by-value, semantics. A ranked alphabet assigns a nonnegative arity to each symbol; a tree node has exactly that many ordered children. A transducer has finitely many states q, each with one input-tree argument and m(q) output-tree parameters, and an initial state q₀ with m(q₀)=0. For each state q and input symbol σ of arity k there is at most one rule q(σ(x₁,…,x_k),y₁,…,y_m)→r. The finite right-hand side follows the grammar r ::= y_j | δ(r₁,…,r_l) | q′(x_i,r₁,…,r_{m(q′)}), with δ an output symbol of arity l and 1≤i≤k. Subtrees and parameters may be copied or deleted, and calls may be nested inside parameter arguments without a fixed nesting bound across instances. On input σ(t₁,…,t_k), evaluate parameter arguments to output trees, then evaluate a call q′ on the indicated child t_i with those parameter values. A missing rule makes the corresponding evaluation undefined, and under call-by-value an undefined argument makes its enclosing evaluation undefined. There is no inspection or pattern matching on parameter trees. Every recursive call processes a proper input child, so evaluation terminates on each finite input, with either a finite tree or undefined. A transducer with a rule for every state/symbol pair is total. There is no regular look-ahead oracle in this chosen syntax. Equality requires identical domains and, on that domain, identical labelled ordered output trees, without identifying different trees by their leaf strings, shapes or origin annotations. Input alphabets, state sets, arities and rules are all part of the finite input to the desired decision algorithm.
6563.answer_criterion: Prove that equivalence of the specified partial deterministic macro tree transducers is decidable by a total algorithm, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Equivalence requires equality of domains and of the labelled ordered output trees on every input in the common domain.

6563.status_note: Primary-source review and a later-work search on 11 September 2026 found no decider or undecidability theorem for the unrestricted model stated here. The inspected 2025–2026 papers classify shape, growth or expressive power. Their claims do not decide ordinary functional equivalence of arbitrary pairs.

context_blocks.text: A macro tree transducer is a small recursive program for transforming structured data. Its input could be a syntax tree, and its output another syntax tree. A state examines the current input symbol and recursively processes child subtrees. Output parameters act as accumulated pieces of the result that can be inserted, duplicated or passed onward. This makes the model more expressive than a finite-state traversal that simply emits output around its recursive calls.

The restriction to proper input children guarantees termination. It does not bound output size by a polynomial, because a rule may copy a parameter or call a state repeatedly. For example, repeatedly replacing an accumulated tree y by b(y,y) along a unary input chain produces an exponentially large output from a small input. The equivalence question must account for that output implicitly if it hopes to avoid constructing every possible result.

The question asks about all finite inputs. Different rule tables can compute the same transformation through different intermediate structures, so syntactic comparison is too restrictive. Testing every tree up to a chosen height can discover a counterexample, but success on that finite collection proves nothing without a theorem giving an adequate height bound. There is no such bound built into the problem statement.

Non-equivalence is semidecidable: enumerate finite input trees, evaluate both programs, and stop when their definedness or outputs differ. Every individual evaluation terminates even if it takes a long time. The missing counterpart is a complete way to confirm equivalence. No terminating equivalence decider is supplied by this semidecision observation.

Maneth’s survey describes three substantial decidable subclasses: ordinary top-down tree transducers without output parameters, macro transducers of linear size increase, and macro transducers with both input and output alphabets monadic. Linear size increase connects to deterministic MSO-definable tree translations. These restrictions remove different difficulties and do not collectively cover all macro transducers. In particular, restricting the input to unary trees alone is not the same as restricting both alphabets.

The survey also records that inverse images of regular tree languages are effectively regular. Taking the inverse image of all output trees gives an effective description of the domain, so domain equality is already decidable. That useful fact does not decide whether two different output functions agree everywhere on their common domain. The hard part is comparing the unbounded structured outputs rather than merely determining where a computation is defined.

Seidl, Maneth and Kemper settle equivalence of deterministic top-down tree-to-string transducers using inductive invariants expressed through polynomial ideals. Their result combines a search for an equivalence proof with a search for a counterexample. That theorem concerns a particular tree-to-string formalism; the present target is the parameterized tree-to-tree model.

The inherited Maneth–Seidl paper studies origin equivalence: each output node also records which input node caused its creation. It decides this stronger equality test for weakly self-nesting transducers. An origin mismatch can occur even when the ordinary output trees are identical, so a negative answer to origin equivalence is not a negative answer to the present question. The paper further shows that for unrestricted unary-input macro transducers, origin equivalence is as difficult as ordinary equivalence.

Gallot and Maneth’s June 2025 paper decides shape preservation for compositions of total deterministic macro tree transducers. Shape preservation means that the output has the input’s ordered tree shape, although labels may change. This property concerns a transformation’s relation to its own input and does not decide equality of two arbitrary transformations.

Gallot, Lhote and Nguyên’s January 2026 revision decides polynomial size-to-height growth and computes its degree. Such a bound compares the height of the output tree with the number of input nodes. Two transformations can satisfy the same growth bound while differing in their output labels or branching, so growth classification is distinct from functional equivalence.

Dartois, Nguyên and Peyrat’s May 2026 paper characterizes a class of functions of linear size-to-height increase using tree-to-tree Hennie machines and a typed lambda calculus. Its equivalence proof concerns the expressive power of two models. It is not an algorithm for deciding whether two arbitrary macro tree transducers produce identical outputs. Keeping these senses of equivalence separate prevents a misleading reading of the recent abstract.

A resolution would locate an important boundary of automatic program comparison. These programs already terminate and have a disciplined recursive structure, but still support nested parameter passing and copying. Decidability would provide a foundation for validating transformations and optimizations in that model; undecidability would demonstrate that structural recursion alone does not make full semantic equality effectively recognizable.

6564.definitions: A tree is a finite nonempty set T of finite words over positive integers, containing the empty word ε, closed under prefixes, and such that ui∈T implies uj∈T for 1≤j≤i. Its root is ε; the children of u are u1,…,uk in that order. Each node has exactly one label from a nonempty finite alphabet Σ. There is no fixed bound on k. Desc(x,y) means x is a proper prefix of y, so y is a strict descendant of x. Sib(x,y) means x=ui and y=uj for the same parent u with i<j; it orders siblings, not all incomparable nodes. Equality and the unary predicates P_a(x), one per label a∈Σ, complete the logical vocabulary. First-order sentences are finite formulas formed from these atomic predicates by Boolean connectives and quantification over individual nodes only, with any finite number of variables and alternations. No quantification over sets, counting quantifier or extra transitive-closure operator is allowed. The parent relation is definable from Desc. The lexicographic order used in the primary paper is equivalent to Desc plus Sib: x precedes y if Desc(x,y), or some sibling s of t precedes it with s equal to or an ancestor of x and t equal to or an ancestor of y. Conversely Sib is definable from parent and lexicographic order. To fix a finite input presentation, a bottom-up automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a binary operation ⊕ and identity 0 making (Q,⊕,0) a monoid, a table δ_a:Q→Q for each a∈Σ, and an accepting subset F⊆Q. A node labeled a with ordered child states q₁,…,q_k receives state δ_a(q₁⊕⋯⊕q_k); the empty sum is 0. The tree is accepted when its root state lies in F. These finite tables, alphabet and state indices are explicitly encoded in binary; this is an algebraic bottom-up presentation of regular unranked tree languages. The algorithm must work for every valid finite presentation, without a complexity bound beyond termination. The sentence φ may depend on A, but must be a single sentence for all finite trees and all their sizes.
6564.answer_criterion: Prove decidability by an algorithm that terminates correctly on every valid automaton description, or prove that this decision problem is undecidable. Recognizing trees with a fixed supplied automaton, deciding whether one supplied sentence agrees with an automaton, or testing definability in a fixed quantifier fragment does not decide existence of an arbitrary first-order definition.

context_blocks.title: Two descriptions of a tree property
context_blocks.text: An automaton combines finitely many states from the children and passes one state to their parent. A first-order sentence instead describes relationships between named nodes. For instance, “every a-labeled node has a b-labeled descendant” is the sentence ∀x(P_a(x)⇒∃y(Desc(x,y)∧P_b(y))). The question asks whether the entire language recognized by a given automaton has some description of this logical kind.

context_blocks.title: Regular does not automatically mean first-order
context_blocks.text: A two-state bottom-up computation can track whether the total number of nodes is even or odd: combine child parities and then count the parent. First-order logic with order cannot express arbitrary parity even on trees that are single paths. Thus finite-state recognition is strictly more expressive. The task is to tell, from an automaton’s finite description, on which side of that expressiveness boundary its language lies.

context_blocks.title: The available relations change the problem
context_blocks.text: A descendant relation permits a sentence to refer directly to nodes arbitrarily far below another node. A child relation concerns just one edge. Decidability results for the child-only vocabulary therefore do not settle this card. Order among siblings is also part of the input structure: permuting subtrees can change the truth of a formula. The chosen vocabulary matches the ordered ancestor-plus-lexicographic setting of the source rather than an unordered or purely local variant.

context_blocks.title: What partial characterizations establish
context_blocks.text: Bojańczyk and Segoufin decide definability in Δ₂, the languages having both an existential-then-universal and a universal-then-existential definition. They do not decide arbitrary first-order definability. Blumensath’s 2024 finite-tree work supplies decidable necessary and sufficient conditions separately, but no one condition that is both. A necessary condition can fail to reject every nondefinable language, while a sufficient condition can fail to accept every definable language. The remaining gap is a complete test.

context_blocks.title: Later results concern other targets
context_blocks.text: The 2025 automata characterization studies first-order logic over unordered infinite trees. The August 2026 result decides a common fragment of particular branching-time and linear-time temporal logics. Their domains or logical restrictions differ from the full finite ordered-tree question. They do not supply the all-input terminating test requested here. A solution would turn an expressiveness boundary into a mechanically checkable property of finite-state tree specifications.

6566.title: Decidability of unbounded Continuous Skolem
6566.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension d≥1, rational matrix A∈Q^{d×d}, and rational column vectors b,c∈Q^d, always halts and correctly decides whether cᵀexp(tA)b=0 for some real t≥0?
6566.definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is exp(tA)=Σ_{j=0}^∞ t^j A^j/j!, and x(t)=exp(tA)b is the unique real solution of x′(t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b. The target is the hyperplane {x:cᵀx=0}; c=0 is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at t=0 counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit t→∞, the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
6566.answer_criterion: Give an unconditional always-halting decision algorithm for every rational input, or prove that no such Turing algorithm exists. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may run forever on some inputs, or a certified answer only under a nonzero distance promise is partial progress. An undecidability theorem allowing more general coefficients or nonlinear differential equations must be reduced to this rational linear model to refute the proposition.

6566.status_note: No unconditional decision procedure or undecidability proof for this rational linear model was found through 11 September 2026. Bounded conditional results, low-order recurrence algorithms, approximate/robust verification and nonlinear-system hardness do not settle the unbounded exact question.

context_blocks.text: Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output cᵀx(t) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system x′=−x, x(0)=1 has output e^{−t}, which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial (t−1)² touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is cᵀb=0. By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when cᵀA^j b=0 for j=0,…,d−1. These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all t≥0.

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at π/2. The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.

6567.title: Can simple stochastic games be solved in polynomial time?
6567.formal: Is the following decision problem in deterministic polynomial time? Given an explicitly represented finite simple stochastic game G, a start vertex s, and a binary rational threshold r∈[0,1], decide whether v_G(s)>r, where v_G(s)=sup_σ inf_τ Pr_s^{σ,τ}[eventually reach the target sink 1]. The game and threshold follow the exact conventions below, and time is polynomial in their total bit length.
6567.definitions: The vertices are partitioned into Max, Min, random, and two distinct terminal sinks 0 and 1. Every nonterminal vertex has two listed successor slots; slots may have the same successor. At a Max or Min vertex its owner chooses a slot. At a random vertex each slot is chosen with probability 1/2, independently at each visit. Both players observe the complete finite history and the current vertex. Strategies may use history and private randomness; there is no bound on play length. Reaching 1 gives Max payoff one; reaching 0, or playing forever without reaching 1, gives payoff zero. Min minimizes the same expected payoff that Max maximizes. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed. All vertices, ownership labels and successor indices are explicit; r=a/b is exact with binary integers 0≤a≤b and b>0. Equality v_G(s)=r is a NO instance. The algorithm is an ordinary uniform deterministic Turing algorithm; its polynomial bound has universal constants independent of the game and threshold. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

context_blocks.text: This game combines three elementary kinds of branching: a controller chooses, an adversary chooses, or a fair coin chooses. Removing one player gives a Markov decision process; fixing both players’ strategies leaves a Markov chain. The hard case is their interaction across cycles. Condon established that the threshold problem has polynomially checkable certificates on both sides, placing it in NP∩coNP. That classification has not yielded a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

Both players have optimal deterministic positional strategies: one successor choice per owned vertex suffices, even though the definition permits history and randomization. A candidate strategy is therefore short. Fixing one player leaves a one-player optimization problem that can be solved in polynomial time, which explains the certificates. The difficulty is finding a suitable strategy among the exponentially many combinations, rather than needing to represent an optimal strategy of enormous length.

The local equations look deceptively simple: a Max vertex takes the maximum successor value, a Min vertex the minimum, and a random vertex their average. In a nonterminating component these equations alone can have multiple solutions. For example, a random vertex whose two slots both lead back to itself satisfies x=(x+x)/2 for every x, but its actual target-reaching probability is zero. A solver must identify the reachability values rather than accept an arbitrary fixed point.

Exact thresholds matter. A chain of k independent fair choices can reach the target with probability 2^(−k), with any failed choice leading to 0. Its graph has only O(k) vertices. Thus an additive error suitable for many numerical applications may be too large to distinguish a positive value from zero or to decide a nearby rational threshold. Polynomially many bits of precision can still require very many iterations if convergence is slow.

Ludwig’s classical randomized algorithm uses an expected 2^{O(√n)} operations on n-vertex games. It demonstrates that straightforward enumeration is not the only way to search the strategy space. It still gives a subexponential bound rather than the polynomial deterministic bound requested here.

Recent progress develops both practical solvers and structural cases. Azeem, Kretinsky and Weininger extend sound value iteration to games with end components, maintaining lower and upper bounds while addressing probabilistic cycles.

Gärtner, Haslebacher and Hoang’s FUN 2026 paper solves stopping binary games on ladders: distance layers toward the sinks contain two vertices, except possibly the last layer. Their algorithm recovers an ordering of optimal values from this special geometry. This restricted-class theorem does not supply a polynomial-time solver for unrestricted games.

The consequences extend to more expressive objectives. Berthon, Katoen and Zhou give a direct polynomial reduction from quantitative stochastic parity games to simple stochastic games, using binary representations of transition probabilities. This strengthens the explanatory connection between recurring long-run conditions and a single reachability target. Their paper invokes the known polynomial equivalence of the usual probability encodings; the reduction does not itself remove the open algorithmic bottleneck.

Baldan, Gurke, König and Wittbold’s 2026 work extends convergent fixed-point iteration to simple stochastic games. Convergence of numerical approximations is a different guarantee from deciding every exact rational threshold using polynomially many bit operations. The iteration theorem does not establish the polynomial-time classification asked here.

6568.title: Can mean-payoff games be solved in polynomial time?
6568.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm, running in time polynomial in the total input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a partition V=V_Max⊔V_Min, integer edge weights w:E→Z, and a start vertex s, determine whether Max has a strategy σ such that every strategy τ of Min produces a play s=v_0,v_1,… satisfying liminf_{T→∞}(1/T) sum_{t=0}^{T−1} w(v_t,v_{t+1})≥0.
6568.definitions: The graph, its ownership partition, its start vertex and all weights are represented explicitly; weights use signed binary. Each vertex has at least one outgoing edge, so plays are infinite. The owner of the current vertex chooses the next edge with full knowledge of the finite history. Strategies are arbitrary deterministic functions of this history. There are no chance vertices, simultaneous moves, hidden observations or multiple payoff coordinates. Max seeks a nonnegative lower limit of average accumulated weight; equality zero is winning. No bound is imposed on intermediate losses or on the size W=max(1,max_e |w(e)|). The running-time requirement concerns ordinary bit operations, so a polynomial dependence on W is not sufficient. Zero threshold loses no generality: a binary rational threshold a/b with b>0 can be absorbed by replacing w(e) with b w(e)−a, with polynomial growth of the encoding.
6568.answer_criterion: Prove that this exact winner-decision language is in P, or prove that it is outside P. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a smoothed or average-case guarantee, or a lower bound for one strategy-improvement rule does not settle the unrestricted worst-case question. Strongly polynomial time would suffice but is a stronger requirement than this card asks for.
6568.why: A foundational complexity question for long-run adversarial optimization. It connects finite graph games, quantitative verification, resource reasoning and tropical algebra, with short optimal strategies but no known polynomial-time method to find the winner on arbitrary binary-weighted inputs.

importance.reason: A canonical NP∩coNP problem central to quantitative synthesis and long-run control; resolving the binary-weight complexity gap would have consequences across several equivalent algebraic and game formulations.

6568.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The July 2026 primary source explicitly states that polynomial-time solution with binary weights remains open. The card fixes a single deterministic mean-payoff objective with a nonnegative liminf threshold. Pseudopolynomial, ergodic smoothed-analysis and framework-specific results do not resolve arbitrary worst-case inputs.

context_blocks.text: Mean payoff measures sustainable long-run performance. Edge weights can represent net resource gains, rewards or the negative of costs; an adversary controls some of the transitions. A finite initial loss disappears from the limiting average, while a repeatedly traversed cycle continues to matter. For example, eventually repeating weights −5 and +7 has mean payoff one, regardless of any fixed initial prefix. This distinguishes the objective from requiring the accumulated sum to remain nonnegative at every step.

Optimal positional strategies exist for both players, so a player can make the same choice whenever a vertex is revisited. With both choices fixed, the resulting path eventually repeats a cycle, and its value is the cycle’s average weight. This yields compact certificates and NP∩coNP membership. It does not make the search easy: the number of positional strategy combinations can be exponential. Zwick and Paterson gave the classical complexity analysis and a polynomial reduction to simple stochastic games.

The size of a weight and the size of its representation differ sharply. A weight 2^b takes only b+1 binary digits. An algorithm using O(nmW) arithmetic operations, where n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, can therefore take exponential time in the input length. Brim and coauthors obtain such a pseudopolynomial bound for the threshold problem through energy-game progress measures. The result is powerful for small weights, but it leaves the dependence needed for this question unresolved.

Universal graphs provide a way to organize and compare value-iteration algorithms. Fijalkow, Gawrychowski and Ohlmann establish tight bounds within that framework, including improved dependence on the largest weight for a fixed number of vertices. Such a matching lower bound identifies a limitation of the framework being analyzed; it does not rule out an unrelated polynomial-time algorithm for mean-payoff games.

Smoothed analysis gives a different kind of progress. Loff and Skomra’s ICALP 2024 theorem obtains polynomial running time with high probability after sufficiently random independent perturbations of rewards, on ergodic game graphs. Here ergodicity is stronger than ordinary strong connectivity: for every reward assignment, the game value is independent of the start vertex. The theorem helps explain efficiency on perturbed inputs while retaining both a graph restriction and distributional assumptions. It does not decide the present worst-case complexity question.

There are also increasingly direct links to linear optimization. Maat’s September 2025 preprint identifies many strategy-improvement variants with instances of the simplex algorithm under nondegeneracy assumptions. This gives a structural bridge between algorithms and their lower-bound constructions. A correspondence between local improvement methods, however, is not a proof that their number of iterations is polynomial.

A July 2026 preprint by Adenwalla and coauthors connects tropical inequality systems and mean-payoff games with deciding chromatic boundedness for certain classes of graphs defined by equality patterns. Its reverse encoding uses a specified succinct representation. This creates another setting in which a solver would be useful. The paper explicitly leaves polynomial-time mean-payoff solving open, and its graph-class reduction should not be mistaken for a polynomial algorithm for games.

6569.title: An internal tower of semisimplicial types in ordinary HoTT
6569.formal: In the fixed ordinary HoTT theory T below, can one define a single internal family S:ℕ→U₁ and restriction maps r_n:S(n+1)→S(n) whose finite stages are equivalent, compatibly with restriction, to the canonical finite semisimplicial telescopes D_n?
6569.definitions: Fix T to be intensional Martin–Löf type theory with dependent function and pair types Π,Σ, identity types with their J eliminator, empty and unit types, finite coproducts, natural numbers and W-types, a cumulative predicative sequence U₀:U₁:⋯ closed under these constructors, and univalence for these universes. Also allow propositional truncation and homotopy pushouts with their ordinary dependent eliminators and propositional computation rules for path constructors, as in the HoTT book. There is no equality reflection, axiom K/UIP, resizing, choice, excluded middle, second equality type, display modality, or additional primitive for semisimplicial types. The question concerns definability in this specified theory; a negative result would apply to this theory, not automatically to every possible extension called HoTT. Define an external, finite family of syntactic telescopes as follows. D₀ is U₀, with element A₀. Given data d=(A₀,…,A_{j−1}) in D_{j−1}, form B_j(d), the dependent type of labelled boundaries of a j-simplex: for every nonempty proper subset F of {0,…,j}, in increasing cardinality and then lexicographic order, choose a label x_F in A_{|F|−1} evaluated on the labels of all nonempty proper subfaces of F. Identify F with {0,…,|F|−1} by its increasing enumeration when supplying these arguments. For singleton F this means x_F:A₀. Set D_j=Σ(d:D_{j−1})(B_j(d)→U₀), whose last field is A_j, and let p_j:D_{j+1}→D_j forget the last field. This describes an ordinary finite T-expression for each external integer j; it does not postulate an internal function j↦D_j. The required output is finite closed T-terms S:ℕ→U₁ and r:Π(n:ℕ)(S(n+1)→S(n)), together with a metatheoretic proof that for every external j there are T-terms e_j:S(j)≃D_j and homotopies e_j∘r_j ~ p_j∘e_{j+1}. Here j inside T denotes its numeral, ≃ is the usual type equivalence, and ~ is pointwise identity. No judgmental equality between S(j) and D_j is required. The equivalences classify the full type-valued telescopes, with arbitrary U₀-small simplex types and no fixed truncation bound.
6569.answer_criterion: Prove that the specified theory T admits finite closed terms S and r together with the external stagewise equivalences and compatibility homotopies required above, or prove that no such terms and witnesses exist in T. The positive conclusion must hold at every external finite stage and allow arbitrary U₀-small simplex types.
6569.why: Determine whether ordinary HoTT can express a fundamental unbounded coherent structure internally, a basic issue for higher categories and foundational proof languages.

importance.reason: A central expressiveness problem for homotopy type theory; precise internal construction would remove a major obstacle to formalizing higher structures without enriching the theory.

6569.status_note: The original question and the May 2026 two-level revision were rechecked on 11 September 2026. No construction in the specified theory T, or nondefinability theorem for T, was located. Results with outer strict equality or display primitives use additional structure and are recorded separately.

context_blocks.text: Homotopy type theory treats identity as mathematical data that can itself have nontrivial identities. This makes it a natural setting for spaces and higher structures, but it changes what it means to give a diagram. In set-level mathematics, equations between composites can be recorded once and used without further information. For general types, chosen identifications can have multiple distinct witnesses, and comparisons between those witnesses may matter in the next dimension.

A semisimplicial type begins with a type A₀ of vertices. For every ordered pair of vertices, A₁ gives a type of edges. For every triangle boundary—three vertices and three specified edges—A₂ gives a type of fillers. At dimension three, a filler is indexed by four vertices, six edges and four triangular fillers sharing their appropriate faces. Nothing forces a filler to exist, and the type of fillers may itself have arbitrarily rich homotopy.

The finite telescope description records shared boundaries through dependent types. A triangle’s three edges are already assigned the required endpoints; one does not choose unrelated edges and then append a collection of endpoint equations. The same idea works at each externally fixed dimension. The difficulty is making the whole construction into one function that accepts an internal natural number, rather than a growing list of separately written definitions.

This is why the card distinguishes its externally specified D_j from the sought internal S. A script can generate the expression for D_100 and a type checker can check it. That does not supply a HoTT term whose argument is an arbitrary n:ℕ. The compatibility requirement also matters: a collection of unrelated types with the right apparent sizes would not tell us how to forget the highest-dimensional data.

The statement deliberately allows equivalence at each stage instead of demanding a particular syntactic normal form. Thus a clever alternative encoding can solve the problem if it represents all the prescribed data and respects truncation. Once the internal tower exists, dependent sums, products and identity types already express a compatible infinite sequence. The missing step is constructing the tower itself, not adding a primitive that merely asserts an infinite sequence exists.

Kraus’s TYPES 2018 discussion identifies uniform finite-dimensional semisimplicial types as a major open problem and explains their role in higher category theory. Adding suitable Segal and completeness conditions to such data provides a route toward internal higher categories. Those conditions are additional structure: this card asks first for unrestricted semisimplicial data, with no composition, identity or horn-filling axioms imposed.

Two-level type theory introduces an outer equality satisfying uniqueness of identity proofs, alongside the homotopical inner theory. It can formalize constructions indexed by outer natural numbers. Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler distinguish this from constructing an inner universe of infinite semisimplicial types; additional hypotheses relating the two natural-number objects support the latter. The May 2026 revision is labelled a typo and reference update, not a new solution in ordinary HoTT.

Displayed Type Theory takes another route. Kolomatskaia and Shulman introduce discrete and simplicial modes together with a primitive display operation, then use it for a coinductive construction of semisimplicial types. This is a substantive solution in their enriched system, with a detailed semantic correctness argument. It does not give a definition from the constructors of T alone, because those additional primitives are precisely what enable the construction.

Chen’s 2025 thesis studies internal models and Reedy-fibrant inverse diagrams directly. It explicitly retains the ordinary-HoTT semisimplicial problem as open. Section 6.1 labels its proposed classifier construction a sketch whose Agda formalization has unresolved termination and definitional-equality issues, and states that it is not intended to solve the unrestricted problem. This is useful progress toward articulating the required coherence, rather than a completed internal classifier.

A set-valued construction also does not suffice. If every simplex type is a set, identities between elements have no higher ambiguity, and ordinary categorical equations behave much more rigidly. The requirement that the simplex types range over U₀ preserves the higher-dimensional content that motivates the problem. Likewise, having a satisfactory semantic construction in a model does not automatically produce a finite term definable in the specified syntax.

A positive answer would show that ordinary dependent types can organize this fundamental form of unbounded coherence without additional structure in the language. A negative answer would identify a precise expressive limitation and help explain why successful alternative foundations introduce new primitives. Either outcome would guide the design of proof assistants intended to support higher category theory and internal constructions of type-theoretic models.

6570.definitions: Terms are generated by variables from a countably infinite set, application MN and abstraction λx.M, modulo renaming bound variables. Beta-convertibility is the least equivalence relation closed under application and abstraction containing (λx.M)N=M[N/x], with capture-avoiding substitution. A directed set is nonempty and every two of its elements have an upper bound in the set. D is a set with a partial order, a least element, and a supremum for every directed subset. Scott-continuous means monotone and preserving directed suprema. [D→D] consists of all Scott-continuous functions, ordered pointwise. An environment ρ assigns an element of D to each variable. Interpret x as ρ(x), MN as F(⟦M⟧ρ)(⟦N⟧ρ), and λx.M as L(d↦⟦M⟧(ρ[x:=d])). The desired condition is ∀M,N: (∀ρ, ⟦M⟧ρ=⟦N⟧ρ) ⇔ M=βN. Models need not be countable, algebraic, effectively presented or extensional; in particular L∘F=id is not required. These are set-based directed-complete orders and all their continuous maps, without a restriction to graph models.
6570.answer_criterion: Prove that a pointed dcpo and continuous retraction F,L satisfying the stated exact-theory condition exist, or prove that none exist. A negative answer must cover all such dcpos, without assuming an effective presentation, algebraicity or extensionality.

context_blocks.text: The untyped lambda calculus describes functions using variables, application and abstraction. Beta-reduction substitutes an argument into a function body. A denotational model assigns mathematical meanings to terms and makes every beta-conversion valid. The question asks whether continuity can coexist with complete precision: no two terms should become equal in the model unless beta-conversion already equates them.

In domain semantics, an order represents increasing information and a directed supremum combines compatible approximations. Scott continuity requires functions to preserve these suprema. The map L represents each continuous self-map by an element of D, and F turns an element back into its associated self-map. The equation F∘L=id ensures that interpreting function application recovers the represented function. This makes beta-reduction sound.

Representability is a semantic condition. The element representing a continuous function need not be denoted by any finite lambda term. Requiring every continuous function to have a finite program would change the question. The model need not have computable elements, a computable ordering or a computable interpretation algorithm.

Extensional equality makes an additional identification. If x is not free in f, eta-conversion equates λx.f x with f, although these terms need not be beta-convertible. Imposing L∘F=id would validate this extra equality. This card therefore requires only the retraction in the other direction and keeps the beta-eta version as a separate target.

Quotienting syntax by beta-conversion gives a term model with exactly the desired equality. It does not automatically provide a pointed dcpo representing all continuous self-maps. The issue is whether the exact syntactic theory can be realized in this particular semantic setting.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra prove that the effective models defined in their paper cannot have theory exactly λβ or λβη. They also prove non-enumerability of the order theory, which records inequalities between denotations. Equational theory records equalities instead. A theorem restricted to effective models, or to order rather than equality, cannot be generalized silently to arbitrary dcpos.

Divergent terms reveal another source of extra equations. A term is unsolvable when no finite reduction exposes a head normal form: an outer variable applied to arguments after any leading abstractions. A sensible model equates all unsolvable closed terms. This is stronger than beta-conversion, which distinguishes some of them. The 2025 filter-model paper studies when unsolvables receive nontrivial interpretations and which type-theoretic conditions govern that behavior.

Lambda Galore, published in 2026, constructs sensible filter models representing all continuous functions whose theories do not contain the full Böhm-tree theory. It separates two semantic properties and resolves a different question about models. Sensibility still identifies unsolvables, so these constructions do not realize exactly λβ. Continuous representability alone does not make their equational theory the one requested here.

6572.title: Is there a polynomial-time simplex pivot rule?
6572.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic primal-simplex pivot algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every rational linear program max{cᵀx: Ax=b, x≥0} with A of full row rank, a finite optimum, and any supplied feasible basis B_0, the algorithm reaches a basis whose reduced costs are all nonpositive using at most p(L) bit operations in total? Here L is the binary input length of A,b,c and B_0, and every basis change must be a legal improving simplex pivot as defined below.
6572.definitions: A has m rows and n columns with 1≤m≤n; all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicit binary integers. A basis B is a set of m columns with invertible A_B. Its basic solution is x_B=A_B^{-1}b and x_j=0 for j∉B, and feasibility means x_B≥0. An entering column j∉B must have reduced cost r_j=c_j−c_BᵀA_B^{-1}A_j>0. Put a=A_B^{-1}A_j. Choose a leaving basic index i attaining θ=min_{k∈B:a_k>0}x_k/a_k, and replace i by j in the basis. The finite-optimum promise ensures that this minimum exists for an improving column. Ties may be resolved by the rule; θ=0 is an allowed degenerate pivot and counts toward the bound. The rule may inspect the whole input and maintain history, with all preprocessing, pivot selection, exact arithmetic, helper computations and memory operations charged to p(L). It must follow these basis exchanges on the supplied LP from B_0: it may not jump to another feasible basis or replace the feasible region by an extended formulation. The required terminal condition r_j≤0 for all j∉B certifies optimality. This is the supplied-feasible-basis optimization version; phase-I feasibility construction is not part of this card.
6572.answer_criterion: Construct such a rule and prove its total polynomial bit complexity for every promised input and initial feasible basis, or prove that no such rule exists. Merely bounding the number of pivots while leaving their selection computationally unbounded is insufficient. A lower bound for a prescribed family of rules, or for nonlinear objectives, does not establish the negative answer for all rules here.
6572.why: A fundamental question about whether local, improving basis exchanges can support efficient global optimization. It would explain a central practical algorithm and sharpen the relationship between polyhedral geometry, degeneracy and algorithmic access to an optimum.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.

6572.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The STACS 2026 and March 2026 primary publications retain the general polynomial simplex question as open. This card fixes deterministic total bit complexity for legal improving primal-simplex pivots from any supplied feasible basis on a finite-optimum rational LP. Strongly polynomial algorithms, nonlinear active-set bounds and distributional performance are distinct formulations.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms with polynomial bit complexity, including ellipsoid and interior-point methods. The unresolved question is whether the same guarantee can be achieved while moving through bases by the simplex method. A pivot rule determines which improving direction to expose next and how to break ties. The STACS 2026 paper on ranking-based rules states that the general question remains open.

There are two obstacles to a polynomial guarantee. First, a short route to an optimal basis must exist under the permitted improving moves. Second, the rule must discover such a route efficiently. Knowing the optimum from another computation does not authorize skipping the route: every intervening basis exchange is still required. Likewise, a short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short path along improving edges.

The bit-complexity requirement is deliberately weaker than strongly polynomial simplex. It permits the running time to depend polynomially on the number of bits in coefficients. A strongly polynomial rule would instead bound its arithmetic work polynomially in m and n, together with appropriate bounds on the sizes of numbers used. Therefore this card does not assert that a positive answer alone settles Smale’s strongly polynomial LP problem or a diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy means several bases can describe the same vertex. A legal pivot with θ=0 changes the basis without improving the objective value, so an algorithm can stall even if the geometric route is short. Kukharenko and Sanità’s March 2026 paper bounds a block of consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by n−m−1, given an improving feasible direction. Such a direction can be obtained using an LP solver. This controls local stalling, but does not bound how many different nonoptimal vertices the method must visit.

Positive average-case results are also substantial. Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm under random perturbations of the input. Smoothed analysis studies the expected behavior around an arbitrary instance as a function of perturbation size. It helps explain good practical performance, but does not give a deterministic worst-case guarantee on every exact rational instance.

The 2026 ranking-based lower bounds exclude broader families than a single greedy rule. One result covers index-ranking rules with a specified limit on their memory states; another covers memoryless rules using rankings by index, reduced cost and objective improvement. Full access to numerical data and unrestricted polynomially bounded history are allowed in this card, so those lower bounds do not cover every candidate.

A striking neighboring result does exclude every pivot rule for the active-set method with a nonlinear objective. Disser and Mosis first use higher-degree polynomial objectives on the hypercube. Bach and coauthors then obtain the phenomenon for maximizing a convex quadratic function, published at SODA 2026. The direction of optimization matters: this is convex maximization. Their construction does not have a linear objective, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a general simplex lower bound.

6573.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture for edge-path diameter
6573.formal: Do universal constants C>0 and k≥1 exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most C(n+d)^k?
6573.definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with R^d, where d≥1, and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph G(P) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
6573.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6573.why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.

importance.reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.
