6573.status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.

context_blocks.text: The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and 2^d vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An n^d upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper n−d bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as Cn² or Cn¹⁰. The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave n^{2+log₂d}; Todd improved it in 2014 to (n−d)^{log₂d}. For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form (n−d)^{log₂d−log₂log d+O(1)}. The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves Π₂^p-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron {x∈R^N:Ax=b,x≥0}, with A having r rows, the stated bound is O(r²log r), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.

6574.title: Is exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time?
6574.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices A_0,A_1,…,A_m∈Q^{n×n} for which there exists a real vector x∈R^m satisfying A_0+sum_{i=1}^m x_i A_i⪰0? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
6574.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size n≥1. A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written M⪰0, when zᵀMz≥0 for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6574.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6574.why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. Resolving it would clarify what semidefinite programming can guarantee without hidden regularity or witness-size assumptions, with consequences for optimization relaxations, algebraic certificates and verification.

6574.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish NP∩coNP membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.

context_blocks.text: Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real n×n matrix Y and impose A_0+sum_i x_i A_i=YYᵀ. These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix M(t) with rows (0,1) and (1,t) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue (t−√(t²+4))/2 tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks [[x,2],[2,2x]] and [[2,x],[x,1]]. The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when x≥√2, and the second when |x|≤√2. The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at x=√2. All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions x_1≥2 and [[x_{i+1},x_i],[x_i,1]]⪰0 force x_{i+1}≥x_i², hence x_k≥2^{2^{k−1}}. A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding NP∩coNP theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.
Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. 6575.title: The deterministic k-server conjecture
6575.formal: For every integer k≥1, every metric space (M,d) with at least k+1 points, and every initial placement C_0 of k servers, does there exist a deterministic online serving rule A and a finite constant β≥0 such that cost_A(σ;C_0)≤k·OPT(σ;C_0)+β for every finite request sequence σ∈M*? The rule and β may depend on M,d,k,C_0, but neither may depend on future requests or on the length of the request sequence.
6575.definitions: The metric is symmetric, has finite real distances, is zero exactly on equal points, and satisfies the triangle inequality; the space may be finite or infinite and is known to the online rule. There are exactly k interchangeable, unweighted servers, whose current positions form a multiset. A request r_t must be served before r_{t+1} is revealed. If a server is already at r_t, no movement is needed; otherwise the rule chooses one of the k servers and moves it to r_t, paying the metric distance. Restriction to these lazy moves loses no competitive power. A deterministic online rule is a function of the known metric, initial placement and revealed request prefix, with arbitrary memory and no access to future requests; this card imposes no running-time bound. OPT is the minimum total movement cost of an offline rule serving the same finite sequence from C_0 with the same k servers and advance knowledge of the sequence. The additive β must be fixed before requests arrive and cannot grow with the number or cost of requests. Randomization, advice about future requests, and extra servers are not supplied.
6575.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6575.why: A central problem in competitive analysis that asks whether the number of available servers exactly captures the worst-case price of future uncertainty. Its techniques and limitations inform caching, online movement and broader metric optimization problems.

importance.reason: A foundational conjecture about online decision-making, with an optimal lower bound, one broadly applicable candidate algorithm, and a persistent gap on general metrics despite many resolved special cases.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé release a potential-discovery benchmark. The four-server circle experiments and finite inequality checks do not resolve the conjecture.

6575.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary source retains the deterministic conjecture and the general (2k−1) upper bound. The 2023 randomized disproof concerns O(log k), not the deterministic factor k. This card fixes all finite request sequences, identical initial placements, exactly k servers and an additive constant independent of requests; it asks for any deterministic online rule, not specifically WFA.

context_blocks.text: The problem isolates the price of making placement decisions without seeing future demand. Servers can represent cache slots, mobile resources or copies of data; a movement pays for changing which demand locations are covered. On a uniform metric, where every distinct pair has distance one, serving a request is precisely the paging problem. The online rule and the offline optimum have the same number of servers. Their difference is information about the future, not available capacity.

The proposed factor k is a sharp target, already forced by paging lower bounds. The classical work of Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator establishes the lower-bound framework and settles the two-server case on general metrics. An additive constant is included so that a fixed initial placement does not distort asymptotic performance. Allowing that constant to depend on the request sequence would make the definition vacuous, which is why its quantifiers are explicit.

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou prove that the work-function algorithm is (2k−1)-competitive on every metric space. Its work function records the minimum offline cost of serving the already revealed prefix and ending in each possible server configuration. The algorithm uses these values to weigh movement against how well a configuration fits the past. This provides a single general strategy and leaves a factor approaching two between the known guarantee and the conjectured optimum.

It is widely conjectured that the same algorithm is actually k-competitive. Proving that stronger statement would settle this card, but the card permits a completely different algorithm. Similarly, failure of one proposed potential function only identifies a gap in that proof method. A potential proof typically compares changes in a quantity assigned to the current work function with the online and offline costs, so that the inequalities telescope over an arbitrarily long request sequence.

Several geometric settings attain the target. Chrobak and Larmore give k-competitive algorithms on tree metrics, covering line-like settings as well. Trees have unique connecting paths, which support movement rules unavailable in arbitrary metrics. This is substantial positive evidence, but arbitrary metric spaces can contain cycles and distance patterns that do not admit the same analysis.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle, with distance measured along the shorter circular arc. Their result first appeared in a 2022 preprint and was published in Theoretical Computer Science in 2024. They also give computer-assisted evidence excluding their defined canonical family of potential functions for the general three-server case. The geometric theorem and the limitation of that proof family are different conclusions.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani’s STOC 2023 theorem disproves the randomized O(log k) conjecture by constructing metrics with randomized competitive ratio Ω(log²k). It does not refute the deterministic target k: these are different claimed rates, and log²k is asymptotically smaller than k. The deterministic lower bound and the (2k−1) upper bound remain the relevant endpoints here.

Brilliantov, Bamas and Abbé’s April 2026 benchmark studies automated searches for potentials, particularly for four servers on a circle. A violated checked inequality refutes a candidate under the chosen formulation, while passing the finite checks is not a proof for every metric configuration and request sequence. Their experiments leave the open case unresolved. This offers concrete research tooling without changing the status of the conjecture.

6577.definitions: Let d,T≥1 be integers and B₂^d={x∈R^d:Σ_i x_i²≤1}. A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of R^d satisfying B₂^d⊆K⊆dB₂^d; the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write F(K) for the Borel-measurable convex functions f:K→[0,1], where convexity means f(λx+(1−λ)y)≤λf(x)+(1−λ)f(y) for x,y∈K and λ∈[0,1]. No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes f₁,…,f_T∈F(K), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses X_t∈K, incurs f_t(X_t), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history (X₁,f₁(X₁),…,X_(t−1),f_(t−1)(X_(t−1))). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define R_K(T)=inf_π sup_(f₁,…,f_T) E_π[Σ_t f_t(X_t)−inf_(x∈K)Σ_t f_t(x)], with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally R*(d,T)=sup_K R_K(T), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function g(d,T) and universal constants a,b>0 with a g(d,T)≤R*(d,T)≤b g(d,T) for all d,T≥1. Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
6577.answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate g(d,T) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.

context_blocks.title: One value does not reveal a direction
context_blocks.text: On the interval [−1,1], the convex losses f(x)=(1+x)/2 and h(x)=(1−x)/2 both equal 1/2 at x=0, but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

context_blocks.title: The benchmark is one fixed decision in hindsight
context_blocks.text: Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

context_blocks.title: Dimension remains a major gap
context_blocks.text: Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order d^(5/2)√T, apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as d√T. The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in [0,1]; an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

context_blocks.title: Normalization and computational cost
context_blocks.text: Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

context_blocks.title: Which newer results change the assumptions
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.

6578.definitions: S²={x∈ℝ³: x₁²+x₂²+x₃²=1}. The energy is E_N(x₁,…,x_N)=Σ_{i≠j}−ln‖x_i−x_j‖₂, counting ordered pairs; collisions have energy +∞. E_N* is the infimum over all N-tuples on S². ln is the natural logarithm and ‖·‖₂ is Euclidean distance. The algorithm is one finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants, independent of N. It has exact real registers and a finite-control tape machine with register copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, and branching on the sign of a register. Tape movements and each scalar arithmetic, comparison or copy operation have unit cost. Input is the integer N as an exact real value; output is a list of 3N real coordinates. Any finite tape/register storage used by the program is charged through its operations. There is no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, random sample or minimization oracle. Polynomial time is in N, not in log N. The inequality is a mathematical condition on the output; the algorithm need not evaluate the energy. This specifies the real-number computation convention in Smale’s problem; coordinates need not be rational and no bit-cost bound is asserted.
6578.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants C,K,k, fixed independently of N, with the stated running time and total-energy guarantee for every integer N≥2. A negative answer proves that no such program and constants exist. Failure of one construction, a lower bound for a restricted method, or energy estimates for finitely many cardinalities do not establish the negation.

Mathematical Problems for the Next Century
references.locator: Problem 7; real-number computation model and logarithmic excess energy.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance C ln N is an additive error in the total energy. It is small compared with its known expansion E_N*=(1/2−ln 2)N²−(N/2)ln N+aN+o(N), where a is a universal constant. Matching only the leading N² term, or even allowing a linear error, leaves far more uncertainty than the target permits. Uniform-looking points and good numerical values for finitely many N do not establish this error bound.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an O(√N ln N) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least 1−exp(−N ln N). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the √N scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

6581.title: Mansour’s conjecture with logarithmic accuracy dependence
6581.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
6581.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C>0 such that, for every n≥1, integer s≥2, Boolean function f:{−1,1}ⁿ→{−1,1} representable by a DNF with at most s terms, and ε∈(0,1/2], some family F⊆2^[n] satisfies |F|≤⌈s^{C log₂(1/ε)}⌉ and Σ_{S∉F} f̂(S)²≤ε?
6581.definitions: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of literals x_i=1 or x_i=−1; a satisfied formula has value +1 and an unsatisfied formula value −1. Term widths, overlaps, and the number of occurrences of a variable are unrestricted. On the uniform probability space {−1,1}ⁿ, χ_S(x)=∏_{i∈S}x_i, χ_∅=1, and f̂(S)=2^{−n}Σ_x f(x)χ_S(x). Parseval gives Σ_S f̂(S)²=1. Thus ε-concentration on F means that the polynomial g=Σ_{S∈F}f̂(S)χ_S has E[(f−g)²]≤ε. The coefficients are ordinary Walsh coefficients, not a basis adapted to a different distribution. The same C must work for all n,s,ε and f. This is an existence question about the spectrum; no efficient algorithm for finding F is part of the proposition.
6581.answer_criterion: An affirmative resolution proves the stated bound with one universal C. A negative resolution must show that for every C some admissible s,n,ε and DNF require more than ⌈s^{C log₂(1/ε)}⌉ coefficients to leave squared Fourier mass at most ε. A polynomial bound whose exponent has an unspecified dependence on ε would settle only the weaker fixed-accuracy form.
6581.why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.

importance.reason: A defining conjecture in Boolean function analysis and learning theory, connecting representation size to approximate Fourier sparsity and agnostic learning.

6581.status_note: Open in the strong logarithmic-accuracy form stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Fixed-error polynomial concentration, restricted DNF models, and generalized-basis learning results do not by themselves settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A DNF describes a function as a short list of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier expansion describes the same function through parity correlations. Mansour’s question asks whether a short description in the first language forces an approximately short description in the second. The number n of available variables may greatly exceed the number s of terms, yet the proposed number of relevant correlations depends only on s and the permitted error.

The approximation is measured in squared error under uniformly random inputs. It does not require exact agreement everywhere, and the approximating polynomial need not have Boolean outputs. Keeping the largest squared coefficients is the best approximation with that many Walsh characters. Consequently the question is a statement about how rapidly the sorted Fourier mass decays, independent of an algorithm’s ability to identify the important characters.

Sparsity and degree are different resources. A parity involving every variable has just one nonzero Fourier coefficient but has degree n. Conversely, restricting a polynomial to degree d can leave a number of possible coefficients that grows like n^d. A theorem saying that high-degree coefficients have little total mass therefore does not by itself give the requested bound, which must avoid such dependence on the ambient dimension.

Even one wide conjunction can have many nonzero coefficients exactly. This does not contradict the conjecture: if the conjunction fixes w distinct coordinates, its satisfying event has probability 2^{−w}. Approximating its ±1-valued function by the constant −1 incurs squared error 4·2^{−w}. Rare accepting terms can therefore produce an exactly dense spectrum while contributing very little approximation error. Combining many overlapping terms is where the simple observation stops being sufficient.

There are two common strengths of the named conjecture. The weaker one allows s^{K(ε)} coefficients for an arbitrary function K of the error. The stronger one in this saved record asks for K(ε)=O(log(1/ε)). O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explicitly distinguish these statements. The card preserves the stronger target instead of treating all polynomial concentration claims as interchangeable.

The connection to Fourier entropy explains that distinction. If the Fourier entropy were O(log s), Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal log(1/f̂(S)²) would capture all but ε of the mass on at most s^{O(1/ε)} coefficients. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture, combined with the influence bound for DNF, would supply such an entropy estimate. This implication gives the weaker form, but its exponent does not establish the logarithmic dependence required here.

Mansour’s classical general bound gives s^{O(log log s)} coefficients at fixed accuracy. Klivans–Lee–Wan proved polynomial concentration for a specified random-DNF model and for every fixed read number. These are substantial structural results, but randomness in the formula cannot be assumed in a worst-case statement about every DNF. Their final May 2010 revision corrects an earlier issue in the read-number argument.

Lecomte–Tan sharpen the fixed-accuracy general estimate to s^{O(log log k)}, where k bounds the number of terms containing a variable. Their stronger small-read theorem gives (s/ε)^{O(log(1/ε))} concentration for read number up to a stated roughly doubly logarithmic range. The explicit s/ε base should be retained when comparing accuracy parameters. Their work also explains how control of term covers improves Fourier estimates beyond a single global norm bound.

The learning consequences depend on access to the target. Through the agnostic-learning reduction described by Klivans–Lee–Wan, suitable sparse Fourier approximation yields efficient agnostic learning under the uniform distribution with membership queries, for fixed approximation accuracy. Such queries allow selected input points; they are stronger access than an ordinary stream of independently sampled labeled examples. This conjecture should not be advertised as automatically solving every version of passive DNF learning.

Recent neighboring results retain these distinctions. Han’s 2025 entropy estimate contains an additional sum involving individual influences, rather than the full conjectured constant times total influence. González–MacManus–Pereyra’s June 2026 revision proves FEI for further classes under structural separation conditions. Neither is a universal theorem with the strong DNF accuracy bound in the question.

Heidari–Khardon’s June 2026 revision studies generalized Fourier representations associated with Bayesian networks. Its DNF learning theorem uses membership queries and a restricted distributional model; its agnostic result concerns decision trees. These changes in basis, distribution and target class are mathematically meaningful, but they do not establish concentration of every DNF in the ordinary uniform Walsh basis used here.

6582.title: Equivalence of deterministic higher-order recursion schemes
6582.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, on every pair of finite deterministic higher-order recursion schemes G,H over the same finite ranked alphabet, halts and decides whether their possibly infinite value trees are exactly equal, including divergence leaves?
6582.definitions: Types are generated by o and τ→σ. A terminal a of rank r has type o→⋯→o with r arguments. A scheme has finitely many typed nonterminals, a start S:o, and exactly one rule F x₁⋯x_k→t for each F:τ₁→⋯→τ_k→o. The distinct parameters x_i have the indicated types; t:o is a well-typed applicative term made from terminals, nonterminals and those parameters. There is no pattern matching, test on constructor values, nondeterministic choice, or restriction called safety. To obtain the value at a node, unfold the head nonterminal with substitution until a terminal a is exposed, then repeat for its r ordered arguments. If no terminal is ever exposed, that node is a nullary ⊥ leaf. This defines a tree over the alphabet extended with ⊥. Equality means identical node domains and labels at every finite address in the ordered tree; evaluation-step counts are ignored. The order of o is 0 and ord(τ→σ)=max(ord(τ)+1,ord(σ)); the maximum nonterminal order is finite but part of the input. Inputs may have different orders. No time bound is imposed beyond halting on every valid pair.
6582.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer is a single effective decision procedure for all finite input orders, with a proof of termination and correctness on equal as well as unequal trees. A negative answer proves this decision problem undecidable. Decidable model checking of one generated tree, a bounded-order subclass, or a conditional reduction to another open problem is not a full resolution.
6582.why: A fundamental decidability boundary for comparing higher-order recursive computations: expressive tree generators admit strong verification procedures, while exact equality of two generated behaviors remains unresolved.

importance.reason: A central equivalence problem joining higher-order functional computation, infinite-tree semantics, and deterministic collapsible pushdown automata.

progress.text: Sénizergues establishes deterministic pushdown equivalence, giving the order-one recursion-scheme boundary described in the inherited survey.

6582.status_note: Open for unrestricted finite-order deterministic schemes with the exact tree semantics stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Conditional Horn reductions, model checking, probabilistic termination and higher-order polyregular functional equivalence do not by themselves settle it.

context_blocks.text: A finite recursive program can describe an infinite object without listing its nodes. The rule S→a S, for unary a, describes an endless chain of a labels. The two-rule system S→a T and T→a S describes exactly the same chain even though its internal call structure differs. This card asks whether such equality of the entire observable unfolding can always be decided when functions may also be passed as arguments.

The output is an uninterpreted constructor tree. A binary constructor named plus is merely a label with two ordered children; the model does not add the arithmetic equation plus(0,x)=x. Likewise, it does not include a program context allowed to inspect generated values. This narrow semantics matters because equivalence questions for richer programming languages can be undecidable for reasons absent from recursion schemes.

Divergence is also observable in a precise way. The rule S→S generates ⊥, while S→a S generates an infinite productive chain. A scheme S→b S c, with binary b and nullary c, can expose infinitely many labels despite never completing its left subtree. Head unfolding therefore differs from an evaluation convention that insists on fully evaluating every argument before producing a constructor.

At order zero, the generated trees are regular and equality can be checked by comparing finite state descriptions. At order one, the problem connects to deterministic pushdown-language equivalence, whose decidability follows from Sénizergues’s theorem. Allowing higher-order parameters makes the finite description much more expressive. The inherited Hague–Murawski–Ong–Serre paper identifies equivalence as a central remaining question.

That paper’s positive equivalence theorem concerns two kinds of representation: higher-order recursion schemes and collapsible pushdown automata generate the same tree class, with effective translations. It transfers the problem to language equivalence for deterministic collapsible pushdown automata. It does not give an algorithm that compares arbitrary trees represented in either formalism. The difference between representation equivalence and instance equivalence is essential here.

Powerful properties of a single tree are nevertheless decidable. Broadbent–Carayol–Ong–Serre provide effective model checking, logical reflection and selection for monadic second-order logic and the modal μ-calculus. Reflection can enrich node labels with the truth of a chosen logical property. Having this machinery does not automatically turn two unrelated infinite descriptions into one object in the same decidable class on which all corresponding nodes can be compared.

Jochems supplies a route through coinductive higher-order constrained Horn clauses. The translation represents the generated tree using predicates interpreted through a greatest model and creates separate positive and negative instances. A suitable semidecision procedure for the resulting coinductive problems would yield a decision procedure by interleaving the two searches. The needed semidecidability is left open, so this is a reduction rather than a completed decision algorithm.

The same work handles divergence constructively: it transforms a scheme so that each ⊥ leaf is replaced by an infinite chain over a fresh unary symbol. Equality is preserved and reflected. Thus treating divergence carefully need not restrict the question to an informal assumption that every program is productive. The present formulation keeps divergence explicit so readers can compare two given schemes without an unstated promise.

Recent results with similar terminology concern other targets. Bojańczyk–Fabiański–Stefański’s April 2026 undecidability theorem compares functions at higher-order types in the polyregular λ-calculus, a language with list-processing operations and extensional input/output semantics. Its theorem is not a stated undecidability result for the closed constructor-tree generators defined above. No reduction identifying the two decision problems is assumed here.

Dal Lago–Fiorillo–Pistone’s LICS 2026 work instead decides almost-sure termination for a typed subclass of probabilistic recursion schemes, using algebraic generating functions. That achievement concerns termination probabilities under additional type restrictions. The inherited question asks exact equality of deterministic value trees at unrestricted finite orders, and remains separate.

6583.title: Does weak normalization imply strong normalization for every pure type system?
6583.formal: For every pure type system (S,A,R) defined below, does weak normalization of every typable term imply strong normalization of every typable term?
6583.why: Normalization connects computation with the metatheory of typed proofs. This conjecture asks whether the pure-type-system rules turn the existence of a terminating computation for every typable term into termination under every reduction order.
6583.status_note: The primary statement and Mull’s 2023 paper leave the unrestricted conjecture open. A later-result and author-publication search on 11 September 2026 found no general proof or counterexample. The positive theorems impose additional PTS structure.

6583.definitions: S is a set of sorts, A⊆S×S is a set of axioms, and R⊆S×S×S is a set of product rules. Terms are finite expressions t ::= x | s | t u | λx:B.t | Πx:B.C, with s∈S and variables from a countably infinite set, modulo renaming bound variables. A context is a finite sequence of declarations of distinct variables. Typing is the least relation Γ⊢t:B generated by the following rules. Axiom: ∅⊢s:t when (s,t)∈A. Start: Γ,x:B⊢x:B when Γ⊢B:s and x is fresh. Weakening: Γ,x:C⊢t:B when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and x is fresh. Product: Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s₃ when Γ⊢B:s₁, Γ,x:B⊢C:s₂ and (s₁,s₂,s₃)∈R. Abstraction: Γ⊢λx:B.t:Πx:B.C when Γ,x:B⊢t:C and Γ⊢Πx:B.C:s for a sort s. Application: Γ⊢t u:C[u/x] when Γ⊢t:Πx:B.C and Γ⊢u:B. Conversion: Γ⊢t:C when Γ⊢t:B, Γ⊢C:s and B=βC. All substitutions avoid capture. A beta step contracts (λx:B.t)u to t[u/x] at any subterm, including inside annotations and product types. =β is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of those steps. A term is typable if Γ⊢t:B for some finite Γ,B. Weak normalization means that each typable term has some finite beta-reduction sequence ending in a term with no beta redex. Strong normalization means that no typable term starts an infinite beta-reduction sequence. Both predicates quantify over open as well as closed terms and over all their reduction choices. The sets S,A,R need not be finite, decidable or functional.
6583.answer_criterion: Prove that every pure type system in which all typable terms are weakly beta-normalizing is strongly beta-normalizing, or exhibit a pure type system that is weakly normalizing for every typable term but has a typable term admitting an infinite beta-reduction sequence.

context_blocks.text: A term can contain several reducible applications, so computation involves choices. Weak normalization says that some sequence reaches a normal form. Strong normalization says that every sequence of beta-reductions terminates. The conjecture asks whether these two system-wide properties coincide for all pure type systems, a common framework for typed lambda calculi.

The distinction is real for untyped terms. Let Ω=(λz.zz)(λz.zz). The term (λx.y)Ω reduces to y in one step if the outer application is chosen, but it can also reduce Ω forever. Thus it is weakly but not strongly normalizing. This only illustrates the distinction: a counterexample to the conjecture needs a pure type system whose entire collection of typable terms is weakly normalizing.

A pure type system specifies which sorts classify other sorts and which dependent function types may be formed, through its sets A and R. The common typing rules generate the resulting calculus. Familiar simply typed, polymorphic and dependent systems fit the framework, but the conjecture also covers unusual specifications, beyond established proof languages.

The global hypothesis concerns every typable term. Confluence cannot replace it: confluence says that two finite reductions can be joined, making normal forms unique when they exist. It does not prevent an infinite path from coexisting with a terminating path. The untyped example already separates these ideas.

Reduction here includes type annotations and components of dependent products. Termination of an implementation’s selected evaluation strategy therefore differs from strong normalization of the calculus. Results after erasing annotations, or for closed programs only, have a different scope from the property of every annotated typable term in every context.

Sørensen’s 1997 work proves the implication for specified classes of typed calculi. Barthe, Hatcliff and Sørensen extend it to a class of non-dependent pure type systems in 2001. Their structural hypotheses are substantive: the theorem does not claim to cover every non-dependent specification, let alone every dependent one. The TLCA list records these as partial results.

Mull’s TYPES 2022 paper, published in 2023, enlarges the known class using a translation preserving typability and infinite reduction paths while removing certain sorts and rules. The theorem includes some systems with dependent rules that earlier results did not cover. The author explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture; the translation’s structural hypotheses cannot be omitted.

A universal implication would connect the existence of normal forms with complete freedom of reduction order throughout this family of type theories. A counterexample would identify a system in which every term can finish, yet some legal choices continue forever. Either outcome would sharpen normalization arguments in proof checking and the metatheory of dependent types.

6584.title: The Li–Li undirected multiple-unicast conjecture
6584.formal: For every finite undirected network with positive rational edge capacities and independent unicast sessions, is the zero-error causal network-coding rate region, under the entropy-capacity convention below, equal to its fractional multicommodity-routing region?
6584.definitions: Let G=(V,E) be a finite connected undirected graph, with capacities c_e>0, and let (s_i,t_i), i=1,…,k, be ordered pairs of distinct vertices. Different pairs may share endpoints. Source s_i initially knows its own message M_i, uniformly distributed over a finite alphabet; the messages are mutually independent. A finite deterministic code specifies in advance a finite sequence of directed edge uses. Each transmitted symbol is a function of messages initially at its sender and symbols previously received there. Every t_i must recover M_i for every message tuple. Local computation and storage are unrestricted; nonlinear functions are permitted. Let X_{u→v} be the whole tuple sent from u to v on edge {u,v}, and measure Shannon entropy H in bits. For a scale b>0, the code supports r∈R_{≥0}^k when H(M_i)≥b r_i for all i and H(X_{u→v})+H(X_{v→u})≤b c_{uv} for every edge. Define C(G) as the closure in R^k of all such supported rate vectors, over all finite alphabets, codes and scales. This explicitly fixes the entropy formulation used in the cited network-coding literature, with exact decoding and capacity shared between directions; it is not a definition using two independent full-capacity arcs. Define R(G) by nonnegative real path flows f_{i,P}, for simple s_i-to-t_i paths P, satisfying Σ_P f_{i,P}≥r_i and Σ_{i,P:e∈P} f_{i,P}≤c_e. The target is C(G)=R(G) for every G and session list. No multicast destinations, correlated sources, initial side information about other messages, or computation of functions in place of message recovery is supplied.
6584.answer_criterion: Prove C(G)⊆R(G) for every specified network and session list; the reverse inclusion follows by routing and closure. Alternatively, exhibit a finite undirected instance with a coding-supported rate vector outside the closed routing polytope, together with a valid causal code and a proof of fractional-routing infeasibility. The latter can use a linear-programming dual certificate. Beating integral edge-disjoint paths, a particular routing algorithm, or a cut bound that is already larger than the routing optimum is insufficient. A multicast or directed-network advantage does not refute this unicast conjecture. A theorem about vanishing-error codes must be related explicitly to this zero-error entropy formulation.
6584.why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.

importance.reason: A central capacity conjecture whose resolution would clarify the power of network coding and influence circuit and data-structure lower bounds.

6584.status_note: The August 2026 primary papers explicitly leave the general conjecture unresolved. This card fixes causal zero-error coding with entropy capacities and closure of rates, as in the cited formal model. Restricted topology results, multicast gains and alternative error conventions are distinguished. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits x and y, it may send x⊕y; a receiver that already knows y can recover x. Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match the best coding rate for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide a necessary upper bound: information needed across a partition must cross its boundary. For multiple commodities, satisfying every cut constraint need not make the demands fractionally routable. Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval study the small K_{3,2} example with four same-side sessions. Its sparsity bound is one, while its maximum concurrent routing rate is 3/4; their entropy inequalities show that coding also cannot exceed 3/4. The gap between cuts and flows therefore does not by itself give a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that a counterexample would have consequences well beyond one small network. Any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family with a gap growing as a positive power of log |V|. A general logarithmic upper bound comes from multicommodity-flow and cut relationships. Thus even a modest strict separation would open the door to much larger asymptotic gains.

The conjecture is also connected to computation rather than communication alone. Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that it implies an Ω(n log n) lower bound for constant-degree Boolean circuits multiplying two n-bit integers. Their reduction turns a sufficiently small circuit into a forbidden network-coding advantage. This is a conditional circuit lower bound, not an already proved consequence of ordinary cut arguments.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.

6585.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
6585.formal: For every fixed integer c≥1, does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm A_c with the following guarantee? Given n≥2, a nonsingular rational n×n matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer 1≤p≤c·ceil(log_2 n), output a rational vector x̂ such that ||Ax̂−b||_2≤2^(−p)||b||_2 with probability at least 2/3. Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most c·ceil(log_2 n) binary digits, and the spectral condition number κ_2(A) is promised at most n^c. The worst-case running time must be O_c(m log^(d_c)n) for some constant d_c independent of the input.
6585.definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence n≤m≤n². The Euclidean norm is ||v||_2=(Σ_i v_i²)^(1/2), and κ_2(A)=σ_max(A)/σ_min(A), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here ε=2^(−p); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target. The output is the full list of n rational coordinates, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; every output bit is charged. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation.
6585.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6585.why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.

importance.reason: A fundamental input-size complexity question for one of the most widely used computational primitives, with meaningful positive results for structured classes and general reductions from apparently special systems.

progress.text: Spielman and Teng develop nearly linear algorithms for graph-structured and symmetric diagonally dominant systems; the expanded solver paper appears in SIAM J. Matrix Analysis and Applications in 2014.

The Simons workshop report is revised to reflect status through 20 August, retaining questions about extending scalable solvers and understanding finite-precision iterative methods. It does not give a universal nearly linear algorithm.

6585.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. This is an editorial, fully specified near-linear target in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime, not a named positive conjecture. The faster-than-matrix-multiplication problem has already been solved. The August 2026 report discusses broader scalable solvers but does not claim this universal guarantee; the simplicial-Laplacian reduction is not a general running-time lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Solving Ax=b is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all n² matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If x*=A^(-1)b, the elementary inequality ||x̂−x*||_2/||x*||_2≤κ_2(A)·||Ax̂−b||_2/||b||_2 relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, A=diag(1,δ), b=(1,δ) and x̂=(1,0) have residual δ while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of Õ(m^((ω−2)/(ω−1))n²) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For m=Õ(n), this becomes Õ(n^((3ω−4)/(ω−1))). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of ω. Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular n×n input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.

6587.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
6587.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
6587.formal: Do there exist a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph G=(V,E) and every integer 1≤k≤|V|, A(G,k) outputs a set S⊆V with |S|=k and |E(G[S])|≥OPT(G,k)/C, where OPT(G,k)=max_{T⊆V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|?
6587.definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. G[S] contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with n=|V| or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree 2|E(G[S])|/k, or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6587.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6587.why: Densest k-Subgraph is a basic test of how well algorithms can identify a concentrated combinatorial structure. Its unresolved approximation landscape influences many reductions and separates strong evidence of difficulty from the hardness consequences currently obtainable from P≠NP.

importance.reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.

6587.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.

context_blocks.text: The task asks for a fixed-size collection of vertices containing as many internal interactions as possible. The cardinality restriction is what turns an otherwise tractable density objective into a central approximation problem. Without a prescribed size, maximizing edges per vertex can be solved in polynomial time. Allowing at least k vertices also changes which solutions compete: a large moderately dense region may be a valid answer even when no comparably useful k-vertex portion can be extracted.

Exact optimization contains CLIQUE: a graph has a k-clique precisely when OPT(G,k)=k(k−1)/2. This observation alone gives almost no multiplicative approximation gap. A k-set missing only one possible edge is nearly optimal as k grows, even though it is not a clique. To rule out a constant-factor algorithm, a reduction must create a substantial separation between the best densities of its YES and NO instances, not merely a one-edge difference.

Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige and Vijayaraghavan achieve O(n^(1/4+ε)) approximation in n^O(1/ε) time for every fixed ε>0. Their method uses small tree patterns and a hierarchy of conditioned information to identify a dense region. The O(n^(1/4)) phrase in the paper’s title needs care: attaining that endpoint in their analysis takes quasipolynomial n^O(log n) time. Neither rate is a constant approximation.

There is substantial evidence against the target. Manurangsi proves that ETH rules out even approximation within n^(1/(log log n)^a), for a universal constant a>0. ETH asserts that 3SAT has no 2^o(N)-time algorithm on N variables. This is a stronger assumption than P≠NP; the result therefore already excludes every fixed constant under ETH, while leaving the weaker-assumption hardness problem unresolved. Its YES instances can contain a k-clique, a property called perfect completeness.

Semidefinite-programming lower bounds supply a different kind of evidence. Bhaskara, Charikar, Guruswami, Vijayaraghavan and Zhou construct polynomial integrality gaps for strong hierarchies of relaxations. A relaxation can assign a large fractional or vector-valued objective even when no genuine k-set has comparable density. Such a gap limits approximation guarantees obtained from that relaxation, but it is not a theorem excluding every polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm.

Chuzhoy, Dalirrooyfard, Grinberg and Tan propose a 2-CSP hardness conjecture that would imply NP-hardness of approximating Densest k-Subgraph within 2^((log n)^ε) for some ε>0. Their paper also connects its approximability to graph partitioning, dense coloring and bounded-crossing subgraphs. Some connections use quasipolynomial reductions, so they should not be read as constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences. The conjectural premise remains a real part of the hardness claim.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi’s May 2026 paper still reports that no NP-hardness of approximation is known for Densest k-Subgraph even at factor 1.001. They show that the absence of any constant-factor DkS algorithm implies a (3/2−ε) barrier for the at-least-k density problem. This transfers a hypothetical negative answer to a neighboring objective; the neighboring problem’s known 2-approximation does not answer this card.

An AAAI 2026 result by Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar gives an exact continuous penalization reformulation and an efficient nonconvex proximal-gradient method. Exactness concerns the relationship between optima of the formulations. It does not mean the method finds a global optimum, or even a fixed approximation ratio, on every graph in polynomial time. The distinction explains how useful practical progress can coexist with the unresolved worst-case guarantee.

6588.title: A polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
6588.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
6588.formal: Do there exist constants a≥1 and C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance with k terminals, outputs a feasible subgraph of cost at most a(log₂(k+2))^C times optimum with probability at least 2/3?
6588.definitions: An instance consists of a finite directed graph G=(V,E), a root r∈V, a nonempty terminal set T⊆V∖{r} with k=|T|, and nonnegative rational arc costs c_e given exactly in binary. Every terminal is promised reachable from r; this can also be checked in polynomial time, with infeasibility reported otherwise. A feasible solution is an arc subset F⊆E such that (V,F) contains a directed path from r to every t∈T. Its cost is Σ_{e∈F}c_e, counting an arc once even if many paths use it. OPT is the minimum such cost. The algorithm must output a feasible subset on every execution and satisfy the approximation guarantee on every instance with probability at least 2/3 over its internal randomness. Its bit running time on every execution is bounded by one fixed polynomial in the entire input encoding length, including cost bits. The constants a,C and the polynomial are independent of n=|V|, k and the costs. If OPT=0, the successful output must also have zero cost. Local computation is ordinary uniform classical computation without advice or free optimization oracles. There is no planarity, acyclicity, bounded depth, bounded treewidth, metric, or supplied fractional-solution promise. The word tree refers to the optimization problem: any feasible subgraph may be returned, and redundant edges can be removed.
6588.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm and fixed constants satisfying these bounds, or prove that no such randomized polynomial-time algorithm exists. An O(k^ε)-approximation for every separately fixed ε>0, a polylogarithmic approximation taking quasipolynomial time, or a guarantee on a restricted graph class is partial progress. A gap for a particular LP relaxation limits that relaxation, not every algorithm. A hardness result ruling out only some smaller powers of log k does not exclude all fixed powers and therefore does not refute this proposition.
6588.why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.

importance.reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.

progress.text: Classical directed Steiner approximation algorithms give O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0 in polynomial time.

Planar and quasipolynomial algorithms do not satisfy this card. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is O(k^ε) for every fixed ε>0, from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting ε to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li obtain an O(log² k/log log k)-approximation in quasipolynomial time. Their techniques combine a structured reduction with a hierarchy of strengthened linear relaxations and dependent rounding. This establishes that a good approximation exists at a slower time scale. The requested advance is to achieve some polylogarithmic factor with a fixed polynomial running-time exponent; matching the sharper quasipolynomial factor is not required.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity x_e for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most x_e on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including Ω(√k) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The inherited Laekhanukit reference requires careful version tracking. Its December 2024 general claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, presents itself as a rectification restricted to a relatively integral fractional solution: each terminal flow on an edge is either zero or the entire purchased capacity. The record still displays the earlier withdrawal comment about a reachability-proof error. This card treats the later restricted statement as a reported claim, not an established general approximation; finding an appropriate fractional solution is an additional requirement.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time O(log k)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by O(log² k). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s July 2026 work extends planar results to length-constrained network design. Its guarantees are bicriteria: they approximate cost while allowing an O(log k) multiplicative violation of the path-length constraint. The paper explicitly retains the general Directed Steiner Tree approximation question as open. Removing a length constraint or changing the objective does not remove the planarity hypothesis needed by those algorithms.
