6589.title: The 4/3 conjecture for the metric TSP subtour relaxation
6589.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
6589.formal: Let Γ=sup_{n≥3,c} OPT_TSP(c)/OPT_LP(c), where c ranges over all metrics on n labeled points and OPT_LP is the subtour relaxation defined below. Is Γ=4/3?
6589.definitions: For V={1,…,n} and E={{u,v}:u≠v}, a metric has c_uu=0, c_uv=c_vu>0 for u≠v, and c_uv≤c_uw+c_wv. Costs are arbitrary real numbers; no Euclidean embedding is assumed. OPT_TSP is the minimum sum of edge costs on a Hamiltonian cycle of the complete undirected graph. For S⊆V, δ(S) contains edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and x(F)=Σ_{e∈F}x_e. Define OPT_LP=min Σ_e c_e x_e subject to x(δ({v}))=2 for every v, x(δ(S))≥2 for every nonempty proper S⊊V, and 0≤x_e≤1 for every e. The LP is feasible and has positive optimum. The supremum ranges over every finite size, not one fixed n. This is the symmetric metric subtour-LP integrality gap, not an approximation ratio measured only against OPT_TSP, an asymmetric TSP relaxation, or a restricted geometric metric.
6589.answer_criterion: Known constructions establish Γ≥4/3. Thus an affirmative resolution proves OPT_TSP(c)≤(4/3)OPT_LP(c) for every finite metric instance. A negative resolution gives an instance with ratio strictly greater than 4/3, or proves such an instance exists. A supremum need not be attained to make the question meaningful. Improving an algorithm’s upper bound while it remains above 4/3 is progress, not a resolution.
6589.why: The exact strength of the principal relaxation for a canonical optimization problem, joining polyhedral structure, probabilistic rounding and approximation. A resolution would explain a longstanding gap between fractional connectivity and integral tours.

importance.reason: A defining integrality-gap conjecture in combinatorial optimization with consequences for LP rounding and the limits of metric TSP approximation methods.

6589.status_note: The general 4/3 equality remains open through the primary-source review of 11 September 2026. The established explicit upper bound recorded here is 3/2−2.18·10^{−34}; a September 2 preprint claims a further small improvement, clearly separated from verified literature. Restricted-class theorems and finite-size verification do not resolve the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.text: The relaxation allows fractional edge purchases while retaining two elementary properties of every tour: each vertex has degree two, and every nontrivial cut is crossed at least twice. It therefore knows much more than a disconnected cycle-cover relaxation, but its feasible points need not be convex combinations of Hamiltonian cycles. The conjecture asks for the exact worst loss caused by that remaining freedom.

For example, a feasible fractional vector may put positive weight on several alternative connections at one vertex without choosing a single predecessor and successor. The cut inequalities ensure aggregate connectivity, yet they do not force these local choices to assemble into one integral cycle. The proposed factor 4/3 says that, in a metric, repairing all such inconsistencies never costs more than one third of the fractional optimum.

The metric assumption is what makes shortcutting possible. If a connected Eulerian multigraph visits a vertex several times, replacing a detour by the direct edge between its endpoints does not increase cost. One can consequently search for a suitably cheap Eulerian structure rather than construct a Hamiltonian cycle at every intermediate step. This observation explains why spanning trees and parity correction recur in approximation algorithms for the problem.

A minimum spanning tree followed by a minimum-cost matching on its odd-degree vertices yields the classical 3/2 guarantee. Wolsey’s analysis measures both components against the LP: the tree costs at most the fractional optimum, and the matching at most half that value. The inherited July 2026 paper recalls this argument before studying a particular randomized refinement.

An algorithmic ratio and an integrality-gap ratio must use the correct denominator. A guarantee cost≤α·OPT_TSP does not establish OPT_TSP≤α·OPT_LP, since the fractional optimum can be smaller. Karlin–Klein–Oveis Gharan’s FOCS 2022 result explicitly supplies an LP-relative guarantee below 3/2, extending the earlier approximation breakthrough. It is this later theorem that directly improves the general gap bound.

The modern approach samples a spanning tree from a distribution constrained by fractional edge marginals, then corrects its parity. Tree cost and parity-repair cost interact, so treating the two separately can lose the desired saving. Gurvits–Klein–Leake strengthen probability estimates using capacities of real stable polynomials. Their Lemma 4.5 is explicitly LP-relative and yields the certified bound Γ≤3/2−2.18·10^{−34}. The small constant reflects a worst-case proof, not a claim that practical tours are that close to 3/2.

A class can have a better integrality gap than the worst ratio of a particular algorithm on it. Jin–Klein–Williamson prove the 4/3 bound for half-integral cycle-cut instances using a specialized construction. Half-integral means that nonzero fractional coordinates are 1/2 or 1, with an additional restriction on the hierarchy of tight cuts. This result does not cover every half-integral instance, still less every subtour solution.

Their July 2026 paper, which supplied the inherited reference, proves a 10/7 guarantee for the maximum-entropy algorithm on that same restricted class. Since 10/7 exceeds 4/3, it improves understanding of the chosen algorithm rather than improving the already-known class gap. The authors also identify examples giving a lower bound of 11/8 on the algorithm’s performance. Such an algorithm-specific obstruction cannot refute the conjecture about the cheapest possible tour.

Two complementary approaches restrict the fractional solution in other ways. Villa–Vercesi–Barta–Mastrolilli prove the 4/3 bound when an optimal solution has at most n+6 nonzero components, combining structural reasoning and computation. This is a support-size condition, not a theorem for every instance on at most n+6 vertices. Larger support remains outside its stated guarantee.

Cook–Hougardy–Petrich’s September 8, 2026 revision reports exact verification for all metric instances through n=16 and for half-integral extreme points through n=18. It also repairs omissions in earlier extreme-point lists. This is stronger evidence than sampling finitely many random metrics, because the computation organizes the relevant polyhedral cases. It still leaves unbounded n, and the catalogue has not rerun that enumeration.

A September 2 preprint by Zhao Song claims a larger universal saving, ε★>2.05522·10^{−30}, through a refined maximum-entropy analysis. Its main theorem is explicitly relative to OPT_LP. The statement was checked, but the lengthy proof and numerical certificate were not independently verified here, so the value is recorded as a recent claim rather than silently replacing the established bound. Even if confirmed, it would remain far above the requested ratio 4/3.

6590.definitions: A directed metric is a function c:V×V→R≥0 with c(i,i)=0 and c(i,k)≤c(i,j)+c(j,k) for all i,j,k. Symmetry is not required, and distinct vertices may have zero distance. The complete directed graph has one arc (i,j) for each i≠j and no loops. A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex once before returning to its start; its cost is the sum of its n arc costs. OPT_ATSP(c) is the minimum over all such cycles. For S⊆V, δ⁺(S)={(i,j):i∈S,j∉S} and δ⁻(S)={(i,j):i∉S,j∈S}; for a set of arcs F write x(F)=Σ_(i,j)∈F x_ij. LP_ATSP(c) minimizes Σ_i≠j c(i,j)x_ij over real variables x_ij≥0 subject to x(δ⁺({v}))=x(δ⁻({v}))=1 for every v, and x(δ⁺(S))≥1 for every nonempty proper S⊊V. The degree equalities imply x(δ⁺(S))=x(δ⁻(S)), so an additional incoming-cut inequality would be redundant. No integrality restriction is placed on x. The feasible set is nonempty and compact; both optima are attained. The inequality, rather than division by LP_ATSP(c), also covers zero-cost instances. For positive LP value, the integrality ratio is OPT_ATSP(c)/LP_ATSP(c), and the overall gap is its supremum over all n and directed metrics. The question is a universal comparison of optimum values, without a running-time restriction on finding the tour. It concerns closed tours, not a prescribed-start/end path.
6590.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed factor-2 inequality for every finite directed metric and every size, or exhibit a finite directed metric with a rigorously proved strict violation. An affirmative answer need not attain ratio 2 on a finite instance: known families approach 2. An approximation algorithm proved only relative to the true tour optimum, or a result restricted to a subset of LP extreme points, does not establish the universal LP inequality.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The question asks whether converting the best fractional cost into an actual tour ever entails a factor larger than two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in {0,1/2,1}. An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical 4/3 conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

6592.title: Is k-Clique fixed-parameter tractable, equivalently FPT=W[1]?
6592.formal: Do there exist a total computable function f:ℕ→ℕ, a constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most f(k)(n+2)ᶜ on every input? Equivalently, is FPT=W[1]?
6592.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on [n], encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with 0≤k≤n, encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; k=0 is a yes-instance. Inputs with k>n are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in f(k)Nᶜ time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of W[1] is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic f(k)Nᶜ-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is W[1]-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.
6592.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6592.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: Downey and Fellows develop the W-hierarchy and the completeness framework that makes parameterized Clique a canonical target for the FPT-versus-W[1] question.

6592.status_note: Explicitly presented as the central open conjecture in Bottesch’s primary paper and the parameterized-algorithms textbook. Research through 10 September 2026 located no proof of equality or separation. Conditional lower bounds and improved fixed-k algorithms are recorded with their distinct quantifiers.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, 2^{2^k}n³ meets the requested form, while n^{k/10} does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If P=NP then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus FPT≠W[1] is a stronger separation conjecture than P≠NP in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every W[1] problem in FPT time. This is why a W[1]-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out f(k)n^{o(k)} algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is W[1]-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove FPT≠W[1].

6595.title: Does the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis hold?
6595.formal: For every real ε∈(0,1), does there exist an integer k≥3 such that no deterministic algorithm decides k-SAT on n variables and input length L in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}L^c)$ for any fixed constant c? Here k is fixed independently of n and L. This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).
6595.definitions: A k-SAT input is an explicitly encoded conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most k literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Variables are relabeled consecutively and n counts the distinct variables actually present; L counts the full binary formula encoding, including literal indices and delimiters. The decision is exact satisfiability, with no promise about clause density, the number of satisfying assignments, or how the formula was generated. Empty clauses make the input unsatisfiable, and the empty conjunction is satisfiable. Running time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time. For a fixed k, the algorithm, polynomial exponent, and hidden constant may depend on k and ε, but not on the individual formula. Define sₖ=inf{α≥0 : k-SAT has an O(2^{αn}Lᶜ)-time deterministic algorithm for some constant c}. SETH equivalently asserts limₖ→∞sₖ=1; monotonicity follows because k-SAT is a restriction of (k+1)-SAT. Polynomial factors are retained explicitly so reading the input is allowed even when clauses are repeated. No advice, oracle, random bits, or quantum computation is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6595.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6595.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates for k-SAT and their growth with clause width, using critical clauses and sparsification.

The parameterized-algorithms textbook gives explicit deterministic definitions of ETH and SETH and separately discusses their randomized analogues.

6595.status_note: The cited primary sources state SETH as an open hypothesis. Research through 10 September 2026 found no deterministic all-width constant-saving refutation or unrestricted proof. Bounds for a fixed width, random instances, restricted solvers, or unique satisfiability are not recorded as resolutions.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all 2ⁿ assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially 2ⁿ time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A 2^{0.9n}-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds 2^{(1−1/k)n} would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond P≠NP, which by itself allows intermediate running times such as 2^{√n}.

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Recent work continues to sharpen small-width algorithms. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports a slightly improved randomized PPSZ bound for general 3-SAT, distinguished from its better bound under a unique-solution promise. Both the fixed width and use of randomness keep this improvement outside the deterministic, all-width saving required to refute the present statement.

6601.title: Do some tautologies require superpolynomial Extended Frege proofs?
6601.formal: Is Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every constants C>0 and c≥1, is there a propositional tautology φ whose shortest Extended Frege proof has bit length greater than C(|φ|+2)ᶜ? Here |φ| is the bit length of the explicitly written formula.
6601.definitions: Fix Boolean formulas over ¬ and →, with → interpreted as material implication and variable indices encoded in binary. Use the Frege axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), together with modus ponens from A and A→B to B. An Extended Frege proof of φ may additionally introduce an abbreviation variable e by the two extension axioms e→θ and θ→e. Here e is fresh, absent from φ, θ, and every preceding line; θ uses original variables of φ and previously introduced extension variables. Extensions are thus acyclic definitions. Other proof lines are axiom instances or applications of modus ponens, and the last line must be φ, with no extension variables. Lines may cite and reuse earlier lines arbitrarily: proofs are not required to be trees. Proof size is the full binary encoding length of all explicitly written formulas, extension definitions, and inference references; there is no depth or per-line-size restriction. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. This fixed presentation is polynomially equivalent to the usual Extended Frege systems, so changing a standard finite Frege basis does not change polynomial boundedness. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6601.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6601.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize propositional proof systems, polynomial simulation, and Extended Frege, proving robustness under the choice of standard rules and connectives.
Strong lower bounds emerge for weaker systems, while even unrestricted Frege lower bounds remain open. EF adds the ability to abbreviate and share formulas.

Pich and Santhanam establish conditional routes from EF proof lower bounds to P≠NP. The assumptions include formally provable computational statements; the result is not an unconditional EF lower bound.
Hsieh, Jain, Li, and Mathialagan obtain SNARGs for NP from derandomization, LWE, SXDH, and a bounded-arithmetic unprovability assumption concerning certificates of EF-hard tautologies.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations in extended polynomial calculus with a square-root rule. Its Section 1 explicitly distinguishes this from propositional Frege and EF lower bounds.

6601.status_note: Explicitly open in the primary proof-complexity sources, including Alekseev’s June 2026 journal article. Research through 10 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution for unrestricted Extended Frege. The algebraic and conditional results cited here retain their stated scope.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If NP≠coNP, every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of NP≠coNP.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to P≠NP under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

6602.title: Superpolynomial AC⁰[p]-Frege lower bounds
6602.formal: For every fixed prime p, does there exist a family of propositional tautologies (τ_{p,n})_{n≥1}, constructible in time polynomial in n, whose encoded lengths lie between n and n^O(1), such that each τ_{p,n} is a DNF and, for every fixed proof-line depth d and every constant r>0, infinitely many n have the following property: every depth-at-most-d Frege proof with MOD_p connectives of τ_{p,n} has total encoded size greater than n^r? The proof system and depth convention are specified below; the family may depend on p but not on d or r.
6602.definitions: A tautology evaluates to true on every Boolean assignment. A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. Fix a conventional sound, implicationally complete finite Frege calculus F over constants 0,1 and connectives NOT, AND, OR. A proof is a sequence of formulas, each a substitution instance of an axiom or obtained from earlier lines by a rule of F; earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily. Extend the language and rules as F(MOD_p) in Krajíček §5: MOD_{p,j}(A_1,…,A_t) is true precisely when the number of true arguments is j modulo p, for 0≤j<p. Besides F’s rules with formulas from this language, permit the empty-list axioms MOD_{p,0}() and NOT MOD_{p,j}() for j≠0, and all instances of MOD_{p,j}(Γ,A) ↔ [(MOD_{p,j}(Γ) AND NOT A) OR (MOD_{p,j−1}(Γ) AND A)], with j−1 taken modulo p and Γ any list of formulas. Constants and variables have depth zero; NOT and MOD increase depth by one, while consecutive ANDs, or consecutive ORs, are flattened and together count as one layer. Every line, including instantiated axioms, obeys the bound d. Proof size counts all symbols and encoded variable indices across all lines, together with rule annotations. Proofs are ordinary Frege proofs, without extension-variable definition axioms; they need not be tree-like or have bounded derivation-graph depth. Standard choices of F give equivalent systems up to polynomial overhead and a constant depth adjustment, immaterial when every fixed d is quantified.
6602.answer_criterion: Exhibit the uniform tautology families and prove the stated superpolynomial proof-size lower bounds, or refute their existence. The tautology condition must itself be established: a formula that has no short proof because it is false is not a hard tautology. A lower bound only for bounded derivation depth, regular proofs, a restricted algebraic subsystem or Boolean circuits alone does not settle this question. A result for one prime is a major partial answer; this single card groups the full fixed-prime frontier rather than duplicating it for each modulus.
6602.why: A central frontier in propositional proof complexity: current methods can handle ordinary bounded-depth reasoning but still cannot establish explicit superpolynomial lower bounds once modular counting is available. The problem tests how circuit lower-bound ideas can constrain entire deductions.

importance.reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.

6602.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary sources retain modular Frege lower bounds as open. ITCS 2026.99 does not prove that its hard-to-prove candidates are tautologies. ECCC TR26-018 restricts derivation depth or proves a polynomial size bound; TR26-070 treats a restricted algebraic certificate representation. None establishes the fully specified tautology families and unrestricted derivation size lower bounds requested here.

context_blocks.text: Proof complexity measures how long a formal explanation of a tautology must be. A short conclusion can require a much longer sequence of intermediate deductions. Restricting the depth of each intermediate formula limits the expressive power of individual statements while still allowing a long derivation and arbitrary reuse of earlier facts. Modular gates add compact statements about counts modulo p, such as parity when p=2. Krajíček gives the explicit modular axiom presentation used in this card.

The corresponding problem without modular gates has been solved. Ajtai’s work gives superpolynomial lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle in bounded-depth Frege, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo strengthen these to exponential bounds. Their argument uses restrictions adapted to the combinatorics of partial matchings. Permitting modular counting defeats the direct extension of that approach: a short parity statement can remain meaningful after many ordinary variables have been fixed.

Circuit complexity provides an analogy but not a solution. Razborov and Smolensky establish lower bounds for constant-depth Boolean circuits with prime modular gates. A proof, however, is a sequence of related formulas, and every tautology itself computes the constant true function. Showing that some nonconstant function requires a large circuit therefore does not directly force long proofs of tautologies. The February 2026 work of Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov explicitly identifies this remaining gap between circuit and proof lower bounds.

Resolution over parities is a much weaker subsystem whose lines are disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. Efremenko and Itsykson’s CCC 2025 work develops amortized closure and strengthens lifting lower bounds for restricted-depth parity-resolution refutations. The restriction there concerns the number of inference steps along a path in the derivation graph. That is different from the constant logical depth of each formula in AC⁰[p]-Frege. A long chain of shallow formulas remains allowed in the present question.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov’s February 2026 lifting theorem gives derivation depth Ω(w²/log S) for size-S parity-resolution proofs when the underlying CNF needs resolution width w. It also gives a pure quadratic size lower bound. These are meaningful advances, but a quadratic bound is polynomial, and a tradeoff requiring sufficiently deep proofs still permits polynomial-size proofs with large derivation depth. Neither gives the superpolynomial unrestricted proof-size target here.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret’s ITCS 2026 result studies explicit DNF formulas expressing the difficulty of proving certain algebraic circuit lower bounds. They show that these formulas do not all have polynomial-size AC⁰[p]-Frege proofs. The unresolved point is whether the formulas are tautologies: the theorem leaves open the possibility that some are simply false. They provide a conditional route to tautologicity through hardness of proving properties related to tensor rank. This separates two obligations that a completed lower-bound construction must satisfy.

Algebraic proof systems offer another route, but their representation restrictions matter. Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret’s May 2026 work gives hard CNF instances for a fragment of the Ideal Proof System represented by read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs. It overcomes the obstacle that earlier lower bounds in that line concerned purely algebraic, non-Boolean instances. It does not remove the restricted representation of certificates or establish lower bounds for full modular Frege.

The quantifiers exclude a fixed-degree lower bound such as n¹⁰ and require failure of every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth. They also keep the target formulas short and efficiently constructible, so hardness cannot come from writing an exponentially large conclusion or searching indefinitely for an unnamed formula. Resolving this frontier would extend lower-bound methods to formal reasoning that can perform modular counting, an ability missing from ordinary bounded-depth Frege.

6603.title: Log-rank conjecture for deterministic two-party communication
6603.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
6603.formal: Do there exist universal constants C>0 and k≥1 such that every total Boolean function f:X×Y→{0,1}, on arbitrary nonempty finite sets X,Y, satisfies $D(f)\le C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k$, where r(f) is the real rank of its 0/1 communication matrix and D(f) is its deterministic communication complexity?
6603.definitions: Alice receives x∈X and Bob receives y∈Y. Both know the complete function f and the protocol. They exchange bits interactively; each next transmitted bit is a deterministic function of the sender’s own input and the previous transcript. A binary protocol tree specifies whose turn it is, and every leaf has a Boolean output that must equal f(x,y) for every input pair reaching it. D(f) is the minimum, over all such exact protocols, of the maximum number of transmitted bits on an input pair. The number of rounds and the local computation are unrestricted; protocol description length is not charged. The communication matrix M_f has rows X, columns Y, and entry f(x,y); r(f)=rank_R(M_f) is ordinary matrix rank over the real numbers. The +2 makes the statement unambiguous for rank zero or one. The same constants C,k must work for all matrix dimensions and all functions. There are no undefined entries, input promises, random bits, quantum messages, approximation errors, or restrictions to one-way protocols. Sign rank and approximate rank are different parameters.
6603.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6603.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

importance.reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.

progress.text: Lovász and Saks formulate the conjecture relating real rank and deterministic communication; the 2026 equivalent-formulations paper gives the original attribution and related graph versions.

Göös, Pitassi, and Watson establish nearly quadratic lower bounds in log-rank, along with separations involving communication partition number.
Sudakov and Tomon improve the universal upper bound to O(√r). The 2023 preprint is published online in 2024 and in Mathematical Programming volume 212 in 2025.

Song reports an explicit lower bound Ω((log r)²/log log r) via alphabet-preserving lifting. The card records this as a preprint refinement, not an independently certified new universal separation record.
The CCC 2026 version of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley gives the O(r log r) signed-rectangle decomposition and equivalent formulations. It explicitly leaves the general conjecture open.

6603.status_note: Explicitly open in the August 2026 CCC version of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley. Checked through 10 September 2026. The established general upper bound is O(√r); recent fixed-polynomial lower-bound refinements and signed-decomposition equivalences do not settle the conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most 2ᵈ leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle A×B. Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents M_f as a sum of at most 2ᵈ rank-one matrices. Consequently log₂r(f)≤D(f) when r(f)≥1. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an O(√r log r) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting O(√r) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.
Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint revisits the construction without first converting its pointer alphabet to Boolean bits and reports a more precise lower bound Ω((log r)²/log log r). This still has a fixed polynomial exponent and therefore supports no refutation of log-rank.

A recent equivalent formulation isolates the role of cancellation more sharply. Hambardzumyan, Lovett, and Shirley show that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of O(r log r) rectangle indicator matrices. The open task can then be expressed as converting such signed decompositions into positive disjoint rectangle decompositions with quasipolynomial growth. This theorem supplies a new formulation, while the needed conversion remains unresolved.

6604.title: The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
6604.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
6604.formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant C>0 such that, for every integer n≥1 and every Boolean function f:{−1,1}ⁿ→{−1,1}, H(f)≤C I(f), where H(f) is the base-two Shannon entropy of its squared Fourier coefficients and I(f) is its total influence under the uniform distribution, as defined below?
6604.definitions: Write [n]={1,…,n}. For S⊆[n], let χ_S(x)=∏_{i∈S}x_i, with χ_∅=1, and let f̂(S)=2⁻ⁿ∑_{x∈{−1,1}ⁿ}f(x)χ_S(x). Put q_S=f̂(S)²; Parseval gives ∑_S q_S=1. Define H(f)=∑_S q_S log₂(1/q_S), with a zero summand when q_S=0. If x is uniform and x^{⊕i} differs only by flipping coordinate i, define I_i(f)=Pr[f(x)≠f(x^{⊕i})] and I(f)=∑_{i=1}ⁿ I_i(f)=∑_S |S|q_S. All Boolean functions are quantified, without circuit-size, monotonicity, balance, or efficient-computability assumptions. The same C must work for all dimensions and all functions. Constant functions have H(f)=I(f)=0 and satisfy the non-strict inequality.
6604.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6604.why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.

importance.reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.

progress.text: Friedgut and Kalai propose the conjecture; the historical attribution and its applications are described by O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou.
The conjecture is verified for symmetric functions and read-once decision trees.

6604.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 primary paper explicitly retains classical FEI as open and proves only specified classes. The August 2026 disproof is of the quantum extension. No classical resolution was found in the checked sources; the formulation uses Shannon entropy, uniform measure and scalar Boolean functions throughout.

context_blocks.text: The Fourier expansion expresses a Boolean rule as a linear combination of parity tests on subsets of its inputs. Squaring the coefficients produces a probability distribution on these subsets. Its entropy measures how dispersed that distribution is; total influence measures the expected size of a subset sampled from it. The conjecture says that the Boolean constraint forces the first quantity to be at most a constant times the second, even though there are exponentially many possible subsets.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy log₂ n but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function g(x)=(x₁+⋯+x_n)/√n, which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

A useful consequence would be spectral concentration: for any 0<δ<1, all but δ of the Fourier mass could be captured by at most 2^{C I(f)/δ} coefficients. This follows by applying Markov’s inequality to the surprisal log₂(1/q_S) of a random spectral subset. It supplies a quantitative connection between stability under individual bit flips and approximation by a short linear combination of parities. The dependence on δ is essential; the claim is not an accuracy-independent support bound.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou establish the conjecture for symmetric Boolean functions and for functions computed by read-once decision trees. Their paper also explains the connection to learning DNF formulas: the conjecture would imply polynomial Fourier concentration for a DNF with polynomially many terms, at each fixed approximation accuracy. This is a structural learning-theory consequence, rather than an assertion that arbitrary Boolean functions become efficiently learnable.

A general bound proved by Han is H(f)≤O(I(f)+∑_i I_i(f) log(1/I_i(f))). The extra term records how influence is distributed across coordinates. It can exceed a constant multiple of I(f), so this does not settle the conjecture. The December 2025 revision adds an acknowledgement of related earlier work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. Bounds on min-entropy concern the largest Fourier coefficient alone and must not be substituted for a Shannon-entropy bound.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s June 2026 revision verifies additional classes, including δ-tribes and functions with specified separation properties. Their method splits on selected coordinates and stops at restrictions already satisfying FEI. It also demonstrates failure of a stronger sufficient inequality when the splitting coordinate is chosen badly. Those examples do satisfy FEI when handled with a suitable coordinate, so they expose a limitation of that inductive route rather than a counterexample to the conjecture.

Slote’s August 2026 preprint disproves a quantum analogue using Hermitian unitary operators with flat, very large Pauli expansions. For the constructed degree-d operators, the spectral entropy grows quadratically in d while the influence grows linearly. These are quantum Boolean functions, not scalar maps on the classical Boolean cube. The result makes the distinction between the two settings concrete and does not provide a classical counterexample.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.

6605.title: The Aaronson–Ambainis influential-variable conjecture
6605.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
6605.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant C≥1 such that, for all integers n≥1 and 1≤d≤n and every real multilinear polynomial f of degree at most d satisfying 0≤f(x)≤1 for every x∈{−1,1}^n, some coordinate i satisfies Inf_i(f)≥(Var(f)/d)^C?
6605.definitions: All expectations use the uniform distribution on {−1,1}^n. Write f(x)=Σ_{S⊆[n]} f̂(S)∏_{j∈S}x_j, with f̂(S)=E_x[f(x)∏_{j∈S}x_j]; degree at most d means f̂(S)=0 when |S|>d. Let x^{⊕i} be x with just coordinate i negated. Define Var(f)=E[(f−E f)²]=Σ_{S≠∅}f̂(S)² and Inf_i(f)=E[(f(x)−f(x^{⊕i}))²]/4=Σ_{S∋i}f̂(S)². This is squared L₂ influence, with the factor 1/4 fixed explicitly. The pointwise range restriction holds on the entire cube, not merely with high probability. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers; no sparsity, coefficient-size, block structure, Boolean-valued-output or quantum-realizability promise is imposed. C must be independent of n,d,f and its variance. Constant polynomials satisfy the inequality trivially with both sides zero. The one-power notation is a normalized version of a polynomial lower bound in variance and inverse degree; because Var(f)≤1/4, fixed positive prefactors can be absorbed by increasing C.
6605.answer_criterion: Prove one universal exponent C works for every admissible polynomial, or show that for every proposed C there is an admissible polynomial of positive variance for which every coordinate has influence smaller than (Var(f)/d)^C. Refuting one particular exponent is insufficient to refute existence of some universal exponent. An exponential-in-degree influence bound, a theorem only after randomly fixing coordinates, or a result for a restricted subclass is partial progress.
6605.why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.

importance.reason: Connects a basic dimension-independent influence bound to almost-everywhere classical simulation of quantum queries, bringing Boolean analysis and quantum complexity together.

6605.status_note: The 4 September 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves the unrestricted Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture open. Recent restricted-model and bounded-round results do not prove it; the 2019 general claim remains withdrawn. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider f(x)=1/2+(x₁+⋯+x_n)/(2n). This degree-one polynomial always lies in [0,1], but Var(f)=1/(4n) and each coordinate has influence 1/(4n²). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

The quantum connection comes from acceptance probabilities. A quantum algorithm making t queries to input bits has an acceptance probability represented by a bounded polynomial of degree at most 2t. If the conjecture holds, a classical procedure can repeatedly query an influential coordinate and restrict the polynomial. After sufficiently many such queries, the remaining uncertainty has small variance, allowing its mean to estimate the acceptance probability on most uniformly sampled inputs.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

One productive restriction is complete boundedness. Roughly, this requires the polynomial to remain bounded even when suitable matrix contractions replace scalar inputs, with products taken in a specified order. It is much stronger than being bounded on the scalar Boolean cube. Bansal, Sinha and de Wolf prove influential-variable bounds for completely bounded block-multilinear forms, a class connected to algorithms querying separate input blocks.

Bhattacharya’s random-restriction theorem approaches the unrestricted class differently. Fix most coordinates independently to random signs and leave roughly a log(d)/d fraction available. Under a lower bound on the original variance, a non-negligible fraction of restrictions have a polynomially influential remaining variable. The accompanying junta theorem approximates restricted functions using few coordinates. Neither assertion directly guarantees such a variable in the original, unrestricted function.

Two recent results clarify the frontier. Blanc and coauthors obtain the desired almost-everywhere classical simulation for a fixed number of quantum query rounds; their exponent depends on the number of rounds. This does not address arbitrary adaptivity or prove the full polynomial inequality. Escudero Gutiérrez, Saucedo and Palazuelos subsequently obtain an optimal root-influence inequality for completely bounded block-multilinear polynomials, improving simulation to allow nonadaptive classical queries for that setting.

The September inequality controls the sum of square roots of influences by the number of blocks times the completely bounded norm. Its extra norm hypothesis is precisely what prevents applying it to every polynomial in this card. The paper explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture. A historical general proof claim by Keller and Klein is withdrawn because of an error in a key lemma, and is recorded as a withdrawal rather than progress establishing the conjecture.

6608.title: Decidability of unconditional Shannon information inequalities
6608.formal: Does a Turing algorithm exist that, given n≥1 and rational coefficients (a_S) for nonempty subsets S⊆{1,…,n}, always halts and decides whether Σ_{∅≠S⊆[n]}a_S H(X_S)≥0 holds for every joint distribution of n finite-valued discrete random variables?
6608.definitions: The finite input lists n and all nonzero coefficients, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, with its subset S encoded explicitly; omitted coefficients are zero. X_S is the tuple (X_i)_{i∈S}. Its Shannon entropy in bits is H(X_S)=−Σ_x p_S(x)log₂ p_S(x), with 0log₂0=0. Each variable has a finite alphabet, but alphabet sizes are unrestricted and are not supplied as bounds in the input. Joint probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers in [0,1] summing to one. No independence, conditional-independence, functional-dependence, fixed-marginal or support-size promise is imposed. The inequality is a single homogeneous linear inequality, with non-strict ≥0 and no affine constant, premise, disjunction or nonlinear entropy term. Runtime may be any computable function of the input length; polynomial time is not required. The number n varies with the input.
6608.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer supplies a total effective procedure for exact validity of every such rational inequality. A negative answer proves that this language of valid inequalities is undecidable. Finding a false input inequality or proving an individual new valid inequality answers an instance, not the meta-question. A procedure that may run forever on valid inputs, or requires a promised numerical gap, does not resolve exact decidability.
6608.why: A basic computability question about the laws of Shannon information, with consequences for automated proofs, network and coding bounds, and database query reasoning.

importance.reason: A foundational decision problem at the intersection of information theory, computability and database theory; it asks whether exact universal entropy reasoning can be fully automated.

6608.status_note: Open for a single unconditional homogeneous rational linear inequality over all finite-valued distributions, based on primary sources and a later-result check through 11 September 2026. Invalidity is semidecidable. Conditional undecidability, restricted set-function domains and inequality-generation algorithms do not establish undecidability or decidability of this exact problem.

context_blocks.text: For a given distribution, each subset of variables has an entropy. Collecting these numbers produces one point in a space with 2^n−1 coordinates. The question asks whether an input linear halfspace contains every such point, across all finite alphabets and distributions. It is therefore a question about all possible information structures, rather than about estimating entropies from a dataset.

Familiar examples are easy to express in this format. Subadditivity is H(X₁)+H(X₂)−H(X₁,X₂)≥0. Conditional mutual information is H(X₁,X₃)+H(X₂,X₃)−H(X₃)−H(X₁,X₂,X₃)≥0. Both hold without a premise. A negative coefficient is perfectly legitimate; it is the full linear combination, rather than each individual summand, whose sign is being decided.

The standard Shannon inequalities give a finite linear-programming proof method for each n. They express nonnegative conditional entropies and conditional mutual informations, or equivalently normalized monotone submodular set functions. If a candidate follows from them, it is universally valid. But the first non-Shannon inequality of Zhang–Yeung showed in 1998 that this proof method is incomplete. Rejecting an attempted Shannon derivation therefore cannot be used as a negative answer about entropy validity.

The unrestricted alphabet quantifier is a major part of the difficulty. A computation on binary variables explores only a small portion of the permitted distributions. Increasing a guessed alphabet bound may discover new counterexamples, but an unsuccessful search at every bound examined so far provides no effective stopping criterion. A solution cannot quietly replace all finite alphabets by one fixed support limit depending on a heuristic.

There is a rigorous semidecision procedure for invalidity. If an inequality is false, it is strictly negative at some distribution with finite alphabets. Entropy is continuous on that finite probability simplex, so a sufficiently close rational distribution still violates it. Enumerate alphabet sizes and rational distributions, and compute certified entropy approximations of increasing precision. Eventually the negative value is certified. The arithmetical-hierarchy study of Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu places validity in co-r.e.

This explains precisely what a positive solution would add: a way to halt on every valid inequality as well. A complete effective enumeration of proofs of all valid inequalities, coupled with the counterexample search, would suffice. Existing automated methods can produce many correct certificates, but no completeness theorem for all rational unconditional inequalities is supplied by the inspected sources.

Taking the topological closure of the entropic region does not change this particular validity problem. A continuous linear form nonnegative on every entropic point is nonnegative on every limit point, and the reverse implication is immediate. Thus the same unconditional linear inequalities hold for entropic and almost-entropic vectors. This observation depends on the exact logical form; it does not authorize replacing the domain inside arbitrary conditional statements.

Cheuk Ting Li’s 2023 theorem establishes undecidability for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those inputs include premises that must hold exactly. Merely deleting a premise changes the statement. The theorem therefore does not by itself establish undecidability of a single unconditional inequality.

Adding a fixed penalty for violating a premise need not capture its limiting behavior. Kaced–Romashchenko explicitly show essentially conditional inequalities that do not extend to unconditional linear inequalities in the proposed manner. Their results explain why this seemingly direct route from conditional to unconditional validity needs additional justification.

Hannula’s 2024 work studies useful decidable simplifications: different classes of set functions and syntactic forms connected to database bounds. Its coNP-completeness result is for normal polymatroids, a restricted semantic domain, while another polynomial-time result uses monotone functions. These are precise complexity results for different domains, not a classification of validity over all entropy vectors.

The connection to databases gives the question an algorithmic role beyond coding theory. Entropy inequalities constrain how large a relational join can be under information about its inputs and degrees. Related logical forms occur in query containment and dependency implication. Understanding which constraints admit complete reasoning procedures helps explain why some query bounds can be computed effectively while broader formulations encounter undecidability.

The 2025 exploration by László Csirmaz compares the Copy Lemma, maximum-entropy constructions and the Ahlswede–Körner method, and leaves their completeness unresolved. Előd P. Csirmaz and László Csirmaz’s 2026 paper derives two infinite collections of five-variable inequalities and computes consequences through nine generations of its construction. Its enumeration concerns that method’s extremal inequalities; even the proposed characterization of the method is not a characterization of the entire entropy region.

6609.title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
6609.formal: Do there exist constants r∈(0,1], δ∈(0,1/2) and A>0 such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with k≤n≤k/r, an encoding C:{0,1}^k→{0,1}^n, and randomized local decoders Dec_i for i∈{1,…,k}, satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word z∈{0,1}^n differing from C(x) in fewer than δn positions, and every requested index i, Dec_i with oracle access to z outputs x_i with probability at least 2/3 while making at most ⌈A log₂(n+1)⌉ bit queries on every execution.
6609.why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
6609.status_note: The 2 April 2026 source explicitly identifies this binary problem as open. The January 2026 HDX result has different decoding guarantees. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated ordinary binary query model; this is a bounded literature check, not an independent proof audit.

Kept an information-theoretic existence target for unbounded lengths rather than adding efficient construction. Primary definition and open-question section read; related 2026 abstract checked.

6609.definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is k/n and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants r, δ and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple (x,z,i); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
6609.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.

context_blocks.title: Recover one item without reading everything
context_blocks.text: A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

context_blocks.title: Why simple repetition does not suffice
context_blocks.text: Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

context_blocks.title: The remaining query gap
context_blocks.text: The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses 2^{O(√(log n·log log n))} queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

context_blocks.title: Related decoding guarantees
context_blocks.text: The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.

6611.title: Does the permanent require determinants of superpolynomial dimension?
6611.formal: Over the complex numbers, is the sequence dc_C(permₙ) unbounded by every polynomial in n? Explicitly, for every C>0 and integer k≥1, must there be n≥1 such that dc_C(permₙ)>C(n+1)^k?
6611.definitions: The polynomial permₙ(X)=Σ_{σ∈Sₙ}∏_{i=1}ⁿx_{i,σ(i)} has n² algebraically independent commuting variables and degree n; Sₙ is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. Its determinantal complexity dc_C(permₙ) is the smallest positive integer m for which there exist constant complex m×m matrices A₀ and Aᵢⱼ satisfying the exact polynomial identity permₙ(X)=det(A₀+Σ_{i,j=1}ⁿxᵢⱼAᵢⱼ). Thus every matrix entry is an arbitrary affine-linear form in all input variables. The representation may depend on n and use arbitrary complex constants without a bit-length or constructibility restriction. The resource is matrix dimension m. No symmetry, sparsity, multilinearity of intermediate expressions, regularity, or read-once restriction is imposed. Equality is in C[X], for every complex substitution, not only on 0/1 inputs. Border complexity, which permits a limit of representations, is a separate measure. Characteristic two is excluded by fixing C: in that characteristic the permanent equals the determinant. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6611.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6611.why: A central concrete target in algebraic complexity: determine whether one canonical efficiently computable polynomial can simulate a canonical algebraic counting polynomial at polynomial cost. Its formulation invites tools from algebraic geometry and representation theory while retaining a precise computational meaning.

importance.reason: The principal permanent-versus-determinant lower-bound problem, connecting algebraic computation, branching programs, geometry, and symmetry.

progress.text: Valiant establishes the foundational algebraic simulation framework: formulas and branching programs have small determinantal representations, and the permanent is complete for VNP.
Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2 using Hessian ranks at zeros. This remains a polynomial lower bound.

Grenet gives a 2ⁿ−1-dimensional representation; Landsberg and Ressayre prove exponential optimality when specified symmetries must be respected. Their unrestricted-versus-equivariant comparison is left open.
Kumar and Volk survey the permanent bounds and develop a new singular-locus method for a different explicit polynomial, a diagonal power sum. That theorem does not raise the permanent lower bound.
The algebraic cost of Boolean summation distinguishes permanent and determinant under a local fixed-additive-size simulation requirement, leaving general polynomial-size representations open.
Bogart and Valero’s journal paper studies generalized permanents and continues to state the superpolynomial ordinary-permanent problem as open.

6611.status_note: Open in the cited foundational and recent papers; checked through 10 September 2026. This card fixes exact unrestricted representations over C. Symmetric, equivariant, real-field, border, and other-polynomial bounds are not substituted for this model.

context_blocks.text: The permanent and determinant sum the same products indexed by permutations; the determinant attaches a permutation sign. Those signs enable cancellations behind efficient determinant computation. A determinantal representation asks whether a larger matrix with carefully chosen affine entries can reproduce the unsigned sum exactly. Merely showing that changing signs in the original n×n matrix fails leaves almost all permitted representations untouched.

The model is nonuniform and algebraic. It asks about the existence of a family of polynomial-size representations even if finding their complex coefficients is computationally difficult. Determinants characterize polynomial-size algebraic branching programs up to polynomial overhead, whereas unrestricted arithmetic circuits define the potentially larger class VP. The requested lower bound separates the permanent from the branching-program model; it should not be identified without qualification with a separation from all of VP.

The unrestricted complex-field lower bound is still quadratic in the original matrix dimension: Mignon and Ressayre prove dc_C(permₙ)≥n²/2. Their argument compares the rank of the matrix of second partial derivatives, the Hessian, at carefully chosen zeros of the two polynomials. Because the permanent has n² input variables, this is only linear in its number of variables, despite being quadratic in n.

There is also an explicit exponential upper bound, dc_C(permₙ)≤2ⁿ−1, due to Grenet. Landsberg and Ressayre prove that this construction is optimal under particular equivariance requirements involving permutations and diagonal rescaling. Removing those requirements is essential: the question allows a representation to break every visible symmetry of the polynomial. Whether symmetry can be imposed with only polynomial overhead is itself another open problem.

Progress can reveal structural differences without giving an unrestricted lower bound. Orzel, Srinivasan, Tavenas, and Yehudayoff show that a local Boolean-summation operation can be absorbed into a permanent by a fixed additive increase in dimension, whereas the analogous uniform fixed-additive-cost property fails for determinants. Their FSTTCS 2025 result explains a step in the VNP-completeness construction; it does not exclude a different, global polynomial-size determinant representation.

Bogart and Valero extend upper- and lower-bound techniques to two generalized permanent families. Their 2026 journal version still identifies the Mignon–Ressayre estimate as the best known characteristic-zero bound for the ordinary permanent for n≥5. This provides a recent status check while illustrating how sensitive the geometric lower-bound method is to the polynomial being studied.

6612.title: VP versus VBP over the complex numbers
6612.formal: Is VP_ℂ=VBP_ℂ? Explicitly, for every family (f_n)_{n≥1} of commutative polynomials over ℂ with a polynomially bounded number of variables and total degree, if f_n has an arithmetic circuit of size n^O(1), must f_n also have an algebraic branching program of size n^O(1)? The polynomial bounds may depend on the family but not on n; all equalities are exact polynomial identities.
6612.definitions: An arithmetic circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one output, input gates labelled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, and binary addition or multiplication gates; subtraction is expressible using the constant −1. Intermediate results may be reused without restriction. Size counts gates and wires, with each field constant of unit cost; no division gates are allowed. An algebraic branching program (ABP) is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source s and sink t, whose edges are labelled by affine linear forms α₀+∑_j α_j x_j over ℂ. Its output is the sum over all directed s-to-t paths of the product of their edge labels. Its size counts vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients and variable occurrences used in those labels. Layering can be imposed with polynomial overhead but is not required here. There is no width, variable-order, read-once, multilinearity, homogeneity, monotonicity or symmetry restriction. Both circuit and ABP families are nonuniform: no efficient algorithm producing them is required, and complex constants need not have bounded bit descriptions. VP_ℂ consists of the stated polynomial-degree families with polynomial circuit size; VBP_ℂ consists of families with polynomial ABP size and polynomially many variables. Polynomial ABP size already bounds the degree.
6612.answer_criterion: Prove that every family in VP_ℂ admits polynomial-size ABPs, or exhibit a family in VP_ℂ whose minimum ABP size is not polynomially bounded: for every constant c, infinitely many n require more than n^c size. A negative answer must retain small general circuits for the separating family and allow arbitrary complex constants in the competing ABPs. Lower bounds only for multilinear, symmetric, noncommutative, monotone or read-once ABPs do not suffice. Approximation in coefficient space, called border complexity, is a different question.
6612.why: One of the central unresolved separations inside algebraic complexity: it asks whether determinant-like path-sum computation captures every efficiently computed polynomial of polynomial degree.

importance.reason: A basic class equality linking general arithmetic circuits, algebraic branching programs and determinant universality; current symmetry and multilinearity results remain model-specific.
