6612.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 survey explicitly leaves the VP–VBP inclusion unresolved. STOC 2026 symmetry separations, multilinear lower-bound methods and min-plus-semiring results use different models. This card fixes characteristic zero over ℂ, unrestricted commutative ABPs and exact nonuniform computation.

context_blocks.text: A circuit can multiply two complicated intermediate results and reuse each of them elsewhere. An ABP has a more linear form of reuse: the polynomial reaching a vertex is obtained by adding predecessor polynomials multiplied by affine edge labels. This is equivalent, with polynomial overhead, to skew circuits, where each multiplication has an input operand that is a variable or constant. The problem asks whether general multiplication and reuse can always be reorganized into this form at only polynomial cost.

The degree restriction rules out an immediate artificial separation. Repeated squaring computes x^{2ⁿ} with n multiplication gates. An ABP with affine labels needs a path of length at least 2ⁿ to produce that degree. This family is excluded from VP because its degree is exponential. The open problem persists when the output degree is polynomial, so a solution must address the structure of efficient computations rather than this simple degree obstruction.

The determinant provides a useful equivalent perspective. Polynomial-size ABPs can be represented by determinants of polynomial-size matrices of affine forms, and the symbolic determinant itself has polynomial-size ABPs. Thus equality would make the determinant universal for all polynomial-degree, polynomial-size circuit computations under polynomial-size affine projections. This differs from the determinant-versus-permanent problem: the permanent is not known to belong to VP, whereas a separation here must already have an efficient circuit on the easy side.

Classical depth reduction supplies a quasipolynomial simulation. If quasipolynomial size is allowed throughout, formulas, ABPs and general circuits compute the same polynomial-degree families. Dutta and coauthors recall this consequence of the Valiant–Skyum–Berkowitz–Rackoff depth reduction in their ITCS 2024 work. What remains unknown is whether the overhead can always be reduced to a fixed polynomial, or whether some efficient circuit computations necessarily resist it.

ABPs also support more algebra than their restricted multiplication rule might suggest. Sinhababu and Thierauf prove that factors of an ABP-computed polynomial have polynomial-size ABPs in characteristic zero. This establishes a closure property that was previously known for general circuits. Sharing factor closure does not establish equality of the models; the June 2026 factoring survey explicitly retains the unresolved chain VF⊆VBP⊆VP.

Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt’s STOC 2026 work separates symmetric analogues of formulas, skew circuits and general circuits and connects them to graph homomorphism polynomials. These analogues require symmetries of the variables to extend to the computation and measure the largest orbit of gates, rather than simply imposing the ordinary total-size bound. Their separations therefore do not establish VP≠VBP. The work also supplies natural complete polynomial families, potentially useful targets for future unrestricted lower bounds.

A January 2026 paper by Fabris, Limaye, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff investigates the min-partition rank method for multilinear ABPs through a combinatorial set-system problem. It recovers a separation between multilinear formulas and multilinear ABPs and studies the potential of the method for stronger lower bounds. The general ABPs in this card can reuse variables along paths and can cancel nonmultilinear terms. A lower bound that forbids those behaviors does not constrain every allowed representation.

A positive answer would show that general efficient algebraic computation can be expressed through path sums and determinants with only polynomial overhead. A negative answer would prove a basic hierarchy inside efficient computation itself. Either result would clarify how much computational power comes from multiplying and reusing rich intermediate expressions, independently of the larger question of whether permanent computation is efficient.

6613.title: Polynomial-size arithmetic formulas for the determinant
6613.formal: Do there exist constants K,C≥1 such that for every n≥1 the symbolic determinant Det_n(X)=Σ_{π∈S_n}sgn(π)∏_{i=1}^n x_{i,π(i)} has an arithmetic formula over the complex numbers with at most K n^C nodes?
6613.definitions: The n² entries x_{ij} of X are distinct commuting indeterminates. S_n is the set of permutations of [n], and sgn(π) is +1 or −1 according to the parity of π. An arithmetic formula is a rooted binary tree. Leaves are labelled by input variables or arbitrary constants from ℂ; internal nodes apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. The output must equal Det_n as a formal polynomial in ℂ[x_{11},…,x_{nn}]. Size counts every node, including each repeated occurrence of a variable, constant or copied subformula. Intermediate results cannot be shared between different parents. Constants are charged unit size, without a bound on their bit description; this is nonuniform algebraic complexity, so no algorithm generating the family is required. Division, comparisons, branching and input-dependent constants are not allowed. Intermediate polynomials may contain higher powers of individual variables and cancellations of those powers; only the final polynomial is required to be the determinant. There is no multilinearity, homogeneity, fixed-depth, monotonicity or bounded-coefficient restriction on intermediate computation. The fixed field ℂ is an explicit characteristic-zero specialization of the inherited question.
6613.answer_criterion: Exhibit polynomial-size formulas with one fixed size exponent for all n, or prove that the minimum formula-size function is not bounded by any polynomial: for every K,C≥1 there is an n for which every allowed formula has more than K n^C nodes. A fixed-power lower bound such as Ω(n³) is insufficient to refute polynomial size. A lower bound restricted to multilinear formulas, noncommuting variables, or bounded depth does not settle this unrestricted commutative formula question.
6613.why: The canonical test of whether reusing intermediate expressions gives a superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic expression trees, even for an efficiently computable polynomial.

importance.reason: A fundamental separation inside algebraic computation, equivalent to the formula-versus-branching-program question through determinant completeness and linked to many explicit polynomial families.

The updated factoring primer explicitly records that polynomial-size symbolic determinant formulas are still unknown, despite new formula-factoring results.

6613.status_note: The June 2026 primary survey explicitly retains the question. Sparse and dense multilinear lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted intermediate computations, and recent factoring progress does not furnish determinant formulas. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The determinant is computationally easy when an algorithm may save intermediate work and reuse it. A formula imposes a stricter discipline: each computed quantity has only one consumer. To use the same expression twice, the expression must be copied. This can turn a compact computation graph into a much larger tree. The problem asks whether the determinant has an alternative expression that avoids this potential blow-up.

The familiar permutation expansion has n! terms, but this does not prove that every formula is that large. Algebraic identities can compress a sum dramatically, just as a product of short sums can represent many expanded monomials. Conversely, Gaussian elimination is not itself a small formula: its usual presentation reuses entries, performs divisions and selects pivots. Its numerical running time therefore cannot answer the stated symbolic question.

Berkowitz’s division-free construction gives polynomial-size arithmetic circuits of depth O(log² n). Unfolding a bounded-fan-in circuit of that depth into a tree gives a formula of size 2^{O(log² n)}=n^{O(log n)}. This is quasipolynomial, already far below the permutation expansion, but still larger than a fixed power of n. A polynomial-size formula would close this remaining gap.

The determinant is also a complete problem for polynomial-size algebraic branching programs, whose outputs are sums of products of edge labels along directed source-to-sink paths. Consequently, polynomial-size determinant formulas would imply VF=VBP: every polynomial family having polynomial-size branching programs would have polynomial-size formulas. The larger class VP allows general arithmetic circuits. The June 2026 factoring primer still lists VF⊆VBP⊆VP without a known strict containment and explicitly leaves small determinant formulas unresolved.

An unrestricted lower bound is known, but it is only a fixed power. Kalorkoti proves Ω(n³) formula size for the n by n determinant, even in a model allowing division. Here n is the matrix dimension; there are n² independent variables. Thus the bound is cubic in dimension and only a power 3/2 in the number of variables. It must not be described as a cubic lower bound in the input-variable count.

Raz proves a much stronger n^{Ω(log n)} lower bound when every intermediate polynomial is multilinear. This restriction is substantive even though the final determinant is multilinear. For a simple illustration, (x+y)²−x²−y² equals 2xy, a multilinear output obtained through nonmultilinear intermediate terms. The example does not establish a size advantage, but it shows why output multilinearity alone cannot justify applying a theorem that assumes multilinearity throughout a computation.

Recent progress tests which determinant features are needed for that restricted lower bound. Boyapati, Chillara and Vempati prove the existence of sparse n by n symbolic matrices with only Θ(n log⁶ n) nonzero entries whose determinants still require n^{Ω(log n)} multilinear formulas. This shows that the dense n²-variable presentation is not essential to Raz’s obstruction. It leaves the permission to use nonmultilinear intermediate computations untouched.

The question also organizes complexity outside generic matrices. Chaugule and coauthors connect small formulas for Schur polynomials and generalized Vandermonde determinants to small formulas for the general determinant. Such reductions make the determinant a useful benchmark for whether apparently special algebraic expressions really admit efficient tree computations. A separation would reveal a basic cost of forbidding reuse, already within problems that possess efficient arithmetic circuits.

6614.title: Deterministic polynomial-time factorization over finite fields
6614.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing algorithm that, for every explicitly represented finite field F_q and every nonzero dense univariate f∈F_q[x] of degree n≥1, outputs its complete irreducible factorization using (n+log₂q)^{O(1)} bit operations, with one absolute polynomial bound?
6614.definitions: The field is supplied as F_q=F_p[t]/(h(t)), where p is a binary-encoded prime, h∈F_p[t] is a supplied monic irreducible polynomial of degree e≥1, and q=p^e. These field promises are part of the input specification; no algorithm for constructing h is required. An element is represented by its e coefficients of degree below e, each in {0,…,p−1}. The polynomial f is given by all n+1 coefficients in this representation. Output a unit u∈F_q\{0}, pairwise distinct monic irreducible polynomials g₁,…,g_r∈F_q[x], and positive integer multiplicities m₁,…,m_r with f=u∏_i g_i^{m_i}. Output order is irrelevant. Arithmetic, conversions, preprocessing and writing the factors all count in bit time. Repeated factors and characteristic-p inseparability are allowed. The running-time exponent must be independent of n,p,e and f. No randomness, number-theoretic hypothesis, factorization oracle or precomputed field-specific advice is allowed.
6614.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives a correct complete-factorization algorithm with the stated uniform worst-case polynomial bit bound for every valid input. A negative answer proves no such algorithm exists in this model; failure of a particular deterministic strategy is insufficient. Polynomial dependence on q or p instead of log q, average-case bounds, fixed-degree results, or conditional algorithms do not resolve the claim.
6614.why: A canonical exact derandomization problem in computer algebra, with broad consequences wherever finite-field factorization is used as a subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem in algebraic computation: randomized polynomial-time search is known, while uniform deterministic polynomial bit complexity remains unresolved even for basic root-finding cases.

progress.text: Berlekamp and subsequent randomized splitting algorithms establish the classical framework for finite-field factorization.

Guo’s P-scheme framework supplies GRH-based polynomial algorithms for additional Galois-group classes and a common treatment of earlier results.
Altman gives unconditional amortized factorization over many primes, with dependence on splitting-field degree.
Umans–Wang propose a number-theoretic route to better degree exponents in fast factorization; general deterministic finite-field factoring is not resolved.
Chuyoon–Shpilka’s sparse multivariate results explicitly retain the univariate-factorization cost and a polynomial dependence on p for the finite-field subroutine.

6614.status_note: Open unconditionally for all explicitly represented finite fields and dense univariate inputs, based on sources checked through 11 September 2026. GRH alone is not known to give the requested general polynomial bound. Amortization over primes, fixed characteristic, special Galois groups and multivariate bounds retaining a univariate oracle do not resolve this exact question.

context_blocks.text: Finite-field polynomial factorization is a setting where randomization already gives efficient exact algorithms. The desired output has a short representation and is unique up to ordering after normalizing the factors. The open issue is therefore whether random choices are essential for guaranteed efficiency, rather than whether factorization is possible or whether its answer is too large to write down.

The logarithm of the field size is the relevant parameter because one coefficient occupies about log₂q bits. Enumerating all q field elements may be reasonable for a tiny field, but is exponential in the coefficient length when q grows. This distinction is already visible for quadratics over a prime field: the general problem includes finding roots of x²−a modulo an arbitrary large odd prime when a is a quadratic residue.

The field presentation makes a potentially hidden prerequisite explicit. Supplying an irreducible h gives a concrete way to add, multiply and invert extension-field elements using polynomial arithmetic modulo h. The algorithm is not being asked to discover a field representation. At the same time, arithmetic operations are not free: the requested complexity includes their bit cost and must remain polynomial as the extension degree and characteristic vary.

Classical algorithms organize the work into squarefree factorization, separation by irreducible-factor degree, and splitting products whose factors have equal degree. The first two stages have deterministic polynomial-time methods. Randomized equal-degree splitting then completes the factorization efficiently. This organization, surveyed by von zur Gathen–Panario, isolates a concrete source of the derandomization difficulty.

A proposed answer can be checked efficiently without solving the search problem from scratch. Multiplying the claimed factors verifies their product, and finite-field irreducibility tests use modular powering and gcd computations. For a monic polynomial g of degree d, one checks divisibility by x^{q^d}−x and excludes common factors with x^{q^{d/ℓ}}−x for prime divisors ℓ of d. The huge exponents are handled by repeated powering modulo g, not by writing enormous polynomials.

Unconditional deterministic methods do work in time polynomial in n, log q and the characteristic p. Consequently fixed characteristic is already a tractable regime even when the extension field is large. The general obstacle is a large characteristic encoded in only log p bits. Guo’s account records a p^{1/2} dependence up to factors polynomial in n and log q for the best general deterministic methods discussed there.

GRH does not currently remove every obstacle. Evdokimov’s algorithm gives quasipolynomial degree dependence under GRH, and Galois-theoretic methods obtain polynomial time for certain supplied lifts with controlled groups. Guo’s P-scheme framework extends those special cases and unifies earlier methods. Neither its polynomial-time subclass theorem nor the general quasipolynomial bound is a general deterministic polynomial-time factorization theorem.

The inherited September 2025 paper by Altman changes the averaging question. Starting from one integer polynomial f, it factors its reductions for every prime below a bound N. The average cost per prime is polynomial in the input parameters and the degree m of the splitting field over Q. This gives a strong amortized result when m is polynomially bounded, but m can be as large as n!, and processing all primes below N does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for one arbitrary prime supplied in binary.

Altman also distinguishes averaging over primes from older averaging over input polynomials. A deterministic procedure can run quickly on most randomly selected polynomials and still have hard individual inputs. The present question requires a worst-case bound for every f over every supplied field. Neither kind of averaging can silently replace that quantifier.

Recent multivariate factorization results sometimes suppress the underlying univariate cost in their headline bounds. Chuyoon–Shpilka’s March 2026 paper explicitly restores this dependence in Remark 1.7 and §2.2. Its finite-field subroutine runs in time polynomial in p, log q and the degree; its multivariate theorem includes a factor T for univariate factorization. Specializing the number of variables does not erase that cost.

Umans–Wang’s November 2025 work pursues a different improvement: a number-theoretic conjecture could reduce the degree exponent in fast polynomial-factorization algorithms below the familiar three-halves bound. It also has a separate consequence for deterministic integer factoring. Those are valuable quantitative directions, but the abstract’s deterministic integer result must not be misread as a general derandomization theorem for finite-field polynomials.

The problem is fundamental because polynomial factorization is repeatedly used as a subroutine in symbolic computation and computational number theory. A deterministic solution would make many algorithms independent of randomized splitting choices. A proof that no such solution exists would instead establish a striking separation for an exact algebraic search problem whose answers are efficiently verifiable.

6617.title: Can a classical randomized algorithm factor every integer in polynomial time?
6617.formal: Do there exist constants C,c and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, on every positive integer N given in binary, outputs its complete prime factorization with probability at least 2/3 and always halts within C(n+1)ᶜ bit operations, where n=⌊log₂N⌋+1?
6617.definitions: For N≥2, the required output is the ordered list (p₁,e₁),…,(pᵣ,eᵣ), with distinct primes p₁<⋯<pᵣ, positive integer exponents eᵢ, and N=∏ᵢpᵢ^{eᵢ}. All output integers are encoded in binary. The factorization of N=1 is the empty list; zero and malformed encodings are outside the positive-integer domain and are rejected. The same finite probabilistic Turing machine must work for all N. Its random tape contains independent fair bits, and the success probability is over these bits separately for each fixed input. The polynomial time bound holds on every random tape. An incorrect output or a failure symbol counts as failure. There are no quantum operations, input-dependent advice, factoring or order-finding oracles, promises of a special form for N, or supplied factors of nearby integers. In particular n is the bit length of N, not its numerical value.
6617.answer_criterion: Answer yes with a proved algorithm meeting the worst-case polynomial running time and per-input success guarantee. Answer no by proving that every uniform classical randomized algorithm fails one of these requirements for some inputs, regardless of its polynomial exponent. Deterministic factoring would suffice for yes, but a deterministic lower bound alone would not suffice for no. Experiments or algorithms for a restricted class of integers do not settle the statement.
6617.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.

progress.text: Sieve methods establish powerful subexponential classical approaches. The standard general number field sieve estimate remains a heuristic expected-time analysis, as summarized in the current large-order paper.

Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena prove deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. The result does not give a polynomial-time factoring algorithm.
Harvey and Hittmeir rigorously factor N in O(N^{1/5}(log N)^{16/5}/(log log N)^{3/5}) deterministic bit operations, improving the preceding exponent-one-fifth bound by a logarithmic factor.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revised large-order algorithm removes earlier power-of-N lower restrictions on its target order parameter. Their introduction still explicitly identifies polynomial-time integer factorization as unknown; the improved subroutine does not provide such a factoring algorithm.

Research through 10 September 2026 found no proved classical polynomial-time algorithm for all integers or impossibility theorem for the stated randomized model. Numerical scaling evidence and quantum algorithms do not establish either answer.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to √N is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Because an output can be checked, a bounded-error polynomial-time factoring algorithm can be repeated until a valid factorization is obtained, giving an always-correct algorithm with polynomial expected time. Conversely, a polynomial expected-time always-correct algorithm can be truncated at a suitable constant multiple of its expected bound to obtain the formulation above. This equivalence concerns performance on every input; success on a sampled family of integers alone is weaker.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate exp(((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(ln N)^{1/3}(ln ln N)^{2/3}). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of N^{1/5+o(1)} make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in a more powerful computational model; it does not establish a classical lower bound. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would undermine factoring-based cryptographic assumptions, but the absence of such an algorithm has not been proved from P≠NP or from the efficiency of multiplication.

6618.title: Are discrete logarithms in prime fields in randomized polynomial time?
6618.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every prime p, every generator g of the multiplicative group Fₚ*, and every h∈Fₚ*, returns the unique integer x∈{0,…,p−2} satisfying gˣ≡h (mod p), with probability at least 2/3 and worst-case running time polynomial in log₂p?
6618.definitions: The input consists of ordinary binary integers (p,g,h), with p prime and 1≤g,h≤p−1, promised that g has multiplicative order p−1. Set n=⌈log₂(p+1)⌉; the total input length is Θ(n). A single probabilistic Turing machine must use at most C(n+1)^c bit operations on every random tape, for fixed constants C,c independent of p,g,h. It may output failure on unsuccessful runs. Success probability is over its own independent fair random bits and must be at least 2/3 separately on every promised input. Its only input is (p,g,h): no factorization of p−1, precomputed logarithm table, advice, special-form description of p, or oracle is supplied. Any preprocessing it performs counts in its runtime. The algorithm may exploit the ordinary integer encoding and all efficiently computable arithmetic modulo p; it is not restricted to generic group operations. The group is multiplication of nonzero residues, not an elliptic-curve group or the additive group. For p=2 the only logarithm is x=0.
6618.answer_criterion: Give and prove a classical algorithm with the specified uniform polynomial worst-case time and per-instance success guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A generic-group lower bound, a fast algorithm for a restricted family of primes, a quantum algorithm, or a polynomial bound in p rather than log p does not settle the question.
6618.why: A fundamental inversion problem in computational number theory and a central candidate for separating efficient classical from quantum computation. Its resolution would clarify which arithmetic structure can overcome generic group barriers and would reshape finite-field cryptographic assumptions.

importance.reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.

context_blocks.text: Computing gˣ mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as p−2. The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute gˣ mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form exp(O((ln p)^{1/3}(ln ln p)^{2/3})). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound (p·d)^{2log₂d+O(1)} for discrete logarithms in F_{p^d}. For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields d=1 and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.

6619.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
6619.formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least 2/3 using at most 2^{Cn}L^d bit operations and L^d bits of working space?
6619.definitions: The input is B∈Q^{m×n}, with m≥n≥1 and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is Λ(B)={Bz:z∈Zⁿ}, and λ₁(Λ)=min_{z∈Zⁿ\{0}}‖Bz‖₂, with the ordinary Euclidean norm in R^m. Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying ‖Bz‖₂=λ₁(Λ); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
6619.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking 2^{Θ(n log n)} time leave the question open.
6619.why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?

importance.reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.

Cryptographic time-space hardness is an assumption, not an unconditional negative resolution.

context_blocks.text: The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is n^{O(n)}. Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve 2^{O(n)} time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: n^{cn}=2^{cn log₂n}. For any fixed C, the factor log₂n eventually makes n^{cn} exceed 2^{Cn}. Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time 2^{100n} would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For B=I, a shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise n^{n/(2e)+o(n)} time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to O(n). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly 2^{2n} time and 2^n space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least 2/3 on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage O((M+K)n) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a 2^{O(n)} iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some 2^{Cn}-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

6621.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with Δ+2 colours
6621.formal: Do absolute constants C,c>0 exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree Δ and every integer q≥Δ+2, the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time t_mix(1/4)≤Cn^c?
6621.definitions: Let n≥1 and Ω={σ:V(G)→[q] : σ(u)≠σ(v) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from V(G), then choose a colour uniformly from [q]\{σ(u):u∈N(v)} and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and π the uniform distribution on Ω. Define t_mix(1/4)=min{t∈Z_{≥0}: max_{σ∈Ω} (1/2)Σ_{τ∈Ω}|P^t(σ,τ)−π(τ)|≤1/4}. This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of n, Δ, q and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
6621.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6621.why: A central boundary question for Markov-chain sampling: does the simplest local recolouring process mix efficiently whenever the universal ergodicity threshold is met?

importance.reason: A longstanding general-graph conjecture linking local algorithms, approximate counting and spin systems; recent near-threshold results still require structural restrictions.

6621.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general-graph Δ+2 conjecture remains open in the checked sources. August 2026 results improve restricted-girth regimes with fixed relative slack; they do not establish the universal additive-two bound.

context_blocks.text: A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold Δ+2 has a concrete role. On a clique with Δ+1 vertices and exactly Δ+1 colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least Δ+2 colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and q/(q−Δ). That factor is at most 1+Δ/2 in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’s q>2Δ regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly 11Δ/6. The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the 11/6 threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains Δ+2 as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes Δ≥125 and q≥1.809Δ and proves O(n log n) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal O(n log n) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on Δ and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves n^{O(tw(G)^3)} mixing with q≥Δ+2, so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses q≥(1+ε)(Δ+1) for a fixed positive ε. Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting ε that shrinks with Δ, does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove O_δ(n log n) mixing for the Metropolis chain when q≥(1+δ)Δ, Δ is sufficiently large in terms of fixed δ>0, and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Chen–Liu’s August 26 preprint reaches girth at least five in the same fixed-relative-slack regime for heat-bath dynamics. Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap Ω_δ(1/n) and mixing time O_δ(n² log q+n log(1/ε)); the sharper O_δ(n log n) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of δ. Both the girth restriction and the dependence on δ matter. Taking δ=2/Δ is not justified by a theorem that first fixes δ and then requires sufficiently large Δ.

The other inherited 2026 source studies an additional constraint: prescribed colour-class sizes. Such a condition changes the sample space, and a single-vertex update generally cannot preserve it. Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained Δ+2 conjecture open.

This is fundamental because it tests whether the basic local sampler remains efficient throughout the universally ergodic range. A proof would connect a simple combinatorial availability condition with global probabilistic convergence. A negative answer would identify an obstruction to efficient local sampling that survives despite spare colours at every vertex and connectivity of the entire state space.

6622.definitions: Ω(a,b) is the set of matrices M∈{0,1}^{r×s} with Σ_j M_ij=a_i and Σ_i M_ij=b_j. The state space is promised nonempty; no restriction on density or balance is imposed. At each discrete step, stay put with probability 1/2. Otherwise choose uniformly an unordered pair of distinct rows and independently an unordered pair of distinct columns. If their 2×2 submatrix is ((1,0),(0,1)) or ((0,1),(1,0)), replace it by the other pattern; otherwise stay put. If r<2 or s<2, the state space is a singleton and each step stays put. P denotes this transition matrix and π the uniform measure on Ω. Define t_mix(1/4)=min{t∈ℕ: max_{M∈Ω} (1/2)Σ_{N∈Ω}|P^t(M,N)−1/|Ω||≤1/4}, with value +∞ if the set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including stays. The maximum is over every initial state. The constants are independent of r,s and all margins; preprocessing, bit costs and sampling algorithms using other transitions are not part of this mixing-time question.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives t_mix(1/4)≤binom(r,2)binom(s,2)(rs ln 2+ln 4), which implies a universal polynomial bound in r+s. The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing [[1,0],[0,1]] by [[0,1],[1,0]] changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a 2×2 matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

6623.title: Polynomial-sample worst-case trace reconstruction
6623.formal: For every fixed deletion probability δ∈(0,1), is there a constant C_δ≥1 and K_δ≥1 such that every unknown n-bit string can be reconstructed exactly with probability at least 2/3 from at most K_δ n^{C_δ} independent deletion traces, for every n≥2?
6623.definitions: For x∈{0,1}^n, a deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability 1−δ and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let μ_{x,δ} be its probability distribution on ⋃_{k=0}^n{0,1}^k. Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given n, δ and m independent samples from μ_{x,δ}; it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of {0,1}^n, and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and δ must succeed for every x with probability at least 2/3 over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let N_δ(n) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The target is N_δ(n)≤K_δ n^{C_δ} for every n≥2. The constants may depend on δ but not on n or x. The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
6623.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6623.why: A fundamental question about how much information random subsequences preserve: can every string be identified from polynomially many observations despite completely hidden alignment?

importance.reason: A defining worst-case recovery problem for synchronization noise, linking string algorithms, information theory, statistics and complex-analytic methods.

The best unrestricted lower bound cited remains polynomial; circular and local-SQ bounds concern different models. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability (1−δ)^n a trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. If even this binary hypothesis test needs many samples, reconstructing an arbitrary string cannot need fewer. Chase gives a lower bound of Ω(n^{3/2}/log⁷ n) for fixed deletion probability. This is a substantial obstruction to near-linear reconstruction, but it remains polynomial and is therefore consistent with the target.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses exp(Õ(n^{1/5})) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint proves a quasipolynomial sample upper bound, including every fixed positive retention probability. Its theorem bounds the number of traces by exp(p^{−7/3}(log₂ n)^c) for an absolute constant c, where p=1−δ. The strategy uses global statistics involving polylogarithmically many trace positions. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since the current card imposes no time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that O(n log n) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly n⁵ is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

6625.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
6625.formal: Does there exist a single deterministic data structure and fixed constants C,c,d>0 such that, for every n≥2, an initially empty undirected simple graph on vertex set [n] can be maintained under any online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, using at most C n^d words of memory and at most C(log₂ n)^c time for each individual operation? Initialization may take at most C n^d time and depends only on n. All connectivity answers must be exact in the word-RAM model specified below.
6625.definitions: An insertion insert(u,v) adds a previously absent unordered edge {u,v}, where u≠v; a deletion delete(u,v) removes an existing edge. A query connected(u,v) returns whether the current graph contains a path from u to v, with connected(u,u)=true. Updates are valid, arrive one at a time and must finish before the next operation is revealed. No future operations or advance description of the sequence is supplied. The data structure must work for every finite sequence, including sequences chosen in response to its previous behavior. The word RAM has word size w=⌈a log₂ n⌉ for a fixed constant a large enough to address its polynomial space. Unit-cost instructions are indirect reads/writes, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient/remainder, comparisons, Boolean bit operations and shifts; arithmetic results stored in one word are reduced modulo 2ʷ where appropriate. Arbitrary-precision computation costs its constituent word operations. All maintenance, rebuilding and query work is charged to the operation performing it. The exponent c is independent of n and of the length or contents of the operation sequence. The graph is unrestricted apart from being undirected and simple; no planarity, bounded-degree or expansion promise is given.
6625.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6625.why: A basic unresolved guarantee for dynamic graph data structures. Connectivity is both a natural maintenance problem and a source of techniques used throughout graph algorithms; combining determinism, exactness and fast individual updates would close a longstanding gap.

importance.reason: A foundational dynamic-graph frontier directly relevant to data structures, with a new randomized breakthrough and an explicit remaining deterministic bottleneck.

Kapron–King–Mountjoy give a Monte Carlo structure with polylogarithmic worst-case operation time and high-probability correctness.
Chuzhoy–Gao–Li–Nanongkai–Peng–Saranurak obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case dynamic connectivity, published at FOCS 2020.
SODA publishes Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s Las Vegas expected polylogarithmic worst-case algorithm and conditional deterministic reduction, first posted 9 October 2025.
SODA also publishes expander pruning with worst-case recourse and update bounds, an ingredient in the connectivity framework.

6625.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The SODA 2026 connectivity paper explicitly retains deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case updates as open. Its unconditional new bound is randomized and expected; its deterministic polylogarithmic conclusion depends on the stated static low-congestion sparsifier construction. Deterministic subpolynomial worst-case bounds and polylogarithmic amortized bounds are already known.

context_blocks.text: The difficulty is deleting an edge that belongs to a maintained spanning forest. Removing it splits one tree into two parts, but the graph might still connect those parts through an edge outside the forest. The data structure must find such a replacement quickly or correctly certify that none exists. A single deletion can expose a large cut, so simply scanning all candidate edges gives no small bound on the time of that update.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give deterministic O(log² n) amortized operation bounds for connectivity, using a hierarchy of forests and edge levels. Their result establishes that long update sequences can be processed efficiently. The accounting permits an individual deletion to spend work paid for by other operations. Guaranteeing low latency after every deletion requires more than redistributing the same amortized accounting on paper.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy obtain polylogarithmic worst-case update time with randomization and a small error probability. Their cutset sampling technique tries to isolate a remaining edge across a cut, which can then be recovered from a compact sketch. Failure to recover an edge may mean either that the cut is empty or that the random samples missed it. Eliminating this uncertainty while keeping every update fast is part of the deterministic challenge.

Chuzhoy and coauthors use deterministic balanced-cut machinery to achieve n^{o(1)} worst-case update time, removing the earlier polynomial barrier. This is a major improvement but still leaves the present target open. For example, exp(√log n) is smaller than every fixed positive power of n and larger than every fixed power of log n. Thus a subpolynomial theorem does not imply the polylogarithmic bound merely by choosing a small exponent.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 algorithm is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest and achieves polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time, even against an adaptive adversary with access to its state. It alternates vertex and edge sparsification in a hierarchy. Each graph update changes the output forest by at most two edges, so maintaining the explicit answer itself does not cause large update costs. The expectation remains a distinction from the deterministic target.

The same paper gives a concrete sufficient condition for derandomization. If a deterministic algorithm constructs a near-linear-edge subgraph together with paths routing the original edges through it in m·polylog(m) time, with congestion at most (m/n)·polylog(m), the framework yields deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity. Congestion counts how many routed paths use the busiest retained edge. Finding any spanning forest is insufficient: its tree edges may carry far too many such paths.

A companion SODA 2026 result by Meierhans, Probst Gutenberg and Saranurak controls both the time and the number of vertices removed when pruning an expander after one edge deletion. This avoids a large burst of changes propagating through a hierarchy. It is an ingredient in the recent randomized progress; it does not by itself supply the deterministic sparsifier construction needed for the full conclusion.

Known lower bounds do not rule out the target. Pătraşcu and Demaine prove logarithmic amortized cell-probe lower bounds, including for connectivity on disjoint paths. Those results show that dynamic connectivity already has a real information-transfer cost in very simple graphs, but a logarithmic barrier is compatible with polylogarithmic upper bounds. The open issue is whether exact connectivity, deterministic computation and a bound on every operation can be achieved simultaneously.

6626.title: Polylogarithmic worst-case updates for exact dynamic minimum spanning forests
6626.formal: Can an exact minimum spanning forest of a fully dynamic n-vertex graph with polynomially bounded integer weights be maintained with polylogarithmic worst-case time per edge update, polynomial preprocessing and space, and high-probability correctness against an oblivious adversary?
6626.definitions: The graph is simple and undirected on the fixed labelled vertex set [n], n≥2, and starts empty. An update inserts one currently absent edge with integer weight in {1,…,n⁴}, or deletes one present edge. Edge weights remain fixed until deletion. A minimum spanning forest consists of one minimum-total-weight spanning tree for each connected component. Break equal-weight ties by the fixed lexicographic order (weight, smaller endpoint, larger endpoint), so the target is the unique forest selected by Kruskal’s algorithm in that order. After each update the data structure must report the edges removed from and added to the maintained forest; on a correct execution at most one edge of each kind changes. These reports specify the entire current forest starting from the empty one. Use a uniform randomized classical word RAM with Θ(log n)-bit words, standard word operations and random-word generation; all input processing and memory accesses count. For every fixed pair of integers a,b≥1, the target permits a separately tuned uniform data structure and constants K,C≥1 whose preprocessing and space are n^{O(1)}, and for which every update takes at most K(log₂(n+2))^C steps on every execution. For every valid update sequence of length at most n^a fixed before its random choices, all reported forests must be correct simultaneously with probability at least 1−n^{−b}. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on a,b, but not on n or the sequence. This is a Monte Carlo worst-case-time formulation; an always-correct deterministic solution would also suffice. The integer range n⁴ is an explicit specialization, and weights occupy O(1) words. There is no advance access to future updates.
6626.answer_criterion: Construct data structures satisfying the stated bounds for every fixed a,b, or prove the proposition false. Amortized polylogarithmic updates, merely subpolynomial worst-case updates, or maintaining an approximate minimum forest are insufficient. A lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone does not rule out the allowed randomization. A data structure that only stores the graph and postpones finding the forest to an expensive query does not meet the required per-update reporting guarantee.
6626.why: A basic dynamic optimization problem with very small changes to its answer but potentially expensive global replacement searches. It tests whether amortized efficiency can be made reliable for every update.

importance.reason: One of the main unresolved worst-case update barriers in dynamic graph algorithms, closely connecting connectivity, weighted optimization, sparsification and expander maintenance.

Nanongkai–Saranurak–Wulff-Nilsen give Las Vegas subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability.
Chuzhoy and coauthors obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates via deterministic expander decomposition.
Meierhans–Probst Gutenberg’s SODA paper gives expected polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity maintenance; its weighted extension is (1+ε)-approximate with inverse-ε overhead.

The inherited ICALP 2021 link was a mismatched matching citation and is identified as such. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all n−1 tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic O(log⁴ n) amortized update bound. Amortization allows occasional expensive operations as long as their cost can be charged across a sequence. The present target limits the time of each individual update, so long rebuilds and large replacement-edge searches must be spread out while keeping the current answer ready.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains O(log⁴ n/log log n) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain Las Vegas maintenance with subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. Their approach combines expander maintenance with a reduction to graphs having few edges beyond a forest. Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently derandomize the needed expander-decomposition component and obtain deterministic n^{o(1)} worst-case updates.

Subpolynomial is still weaker than polylogarithmic. For example, exp(√log n) grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of n but faster than every fixed power of log n. Thus a statement of n^{o(1)} update time does not automatically meet this card’s bound. The 2020 deterministic theorem resolves an earlier polynomial-exponent barrier while leaving the sharper target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a (1+ε)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to log(U)/ε for weights in [1,U]. The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

For integer weights, one could force an approximation guarantee to become exact by taking ε smaller than the reciprocal of a polynomial upper bound on the optimum cost. But the displayed 1/ε overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

6627.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
6627.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |M|≥ν(G)/(1+ε) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
6627.definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set [n], n≥2; ν(G) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed ε and constant a≥1, require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm A_{ε,a} such that every sequence of T≤n^a updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most K[n+T(log₂(n+2))^d]. Words have B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least 1−n^{−3}, after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes O(1) time; enumerating all matching edges costs O(n) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on ε and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. 6627.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to ν(G) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to n^{1/2+o(1)} amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a 2−√2−η fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed η>0. The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly n^{o(1)} times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: n^{o(1)} can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time n/2^{Ω(√log n)} times a polynomial in 1/ε. It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-ε question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.

6628.title: An FPRAS for perfect matchings in general graphs
6628.formal: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number Z(G) of perfect matchings in every finite undirected simple graph G? More precisely, is there one randomized algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every explicitly encoded graph G and rational 0<ε<1, A halts within p(L,⌈1/ε⌉) bit operations and outputs a nonnegative rational Ẑ satisfying Pr[(1−ε)Z(G)≤Ẑ≤(1+ε)Z(G)]≥3/4, where L is the total binary input length?
6628.definitions: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. It is perfect if every vertex is incident to exactly one selected edge. Z(G) is the number of distinct such edge sets; edges and vertices are unweighted. The graph is specified by a labeled vertex set and its full edge list, without bipartiteness, density, degree, expansion or planarity promises. For an odd number of vertices Z(G)=0; for the empty graph Z(G)=1. The random bits are independent fair bits, all computational and output costs are counted, and the time bound holds for every random tape. When Z(G)=0, require output zero with probability one; this causes no loss of generality because existence of a perfect matching can be decided deterministically in polynomial time before approximation begins. The fixed success probability 3/4 can be amplified to 1−δ by independent repetitions and a median, with an O(log(1/δ)) multiplicative overhead. The same polynomial p must work for all graphs and all requested accuracies. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6628.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6628.why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.
