6628.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general-graph question remains open in the checked primary literature. The August 2026 improvement is a permanent algorithm for bipartite graphs. Slow mixing of the particular general-graph Markov chains does not establish impossibility of all FPRAS approaches.

context_blocks.text: Finding a perfect matching and estimating how many exist are different tasks. Edmonds’ algorithm handles existence and maximum cardinality in general graphs, whereas exact counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs. Approximation avoids asking for every digit of a potentially exponential count, but still requires a reliable multiplicative estimate. The 2018 paper of Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes places this gap at the center of general matching-counting research.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda resolve the bipartite case through an FPRAS for the permanent of any nonnegative matrix. A square bipartite adjacency matrix records allowed pairs between two fixed vertex classes; a permutation chooses one partner for every vertex. The algorithm combines a Markov chain on perfect and near-perfect matchings with simulated annealing and weights that balance different pairs of unmatched vertices.

Applying that theorem to the ordinary adjacency matrix of a nonbipartite graph does not count its perfect matchings. For example, K₄ has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine: the latter also counts directed cycle-cover patterns. The corresponding general-graph quantity is a hafnian, a sum over partitions of the vertex set into unordered pairs. The distinction is combinatorial, not a matter of merely changing the matrix dimensions.

Counting all matchings is another solved neighboring problem: Jerrum and Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function. The desired perfect matchings may form a very small fraction of that distribution. A disjoint union of k edges already has 2ᵏ matchings and just one perfect matching. Thus approximate uniform sampling from all matchings, followed by waiting for a perfect one, need not run in polynomial time. This example concerns that proposed reduction, not hardness of counting on the example graph.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes show that the straightforward extension of the JSV chain encounters exponential mixing bottlenecks on general graphs; changing weights based only on the unmatched-vertex pattern does not give a universal remedy. They also use the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition to obtain algorithms for structurally restricted graphs. A factor-critical component is one whose deletion of any one vertex leaves a perfect matching. Their parameter concerns the number of ears in such a component’s ear decomposition, not simply its vertex count.

The problem matters beyond matching counts themselves. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s 2025 journal paper classifies approximation of several two-state spin-system partition functions. Some parameter settings are linked by approximation-preserving reductions to perfect-matching counting in general graphs, and the paper explicitly retains that task as a central open question. A resolution would therefore determine tractability for related counting models as well.

On 27 August 2026, Chen, Vigoda and Yang post an improved permanent FPRAS. For an r×r zero–one matrix their stated bound is O(r⁶ ε⁻² log⁵ r log(2/δ)), improving the previous leading dependence at fixed accuracy and success probability. Their analysis controls mixing of observables describing unmatched-vertex patterns through a restricted Poincaré inequality and coupled flows. The state space remains bipartite; the new theorem does not remove the general-graph obstruction.

The central issue is whether the extra structure available in bipartite graphs is essential for efficient approximate counting. A positive result would extend one of the landmark successes of randomized counting to all graphs. A negative result would establish a striking boundary: even though perfect matching existence remains efficiently decidable on both sides, relative counting would become computationally harder once arbitrary odd-cycle structure is permitted.

6629.title: A deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
6629.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given nonnegative rational n×n matrix A and every rational ε∈(0,1), outputs a rational Z satisfying (1−ε)per(A)≤Z≤(1+ε)per(A) in time polynomial in the input bit length and 1/ε?
6629.definitions: For n≥1, per(A)=Σ_{π∈S_n}∏_{i=1}^n A_{i,π(i)}, where S_n is the set of permutations of [n]. Each entry is represented by a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Let L be the total binary description length of A and ε. There must be one fixed polynomial P such that the algorithm uses at most P(L,1/ε) bit operations on every input. Ordinary deterministic Turing computation is intended, with output bits and arithmetic costs counted; there are no random bits, nonuniform advice, counting oracles or exact-real unit-cost operations. No density, expansion, lower-bound-on-positive-entries, bounded-degree or matrix-scaling promise is imposed. Zero entries are allowed. If per(A)=0, the algorithm must return Z=0 exactly. This zero case is decidable in polynomial time by checking whether the bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. FPTAS means fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: the running-time exponent must be independent of ε, and the error is relative to per(A), not additive relative to n!, a matrix norm, or another normalization.
6629.answer_criterion: Construct such a deterministic approximation scheme or prove that none exists. A randomized FPRAS does not settle the deterministic question. An approximation within a factor depending superconstantly on n, or a scheme with running time n^{g(1/ε)}, does not meet the stated guarantee. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a refutation, since using exponentially small ε is allowed to take exponential time under the FPTAS bound.
6629.why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.

6629.status_note: The 9 September 2026 primary preprint explicitly leaves a deterministic FPTAS open. Its new general subexponential-factor guarantee improves the late-August exponential-base results without yielding arbitrary relative accuracy. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: For a zero–one matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph: rows and columns are the two vertex classes, and a permutation chooses one allowed partner for every row. With nonnegative weights it sums the products of edge weights over these matchings. Finding one perfect matching is efficient, but estimating how much total weight all perfect matchings contribute is a different task.

Unlike the determinant, the permanent has no alternating signs in its permutation sum. Nonnegativity makes multiplicative approximation meaningful even when the total is very small. It also makes zero detection easy: a positive permanent is equivalent to existence of a perfect matching using positive entries. The hard part is accurate quantitative estimation on positive instances, not distinguishing an arbitrary exponentially tiny value from zero by floating-point tolerance.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda provide a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme for every nonnegative matrix. Their method combines weighted perfect and near-perfect matchings, sampling and simulated annealing. Thus a solution need not discover that approximate counting is possible; it must remove randomness while retaining arbitrary relative accuracy and polynomial dependence on the requested inverse accuracy.

The randomized side continues to improve. Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s August 2026 preprint reduces the reported running time for zero–one matrices to O(n⁶ log⁵ n) when the relative accuracy and success probability are fixed, with an extension to general nonnegative matrices. The better analysis concerns a restricted Poincaré inequality for the Markov chain. It remains a sampling-based randomized algorithm.

A major deterministic approach is the Bethe permanent, obtained from a variational optimization over doubly stochastic matrices. Anari and Rezaei prove that it lower-bounds the permanent and loses at most a factor 2^{n/2}. This factor is attained on block-diagonal matrices built from two-by-two all-ones blocks. The tight example limits the unmodified Bethe estimate, rather than proving that every deterministic approximation algorithm must lose that much.

In late August 2026, Anari and independently Narang and Perkins go beyond the canonical Bethe estimate. Both approaches exploit structure near the bad two-by-two blocks and achieve a factor c^n for some absolute c<√2. This improves the exponential base. A fixed positive base above one, however, still gives an error factor growing exponentially with the matrix dimension.

The September 9 preprint of Kudria, Luo and Majid improves the general deterministic polynomial-time guarantee to exp(O(n(log log n)²/log n))=exp(o(n)). Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than 1+ε.

There is a useful amplification threshold. Make a block-diagonal matrix containing r copies of A; its permanent is per(A)^r. If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximated an N by N permanent within exp(O(N^{1−γ})) for one fixed γ>0, applying it at N=rn and taking an rth root would reduce the logarithmic error to O(n^{1−γ}/r^γ). Polynomially many copies in n and 1/ε would then suffice for an FPTAS.

The September theorem’s logarithmic saving does not cross that threshold: polynomially many copies increase log(rn) by only a constant-factor scale, leaving a large logarithmic error after root extraction. Consequently, subexponential approximation and arbitrary relative accuracy remain distinct milestones. A solution would remove one of the most prominent uses of randomness in approximate counting while clarifying how much global matching information deterministic optimization can recover.

A statistical query is a bounded average. For a database of categories, an indicator query asks what fraction of records belong to a selected set of categories. Several queries can ask about overlapping sets, so their answers concern the same individuals. Privacy constrains the distribution of the entire released vector under replacement of any one record. Protecting each coordinate separately with the full privacy budget would not establish the required joint guarantee.

The normalized Euclidean error is the square root of the average squared coordinate error for one output, followed by expectation over the mechanism. If the error vector is (1,0,…,0), its normalized Euclidean error is 1/√k, whereas its maximum-coordinate error is one. Thus one badly estimated query can have much less effect on the average criterion. The position of the expectation also matters: this is not the square root of the expected squared error.

The 2021 question sought a bound independent of k, the number of queries. Its shifted logarithm handles a singleton universe, and the minimum with one reflects a trivial data-independent release: outputting the zero vector has normalized error at most one. A singleton universe in fact permits exact release, because all databases have the same answer vector. These conventions do not assert a matching lower bound in every parameter regime.

Nikolov proves sample complexity O(log T/(εα²)) for normalized error α, alongside sharper alternatives for some parameters. Rearranging gives the square-root accuracy bound. His definitions use bounded real queries, replacement adjacency and the expected norm divided by √k, matching this card. The mechanism exploits a lower-dimensional representation of the feasible answer vectors and also has an efficiency guarantee beyond this card’s existence requirement.

The July 2026 version of Fitzsimons’s paper focused on the maximum-coordinate problem and retained a √log(2k) factor. Its 3 August revision adds Theorem 1.2 with the exact Euclidean rate and explicitly acknowledges Nikolov’s earlier solution. The Euclidean conclusion therefore must not be classified as still open by reading only the first version or the abstract-page summary. The newer paper’s claimed formalization was not independently built or audited here.

6632.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
6632.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
6632.formal: Does there exist a universal constant C≥1 and a randomized, universally truthful combinatorial-auction mechanism that, for every number n of bidders, number m of items and normalized monotone submodular valuation profile, uses polynomial communication and produces an allocation of expected social welfare at least OPT/C?
6632.definitions: There are m≥1 distinct indivisible items and n≥1 bidders. Bidder i privately knows v_i:2^[m]→Q_{≥0}, with v_i(∅)=0, v_i(S)≤v_i(T) for S⊆T, and v_i(S)+v_i(T)≥v_i(S∪T)+v_i(S∩T) for all S,T. To make communication in bits precise, a public integer B≥1 bounds the binary lengths of the numerator and positive denominator of each value. This is a bound per value, not permission to transmit the exponential table. One uniform protocol must work for every n,m,B with at most P(n,m,B) communicated bits in the worst case, for one fixed polynomial P. Arbitrary interactive messages and demand queries are allowed; all query descriptions, replies, allocations and payments count toward communication. Local computation by bidders and auctioneer is unrestricted but must terminate. An outcome consists of pairwise disjoint bundles S_1,…,S_n and rational payments p_1,…,p_n; unallocated items are allowed. Utilities are quasilinear, u_i=v_i(S_i)−p_i. There are no private budgets or distributional assumptions. Universal truthfulness means the mechanism is a report-independent distribution over deterministic dominant-strategy truthful mechanisms: for every fixed random seed r, every i, every admissible true and alternative reported type v_i,v_i′, and every v_{−i}, v_i(S_i(v_i,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i,v_{−i};r)≥v_i(S_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r))−p_i(v_i′,v_{−i};r). A low-communication protocol implements this outcome and payment rule on the distributed reported types. OPT=max Σ_i v_i(T_i), where the maximum is over pairwise disjoint T_i⊆[m]. The expected welfare guarantee holds for every truthful valuation profile, with expectation only over the mechanism’s randomness; C is independent of n,m,B. No additional individual-rationality or transfer-sign restriction is imposed in this formulation.
6632.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6632.why: Determine whether exact truthful incentives inherently cause an unbounded loss of allocative efficiency, even when arbitrary compact communication and unlimited local optimization are available.

importance.reason: A central multi-parameter mechanism-design problem linking truthful incentives, submodular optimization, information elicitation and the communication cost of welfare approximation.

Assadi–Singla obtain expected O((log log m)³)-approximation with universal truthfulness and O(n) demand queries.
Assadi–Kesselheim–Singla improve the submodular and XOS factor to O((log log m)²); Theorem 2 uses at most n value and demand queries.

6632.status_note: The checked primary literature retains a gap between constant nontruthful welfare approximation and the general universally truthful guarantee. Theorem 2 of the SODA 2021 paper supplies O((log log m)²) for submodular bidders. The 2026 graph-auction results impose eligibility restrictions. No general constant-factor resolution found through 11 September 2026. The public per-value precision parameter makes the inherited polynomial-communication question explicit in bits.

context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand query offers item prices and asks a bidder to choose a bundle maximizing its value minus its total price. Sending that bundle requires only m membership bits, even when finding it takes enormous local computation. This is why allowing demand queries changes the problem substantially. The formulation deliberately measures communication: an algorithm that delegates difficult optimization to a bidder can qualify. It would need further work to become computationally efficient for that bidder.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful m^{1/2−ε}-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed ε>0. A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla reached an expected O((log log m)³) approximation using O(n) demand queries, at FOCS 2019. Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla subsequently improved the submodular guarantee to O((log log m)²), while obtaining O((log log m)³) for the broader subadditive class. These asymptotic factors grow with the number of items, despite growing very slowly.

The latter mechanism learns approximate item prices through random groups of bidders. A bidder participates in a single fixed-price auction, so its own report cannot manipulate the menu it faces. Some price-learning rounds can become the final allocation rather than merely gathering information; the analysis accounts for welfare earned in those rounds. This makes price discovery compatible with truthfulness, but leaves a loss between the learned allocation and optimal welfare.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

6633.title: Polynomial query complexity of exact envy-free cake cutting
6633.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
6633.formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol exist that, for every n and every profile of n nonatomic additive cake valuations, use at most Cn^d queries to produce a complete exactly envy-free allocation, allowing disconnected pieces?
6633.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Agent i has an arbitrary nonatomic Borel probability measure μ_i: values are nonnegative, countably additive, μ_i([0,1])=1 and μ_i({x})=0 for every point x. No density formula, bounded-density promise or random valuation model is supplied. The protocol learns valuations only through exact queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μ_i([x,y]); Cut(i,x,α), with 0≤α≤μ_i([x,1]), returns a point y≥x for which μ_i([x,y])=α. Endpoints used by the protocol are 0, 1 and previously returned cut marks; interval values can be combined by additivity. If several cut points satisfy a query, the protocol must remain correct for any valid response. Count each evaluation or cut query as one; finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-complexity bound. Output a partition (A₁,…,A_n) of the entire cake into finite unions of intervals with endpoints among the known marks. Assign cut endpoints arbitrarily, since every agent values them at zero. Require μ_i(A_i)≥μ_i(A_j) for every ordered pair i,j. There is no unallocated residue, approximation error, randomization, or connected-piece requirement. The bound Cn^d is uniform over all valuation profiles and valid query responses.
6633.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic protocol with the stated worst-case polynomial query bound, or prove that every such protocol has superpolynomial worst-case query complexity as n grows. A lower bound on the number of queries used by one known protocol is not a general impossibility result. A finite bound depending arbitrarily on n, an average-case polynomial bound, or a polynomial protocol permitting positive envy or discarded cake leaves this question open.
6633.why: A central information-complexity question in fair division: how many exact preference queries are necessary to allocate an entire divisible resource without envy?

importance.reason: The main worst-case complexity gap for exact envy-free cake cutting; recent single-exponential and average-case results sharpen the boundary without settling polynomial query complexity.

6633.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Polynomial worst-case query complexity remains open. The latest checked general upper bound is the n^{O(1)}2^n protocol reported in the Ye–Bai preprint of 4 September 2026; Chèze’s polynomial result is over random valuation profiles.

context_blocks.text: Envy-freeness asks each person to compare the allocated pieces using their own valuation. It does not require different people to agree on values or to receive pieces of equal geometric length. For two agents, cut-and-choose works: one divides the cake into two equally valued parts and the other selects a preferred part. Extending this idea while controlling every pairwise comparison becomes much harder as the number of agents grows.

Completeness prevents a trivial answer. If the protocol could discard everything, giving everyone an empty piece would create no envy. Allocating the full cake also makes envy-freeness imply proportionality: for each agent, the value of their own piece is at least the average value of the n allocated pieces, namely 1/n. The converse fails because receiving a fair share does not prevent preferring someone else’s larger-valued share.

Disconnected pieces are essential to the computational question being asked. Exact envy-free allocations with connected pieces cannot, in general, be obtained by finite Robertson–Webb protocols once there are at least three agents. That obstruction does not apply when an agent may receive several intervals. Likewise, a bound on the number of final cut locations alone is not a bound on the number of valuation questions needed to discover suitable locations.

Nonatomicity gives the cut oracle its power: an interval can be cut to achieve any intermediate value. It does not impose a simple shape on preferences. A valuation may put almost all its mass in a very small region or have intervals of zero value. Exact comparisons must remain valid on these profiles, so a fixed numerical mesh or a small positive tolerance cannot silently substitute for an exact protocol.

Procaccia’s general lower bound is Ω(n²) Robertson–Webb queries. This already separates envy-free division from the Θ(n log n) query complexity of proportional division, but it remains compatible with a polynomial protocol. A quadratic lower bound cannot justify describing the target as impossible or necessarily exponential.

Aziz–Mackenzie’s FOCS 2016 breakthrough establishes a bound depending only on n for every profile, resolving the earlier question of whether any bounded protocol exists. Their displayed upper bound is a tower of six copies of n. This is stronger than merely terminating on each profile: earlier finite procedures could require arbitrarily many queries while n stayed fixed. The existence of a bounded protocol leaves the growth rate of that bound open.

Sokolov’s June 2023 preprint revises parts of the protocol and sharpens the analysis to n^{8n²(1+o(1))}. That is a major quantitative reduction, equal to 2^{(8+o(1))n² log₂n}, although it remains far above polynomial. The inherited 2025/2026 average-case article still quotes the older tower benchmark; the progress account here therefore also checks subsequent and separately posted algorithmic work.

A very recent advance is Ye–Bai’s September 4, 2026 preprint. Its Theorem 1.1 states a deterministic protocol using n^{O(1)}2^n queries for complete envy-free allocation with arbitrary nonnegative additive nonatomic valuations. The proof replaces a very large family of partial allocations by a polynomial-sized collection and controls how their pieces can be reassigned without conflicts. This is the latest reported general upper bound found in the review, and is identified as a preprint.

The same paper distinguishes query complexity from local computation. A helper construction uses exhaustive search after the relevant values have been elicited; Appendix C explains its deterministic choices and implementation through ordinary Robertson–Webb queries. Expensive transcript processing is allowed in the present question. Thus the reported single-exponential query bound should not be advertised as an equally fast bit-time algorithm, and it still does not give polynomially many queries.

Chèze’s inherited article studies a probability distribution on valuation profiles, following a full-independence framework. Under its uniform model, the probability of needing at least n^{12} queries tends to zero. This probability concerns the sampled preferences, rather than random bits used by a protocol facing an arbitrary fixed profile. Rare or specially chosen valuations remain relevant to the worst-case question. The article appeared online in September 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume.

Approximate envy-freeness creates another distinct regime. Bounds polynomial in n and inverse tolerance can produce small positive envy, including versions with connected pieces. Sending the tolerance to zero does not yield a finite exact protocol if the query count diverges. Exactness, completeness, access through queries and unrestricted disconnected allocations are therefore all part of this card’s answer criterion.

The fundamental issue is the amount of preference information needed for an exact global fairness guarantee. A polynomial protocol would show that the enormous historical bounds reflect limitations of the constructions rather than an intrinsic elicitation barrier. A superpolynomial lower bound would reveal a sharp information cost of exact envy-freeness even when computational work between queries is unrestricted.

6634.definitions: An election E consists of disjoint finite labeled sets V of n≥1 voters and C of m≥1 candidates, and a strict total order ≻_v on C for each v∈V. A consistent distance d is a pseudometric on V∪C: d(x,x)=0, d(x,y)=d(y,x)≥0, and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z) for all points, with a≻_v b implying d(v,a)≤d(v,b). Distinct named points may be colocated. Equal distances may be broken in any order in the reported ranking; the guarantee must hold for every consistent pair (E,d). The social cost SC_d(a)=Σ_v∈V d(v,a), and OPT_d=min_a∈C SC_d(a). A randomized ordinal rule f assigns each election E a lottery p=f(E), where p_a≥0 and Σ_a p_a=1. Its expected cost is Σ_a p_a SC_d(a). The lottery depends only on n,m and the full rankings, not on d or additional distance queries. It may use arbitrary real probabilities and unbounded computation. No anonymity, neutrality, incentive-compatibility or tournament-only restriction is imposed. Define Dist(f)=inf{D≥1: for every E and every consistent d, Σ_a f(E)_a SC_d(a)≤D·OPT_d}, taking inf∅=+∞. This inequality requires zero expected cost if OPT_d=0 and avoids dividing by zero. Set D*=inf_f Dist(f), over single rule families defined on all finite elections. The expectation is over the selected candidate, while elections and consistent metrics are worst-case choices. Replacing total cost by average cost divides both sides by n and gives the same distortion.
6634.answer_criterion: Give an exact real value or unambiguous exact expression for D* and prove equality: for every η>0 there must be a rule with universal distortion at most D*+η, and every rule must have distortion at least D*. An attained optimum with the matching lower bound also suffices. A numerical interval, a better upper bound alone, or an exact optimum within a restricted family of rules does not determine the unrestricted infimum.

context_blocks.title: Rankings hide the size of a preference
context_blocks.text: Two voters rank candidates a and b in opposite orders. Put a at 0 and b at 2 on a line. If voter 1 is at 0 and voter 2 at 1, the total costs of a and b are 1 and 3; if voter 1 is at 1 and voter 2 at 2, they are 3 and 1. Both arrangements fit the same rankings when a distance tie is resolved in the reported direction. The rule therefore has to make one choice of lottery that works in both possible geometries.

context_blocks.title: What randomization changes
context_blocks.text: If the lottery selects a with probability p, its distortion in these two examples is respectively 3−2p and 1+2p. At least one is at least 2. Choosing each candidate with probability one half reaches 2 for this pair of examples, whereas a deterministic choice suffers factor 3 in one of them. This demonstrates why randomization can help, but it is only a small lower-bound example. It does not establish the optimum over all elections.

context_blocks.title: The old value-2 conjecture is false
context_blocks.text: Charikar and Ramakrishnan construct larger elections giving a universal randomized lower bound of approximately 2.11264. Consequently, the target is to identify the optimal value above two, not prove the former conjecture. The lower bound concerns all randomized rules that use rankings, with no restriction to a particular named procedure or to pairwise summaries.

context_blocks.title: Recent upper bounds leave a smaller gap
context_blocks.text: Frank’s August 2026 preprint gives an upper bound of 2.5. Shah’s revision of 6 September improves this to 2.1441; its first version had the weaker value 2.3282. The 8 September preprint of Cai and coauthors states an upper bound of 2.13713, leaving a gap of less than 0.025 above the reported general lower bound. These are recent theorem claims with checked model matches; this review has not independently verified their proofs or numerical certificates. They still leave an interval rather than an exact value.

context_blocks.title: Restricted rules answer different questions
context_blocks.text: A weighted tournament records how many voters prefer a to b for each pair. It need not preserve all the information in their complete rankings. The optimal factor 3 for randomized tournament rules therefore does not bound what full-ranking rules can achieve. Similarly, Shah’s lower bound of 2.136 concerns his random-size-stable-lottery family; it is not a new universal lower bound for every rule. The scope of both upper and lower bounds matters when comparing them with D*.

context_blocks.title: Why this constant matters
context_blocks.text: D* measures how much total distance can be lost solely because a decision rule knows the order of preferences but not their intensities. It makes no assumption that voters behave strategically, and it does not require a truthful mechanism. The mathematical guarantee is robust across every metric consistent with the ballots, rather than an average over a chosen model of elections.

6635.title: Does every finite-template decision promise CSP have a P/NP-hard dichotomy?
6635.formal: For every pair of fixed finite relational structures A,B of the same finite signature, with a homomorphism A→B, is the decision promise problem of distinguishing I→A from I↛B either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions?
6635.definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols R with fixed positive arities a_R. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and, for each R, a relation R^A⊆A^{a_R}. A homomorphism h:I→A is a map on domains such that (v₁,…,v_a)∈R^I implies (h(v₁),…,h(v_a))∈R^A for every R and tuple. The templates A,B and their relations are fixed for each computational problem. Only I varies; its domain and relation tuples are explicitly listed in binary, of total length L. The algorithm must accept all I admitting a homomorphism to A and reject all I admitting no homomorphism to B. On I→B but I↛A, either answer is allowed. A→B makes the yes and no sets disjoint. Polynomial time means one deterministic algorithm for the fixed pair, halting on every input in O(L^c), with c and hidden constants allowed to depend on A,B. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time map from 3-SAT formulas φ to structures I_φ such that satisfiable φ yield I_φ→A and unsatisfiable φ yield I_φ↛B. The question is about deciding the promise, not producing a B-valued assignment. No uniform algorithm for classifying templates is required. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

6635.status_note: Open classification question in the cited survey, with relevant partial results checked through 10 September 2026. The card asks for an unconditional decision dichotomy over all fixed finite template pairs; it does not assume decision/search equivalence or a complete algebraic classification.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary constraint satisfaction asks whether a collection of local requirements can all hold simultaneously. Promise CSPs keep two versions of each requirement: the input is guaranteed to admit a solution satisfying the stronger version, while the relaxed task uses the weaker one. For graph colouring, A=Kₖ and B=K_c with k≤c produces the decision task of distinguishing k-colourable graphs from graphs that are not c-colourable. Graphs in between impose no decision requirement.

When A=B, the promise disappears. Bulatov and Zhuk independently proved in 2017 that every finite-template CSP is either in P or NP-complete. The present question asks whether a comparable exclusion of intermediate complexity survives arbitrary finite promises. It does not follow merely by applying the classical theorem to A and B separately: the relaxed task can be easier than either endpoint CSP.

A concrete tractable example promises that each listed triple of Boolean variables can have exactly one 1 and asks only for a not-all-equal assignment. Solve the equations x+y+z=1 over the integers, then map positive values to 1 and nonpositive values to 0. No such triple can become all zero or all one. Barto proves that this tractability cannot be explained by sandwiching the pair through a tractable finite-domain CSP, unless P=NP. Finite templates can therefore need an infinite intermediate domain in this natural algorithmic framework.

The algebraic approach studies operations that combine several A-solutions coordinatewise into one B-solution. These polymorphisms capture useful structure for algorithms and reductions, but their input and output domains can differ, preventing the direct use of all the composition arguments available in ordinary CSP. The survey emphasizes that a full dichotomy was not yet backed by enough evidence to be asserted as a settled consensus conjecture; this card poses it as a precise open question.

Important subclasses are classified. Brakensiek and Guruswami obtain a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise CSPs allowing negations, with tractable cases going beyond a direct reuse of Schaefer’s classical Boolean CSP classification. That theorem does not classify all Boolean templates or all finite domains.

The 2026 work of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima expands the logical viewpoint by relating Promise MMSNP to finite-domain PCSPs. It also classifies a family defined by forbidden monochromatic cliques under the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture. Both the restricted family and the additional assumption matter: this is not an unconditional classification of every finite template pair.

6636.title: The Bodirsky–Pinsker infinite-domain CSP dichotomy
6636.formal: For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous structure A over a finite relational signature, and every finite-signature first-order reduct B of A, is CSP(B) either decidable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
6636.definitions: A relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed finite arities. A is homogeneous if every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of A. It is finitely bounded if there is a finite set F of finite structures in its signature such that a finite structure embeds into A exactly when none of the structures in F embeds into it; embeddings preserve both relations and their complements. Countable allows finite or countably infinite domains. B has the same domain as A, with finitely many relations each definable by a first-order formula over A without parameters; it may forget original relations and introduce definable ones. For each fixed B, an input to CSP(B) is an explicitly encoded finite structure I in B’s signature. Accept exactly when there is a map h from the domain of I to that of B preserving every relation tuple. Equivalently, a finite conjunction of atomic B-constraints must have a satisfying assignment. h need not be injective. A, B and their defining formulas are fixed, not part of the input; running times are measured in the finite instance’s bit length. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6636.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

6636.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The latest checked primary papers explicitly retain the general dichotomy as open. The July FO/L-hard classification has both a different complexity boundary and an expansion hypothesis; the August interpretability result does not settle tractability.

context_blocks.text: The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers (ℚ;<) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare P/NP-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

6637.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
6637.formal: Is there a fixed integer C≥3 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph G promised to be 3-colourable, outputs a proper vertex colouring using at most C colours with probability at least 2/3?
6637.definitions: The input is an explicitly given graph G=([n],E), n≥1, with no loops or parallel edges, encoded by its adjacency matrix. A proper k-colouring is a map c:[n]→[k] such that c(u)≠c(v) for every {u,v}∈E. The promise is existence of a proper 3-colouring; such a colouring is not supplied. There must be one C, one randomized Turing machine A, and fixed constants K,d such that A uses at most K(n+1)^d bit operations on every graph and every random tape. On each promised input, the probability, over independent unbiased internal random bits, of outputting a proper C-colouring is at least 2/3. Invalid outputs can be replaced by a failure symbol after checking all edges. No correctness requirement is imposed on non-3-colourable inputs, but the time bound still applies. The algorithm may colour such an input whenever it can; it need not recognize the promise. C is independent of n, degree, density and the input graph. No planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition promise is available. Randomization is explicitly permitted in this version of the inherited question; a deterministic algorithm would be a stronger positive result. The algorithm must colour every vertex and avoid every monochromatic edge on a successful run.
6637.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm for at least one fixed C, or prove that no such C and randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist. A growing colour bound, a partial colouring of most vertices, or a guarantee only on a restricted graph family is insufficient. NP-hardness of the 3-versus-C promise for every fixed C would establish the usual complexity-theoretic obstruction; excluding randomized algorithms from that obstruction additionally uses NP≠RP. Hardness for C=5 alone leaves all larger constants unresolved. Conditional hardness results must keep their assumptions explicit.
6637.why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

6637.status_note: No constant-colour algorithm or unrestricted all-constant hardness resolution found through 11 September 2026. The February 2026 primary paper retains the gap between five-colour NP-hardness and a growing O(n^{0.19539}) algorithmic bound. The March logic result is restricted to fixed-point logic with counting. This card explicitly allows bounded-error randomized algorithms.

context_blocks.text: The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to K₃ and the output must provide a map to K_C. The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to K₃ from graphs not mapping to K_C.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove NP-hardness of finding a five-colouring of a three-colourable graph, as part of a broader algebraic framework. This is far stronger than hardness of finding the promised three-colouring, yet it excludes only particular small output domains under standard complexity assumptions. It does not rule out a successful algorithm using six, 100 or any other larger fixed number of colours.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an O(√n)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains Õ(n^{0.19747}) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector 5/2-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives O(n^{0.19539}) colours. A vector 5/2-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

6638.title: A constant improvement over factor 2 for unrelated-machine makespan
6638.formal: Does there exist a constant ε with 0<ε<1 and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm which, for every unrelated-machine scheduling instance, assigns all jobs to machines with makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
6638.definitions: An instance consists of m≥1 machines, n≥0 independent jobs, and an explicitly given m×n matrix of processing times pᵢⱼ in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} with p_{σ(j),j}<∞. Its makespan is Cmax(σ)=maxᵢ Σ_{j:σ(j)=i} pᵢⱼ, and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output σ, not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. ε and the polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6638.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6638.why: A defining unresolved approximation barrier in scheduling. Beating two by any fixed constant would also imply a constant approximation for general Santa Claus allocation, while known relaxation gaps rule out a large family of straightforward proofs.

6638.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The full worst-case constant-improvement question remains open in the checked primary literature. The known 2−1/m ratio and prediction-assisted results have different quantifiers from the fixed-ε target. The 3/2 hardness is conditional on P≠NP.

context_blocks.text: Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.

6640.title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
6640.formal: Do a universal integer C≥0 and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist that pack every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance into at most OPT+C unit-capacity bins with probability at least 2/3?
6640.definitions: The input is a list of n≥1 rational item sizes s₁,…,s_n∈(0,1], each encoded as a binary numerator and positive binary denominator; L is the total encoding length. A feasible packing is a map b:[n]→[k] with Σ_{i:b(i)=j}s_i≤1 for every bin j. OPT is the minimum feasible integer k. The algorithm is uniform and classical, has access to the entire input before assigning items, and must output an explicit feasible packing. For absolute constants K,d, every execution must take at most KL^d bit operations. Its output is always feasible, and on each fixed input it uses at most OPT+C bins with probability at least 2/3 over its private random bits. C,K,d are independent of n, the number of distinct sizes, OPT and coefficient precision. No capacity augmentation, splitting of items, cardinality constraint or promise on the input distribution is allowed. Repeated items are explicitly listed rather than represented by binary multiplicities. Randomization is expressly allowed; a deterministic algorithm would also resolve the question. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6640.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6640.why: A basic boundary between asymptotic approximation and almost exact combinatorial optimization: can efficient packing lose only a fixed number of bins on every instance?

6640.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No universal constant-additive polynomial-time algorithm or general impossibility result was found in the checked primary sources. The logarithmic-additive guarantee and recent high-multiplicity/support results do not settle this explicitly listed, randomized formulation.

context_blocks.text: The objective is to minimize the number of identical containers needed to hold indivisible items. Each bin has a single numerical capacity constraint, so the model contains no geometric placement issue. Nevertheless, many different combinations of small and large items can fit exactly or almost exactly, and choices that look locally efficient can leave unusable capacity elsewhere. The inherited invited survey explicitly asks for an OPT+O(1) guarantee.

Additive and multiplicative errors behave differently as the optimum grows. A one-percent excess can mean thousands of unnecessary bins on a large instance; an additive constant remains fixed. Conversely, this card allows any universal constant, even a very large one. It does not ask for an additive-one algorithm or for exact optimization on small instances.

The elementary hardness example is distinguishing instances needing two bins from those needing three, through Partition. This rules out exact polynomial optimization under the usual complexity assumptions, but it does not settle constant additive approximation. With allowance C=1, a valid three-bin answer is permitted in both cases. A stronger hardness argument would need a gap that survives the particular additive allowance.

Asymptotic approximation schemes achieve a ratio approaching one, with additional losses depending on their accuracy parameter. This does not automatically give OPT+C. Choosing ε on the order of 1/OPT makes ε·OPT small, but the additive term and the running time may worsen as ε shrinks. The dependence on every parameter must be controlled simultaneously; the existence of a scheme alone does not establish the desired fixed loss.

Several published bounds use the Gilmore–Gomory configuration LP. A configuration specifies a multiset of item types that fits in one bin. The LP permits fractional numbers of such bins while covering all required items. Its optimum OPT_f is a lower bound on the integral optimum. Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with O(log² OPT) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to OPT_f+O(log OPT_f), and hence OPT+O(log OPT). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of OPT_f would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring Ω(log n). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.

6641.title: The uniform word problem for one-relation monoids
6641.formal: Is there a single algorithm that, given a finite alphabet A and four finite words u,v,s,t∈A*, always halts and decides whether s and t represent the same element of the monoid presented by ⟨A | u=v⟩?
6641.definitions: A* consists of all finite strings over A, including the empty word ε, with concatenation as multiplication and ε as identity. The presentation ⟨A | u=v⟩ denotes A*/≡, where ≡ is the least equivalence relation containing u≡v that is compatible with concatenation on both sides. Equivalently, s≡t exactly when some finite sequence s=w_0,w_1,…,w_k=t exists in which each adjacent pair is xu y,xv y in either order for some x,y∈A*. The fixed words u and v are literal strings, not variables that can be substituted by arbitrary words. Empty sides are permitted: replacing ε means inserting the other side at a gap in the current string. The alphabet and all four words form a finite explicit input; one may encode A as {1,…,a} and its letters as integers. The requested algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine for all presentations and all word pairs, with no oracle and no unbounded advice. There is no polynomial-time or other prescribed resource bound, but termination is required on both equal and unequal pairs. This is an ordinary monoid presentation. No inverse operation, cancellation law, group axiom or commutativity assumption is present. The presentation itself varies with the input: the card asks for uniform decidability, not merely a separate non-effectively selected procedure for each fixed presentation.
6641.answer_criterion: Construct an always-terminating uniform decision procedure with a correctness proof, or prove that the language of positive presentation-and-word-pair instances is undecidable. One explicit fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem would suffice for a negative answer, but is stronger than is logically required to refute uniform decidability. Enumeration that halts only on equal words, or a procedure whose termination on unequal words is unproved, is insufficient. An exponential derivation-length lower bound is compatible with decidability.
6641.why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?

importance.reason: One of the central minimal-presentation decision problems, connecting string rewriting, algebraic normal forms, computability and reductions between monoids, inverse monoids and groups.

6641.status_note: The August 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the ordinary one-relation-monoid word problem as open. Its inverse-monoid undecidability theorem does not resolve this ordinary presentation problem. Checked through 11 September 2026. The inherited input includes the presentation, so the card explicitly targets uniform decidability and distinguishes it from the per-presentation quantifier.

context_blocks.text: This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

Positive answers are always semidecidable. Enumerate all finite replacement sequences from s and stop if t appears. Every individual stage has finitely many choices, even when one side of the relation is empty. The missing ingredient is an effective stopping argument for negative instances. Seeing no derivation within a long search does not establish inequality when intermediate words may continue to grow.

Length-preserving relations illustrate an easy case. If |u|=|v|, every reachable word has length |s|, so exhaustive search takes place in a finite graph. Unequal input lengths immediately imply inequality. When the relation changes length, that finite-state argument disappears. The question permits enormous running times, so even an impractical computable bound on the needed search would be a meaningful resolution.

Simply orienting a rule toward shorter words need not produce unique normal forms. For the relation baba=aba, the word bababa can shorten through ababa to aaba, or directly to baaba. Neither aaba nor baaba contains baba, so both are irreducible under the shortening rule, although they are equal in the presented monoid. This example shows why termination of one chosen reduction strategy is different from a complete equality test.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family ⟨a,b | baa(ba)^N=a⟩ for N≥2 with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

The inverse-monoid connection is still useful: positive decidability results for the appropriate intermediate class would imply positive results for ordinary one-relation monoids. A negative result in a broader intermediate class need not transfer backwards through that implication. The fundamental goal remains an exact boundary for algorithmic equality under extremely small presentations, with consequences for rewriting systems, normal forms and the ways finite algebraic syntax can encode unbounded computation.

6643.definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables p_i (i∈ℕ), ⊥, negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in φ, may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation R⊆W×W, finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and w⊨□ψ iff v⊨ψ for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
6643.answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.

context_blocks.text: A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇ψ is false for every replacement ψ. Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula p→□p, unifiers exist, including p↦⊤, but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.

6645.title: The full constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
6645.area: Database theory and finite model theory
6645.formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given any conjunctive query q with self-joins allowed, decides whether q admits enumeration of all distinct answers with O_q(N) preprocessing and O_q(1) worst-case delay on every database of size N?
6645.definitions: A query is a finite formula q(x̄)=∃ȳ ∧ᵢ Rᵢ(z̄ᵢ), with no constants, negation, disequalities or aggregation. The head x̄ lists distinct variables; every variable occurs in a relational atom. Relation symbols have fixed positive finite arities within q and may occur repeatedly; repeated variables within atoms are allowed. Boolean queries have an empty head. A database D explicitly lists finite set-valued relations over a domain [n]; N=1+n+the total number of tuple entries in these lists. Each domain identifier fits in O(log(N+2)) bits. q(D) is the set of head tuples extendible to an assignment satisfying all atoms. Fix the deterministic word-RAM convention with addition, multiplication, comparison, Boolean word operations and indirect access costing one step, words of O_q(log(N+2)) bits, and a polynomial address universe of initially zero cells. Accessed cells and operations are charged; no linear-space or constant-extra-space restriction is imposed. This allows direct tuple-membership tables without charging for touching every unused address. Membership in the target class means that for this fixed q there are an enumerator and constants C_q,B_q whose preprocessing takes at most C_q N steps, whose word length is at most B_q log₂(N+2), and whose time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to termination is at most C_q after preprocessing. Empty output must be reported within the same delay bound. Output order is arbitrary and each tuple appears exactly once. The classifier takes q, not D, as input and must halt on every query; it has no prescribed runtime bound and need not output the enumerator. This is an explicit effective yes/no formulation of the source’s broader request for a complete tractability classification. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
