6645.why: A missing general tractability boundary for relational query evaluation, connecting logical syntax, enumeration algorithms and fine-grained lower bounds.

importance.reason: A central database-theory classification question: identify exactly which fixed queries permit optimal preprocessing and delay, including the self-joins excluded by classical dichotomies.

6645.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked primary sources leave the general self-join classification unresolved. The exact target is an editorial effective formulation, with a specified RAM and permissive polynomial memory. Known negative classifications use stated fine-grained hypotheses; newer projected-query and dynamic results do not cover the whole class.

context_blocks.text: A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, q(x,z)=∃y R(x,y)∧S(y,z) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer (x,z), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example ∃y R(x,y)∧S(y,z), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge {x,z} creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query R(x,y)∧R(y,z)∧R(x,t)∧R(t,z). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with t=y. When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang’s June 2026 preprint studies insertions into semiring-annotated databases and classifies a self-join-free setting using acyclicity and p-hierarchy. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.

6646.title: Martin’s full conjecture for Turing-invariant functions under determinacy
6646.formal: Assume ZF+DC+AD. Do both assertions hold? (I) Every Turing-invariant function f:2^ω→2^ω is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies x≤_T f(x) on a cone. (II) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump f′ has rank exactly rank(f)+1 in this prewellorder.
6646.definitions: A real x∈2^ω is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write x≤_T y if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and x≡_T y for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when x≡_T y implies f(x)≡_T f(y). A cone above a real a is {x:a≤_T x}. Being constant on a cone means ∃a,b ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≡_T b; the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define f≤_M g by ∃a ∀x≥_T a, f(x)≤_T g(x), and f≡_M g by mutual ≤_M. Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which id≤_M f, where id(x)=x. The prewellorder assertion says that ≤_M is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding [f]. The jump of a real y is y′={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; f′(x)=f(x)′. ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.
6646.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6646.why: A central structural problem in computability theory: whether invariance alone, under determinacy, forces nontrivial operations on computational degrees into a well-ordered hierarchy. It connects relative computability, definability, descriptive set theory, and analogies with hierarchies of proof-theoretic strength.

importance.reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for order-preserving and measure-preserving functions. Their 2024 version explicitly distinguishes the remaining unrestricted conjecture.

6646.status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. Determinacy, degree-wise constancy, and restrictions in the partial results are stated explicitly.

context_blocks.text: The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying f(x)≤_T x on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing x≡_T y into indices witnessing f(x)≡_T f(y), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which f(x) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.
The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.

6648.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
6648.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
6648.definitions: Work in Cantor space 2^N, with coordinates numbered 0,1,… and fair-coin product measure μ. For a finite binary string σ, the cylinder [σ]={X:σ is a prefix of X} has measure 2^{−|σ|}. A Martin-Löf test is a sequence (U_k)_{k≥1} of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs (k,σ), with U_k equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and μ(U_k)≤2^{−k}. A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test X∉⋂_k U_k. A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier q∈[0,2], before seeing X(j). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After X(j) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by 2−q if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. q=1 allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.
6648.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

6648.status_note: The revised 2025 primary paper and its journal version explicitly retain KLR=MLR as a major open problem. Its finite-family/open-set obstruction is not a separating infinite sequence. No later resolution found through 11 September 2026. The formulation fixes fair-coin measure, fresh adaptive coordinates, rational fair bets, partial computability and unbounded-capital success.

context_blocks.text: These are two ways to say that an individual infinite sequence behaves randomly. Martin-Löf tests describe effectively recognizable events of arbitrarily small probability, and a sequence is nonrandom if one test catches it at every level. The betting definition instead asks whether an algorithm can turn knowledge of selected bits into unbounded profit. It measures mathematical unpredictability of a whole sequence, rather than a statistical confidence score assigned to a finite data sample.

The betting order is adaptive. A strategy may inspect a faraway coordinate before deciding which earlier, still unseen coordinate to bet on. It may also read a coordinate with a zero wager to gather information. It cannot bet on a bit already revealed, since that would permit guaranteed profit even from a fair-coin sequence. Its choice of the next position must be computed using only the information it has actually observed.

The known implication from Martin-Löf randomness follows from the fairness of the bets. For a fixed strategy starting with capital one, the set of sequences on which capital ever reaches a threshold R has measure at most 1/R. Reaching a threshold is witnessed after finitely many completed actions and can be effectively enumerated. Taking increasing thresholds produces a Martin-Löf test covering the sequences on which this strategy succeeds. The unresolved direction would convert every effective failure of randomness into success of some permitted gambler.

Choosing the query order in advance is insufficient. Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.

6651.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture: high chromatic number forces a clique minor
6651.formal: For every integer t≥1 and every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G, does χ(G)≥t imply that G contains K_t as a graph minor? Equivalently, is every K_t-minor-free graph (t−1)-colorable?
6651.definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A proper coloring assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors; χ(G) is the minimum number of colors. K_t is the complete graph on t vertices. A K_t minor is witnessed by t pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets B_1,…,B_t such that each induced subgraph G[B_i] is connected and every pair B_i,B_j has at least one edge between it. These branch sets can be contracted and all unwanted vertices or edges deleted. They may have arbitrary sizes; the minor need not be induced and no parity condition is imposed. Equivalently, the Hadwiger number h(G), the largest t for which G has a K_t minor, must satisfy h(G)≥χ(G). The statement concerns existence, with no running-time requirement on finding the coloring or branch sets.

context_blocks.text: A graph can have very few large complete subgraphs and still need many colors. Hadwiger asks whether contracting connected pieces always reveals a complete graph as large as the number of colors originally needed. This would make a global obstruction to coloring visible through a precise structural certificate: disjoint connected regions linked in every pair. The complete graph K_(t−1) shows that the proposed upper bound for K_t-minor-free graphs cannot be reduced.

The conjecture encompasses the Four-Color Theorem because planar graphs exclude K_5 minors. Wagner’s structure theorem makes the t=5 case equivalent to four-colorability of planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas extended this equivalence to t=6 by proving that a minimal counterexample in that case would be apex: deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. Thus the known exact cases extend through K_6 minors; the first unresolved case is t=7.

The earlier general approach forced clique minors from high average degree. The resulting O(t√log t) degeneracy bound gives a coloring bound of the same order by repeatedly removing a low-degree vertex and coloring in reverse. That density threshold is sharp, so simply improving its numerical constant cannot yield Hadwiger’s linear target. The chromatic-number question requires using structure beyond this degree argument.

Delcourt and Postle obtain O(t log log t) colors through a reduction to coloring much smaller minor-free subgraphs, on roughly t times a polylogarithmic number of vertices. Their reduction also shows that proving a linear bound on these small graphs would imply a linear bound without a size restriction. It narrows where a genuinely new coloring argument is needed, without imposing the small-size hypothesis on the conjecture itself.

Liu and Luo’s September 2026 preprint builds on that reduction and claims O(t log log log t). Its proof combines contractions that reduce degeneracy with fractional colorings, which distribute weight across independent sets. Even this extra logarithm removed leaves both the O(t) weakening and the sharp coefficient in the original conjecture unresolved. The result is recorded as a new preprint claim, not as an independently verified proof.

An odd clique minor imposes additional compatibility conditions on two-colorings inside its branch trees. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson construct graphs with no odd K_t minor and chromatic number approximately 1.5t, disproving the odd Hadwiger conjecture. Their graphs are not counterexamples to the ordinary-minor assertion asked here: forbidding odd minors permits more graphs than forbidding all clique minors.

6652.title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for every forbidden induced graph
6652.formal: For every finite undirected simple graph H with at least two vertices, does there exist a real constant c(H)>0 such that every n-vertex undirected simple graph G with n≥1 and no induced copy of H satisfies max{α(G),ω(G)}≥n^{c(H)}?
6652.definitions: An induced copy of H is an injective map f:V(H)→V(G) such that distinct u,v are adjacent in H if and only if f(u),f(v) are adjacent in G. Thus both edges and nonedges must match. α(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices, and ω(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise adjacent vertices. The constant c(H) may depend arbitrarily on the entire fixed graph H, but not on G or n. No density, degree, dimension or algorithmic promise is imposed on G. The claim concerns existence of a clique or independent set, without requiring a polynomial-time construction. A hereditary graph class is one closed under taking induced subgraphs; the class of H-free graphs is hereditary.
6652.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6652.why: A foundational prediction that forbidding any fixed induced pattern forces polynomial-size order inside a graph. Its links to hereditary classes, neighborhood complexity and sparse/dense decompositions make it a central structural question with connections to algorithmic graph theory.

importance.reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.

6652.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary literature explicitly retains the full conjecture as open. Sági’s historical revised claim is recorded separately and is not treated as a verified solution; the withdrawal of its earlier version does not itself refute the revision. New six-vertex and bounded-VC-dimension results have restricted scope.

context_blocks.text: Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of logarithmic size in every sufficiently large graph, and random graphs show that this order of magnitude is unavoidable without further restrictions. Erdős–Hajnal predicts a dramatic change after forbidding even one fixed induced pattern: the guaranteed set should grow as a positive power of the number of vertices. The conjecture therefore asks how much global organization a single local structural exclusion forces.

For a simple example, a graph with no induced three-vertex path is a disjoint union of cliques. If it has t components, choosing one vertex from each gives an independent set of size t, while the largest component has at least n/t vertices and is a clique. One of these sets has size at least √n. This proves the conjecture for that forbidden graph and illustrates the desired polynomial gain through a structural decomposition.

The general theorem of Erdős and Hajnal gives a lower bound exp(c_H√log n). Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improve it to exp(c_H√(log n·log log n)) for a positive constant depending on H. Their 2024 journal paper is the first improvement of this general bound. It is still smaller than nᵟ for every fixed δ>0 as n grows, so the extra logarithmic factor does not reach the conjectured scale.

Closure under complementation and vertex substitution lets proofs for a few building blocks settle many further forbidden graphs. Substitution replaces one vertex by a graph whose vertices all have the same neighbors outside the replacement. The remaining five-vertex building blocks were the bull, the five-cycle and the five-vertex path, together with its complement. Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s proof for the path, published in March 2026, completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices.

For longer fixed paths, their separate all-path theorem gives homogeneous sets of size 2^{(log n)^{1−o(1)}}. This is close to the polynomial scale in its exponent but still does not assert n^c for any fixed positive c. In particular, the five-vertex result should not be described as resolving the conjecture for paths of arbitrary length.

Huang, Ju and Zhou’s August 2026 revision proves two additional six-vertex cases using an extension of iterative sparsification. The E-graph is a five-vertex path with a new leaf attached to its middle vertex. The Bird starts from a triangle with leaves attached to two different triangle vertices, then extends one of those leaves by one more edge. Both contain an induced five-vertex path, so excluding either permits a larger class than excluding the path itself.

A 28 August 2026 preprint by Tran and Nguyen reports another six-vertex case, specified without a drawing by vertex set {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edge set {ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df}. It develops the comb and sparsification framework further. This is an individual new forbidden pattern, rather than a proof for every six-vertex graph.

Another strand connects the conjecture with finding large nearly empty or nearly complete induced subgraphs. Bucić, Fox and Pham prove equivalence with polynomial quantitative versions of the Rödl and Nikiforov statements. This makes the problem relevant to structural decompositions and induced-pattern density, beyond locating a single clique or independent set.

There are also stronger quantitative results under additional hypotheses. Sun, Wang and Zeng’s July 2026 preprint gives exponent at least (Cd)⁻ᵈ for graphs of neighborhood VC-dimension at most d. This dimension bounds the size of a vertex set on which neighborhoods realize every possible subset. Such a restriction controls neighborhood complexity; arbitrary H-free graphs are not assumed to satisfy a fixed VC-dimension bound.

6653.title: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
6653.formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer r≥1, does there exist a finite integer B(T,r) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most B(T,r)?
6653.definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number ω(G) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For S⊆V(G), the induced graph G[S] retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map φ:V(T)→V(G) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if φ(x)φ(y) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is ∀T ∀r ∃B ∀G: the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |V(G)|, maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function f_T:N→N with χ(G)≤f_T(ω(G)) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for f_T, or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
6653.answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs G_k satisfying ω(G_k)≤r and χ(G_k)→∞. A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |V(G)|, or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
6653.why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.

context_blocks.text: A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known. Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size n^{1−o(1)}, and consequently a chromatic bound n^{o(1)}, where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power n^ε eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also n^{o(1)} and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant B(T,r) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.

6654.title: Seese’s conjecture for MSO₁ and clique-width
6654.formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO₁ satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
6654.definitions: An MSO₁ sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency E(x,y), membership x∈X in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class C, Sat_MSO₁(C) consists of all finite encoded MSO₁ sentences φ for which some G∈C satisfies φ. Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory Th_MSO₁(C)={φ: every G∈C satisfies φ}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in [k], disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width cw(G) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set cw(∅)=0. The conclusion is ∃k∀G∈C cw(G)≤k, with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
6654.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO₁ satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.

6654.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO₁ decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.

context_blocks.text: An MSO₁ sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO₁ conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO₁ satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether n∈S if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO₁ with the predicate Even(X), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO₁ sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO₁ formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO₁ decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

6656.title: Planted clique: can polynomial time detect a clique below the square-root scale?
6656.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed ε∈(0,1/2), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm A whose success probability in the experiment below is at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large n, with k=⌊n^(1/2−ε)⌋.
6656.definitions: Set [n]={1,…,n}. The null distribution N_n draws a simple undirected labeled graph by including each unordered pair independently with probability 1/2. The planted distribution P_(n,k) first chooses S uniformly among all k-element subsets of [n], includes all edges inside S, and includes every other edge independently with probability 1/2. Draw b uniformly from {0,1}; draw G from N_n if b=0 and P_(n,k) if b=1. Give A the binary integers n,k and the full adjacency matrix of G, but neither b nor S. It outputs a bit b̂. Success means Pr[b̂=b], averaged over b, the graph, S when present, and A’s independent random bits. Equivalently success is (Pr_N[A=0]+Pr_P[A=1])/2. Polynomial time means at most C(n+1)^c bit operations for every input and random tape, with fixed C,c; they and A may depend on the fixed ε. The forbidden guarantee is ∃A,C,c,N ∀n≥N, success≥2/3. This is a one-graph detection problem; A may generate its own random graphs at its own computational cost. The size of S is exactly k, not an independent per-vertex planting probability. No advice, quantum computation, oracle, side information, or algorithm-family restriction is allowed.
6656.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6656.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis and a central test case for statistical–computational gaps. It asks for a clean separation between the presence of information and efficient extraction of that information; reductions transfer related assumptions to sparse estimation and latent-structure learning. Proving this formulation would in particular imply P≠NP, since a polynomial algorithm for maximum clique would distinguish the distributions.

importance.reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.

progress.text: Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery for k≥c√n for any fixed c>0, using spectral methods and boosting.

Barak, Hopkins, Kelner, Kothari, Moitra, and Potechin prove a nearly tight sum-of-squares integrality gap: degree d=o(log n) assigns random graphs clique value n^(1/2−o(1)). This is a restricted-model lower bound.

Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu show that an appropriate discrete gradient descent and low-temperature local chain recover at the √n scale from the full-graph initialization; the final preprint version is dated 15 May 2025.
Nagda and Raghavendra derive optimal efficient distinguishing advantages conditional on a planted-clique hypothesis, in the independent-vertex planting model.

Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller give robust sum-of-squares algorithms for multiple overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs when clique size is much larger than √(n log n). This is progress in a related model, not below the threshold fixed here.

6656.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026; no unrestricted polynomial-time solution below n^(1/2−ε) or unconditional hardness proof was identified. The exact formulation fixes constant-success detection and exactly k planted vertices. Low-degree and sum-of-squares bounds remain scoped to their models; the optimal-advantage result is conditional.

context_blocks.text: This asks whether a planted structure can be statistically obvious yet computationally inaccessible. In the specified regime, k grows as a positive power of n, while an unplanted graph has no clique of size r=⌈3 log_2 n⌉ with probability tending to one: a union bound is at most n^r·2^(−r(r−1)/2), which tends to zero. Enumerating all r-subsets therefore distinguishes the two distributions with success tending to one in quasipolynomial time n^O(log n). The obstacle is reducing that computation to polynomial time, not a lack of information in the graph.

The classical spectral algorithm of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov recovers the hidden vertex set for every fixed positive constant times √n, with a polynomial whose exponent can depend on that constant. Recovery immediately yields detection here by checking that the reported set is a sufficiently large clique. Letting the constant shrink as n^(−ε) does not keep that analysis polynomial with a fixed exponent.

Substantial evidence comes from provable failures of general algorithmic frameworks. Barak and coauthors show that low-degree sum-of-squares relaxations assign a random graph an implausibly large clique value near √n, despite its true largest clique having only logarithmic size. This is an unconditional limitation of that relaxation. It does not rule out every algorithm allowed in this card.

Recent positive work also illustrates why an algorithmic barrier must state its model. Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu permit local optimization to pass through vertex sets that are not cliques, penalizing missing edges. Starting from the whole graph, their procedure reaches the planted clique at a sufficiently large constant times √n. Restrictions to moves among actual cliques can fail even in easier regimes; those failures do not establish the unrestricted conjecture.

Nagda and Raghavendra obtain sharp bounds on efficient distinguishing advantage assuming planted-clique hardness. Their paper uses independent vertex planting, so the planted size fluctuates around its mean, and uses a different normalization of advantage. It strengthens consequences of a hypothesis in that related model. It is not an unconditional lower bound for the fixed-size experiment here.

The question isolates detection from stronger output requirements such as recovering every planted vertex. It also fixes the random background: arbitrary base graphs, geometric random graphs, and adversarially modified edges describe different experiments. Work on robust recovery of overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs continued in COLT 2026, but its distribution and signal regime do not settle this question.

6657.title: The computational threshold for dense tensor PCA
6657.formal: For every fixed integer k≥3, rational ε with 0<ε<(k−2)/4, and rational c∈(0,1), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of Y=n^{k/4−ε}v^{⊗k}+Z specified below, achieves |⟨u,v⟩|≥c with probability at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in R^n and the n^k ordered entries of Z are independent N(0,1) variables.
6657.definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple (i₁,…,i_k)∈{1,…,n}^k, the signal entry is n^{k/4−ε}v_{i₁}⋯v_{i_k}. Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for n≥2 set b=⌈10k log₂n⌉ and Q_b(x)=2^{−b}⌊2^b max(−2^b,min(x,2^b))⌋. The input consists of n and all entries Q_b(Y_{i₁,…,i_k}), represented as signed dyadic rationals with O(log n) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants k, ε and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector u=w/‖w‖₂; zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |⟨w,v⟩|≥c‖w‖₂. The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
6657.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed (k,ε,c) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below 2/3 for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least 2/3 for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at n^{k/4} does not supply the fixed power saving n^ε requested here.
6657.why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

importance.reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.

progress.text: Montanari–Richard introduce and analyze the spiked tensor model, exhibiting a gap between information-theoretic recovery and the analyzed polynomial-time methods.

Wu–Zhou sharpen the analysis and stopping rule for randomly initialized power iteration; its threshold improves by a polylogarithmic factor.
Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang improve stochastic-gradient guarantees in a multiple-observation model; the even-order bound reaches the familiar conjectured computational scale.
Fu–Sohn establish low-degree estimation bounds for independent-coordinate priors, with the predicted degree–signal dependence and an additional technical restriction on degree.

6657.status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below n^{k/4}. No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order √n. Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order √n here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around n^{k/4}, up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from √n. The interval for ε deliberately places our target strictly between them: λ/√n=n^{(k−2)/4−ε} grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and ε=1/8, the observation contains n^4 noisy numbers and signal strength n^{7/8}. The statistical scale is n^{1/2}, and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all n^4 entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as vvᵀ and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar n^{k/4} scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most n^{k/2}2^{−b}, an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

6659.title: Can metric k-Median reach the 1+2/e threshold?
6659.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
6659.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), does a randomized polynomial-time (1+2/e+ε)-approximation algorithm exist for general metric k-Median that always opens at most k facilities?
6659.definitions: An input consists of a finite set V, a full table of nonnegative rational distances d on V encoded in binary, nonempty subsets C,F⊆V of clients and allowable facilities with C∪F=V, and an integer 1≤k≤|F|. The table is promised to satisfy d(u,v)=d(v,u), d(u,v)=0 exactly when u=v, and the triangle inequality. Each client has unit demand. For nonempty S⊆F define cost(S)=Σ_{c∈C}min_{s∈S}d(c,s), and OPT=min{cost(S):S⊆F,1≤|S|≤k}. L is the total bit length of the input. For each fixed ε the target is one uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε, with constants K_ε,d_ε such that every execution takes at most K_ε L^{d_ε} bit operations. It always returns an explicit nonempty S⊆F with |S|≤k, and on each input Pr[cost(S)≤(1+2/e+ε)OPT]≥2/3. Here e is the base of the natural logarithm. The constants may depend on ε but not on k, |C|, |F| or distance precision. No Euclidean, low-dimensional, stability, capacity or input-distribution promise is made. Candidate facilities are part of the input and cannot be enlarged. The guarantee also covers OPT=0.
6659.answer_criterion: Give the stated algorithms for every fixed ε>0, or rule them out for at least one fixed ε, explicitly identifying any complexity assumption used. This card fixes the yes/no question of approaching the known hardness threshold; it does not additionally require finding a different exact threshold after a negative answer. An algorithm opening k facilities only in expectation, one allowing k+o(k) facilities, or an FPT algorithm with unrestricted dependence on k does not prove the claim.
6659.why: A central unresolved approximation threshold for metric clustering, separating known coverage hardness from the best algorithms with a strict facility budget.

importance.reason: A major optimization problem with a substantial remaining algorithm–hardness gap and connections to coverage, facility location, LP rounding and parameterized approximation.

progress.text: Feige proves the 1−1/e hardness threshold for Max k-Cover, which yields the 1+2/e metric k-Median gap through a client–facility metric construction.

Cohen-Addad–Grandoni–Lee–Schwiegelshohn–Svensson obtain a randomized polynomial-time 2+ε approximation with at most k facilities; the May 2026 full-version revision retains the theorem.
Improved approximation-scheme runtimes apply to low-dimensional Euclidean clustering, a restricted metric setting.
Spectral dual fitting improves k-Means approximation; squared-distance clustering is a different objective.

6659.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked general-metric result remains 2+ε with a strict budget, while the classical hardness threshold is 1+2/e. The FPT algorithm, Euclidean schemes and 2026 k-Means results do not settle the polynomial-time target here.

context_blocks.text: Metric k-Median selects a limited number of service locations and minimizes total distance to the nearest selected location. The number of clients and the number of candidate facilities may differ, and the distance table need not come from a Euclidean embedding. The same formulation models representative selection for clustering and placement of facilities. Its simplicity makes the unresolved approximation threshold a central benchmark for algorithm design.

The two endpoint numbers are approximately 1.73576 and 2. The lower endpoint is the classical hardness threshold 1+2/e; the best general feasible guarantee in the checked literature is 2+ε. The inherited STOC 2025 paper explicitly asks for a tight approximation result after obtaining that upper bound. Asking for 1+2/e+ε for every fixed ε avoids requiring that an infimum approximation ratio be achieved exactly.

The coverage origin of the lower endpoint can be seen directly. Represent each set as a candidate facility and each universe element as a client. Give a client–facility pair distance one when the set contains the element and distance three otherwise, and give distinct pairs on the same side distance two. These distances satisfy the triangle inequality. A collection of k sets covering a fraction p of the elements then has clustering cost (3−2p) times the universe size.

Feige’s Max k-Cover gap distinguishes complete coverage from coverage of at most 1−1/e+η, for any fixed η>0. Under the preceding metric construction this becomes a gap between cost one per client and cost at least 1+2/e−2η per client. This is why the constant is not an arbitrary numerical target. A randomized algorithm beating that gap on every input would yield randomized algorithms for the underlying NP-hard decision problem; the appropriate exclusion is NP≠RP for this card’s success convention.

Jain–Mahdian–Saberi’s 2002 paper gives the classical metric k-Median lower bound through a reduction to approximating Set Cover. Its historical statement uses the then-known slightly-superpolynomial-time assumption for Set Cover hardness. The coverage reduction above explains the stronger ordinary NP-hardness formulation without silently changing the assumption in the original theorem. Neither lower-bound route excludes approximation from just above 1+2/e.

The 2025 algorithm combines two components. One permits a logarithmic number of extra centers while retaining a 2+ε cost bound; another handles instances where deleting one optimal center increases the optimum substantially. Combining them returns a feasible solution opening at most k centers. The full paper’s May 2026 revision retains this result. It is therefore incorrect to describe the headline 2+ε theorem as only a bicriteria approximation.

The usual linear relaxation has a separate barrier near two. It uses fractional openings y_s, assignments x_{c,s}≤y_s, unit total assignment for each client, and Σ_s y_s≤k. For a star with q≥3 leaves, all vertices available as facilities, clients at the leaves and k=q−1, every integral optimum has cost two. Set the central opening to 1/(q−1), each leaf opening to (q−2)/(q−1), and assign each client’s remaining fraction to the center. This feasible LP solution costs q/(q−1), giving an integrality gap approaching two.

That explicit example limits a guarantee measured against this relaxation, not every polynomial algorithm measured against OPT. A sharper algorithm might use additional constraints, a different relaxation, or another method. Likewise, a lower bound for one rounding framework is not a computational impossibility theorem for the original optimization problem. The card’s target is deliberately stated using the true integral optimum.

There is already a matching-threshold algorithm in a different runtime regime. Cohen-Addad–Gupta–Kumar–Lee–Li’s ICALP 2019 work achieves 1+2/e+ε in fixed-parameter time with respect to k. The potentially large dependence on the number of opened facilities is permitted there. This does not supply a polynomial-time algorithm when k grows as part of the input, but it shows that the target ratio has meaningful algorithmic support.

A 2026 development concerns geometric input. Cohen-Addad and coauthors improve approximation-scheme runtimes in low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where additional structure is available. Such a scheme does not apply to arbitrary distance tables.

Anand and coauthors’ July 2026 spectral dual-fitting paper improves k-Means guarantees, including in general metrics. That objective sums squared distances; squaring changes both the analysis and the hardness constants. It does not establish the stated k-Median ratio.

Resolving this question would determine whether the coverage obstruction captures the full cost of efficient metric clustering. A positive answer would bridge the remaining gap beyond the familiar LP benchmark. A stronger hardness threshold would reveal an obstruction not expressed by coverage alone. The exact facility budget is essential to either conclusion: averaging an excessive number of facilities over random choices changes the feasible problem.

6662.title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
6662.formal: Do there exist universal constants C,B,b>0 and a deterministic algorithm which, for every pair of integers N≥2 and 2≤s≤N, outputs in at most B N^b bit operations a rational m×N matrix A, with m≤C s ln(eN/s), such that (2/3)‖x‖₂²≤‖Ax‖₂²≤(4/3)‖x‖₂² for every real vector x∈ℝ^N with at most s nonzero coordinates?
6662.definitions: The input consists of N and s in binary. The output is an explicit list of all entries of A, each encoded as a signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Its total encoding length must also be at most B N^b. Time is ordinary deterministic Turing-machine bit complexity, polynomial in N; randomness, advice and unit-cost exact real arithmetic are unavailable. The row count m is a positive integer chosen by the algorithm. The same constants and algorithm work for all allowed pairs N,s. The norm is Euclidean, and the displayed inequalities concern squared norms. They define restricted isometry of order s and distortion δ=1/3. The condition must hold simultaneously for every support of size at most s and every real choice of coefficients on that support. No probability over supports or signals is permitted. The natural logarithm and the factor e ensure a nonzero expression when s is close to N. The omitted case s=1 is trivial and can be handled by a single row of ones.
6662.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm satisfying all the uniform dimension, encoding, time and restricted-isometry requirements, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A negative result conditional on a complexity assumption must state it. An existence proof, a construction using random bits, success for most sparse signals, or a deterministic construction with a larger asymptotic row count does not settle the stated question.
6662.why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.

context_blocks.text: Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of A_SᵀA_S must lie between 2/3 and 4/3. Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion 1/3, then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by ℓ₁ minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain m=O(s log(eN/s)) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for s≥2. Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square t² within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±1/t. This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence μ, the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most (s−1)μ. When μ is about 1/√m, this argument certifies only s on the order of √m. This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal s log(eN/s) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with O(s log(N/s) log s) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the m+1 unit vertices of a regular simplex in ℝ^m have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and ℓ₁-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.

6663.title: Does Frege simulate Extended Frege with polynomial proof size?
6663.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 such that every Extended Frege proof π of a propositional tautology φ has some ordinary Frege proof ρ of the same formula with |ρ|≤C(|π|+2)ᵏ? Equivalently, if sF(φ) and sEF(φ) are the minimum proof sizes in the two systems, is sF(φ) polynomially bounded in sEF(φ), uniformly over all tautologies?
6663.definitions: Fix formulas over negation ¬ and material implication →, with binary-encoded variable indices. Ordinary Frege uses the axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), and modus ponens: infer B from A and A→B. A proof is a finite sequence ending with φ; earlier lines may be cited and reused without restriction. Extended Frege adds acyclic definitions, introducing the pair e→θ and θ→e, where e is a new variable absent from φ, θ and all preceding lines. θ may use variables of φ and earlier extension variables. The final formula contains no extension variables. Proof size is the complete binary encoding length of every explicitly written line, definition and inference reference. No formula-depth, proof-depth or tree-shape bound is imposed. These presentations are polynomially equivalent to the usual finite-basis Frege and Extended Frege systems. The target is existence of short translated proofs: it does not require a polynomial-time function that finds ρ from π. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
6663.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
6663.why: This asks whether reusable definitions fundamentally shorten mathematical proofs, beyond any polynomial factor. It is one of the central comparisons between strong propositional proof systems and captures the difficulty of reasoning with shared circuits versus explicit formulas.

6663.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No polynomial size simulation or superpolynomial separation of unrestricted Frege and EF was found in the primary literature. The newest checked simulation, TR26-166, concerns a restricted algebraic formula system and has quasipolynomial overhead.

context_blocks.text: The extension rule gives reusable names to intermediate computations. If a subformula is used many times, ordinary formula syntax writes out each occurrence; Extended Frege can define it once and refer to its name. A network of such definitions represents a Boolean circuit with shared gates. The rule does not permit a false final theorem: every assignment to the original variables uniquely extends through the definitions, and the conclusion uses only original variables.

Repeated substitution eliminates definitions, but can create exponentially large formula trees. This explains why the obvious simulation is expensive; it does not prove that all ordinary Frege proofs must be expensive. The challenge is to compare the shortest proofs, not one syntactic expansion procedure.

The distinction between proof size and proof-search time is essential. The quantifiers are “for every EF proof there exists a short Frege proof.” They do not supply an algorithm for locating that proof. The stronger notion usually called p-simulation requires a polynomial-time transformation. A size simulation alone can hold even if the available methods for finding the translated proof are much slower.

Buss connects the comparison to finite consistency statements. Frege has polynomial-size proofs of its own partial consistency, meaning the corresponding finite statements that no contradiction has a proof up to a specified length. His theorem characterizes Frege simulation of EF by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the analogous partial consistency statements for EF. This turns a comparison of all proofs into a canonical family of propositional statements; it is not a general proof of the desired simulation.

For example, Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs of propositional Kneser–Lovász coloring principles. That upper bound constrains possible lower bounds for the family, but it does not demonstrate a separation and does not rule out a polynomial Frege upper bound. Quasipolynomial and polynomial must remain distinct in this problem.

Krajíček’s June 2026 paper gives a circuit-rewriting description of EF reasoning. An EF proof of circuit equivalence yields a polynomially long chain of equivalence-preserving rewrites; each rewrite adds at most seven gates and may delete gates. This is a normal-form result about circuit reasoning. The intermediate objects still retain circuit sharing, so it does not turn an arbitrary EF proof into a polynomial-size formula-based Frege proof.

A September 2026 preprint by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay proves a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a partially commutative formula version of the Ideal Proof System over GF(2). Variables lie in two groups: they commute across groups but not within a group. The proof formalizes an identity-testing algorithm inside Frege. The restrictions on the algebraic certificates, and the quasipolynomial overhead, both matter; the theorem is not the full EF simulation asked for here.

A negative answer would establish a concrete benefit of reusable definitions for strong propositional reasoning. It would also imply superpolynomial Frege lower bounds, since the final formula is part of every EF proof. By contrast, proving that Frege has some hard tautologies, or assuming NP≠coNP, does not automatically separate it from EF: those same tautologies might require equally long EF proofs. The separate question of whether EF itself is polynomially bounded asks about a different comparison.

6664.title: The asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture
6664.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
6664.formal: Is there a universal constant C>0 such that, for every n≥1, every integer 1≤d≤n and every Boolean polynomial threshold function f=sign(p):{−1,1}^n→{−1,1} of degree at most d, its total influence satisfies I(f)≤C d√n?
6664.definitions: A realizing polynomial p is a real polynomial in n variables of total degree at most d, with p(x)≠0 at every Boolean input. The sign is +1 for positive values and −1 for negative values. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; no bound on coefficient magnitude, description length, margin or number of monomials is assumed. One may take p multilinear by reducing x_i² to 1 on the cube. The nonzero convention loses no threshold functions under a fixed sign-at-zero convention, since a sufficiently small constant perturbation preserves all assigned signs. If x is uniform on {−1,1}^n, let x^(i) denote x with coordinate i flipped. Define Inf_i(f)=Pr[f(x)≠f(x^(i))], pointwise sensitivity s_f(x)=|{i:f(x)≠f(x^(i))}|, and I(f)=Σ_i Inf_i(f)=E[s_f(x)]. The constant C is independent of n,d,f and the realizing polynomial. Constant functions have zero influence; allowing d=0 adds only these trivial cases. This is the asymptotic influence conjecture, not the disproved claim specifying an exact extremizing function.
6664.answer_criterion: Prove one universal C works for all n,d and all such functions, or show that the ratios I(f)/(d√n) are unbounded over this class. A counterexample to a particular proposed numerical C, or to the original exact symmetric extremizer, does not by itself refute this existential-constant statement. A bound C_d√n with unrestricted dependence on d, or √n times a growing polylogarithmic factor, is partial progress rather than the claimed uniform bound.
6664.why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.

importance.reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.
