7179.definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. ED(x,y) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has w=ceil(4 log₂(n+2)) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo 2^w, integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving ε cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
7179.answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case O(n^(2−ε)) bound for some fixed ε>0 in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Edits can shift an entire alignment
context_blocks.text: The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

context_blocks.title: What the quadratic barrier means
context_blocks.text: The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes O(n²) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as n²/log n is smaller than n² but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for n^(2−ε) with one ε>0 that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

context_blocks.title: A precise conditional obstacle
context_blocks.text: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every δ>0 there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in O(2^((1−δ)N) poly(L)) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Why recent approximation is different
context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized (1+η)-approximation for each fixed η>0, with running time n²/2^(log^Ω(1) n). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on η cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

context_blocks.title: Scope of the benchmark
context_blocks.text: The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

Each insertion, deletion and substitution costs one, and the algorithm must always return the exact minimum.

Known reductions rule out such an algorithm if SETH is true, but that hypothesis remains unproved.

7195.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary τ lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite τ-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of A^r. An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by [n] and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence φ has a truth value A⊨φ invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid (τ,φ), outputs a deterministic machine M_φ and integers C_φ,k_φ≥1 such that M_φ decides A⊨φ in at most C_φ(N+1)^{k_φ} steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite τ and every PTIME Boolean property Q of τ-structures, some fixed τ-sentence φ satisfies A⊨φ exactly when A∈Q for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input (φ,A) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
7195.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.

context_blocks.title: Properties should survive renaming
context_blocks.text: A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

context_blocks.title: Why an effective syntax matters
context_blocks.text: One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

context_blocks.title: The known ordered theorem
context_blocks.text: The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

context_blocks.title: Capturing is not one universal time bound
context_blocks.text: One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

context_blocks.title: The remaining gap
context_blocks.text: Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if P=NP, existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.

sentences: Is there an effective logic for all polynomial-time properties of finite unordered structures?
Its sentences must describe properties unchanged by renaming domain elements.
Each sentence must compile effectively to an evaluation algorithm with a polynomial time bound.
Fixed-point logic captures polynomial time when an order is supplied, but that is a different input model.
Current candidate and restricted-class results leave the general existence question open.

7220.title: A (1+ε)-approximation for edit distance in truly subquadratic time
7220.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), do there exist constants δ_ε∈(0,1), K_ε>0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε such that, for every n≥1 and every pair of length-n strings x,y, A_ε runs in at most K_ε(n+2)^(2−δ_ε) time and outputs an integer D satisfying ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3? ED is unit-cost Levenshtein distance in the model below.
7220.definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions converting x to y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input strings are explicitly stored arrays over {0,…,n²+1}, including binary and fixed finite alphabets. Symbols occupy O(log n) bits. Use a word RAM with word length B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed sufficiently large constant B, with random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may use independent random bits but no input-dependent advice, preprocessing oracle or preprocessed database. The runtime bound includes all preprocessing and holds on every execution; success is required separately on every input pair. Output a numerical distance estimate, with no additive error and no promise on the distance or input distribution. An edit script is not required. For each fixed ε the algorithm is uniform in n and the strings; its constants and exponent saving may depend on ε. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, common positive saving for all ε, or efficient procedure generating A_ε is required. Rational ε suffice for every positive fixed accuracy by choosing a smaller rational parameter.
7220.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence statement for every fixed positive accuracy, or prove that for some fixed ε>0 no randomized algorithm achieves that multiplicative guarantee in O(n^(2−δ)) time for any fixed δ>0. A result for just one constant approximation factor does not establish the universal accuracy claim. A savings factor that is subpolynomial in n, an additive approximation, or a guarantee confined to special input distributions is insufficient. A deterministic algorithm would suffice for the positive direction, but a lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone would not settle the negative direction. Any conditional lower bound must retain its explicit assumption.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing ε=0.01 fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired δ_ε must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as n²/logⁱ n, for fixed i, is n^(2−o(1)) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as ε approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized (1+ε)-approximation for each constant ε in n²/2^{log^{Ω(1)} n} time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed δ_ε>0. The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed η>0, a constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time. The approximation constant depends on η and is not guaranteed to be 1+ε for an arbitrarily prescribed ε. Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in O(n polylog n) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary 1+ε accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter ε is fixed before the input length grows; choosing ε below 1/n to force exactness is outside any fixed-ε runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When ED=0 a successful estimate must be zero, and when ED=1 and ε<1 an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.

7220.why: Determine whether arbitrarily accurate fixed-factor approximation can break the quadratic exponent for a central sequence-alignment problem. This tests a different computational boundary from constant-factor estimation with nearly linear overhead.

Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.

The main unresolved issue is whether this intermediate status hides a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme.

The relative-error requirement matters when the graph has few independent sets as well as when it has exponentially many. The algorithm must work for every explicitly encoded graph and every requested accuracy, with no structural promise that would make local sampling mix rapidly. A polynomial bound in |V| alone, an additive approximation, or an algorithm whose polynomial degree depends on the graph family would be a different statement.

Several restricted classes do admit efficient approximation schemes. For example, results for almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph and for dense regular bipartite graphs exploit expansion or spectral structure. These theorems demonstrate that the target is achievable on substantial subclasses, but they do not provide a worst-case FPRAS for arbitrary bipartite inputs.

The conjectured difficulty is deliberately weaker than #P-hardness of approximation. #BIS is believed not to have an FPRAS, yet it is also believed not to be NP-hard under the usual approximation-preserving reductions. Resolving the card would therefore locate a central intermediate point between problems with known FPRASes and problems with robust hardness barriers.

7223.title: Does integer multiplication have linear-size Boolean circuits?
7223.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and n₀≥1 such that, for every integer n≥n₀, a Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
7223.definitions: The circuit has input bits a₀,…,a_{n−1},b₀,…,b_{n−1}, representing a=Σᵢaᵢ2ⁱ and b=Σᵢbᵢ2ⁱ, and output bits c₀,…,c_{2n−1} satisfying Σⱼcⱼ2ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let M(n) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is M(n)=O(n). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
7223.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every n₀ there is n≥n₀ with M(n)>Cn. A lower bound c·n with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.

context_blocks.text: Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. 7229.title: Do one-way functions imply classical key agreement?
7229.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol with negligible disagreement and computationally secret shared keys, against passive probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdroppers, in the plain public-channel model defined below?
7229.definitions: All algorithms are uniform classical probabilistic Turing machines; security parameter λ is supplied in unary. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time I, Pr[f(Y)=f(X) and |Y|=λ] is negligible in λ, where X is uniform in {0,1}^λ and Y is the single output of I(1^λ,f(X)); probability also includes I’s private coins. A function μ:N→[0,1] is negligible if for every integer d≥1 there is λ₀ such that μ(λ)≤λ^(−d) for all λ≥λ₀. The protocol consists of two interactive machines A,B with independent private fair coins and total worst-case computation and communication polynomial in λ. They exchange classical messages on a noiseless public channel, with no correlated initial secrets, trusted setup, random oracle or quantum communication. At termination each outputs a λ-bit string K_A,K_B. Correctness requires Pr[K_A≠K_B] to be negligible. Let T be the full public transcript, and let U_λ be an independent uniform λ-bit string. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D, |Pr[D(1^λ,T,K_A)=1]−Pr[D(1^λ,T,U_λ)=1]| must be negligible, over the honest coins, D’s coins and U_λ. The eavesdropper observes T but does not alter the messages. The target is the unrelativized existence implication; neither the construction nor its proof is required to treat f as a black box. Both premise and conclusion use the same uniform adversary convention.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. context_blocks.text: A spectrum forgets the internal structure of a model and remembers only its possible finite sizes. A sentence can impose substantial combinatorial conditions on its relations, but the resulting object is just a subset of the positive integers. Asser’s question asks whether sizes excluded by one finite description can themselves be the allowed sizes of another finite description.

Negating the sentence does not solve the problem. If φ describes a graph consisting of disjoint edges covering all vertices, its spectrum contains the positive even numbers. An even-sized edgeless graph nevertheless satisfies ¬φ, so even numbers also belong to Spec(¬φ). Existence of a countermodel at a given size is different from absence of every model at that size.

The quantifier order is therefore essential. The target permits a new sentence ψ, chosen after φ but before n, which represents the entire complement simultaneously. It is not enough to provide a separate sentence for each excluded size. Allowing ψ a different vocabulary also prevents an arbitrary choice of representation from imposing an unintended extra restriction.

The spectrum problem helped shape finite model theory and descriptive complexity. The survey by Durand, Jones, Makowsky and More records Asser’s complement question as unresolved and connects the subject with bounded computational resources and structural restrictions on models. The importance here is the closure operation on the full expressive class, rather than one particular encoding of a graph family.

The existing logic-for-PTIME card asks for a logical characterization of efficient properties of individual finite structures. This card instead concerns the sets of cardinalities admitting some structure satisfying a sentence. It adds a different foundational question to the database and finite-model-theory bucket, even though both connect logic with computation.

7233.title: Can general weighted TSP be solved in O*((2−ε)^n) time?
7233.formal: Do there exist constants ε∈(0,1), c≥1 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on n≥3 labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((2−ε)^n(n+L)^c)?
7233.definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with w=B⌈n+log₂(L+2)⌉ bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in n+L. The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants ε,c,B and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.

context_blocks.text: The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar O(2^n n²) time by a factor 2^{Ω(√log n)}. Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield O*((2−ε)^n) for any fixed positive ε.

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.

7235.title: A (1+ε)-approximation for edit distance in n^(1+o(1)) time
7235.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length n≥2, outputs an integer D with ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3, using worst-case time n^(1+o(1))?
7235.definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in {0,…,n²+1}, stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with w=B_ε⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer B_ε; unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed ε there is one algorithm A_ε, and for every rational η>0 there are constants C_{ε,η},N_{ε,η} such that every execution on every pair of total length n≥N_{ε,η} uses at most C_{ε,η} n^(1+η) operations. A_ε halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on ε and η; the algorithm may depend on ε but not on η. All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. There is no additive error or promise that ED is large. Only a numerical estimate is required, not an edit script. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε or effective procedure generating A_ε from ε is required.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a (1+ε)-approximation in n^(2−δ_ε) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in O(n polylog n) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its n^(1+o(1)) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy ε, one algorithm must meet n^(1+η) bounds for every fixed η>0 once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each η, with uncontrolled dependence on η, is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time for each fixed η. Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 approximation scheme moves toward arbitrarily accurate approximation, but its stated runtime is quasi-strongly subquadratic. Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.

7236.title: Can all marginals be privately released in polynomial time from a polynomial-size database?
7236.formal: Do there exist an integer C≥1, a function α:N_{≥2}→[0,1] with lim_{d→∞}α(d)=0, a uniform randomized mechanism M and a uniform deterministic evaluator E, such that for every d≥2 and every database D∈({0,1}^d)^n with n=d^C, M runs in time polynomial in n,d, satisfies (1,1/(100n²))-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite synopsis S for which, with probability at least 2/3, E(S,q) approximates q(D) within α(d) simultaneously for every marginal query q?
7236.definitions: A marginal query is a pair (J,a), where J⊆{1,…,d} and a∈{0,1}^J, and q_{J,a}(D)=|{i∈{1,…,n}:D_{ij}=a_j for all j∈J}|/n. The empty J query has value one. Queries of every order up to d are included. The database is an explicitly stored ordered n-by-d bit matrix; neighbouring databases have the same dimensions and differ in exactly one row. Differential privacy means that for every ordered pair of neighbours D,D′ and every set O of output strings, Pr[M(D)∈O]≤e·Pr[M(D′)∈O]+1/(100n²). M uses independent fair random bits and has one worst-case polynomial bound p(n+d) on bit operations, output length and random bits. Its output is a finite binary string S. E receives d,S,J,a, has a worst-case bound given by one polynomial in d+|S| and outputs a binary-encoded rational number. E has no access to D, private state of M or an additional oracle. Both algorithms are ordinary classical Turing machines, with no nonuniform advice. The accuracy event is simultaneous over all queries and its probability is over M’s randomness alone, separately for every D. S need not encode a synthetic database or a consistent probability distribution. C,α,p,M,E and the evaluator’s polynomial are fixed before d,D are chosen. No algorithm to compute α and no prescribed rate of its convergence are required.

context_blocks.text: A marginal measures the fraction of records matching a pattern on selected coordinates. Low-order marginals describe small groups of attributes, while all marginals permit every such pattern. The family contains exponentially many queries even though one query has a short description. A synopsis is therefore an efficiently evaluable representation, rather than a literal list of exponentially many answers.

Privacy and accuracy quantify different objects. The privacy guarantee compares the complete output distributions after changing one person’s row. Accuracy concerns all queries simultaneously on each fixed database. Once a successful synopsis has been released, its deterministic evaluation reveals no additional access to the original records. An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. The present card fixes approximate-DP parameters, replacement adjacency and a noninteractive evaluable synopsis. These choices state one concrete version of the proposal; they are not asserted to be equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order formulation.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.

7237.title: Is distinguishing 3-colourable graphs from graphs needing more than six colours NP-hard?
7237.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction R from Boolean 3-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every 3-CNF formula F, satisfiability of F implies χ(R(F))≤3 and unsatisfiability of F implies χ(R(F))>6?
7237.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses containing at most three literals, each literal being a Boolean variable or its negation; the formula and variable indices have a standard explicit finite binary encoding. R is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that outputs a graph as a labelled vertex set {1,…,n} and a list of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no repeated edges. Its total running time and output length are bounded by one polynomial in the formula’s encoding length. A proper k-colouring assigns one of {1,…,k} to each vertex so that endpoints of every edge receive different colours. χ(G) is the least such k, with χ of the empty graph taken to be zero. The promise decision problem, also denoted PCSP(K₃,K₆), has yes-instances χ≤3 and no-instances χ>6; graphs with χ=4,5,6 are outside the promise. K_k is the loopless complete graph on k vertices. No colouring or satisfiability witness is supplied as input. The reduction must satisfy the two implications unconditionally, without a Unique Games or Label Cover hardness hypothesis. Because 3-SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is precisely the usual deterministic many-one NP-hardness target for the promise problem.

context_blocks.text: The input promise says that three colours suffice, but it does not reveal the three colour classes. Allowing a larger palette relaxes the output condition. The associated gap decision task distinguishes such promised yes-instances from graphs that cannot be coloured even with six colours. This isolates a small finite-template promise CSP with a particularly clear combinatorial meaning.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal establish hardness for colouring k-colourable graphs with 2k−1 colours, including the 3-versus-5 case. The 3-versus-6 question remains explicitly posed in subsequent work. Increasing the permitted palette weakens the output requirement, so hardness at five colours does not imply hardness at six.

TCS-6637 asks whether some fixed constant C admits a polynomial-time colouring algorithm for every 3-colourable graph. A negative result for six colours alone does not exclude algorithms using seven, one hundred or another fixed palette. Conversely, an algorithm with a growing number of colours does not settle even the six-colour search problem. The new card is a precise frontier case, rather than a duplicate of the quantifier over arbitrary constants.

The decision and search tasks should also be kept distinct. A polynomial-time six-colouring algorithm on 3-colourable inputs would decide the gap by checking its output: on a graph requiring more than six colours, no valid output exists. This implication explains the algorithmic relevance of the decision hardness target without redefining NP-hardness as a blanket statement about every search reduction.

The six-colour case has value beyond its small numerical parameters. It tests how far promise relaxation can preserve intractability after the classical CSP dichotomy, and it provides a fixed finite object on which algebraic and combinatorial limitations can be stated. Its specialist home remains Constraint satisfaction under the catalogue’s graph-category expansion.

7238.title: Can random 3-SAT at constant density be refuted in polynomial time?
7238.formal: Do there exist an integer C≥6 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and Pr[A(F)=UNSAT]→1 as n→∞ for F drawn from R_3(n,Cn)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
7238.definitions: For n≥3, R_3(n,m) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of {1,…,n} and independently negates each of its three variables with probability 1/2. Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every η>0 there is n0 such that the probability is at least 1−η for all n≥n0. There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers C≥6 loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.

context_blocks.text: At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.

7238.why: Separate the typical absence of satisfying assignments from the computational ability to certify that absence soundly.
7238.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.

7239.title: Does greedy CDCL without restarts p-simulate resolution?
7239.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time transformation which, given a CNF formula F and a resolution refutation π of F, outputs a legal greedy CDCL refutation of the same F, without restarts, in the asserting-learning model defined below? Both the transformation time and the output length are polynomial in the binary length of (F,π).
7239.definitions:
Literals are x_i or ¬x_i for i∈{1,…,n}; clauses are sets of literals and F is a finite set of clauses. A resolution inference derives (C∖{x})∪(D∖{¬x}) from clauses C containing x and D containing ¬x. A refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each entry being an input clause or an inference from earlier entries, with parent indices and pivot recorded. Variable indices and pointers use binary notation. Clause and formula encodings explicitly list their literals.

A CDCL state consists of a database D containing F and an ordered trail of assignments to distinct variables of F. Each assignment is marked either as a decision or with its reason clause in D. Its decision level is the number of decisions up to that assignment. Initially D=F and the trail is empty. A clause is falsified if all its literals are false on the trail; it is unit if exactly one literal is unassigned and all others are false. The following priority of actions is mandatory.

If D has a falsified clause, a conflict must be processed before any other action. At decision level zero the run ends with UNSAT. Otherwise choose a falsified clause K and a trivial resolution analysis: start with K and repeatedly resolve the current clause with a reason clause recorded on the current trail, using a distinct pivot at each step. Every intermediate clause must be falsified by the current trail. Stop at a nonempty asserting clause C, meaning that exactly one of its variables has the current highest decision level. The trace records the full analysis. Add C to D and erase the suffix of the trail whose decision levels exceed a, where a is the maximum level of the other literals of C, or zero if there are none. Then perform one legal unit propagation and return to the conflict-first priority check.

If there is no conflict but a unit clause exists, choose such a clause, assign its unassigned literal to true, record that clause as the reason, and repeat the priority check. Only when neither conflicts nor units exist may a new decision assign either value to an unassigned variable. At such a stable state the run may first delete any subset of learned clauses, retaining all input clauses and all reasons appearing on the current trail, and must then make a decision. A satisfying complete trail ends with SAT, not a refutation. There is no independent operation clearing or shortening the trail: backjumping is allowed only after a conflict and only to the assertion level.

All choices of decisions, unit reasons, conflict clauses, trivial asserting analyses and permitted deletions are free components of the output trace. No fixed branching heuristic or first-UIP policy is imposed. No new variables, preprocessed replacement formula, unrecorded learned axioms or restarts are permitted. The only learned clauses are those derived by the recorded conflict analyses. The trace length counts all clauses, literals, assignments, analysis steps and pointers in an explicit binary encoding, so expensive analysis cannot be hidden in one step. This is the restart-free instantiation of the Vinyals model with arbitrary trivial asserting learning. The requested p-simulation is a uniform translation supplied with π; mere existence of a short trace, or finding one from F alone, is a different claim.

context_blocks.text: Clause learning stores consequences of encountered conflicts and reuses them during a SAT search. General resolution permits arbitrary reuse of earlier clauses, without requiring that they arise along a current partial assignment. This question asks whether the constraints of a greedy search, even with freely chosen decisions and learning, impose a superpolynomial cost when restarting is unavailable.

The operational model matters. Exhaustive unit propagation and immediate conflict processing constrain which trails are reachable. A restart discards the current trail while retaining learned information, whereas a backjump must be justified by the newly learned asserting clause. The statement specifies those actions separately rather than treating every return to decision level zero as a prohibited restart.

Vinyals gives an execution-trace proof system with explicit propagation reasons, conflict-analysis derivations, deletion rules and cost measures. The present card selects its no-restart policy and allows arbitrary trivial asserting analyses. This avoids making the question depend on a particular solver implementation, while retaining actual greedy search restrictions.

The supplied resolution proof is part of the translator’s input. An affirmative answer therefore would not give a polynomial-time SAT solver or a practical heuristic that discovers short proofs unaided. A theorem guaranteeing only polynomial-size traces, without a polynomial-time translation, would establish the corresponding size-simulation statement rather than the full p-simulation asked here.

Vinyals’ 2022 exposition distinguishes known simulations using non-greedy propagation or preprocessing from the unresolved greedy no-restart comparison. Buss and Thapen’s later work identifies candidate formulas for separating related resolution systems but does not prove that separation. These results motivate the target without establishing a resolution of the operational model on this card.

7240.title: Can all vertices of a rational polytope be enumerated in output-polynomial time?
7240.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every rational matrix M and rational vector b with P={x∈R^d:Mx≤b} bounded, A lists each vertex of P exactly once and halts within p(L+S) bit operations, where L is the binary input length and S is the total binary length of the required vertex list? The dimension d is part of the input.
7240.definitions: The input specifies integers m,d≥1, M∈Q^(m×d), and b∈Q^m. Every rational is written as a reduced signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary, with delimiters; L includes this entire explicit representation. P may be empty or lower-dimensional, and redundant inequalities and degeneracy are allowed. A vertex is an extreme point: v∈P such that v=(x+y)/2 with x,y∈P implies x=y=v. Every vertex is rational. The output is a finite list in arbitrary order of these vectors, with each coordinate in the same reduced rational encoding, followed by an end marker. S includes separators and the end marker; it is determined independently of the algorithm, so padding or duplicate outputs cannot enlarge the permitted bound. The empty polytope has an empty vertex list. The bound concerns total running time, including writing the output, without a polynomial-delay or polynomial-workspace requirement. Correctness and the bound are required on the bounded-polyhedron promise; behavior outside that promise is immaterial.

context_blocks.text: A finite system of inequalities describes a convex region implicitly, while a vertex list describes its extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without producing that list. Enumerating the list asks whether the entire conversion can be performed with only polynomial overhead relative to the information that must actually be returned.

The number of vertices can be exponential in the input length, so a running-time bound polynomial in the input alone would be inappropriate. Output-polynomial time allows that unavoidable cost. It still excludes an algorithm that examines exponentially many intermediate objects when the final list is short. Degeneracy is particularly relevant because many collections of tight inequalities can describe the same vertex.

Reimers and Stougie explicitly identify total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polyhedra as a longstanding open question. They obtain such an algorithm under a bounded branch-width condition. Their paper also distinguishes the general unbounded-polyhedron problem, for which output-polynomial enumeration would imply P=NP. That hardness statement does not resolve the bounded target here.

Dong, Fan, Xiong and Zeng study vertices of hyperplane arrangements. An arrangement includes intersections that may lie outside the feasible region selected by a system of inequalities. Consequently, an output-sensitive bound for the entire arrangement is measured against a different output and does not establish the required bound in the number of vertices of this polytope.

This card adds geometric enumeration to a category that already contains counting and hypergraph-transversal questions. Its target is the exact finite output of an algorithm in variable dimension. Neither approximate vertices nor a fast method restricted to simple polytopes meets that target.

7241.title: Can twin-width be approximated in fixed-parameter time?
7241.formal: Do there exist total computable functions f,g:N→N and a constant c≥1, and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer k≥0, A halts within f(k)(n+1)^c bit operations and either correctly reports tww(G)>k or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most g(k)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
7241.definitions: The input gives n, the n×n adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of V(G), starting with the singleton partition and ending with {V(G)}, each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair x∈X,y∈Y and a nonadjacent pair x′∈X,y′∈Y in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width tww(G) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the n−1 merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If tww(G)≤k, rejection is forbidden. If tww(G)>k, either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.

7262.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture for concise cubic tensors
7262.formal: For every n≥1 and every tensor T∈ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n⊗ℂ^n whose three flattenings all have rank n, is lim_{k→∞} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k)=n?
7262.definitions: R(T) is the least r such that T=Σ_{i=1}^r a_i⊗b_i⊗c_i with a_i,b_i,c_i∈ℂ^n. Each flattening views the tensor as a linear map from the dual of one factor into the tensor product of the other two. In T^⊗k the first, second and third tensor factors are respectively grouped, producing a tensor with three factors ℂ^(n^k). Submultiplicativity of rank makes the displayed limit equal to inf_{k≥1} R(T^⊗k)^(1/k). This is exact rank over ℂ, not border rank, and there is no explicitness or computational requirement on T.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank has a simple algebraic characterization, whereas tensor rank changes substantially when many independent copies are considered jointly. Strassen’s conjecture says that in the asymptotic setting the three flattening dimensions already determine the answer.

7268.formal: Do constants a,b,c>0 and q≥1 exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a log₂(N+2) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most (N+2)^b symbols over an alphabet of size at most (N+2)^b, with perfect completeness and soundness at most (N+2)^(−c)?
7268.definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with O(log N) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most (N+2)^(−c). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.

context_blocks.text: The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. This is different from asking that a constant-error PCP have linear proof length.

7269.title: Exponential multilinear-formula lower bounds for the permanent
7269.formal: Does there exist c>0 such that, for every sufficiently large n, every multilinear arithmetic formula over ℂ computing perm_n has at least 2^(cn) gates?

Every gate must compute a multilinear polynomial: every variable has degree at most one in every monomial after cancellation. 7271.title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
7271.formal: Do a constant C and a deterministic algorithm running in poly(n) time exist that compute E_n:{0,1}^n×{0,1}^n→{0,1} with |Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]−1/2|≤0.01 for every pair of independent sources X,Y of min-entropy at least log₂n+C?

7273.title: A complete disjoint NP pair
7273.formal: Do disjoint languages A,B∈NP exist such that, for every disjoint pair C,D∈NP, there is a deterministic polynomial-time function f with f(C)⊆A and f(D)⊆B?

7274.title: Do arbitrary one-way functions imply one-way functions in NC⁰?
7274.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ circuit family?
7274.definitions: The security parameter λ is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function ν(λ) is negligible if for every c>0, ν(λ)≤λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* of polynomially bounded, length-dependent output size, such that every allowed inverter on (1^n,f(U_n)) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability, for uniform U_n. A polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ family is generated from 1^n in poly(n) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT gates. Inversion security quantifies over all polynomial-size adversaries, not just shallow ones.

context_blocks.text: Local evaluation and global inversion difficulty are strikingly different requirements. An NC⁰ one-way function has each output bit depend on only a constant number of input bits, while inverting the full output must defeat every polynomial-size adversary.

Known locality transformations start from stronger assumptions such as one-way functions in NC¹. Those constructions establish plausible NC⁰ cryptography, but they do not derive it from an arbitrary sequentially computable one-way function. The implication therefore asks whether cryptographic hardness can always be made local.

7274.why: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.

7281.title: Unconditional NP-hardness at the Goemans–Williamson Max-Cut threshold

The reduction and constants may depend on ε. No Unique Games or other hardness conjecture is assumed.

context_blocks.text: The Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio is a landmark in semidefinite optimization. Matching hardness from ordinary NP-hardness would identify that ratio as an intrinsic computational threshold under P≠NP.

The target deliberately concerns the reduction itself, so a conditional implication from UGC does not count as a solution. This separates the problem from the Unique Games conjecture and from improving a particular rounding algorithm.

7283.title: Superpolynomial semidefinite extension complexity of perfect matching
7283.formal: For every C,c>0, does some even n≥2 satisfy xc_SDP(P_n)>Cn^c, where P_n is the perfect-matching polytope of K_n?
7283.definitions: P_n⊆ℝ^(n choose 2) is the convex hull of the zero-one incidence vectors of all perfect matchings of the complete graph on n labeled vertices. A size-r semidefinite lift is an affine subspace L of the real symmetric r×r matrices and an affine map π into ℝ^(n choose 2) such that P_n=π(L∩S_+^r), where S_+^r consists of positive semidefinite matrices. xc_SDP is the smallest such integer r. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers and need not be efficiently generated. The representation is exact; approximate relaxations and linear lifts are different notions.

context_blocks.text: Perfect matching can be optimized in polynomial time, yet exact linear descriptions in higher-dimensional spaces can require exponentially many inequalities. The question asks whether positive semidefinite constraints also suffer a superpolynomial representation barrier.

A linear extension-complexity lower bound is not a semidefinite one. Allowing an arbitrary affine slice of a positive semidefinite cone makes the model substantially stronger. A lower bound here would separate efficient optimization from compact exact SDP representation for a canonical tractable polytope.

7283.why: Identify a fundamental limitation of exact semidefinite optimization representations.

7284.formal: Is computing an exact Hylland–Zeckhauser equilibrium for a one-sided matching market FIXP-hard under the standard FIXP reductions?

7288.title: Constant adaptivity gap for influence maximization with full feedback
7288.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that OPT_adaptive(G,p,k)≤C·OPT_nonadaptive(G,p,k) for every independent-cascade influence instance under full-adoption feedback?
7288.definitions: The input is any finite directed graph, an independent retention probability p_e∈[0,1] for each edge, and a budget 1≤k≤|V|. Sample a live-edge subgraph once. A seed activates all vertices reachable from it along live edges. A nonadaptive strategy selects at most k seeds before observing the subgraph. An adaptive strategy selects seeds sequentially, observing after each choice the resulting activated set and the outcomes of edges explored by its completed cascade. Both objectives maximize the expected total number of activated vertices over strategies with no computational restriction. The expectation is over the live-edge graph and strategy coins. Failed transmissions into vertices already active reveal no additional state.

context_blocks.text: Feedback may allow later interventions to respond to the success of earlier ones. The adaptivity gap measures the value of that information, independently of the difficulty of finding an optimal strategy.

The cited research obtains bounds for full-adoption feedback and distinguishes it from the myopic-feedback model, where constant bounds are known. A constant full-feedback gap would say that a preselected seed set always captures a fixed share of the best adaptive policy. The source model’s precise observation convention remains important.

7303.title: Quadratic expected message complexity for asynchronous crash consensus
7303.formal: Does a randomized asynchronous binary consensus protocol exist with expected O(n²) messages against a strong adaptive adversary, tolerating every t<n/2 crash failures?
7303.definitions: The n processes communicate by reliable asynchronous point-to-point messages and start with binary inputs. A crashed process takes no further steps. Every process that does not crash must eventually decide with probability one under fair scheduling; all decisions agree, and when all initial inputs are b every decision is b. A strong adversary observes past states, messages and revealed random outcomes and chooses subsequent process steps, message deliveries and crashes without seeing future coins. The bound counts all messages sent before protocol termination and must hold in expectation for every admissible adversary. It does not impose a bit bound on each message.

context_blocks.text: Randomization makes asynchronous agreement possible despite crash failures, but robustness to a strong scheduler affects its communication cost. A quadratic bound would reach a central efficiency frontier in the standard message-passing model.

Alistarh, Aspnes, King and Saia give nearly quadratic expected communication against a strong adversary. Their logarithmic overhead is not a proof of the exact quadratic target. This question concerns crash failures, separately from Byzantine behavior or private-channel security.

7304.title: Robustness of the deterministic consensus hierarchy

7305.title: Compact routing at stretch 2k−1 and n^(1/k) storage
7305.formal: For every integer k≥2, do universal graph-routing schemes exist with stretch at most 2k−1 and Õ(n^(1/k)) words of routing information per vertex, without a preliminary handshake?
7305.definitions: A routing scheme preprocesses a connected undirected weighted graph and assigns local routing tables and destination labels. 7306.title: A recursively enumerable theory for an effective continuous lambda-model
7306.formal: Does an effective model of the untyped λ-calculus in Scott’s continuous semantics have a recursively enumerable equational theory?
7306.definitions: The equational theory of a model is the set of encoded pairs of λ-terms with equal denotations, under the source’s convention for free variables. Recursively enumerable means that a Turing machine can enumerate exactly those pairs. A continuous model interprets function abstraction and application using a reflexive object in an appropriate category of domains and continuous maps. Effectiveness is the additional computability structure defined in the source, not merely a countable presentation.

context_blocks.text: Denotational semantics assigns mathematical meanings to programs. An enumerable complete equality theory would connect those meanings to a mechanically enumerable calculus of program equations.

Berline, Manzonetto and Salibra rule out recursively enumerable order theories for their effective models and obtain stronger equational impossibility results in stable settings. The order theory and equality theory are different objects, and Scott-continuous semantics is broader than the stable settings covered by those negative theorems.

7309.title: Decidability with two parametric clocks and arbitrarily many integer parameters
7309.formal: Is reachability decidable for discrete-time parametric timed automata with at most two parametric clocks and an arbitrary finite number of nonnegative integer parameters?
7309.definitions: An input has finitely many locations, clocks initially zero, parameter symbols, guarded transitions and an initial and target location. A time-elapse step adds the same nonnegative integer to every clock. A transition guard is a conjunction of comparisons x⋈c or x⋈p, where c is a nonnegative integer, p a parameter and ⋈∈{<,≤,=,≥,>}; the transition may reset designated clocks to zero. Other clocks are unchanged. At most two clocks appear in comparisons to parameters; arbitrarily many clocks compared only with constants are allowed. A parameter valuation assigns a nonnegative integer to every parameter once for the entire run. The algorithm must halt on every finite binary encoding and answer whether some valuation permits a finite run to the target. This transition-guard presentation has no extra diagonal or parameter-arithmetic guards.

context_blocks.text: Parametric clocks describe systems whose timing constants are not fixed in advance. Decidability asks whether some assignment of those constants can make a target behavior reachable.

Göller and Hilaire establish EXPSPACE-completeness with two parametric clocks and one parameter in discrete time. They explicitly leave arbitrary numbers of parameters open. Dense-time results and infinite-word acceptance questions use different semantics and cannot be substituted for this finite-reachability target.

7310.title: Unconditional decidability of exact time-bounded CTMDP reachability
7310.formal: Is there an unconditional algorithm deciding whether the optimal probability of reaching a designated target by rational time T in a finite rational-rate continuous-time Markov decision process is at least a rational threshold p?
7310.definitions: A CTMDP has a finite state set, finitely many available actions and nonnegative rational transition rates. A policy resolves action choices based on admissible observations of the elapsed-time stochastic process. Reachability asks whether a target state is visited by the deadline, and the optimum is over all policies in the selected model. The comparison is exact; producing an additive approximation to the optimum alone does not decide threshold equality.

context_blocks.text: Quantitative verification often asks whether a stochastic system meets a probability requirement before a deadline. Exact comparison creates difficulties that can survive even for a finite model with rational data.

7311.title: Does choiceless polynomial time with counting capture PTIME?
7311.area: Database theory and finite model theory
7311.formal: Is every isomorphism-invariant polynomial-time property of finite relational structures definable in choiceless polynomial time with counting?

7313.title: Does ETH imply Gap-ETH?
7313.formal: Does the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis imply the deterministic Gap Exponential Time Hypothesis for sparse 3-CNF formulas?
7313.definitions: For a 3-CNF formula F with n variables, let val(F) be the maximum fraction of clauses simultaneously satisfiable. The ETH convention here asserts that there is c>0 for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas in time O(2^(cn) poly(L)), where L is the binary encoding length. Gap-ETH asserts that there exist constants B≥1, δ∈(0,1) and c′>0 for which no deterministic algorithm in time O(2^(c′n) poly(L)) distinguishes val(F)=1 from val(F)≤1−δ on formulas with at most Bn clauses. Its inputs are promised to satisfy one of those two alternatives. Empty formulas are satisfiable. All constants are fixed independently of F; randomized versions are not asserted.

context_blocks.text: ETH concerns exact satisfiability, while Gap-ETH postulates comparable exponential hardness even when unsatisfiable inputs violate a fixed fraction of clauses. Their equivalence would unify many exact and approximation lower-bound assumptions.

Bitansky and coauthors distinguish ETH from the stronger gap hypothesis while obtaining exponential hardness for particular approximation tasks. Hardness for those tasks does not imply a gap-preserving sparse 3-CNF statement. This implication is distinct from asking whether either hypothesis is true.

7313.why: Clarify whether a major approximation-hardness assumption adds strength to the standard exact exponential-time hypothesis.
